text:
Now, this here week, it weren’t a week at all, not by a long sight. More like a sliver of time snatched by a particularly ornery current. Old Man Tiber, he was in a mood, I tell you. A right proper snit. We’d been chugging along on the *Belle of Baton Rouge*, peaceful enough, when the sky commenced to look like a bruised plum. 

My souls, how the wind did scream along! And every second or two there’d come a glare that lit up the white-caps for a half mile, showin’ you the river wasn’t water at all, but a boilin’ pot of trouble. Folks were clutchin’ their hats and prayin’ to whatever deity they favored, though I reckon even *they* were wonderin’ if it’d do any good.

Captain Peabody, bless his grizzled heart, he just stood there, lookin’ like a statue carved from worry. Said somethin’ about “respectin’ the river’s temper,” which is a fancy way of sayin’ we were all at her mercy. It passed, of course. They always do. But that little stretch? Felt like a lifetime crammed into a handful of hours. A lifetime, and not a pleasant one, neither.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The chipped porcelain of the recovered photographs felt disturbingly cold, even through gloved hands. They depicted a cyclopean conflict waged not amongst stars, but *within* the abyssal currents. Structures of basalt, geometrically abhorrent to Euclidean comprehension, crumbled under assaults of bioluminescent weaponry – pulsing, sickly green against the eternal black. 

But it was the *figures* that clung to the sanity. Not human, not wholly animal, but… *constructed*. Vast, ichorous beings of segmented chitin and phosphorescent membrane, locked in a silent, writhing ballet of destruction. They were the servitors, undoubtedly, of entities far older, far more terrible.

And the aftermath. Oh, the aftermath. The images, blurred by the pressure and the… *something else* clinging to the lenses, showed the results of Shoggoth intervention. Not clean severance, but a dissolution, a spreading slick of iridescent slime where form had once been. Bodies – or what remained of them – were left headless, the spinal columns extruded and coiled like obscene, glistening ropes. 

A mar, indeed. A psychic residue clung to the prints, a whispering dread that spoke of geometries best left unseen, and of a war whose victors were, and always would be, utterly alien to the fragile concerns of mankind.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, Mrs. Phelps, she was a woman built on good intentions and a heap of fluster. Always fussin’ over somethin’, she was, like a hen with one chick too many. She’d been hankerin’ for a bit of excitement, a real chance to *do* somethin’ beyond starchin’ collars and frettin’ over the parlor curtains. And Lord, did she get it.

It all commenced with a mistaken identity, naturally. A fella, lookin’ remarkably like a nephew she was expectin’ from the Territories, showed up. A right scamp, he was, full of tall tales and a glint in his eye that’d charm the bloom off a rose. She took to him like a duck to water, bless her heart.

Then came the moment. She stooped down quick at the foot of the bed and give me a pull, and out I come; and when he turned back from the window, expectin’ young Tom, well, he near jumped out of his skin. A sight to behold, I tell you. A proper hullabaloo. She’d finally got her chance, alright – a chance to be mistaken, a chance to be flustered, and a chance to create a story folks would be tellin’ for years to come. A right comical mess, it was.

He had been much less in his own apartment had they sat in one equally lively; and she gave Charlotte credit for the arrangement. It was, after all, Charlotte’s particular talent to discern the precise degree of social stimulus required for each individual, and to administer it with a delicate hand. 

Mr. Ashworth, though possessed of a fortune undeniably handsome, was prone to a melancholy which threatened to consume him entirely. Miss Eleanor, observing his hesitant entrance, felt a pang of sympathy, quickly followed by a more practical consideration. He needed distraction, and plentiful conversation.

Fortunately, Mrs. Penhaligon, ever eager to display her accomplishments, had launched into a detailed account of her recent visit to Bath. Mr. Ashworth, though initially reserved, found himself drawn into a discussion of the Pump Room, and even offered a tentative opinion on the merits of the circulating library. A small victory, perhaps, but one which Eleanor deemed entirely satisfactory. Charlotte, observing from her favoured corner, offered a subtle, approving nod.

text:
The arrangements for the morrow’s excursion to the vicarage were, it must be confessed, remarkably ill-conceived. They had just been preparing to walk, Miss Eleanor having selected her most serviceable pelisse and Miss Marianne lamenting the dust which would inevitably cling to her favourite muslin, when the letters arrived. And her uncle and aunt, leaving unexpectedly for London on pressing business concerning a distant cousin’s entail, threw the entire plan into disarray.

A sigh escaped Miss Eleanor’s lips, though she schooled her features to a composure she did not entirely feel. Marianne, however, was less restrained. “London!” she exclaimed, with a dramatic flutter of her hand. “Just as we were to enjoy the fresh air and Mr. Harris’s improved shrubbery! It is most provoking.”

Their mother, ever practical, attempted to soothe. “Provoking, perhaps, but unavoidable. We must make the best of it. A quiet evening with our books, then. Though I confess, a little society would have been a welcome diversion from the monotony.” 

The prospect, however, held little charm for Marianne, who considered books a poor substitute for animated conversation and the possibility of a certain gentleman’s company.
author: Jane Austen

Now, Old Man Hemlock and young Silas Peabody, they had a disagreement. Not a fisticuffs kind, mind you, but a *peculiar* one. It weren’t ‘bout land, nor livestock, nor even a woman – though Silas *did* have a fondness for Hemlock’s daughter, Bessie, a fact Hemlock weren’t shy ‘bout remindin’ him of. No sir. This here ’spute wuz ‘bout pints.

Specifically, the pints of buttermilk Hemlock sold. Silas claimed they weren’t *true* pints. Said Hemlock wuz shortin’ folks, slippin’ a finger’s width o’ air into each measure. Hemlock, he scoffed. “Boy,” he said, puffin’ on his pipe, “I been sellin’ pints since afore you wuz born! My measure’s honest as the day is long.”

But Silas, he’d brought a plumb bob and a ruler. He measured. He calculated. He declared Hemlock a scoundrel. I reck’n I knows sense when I sees it; en dey ain’ no sense in sich doin’s as dat. The whole town gathered, watchin’ Silas fuss over buttermilk like it wuz gold. A right foolishness, I tell ya. A man arguin’ over a dribble.

Old Man Tiber, he was a sight. Claimed he could still pitch a bluegill clear over the courthouse, though his arm hadn’t known a proper stretch since Grant was a corporal. Now, young Jedediah, fresh off the farm and full of vinegar, was tryin’ to show Tiber how a man *actually* throws a ball.

“No, no, see here!” Jedediah’d holler, windin’ up like he was launchin’ a cannonball. “Wrist snap, elbow drive! Gotta put your back into it!”

Tiber just shook his head, slow and deliberate. “Lordy, boy, you throw like a woman fendin’ off a suitor. All wrist and flail. A proper throw, now, that’s from the *shoulder*. Stiff-armed, see? Like there’s a hinge right there, a pivot point. Not all flung out like you’re reachin’ for a biscuit.”

He demonstrated, a pathetic little lob that barely cleared Jedediah’s boot. “It’s about control, son. Precision. Not showin’ off. A girl throws like *that*,” he said, gesturing wildly at Jedediah’s form, “a man throws…well, a man throws with a bit more dignity.” 

Jedediah just grinned, wound up again, and nearly took Tiber’s hat off with a fastball. Some lessons, it seemed, were lost on the young’uns.
author: Mark Twain

text:
It was, I confess, a matter of some small satisfaction to find myself, once again, situated through my means; and it was but the other day that I recommended another young person, who was merely accidentally mentioned to me, and the particulars of whose disposition appeared, upon brief enquiry, entirely suitable. Miss Eleanor Finch, a niece to the Rector of Upper Bramble, possessed a modest fortune, and, more importantly, a sensibility not prone to flights of fancy. 

Mrs. Hawthorne, you see, had been lamenting the lack of a companion for her nephew, young Mr. Cecil, a gentleman of amiable, though somewhat melancholic, temperament. He required, she declared, a lady who could appreciate a quiet evening with a book, rather than a bustling assembly. Miss Finch, therefore, presented herself as a most eligible candidate. 

One hopes, naturally, that the connection will prove felicitous. Mr. Cecil, though possessing a comfortable income, is not a man to pursue with undue eagerness. A gentle encouragement, a shared appreciation for Virgil, and a willingness to overlook his occasional fits of abstraction – these, I suspect, will be the keys to his affections. It is a delicate matter, certainly, but one I believe Miss Finch is well-equipped to manage.
author: Jane Austen

Now, the rain was comin’ down in sheets, a proper Missouri soaker, and Old Man Hemlock’s porch was the only dry spot for a mile, so naturally, folks lingered. This feller, see, he stood just at the edge, lookin’ like a drowned rat tryin’ to decide if catchin’ pneumonia was worth a moment’s respite. I figured a man that hesitant needed persuadin’.

“Come in, come in, sir!” I hollered, loud enough to cut through the storm. “No sense standin’ out there gettin’ yourself addled. Coffee’s hot, and the company’s…well, it’s company.”

He shuffled in, lookin’ sheepish as a hound dog caught in the pantry. “Much obliged,” he says, wringin’ water from his coat. “Name’s William Thompson, from Hicksville, Ohio. A right awful journey, it was.” 

Then he paused, cleared his throat, and added, with a little flourish, “And might I add, a rather *blessed* journey, too. William Thompson, at your service…and William Thompson, the Second, if you please.” 

A man with two names, and a story already spinnin’ like a top. I had a feelin’ this wasn’t just the rain bringin’ the dampness into the room.

text:
The pronouncement, delivered with a gravity quite unbecoming the occasion, struck Miss Elizabeth with a force that rendered her momentarily incapable of reply. “Ardently I admire and love you.” The words, though not entirely unwelcome, possessed a boldness so unexpected, so utterly devoid of the customary preamble, as to leave her faculties in a delightful, yet unsettling, disarray. 

She stared, coloured a becoming rose, and then, finding no suitable response readily available, remained, to her own mortification, silent. Mr. Darcy, however, appeared to consider this lack of immediate effusiveness as quite sufficient. A slight inclination of his head, a barely perceptible tightening of his lips, suggested a satisfaction derived not from her acceptance, but from the *delivery* of his sentiment. 

It was, she thought, a most singular declaration. One might expect protestations of worthiness, assurances of devotion extending beyond mere admiration. Instead, a bluntness, a confidence bordering on presumption. Yet, despite the impropriety of the manner, a warmth began to spread within her, a curious mingling of amusement and… something far more significant. He simply *believed* her response would follow, and in that belief, perhaps, lay a charm of its own.
author: Jane Austen

text:
“Word,” said her Ladyship, her lips pursed with a disapproval barely veiled by politeness, “you give your opinion very decidedly for so young a person. Pray, what is your age?”

Miss Eleanor, though startled by the directness, met the gaze unflinchingly. “With three younger sisters grown up,” she replied, a slight flush rising in her cheeks, “one is perpetually engaged in matters of consequence, even if those consequences are merely the proper arrangement of ribbons or the suitable selection of a pianoforte piece. I am, Madam, but seventeen years of age.”

A delicate sniff escaped her Ladyship. “Seventeen! A mere bud, then, to be offering pronouncements on the merits of Mr. Hawthorne’s estate. Such forwardness is…uncommon.” 

Eleanor bit back a retort regarding the uncommonness of judging a property solely on the size of its ballroom. “I merely observed, Madam, that the land appears to lack sufficient drainage. A dampness, I fear, would prove detrimental to the rose garden.” 

Her Ladyship’s eyes narrowed. “A rose garden, indeed. A most practical concern for a young lady on the brink of…establishment.” The implication hung heavy in the air, a subtle barb aimed at Eleanor’s decidedly un-marriageable independence.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth possessed a talent for pleasing, not through artifice or calculated display, but rather a natural warmth which seemed to emanate from her very being. It was a quality Mr. Hawthorne, a gentleman of decidedly rigid principles and a staunch advocate for propriety, had initially dismissed as a lack of polish. He had, with a pointedness that bordered on rudeness, declared her manners wanting in the sophistication demanded by London society. 

Yet, despite his assertions, he found himself increasingly…distracted. Her conversation, though devoid of the studied wit favoured in drawing-rooms, possessed an easy playfulness, a quickness of observation that disarmed even his most critical faculties. She spoke of village life with a genuine affection, of small kindnesses and quiet amusements, and he, accustomed to the cynical pronouncements of the ton, found it unexpectedly refreshing.

He observed, with a growing discomfort he dared not acknowledge, that his gaze frequently sought hers across the room. It was, he told himself, merely a study of character – a gentlemanly attempt to understand so singular a disposition. But the blush that rose to *her* cheeks when their eyes met suggested a different understanding altogether.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The drawing-room at Rosings Park held a chill despite the roaring fire, a chill not entirely attributable to the November air. Miss Bennet, seated a discreet distance from him, had just remarked upon the anticipated pleasure of seeing a certain friend in January. He found himself, against his better judgement, observing the delicate flush that rose in her cheeks as she spoke of it.

“Shall see her in January,” she repeated, a wistful note colouring her voice. He offered a curt acknowledgement, then found himself subjected to a most unexpected query.

“But do you always write such charming long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

A most impertinent question, and yet… delivered with such artless sincerity. He felt a tightening in his chest, a sensation he found exceedingly disagreeable. 

“They are generally long,” he replied, striving for a composure he did not entirely feel. “But whether always charming… Do not mention the author by name.” 

He observed her closely. A slight widening of the eyes, a barely perceptible inclination of the head. It was, he conceded, a most unsettling exchange. And, confound it all, rather *interesting*.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, I reckon I’ve seen a passel of characters in my time, driftin’ along the Mississippi and beyond, but Old Man Hemlock… well, he was a study. Glidin’est, stealthiest man I ever see. Not a footfall you could hear, not a twig would snap under his weight. Moved like a shadow stretched too thin, he did. And there warn’t no more smile to him than there is to a ham. A fella could look at him and figure he’d been weaned on vinegar and regret.

They had borrowed a melodeum—a sick one, mind you, wheezin’ and groanin’ like a consumptive mule—from Widow Peabody for the church social. Hemlock was tasked with movin’ it. Now, a normal man would *struggle* with that instrument, makin’ a racket fit to wake the dead. Not Hemlock. He just… *shifted* it. Like he was willin’ it across the floor with his gaze. 

Folks swore they blinked and it was in a different spot. Didn’t grunt, didn’t strain, didn’t even *breathe* hard. Just a silent, unsettling glide. Gave a body the creeps, it did. Made you wonder what else he could move without a sound.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, I reckon some folks are powerful fond of watchin’ other folks, thinkin’ it’s a sign of responsibility or somethin’. A foolish notion, if you ask me. Old Man Hemlock, he was one for the watchin’, see? Had a fella posted to keep an eye on Jim, our… well, let’s just say a man of color who’d taken a notion to find his own freedom. 

A right waste of good wages, that was. Jim could’ve slipped out that there window-hole hours ago, easy as a catfish slidin’ through weeds. But he didn’t. Why? Not because of the fella watchin’, no sir. Jim’s a sensible man. He was waitin’ on the boy, a ten-year-old sprout with a heart bigger than a watermelon and a knack for gettin’ into trouble.

Mr. Alistair Finch, a gentleman possessed of a comfortable fortune and a sensibility perhaps *too* easily stirred, found himself in a most vexing predicament. Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, newly arrived in the village, had, with an artlessness he deemed both charming and dangerous, elicited a warmth within him he had long believed extinguished. He had, in a moment of regrettable candour during a discussion of botanical illustrations, allowed a compliment to slip – a remark upon the delicate precision of her watercolouring, which, though perfectly proper, had been delivered with, he now acknowledged, an undue enthusiasm.

He wisely resolved to be particularly careful that no sign of admiration should *now* escape him—nothing that could elevate her with the hope of reciprocation. To appear indifferent, even slightly cool, was the only course. It was a difficult undertaking, for Miss Ainsworth possessed a habit of asking questions that demanded thoughtful responses, and her eyes… her eyes held a disconcerting capacity to draw forth sincerity. He practiced a studied neutrality, offering only the most commonplace observations, and praying she might attribute his reserve to a natural lack of conversational skill, rather than a wounded pride. The task, he suspected, would prove far more arduous than any he had yet encountered.

He had accepted an invitation to Lady Beatrice’s musicale, anticipating an evening of polite conversation and accomplished pianoforte. He had fully expected, naturally, to make his excuses and withdraw at the first opportunity, without the expectation of his decamping as fast as he could from such disgraceful companions. That he was _surprised_ by the connection was evident: Miss Penelope Plumtree, the elder and generally the more voluble of the two, possessed a remarkably astute understanding of the intricacies of the local land holdings. 

Indeed, her observations regarding the recent sale of the Hargrave estate were not merely informed, but insightful. Mr. Finch, whose own investments were considerably tied to the area, found himself reluctantly drawn into a discussion, his initial disdain slowly yielding to a grudging respect. A most peculiar evening, he thought, and one which promised to complicate his carefully constructed notions of society considerably.

Old Man Tiber, he had a notion. A powerful, peculiar notion. Said he’d struck it rich, not with gold nor silver, mind you, but with *location*. “I’m buildin’ a palace,” he declared, puffin’ on a clay pipe that smelled like burnt hickory, “but not *here*. No sir. That palace around over the country wherever you want it, you understand.”

Folks just scratched their heads. Tiber, you see, wasn’t known for his clarity. He’d explain it further, though. A system of rails, he said, and a steam engine powerful enough to haul the whole shebang – parlor, kitchen, the works – to wherever a fella felt a hankerin’ for a view. 

“Think of it!” he’d bellow, spittin’ a stream of tobacco juice. “Breakfast in Missouri, supper in Maine! No more settlin’ down, no more roots! Just…movin’!”

“Well,” says I, “I think they are a pack of flat-heads for not keeping the blueprints under lock and key. Word got out, and now every Tom, Dick, and Harry’s claimin’ they invented the notion first. Lawyers swarmin’ like flies on a molasses barrel, all lookin’ to get a piece of Tiber’s foolish dream.” 

It was a spectacle, I tell you. A right comical spectacle.

“She seems a very pleasant young woman,” said Bingley, his countenance radiating a warmth that Miss Bennet found excessively flattering, though she endeavoured to appear indifferent. “Oh dear, yes; but you must own she is very plain. Lady Lucas herself observed as much, though with a delicacy, of course, befitting her station.”

Charlotte, ever the pragmatist, offered a small, knowing smile. “Plainness, Mr. Bingley, is often a shield against expectation. A lady unburdened by excessive beauty may find herself judged on her merits, rather than her complexion.” 

Miss Bennet, however, felt a blush rise despite herself. It was not vanity, precisely, that stung, but the bluntness of the assessment. She valued her own quiet observances, her skill at the pianoforte, her attempts at watercolour – qualities, she believed, far exceeding the importance of a rosy cheek. 

“Indeed,” Bingley continued, oblivious to the subtle currents of feeling, “her conversation is most agreeable. Though, perhaps, a little… earnest. One does not often encounter such forthright opinions.” Charlotte stifled a laugh. Earnestness, in a female, was frequently mistaken for a fault.

It was a truth universally acknowledged, that a gentleman of Mr. Darcy’s consequence must possess a certain sway over those within his sphere. Yet, Miss Elizabeth found herself contemplating a peculiarity most unsettling. Could there truly exist *two* men over whom his influence could be so boundless, so readily exerted? It seemed a proposition quite beyond the bounds of reasonable expectation. 

Her mind, naturally inclined to observation, recalled the unfortunate Mr. Wickham, so easily led, or perhaps *allowed* to lead himself, into imprudence. And now, the revelation concerning Mr. Bingley’s hasty departure from Netherfield… it spoke of a direction, a subtle steering, that bordered on the manipulative. 

To think that Mr. Darcy, a man of such acknowledged integrity, should be concerned in the measures taken to separate two hearts! It was a disquieting thought. One might forgive a slight indulgence in pride, a reserve of manner, but to actively intervene in the affections of others… surely, such a course could only be justified by the most pressing necessity. And what necessity, she wondered, could be weighty enough to warrant such interference?

The arrival of Mr. Bingley at Netherfield Park occasioned a degree of agitation within Longbourn that, whilst not openly displayed, was keenly felt by Mrs. Bennet. “He came down to see the place,” she announced to her husband, a statement delivered with the air of a momentous discovery. Kitty, ever eager to contribute, piped up, “I’m the tallest, Mama! Perhaps he’ll notice.” A remark met with a withering glance from Jane. 

News arrived via a breathless servant that he had ridden a black horse, a detail deemed of utmost importance. The anticipation grew with each passing hour. “When the party does call,” Mrs. Bennet declared, adjusting her cap, “we must all be at our best. A favourable first impression is everything, you know. Everything!” Mr. Bennet merely retreated further into his book, a silent observer of the domestic flurry.

text:
## CHAPTER VI.

[Illustration: *A delicately rendered sketch of Miss Elizabeth Bennet observing Mr. Darcy from across a crowded drawing-room.*]

The civilities between Longbourn and Netherfield, once commenced, proceeded with a regularity most pleasing to Mrs. Bennet, and, it must be confessed, not entirely displeasing to her daughters. A morning call, returned with equal promptness, established a footing, though not, perhaps, a particularly *firm* one. Miss Elizabeth, however, found herself observing Mr. Darcy with a degree of curiosity that bordered, she feared, upon imprudence. 

He possessed, undeniably, a countenance of striking, though severe, elegance. Yet his manner, whilst not actively rude, lacked that warmth and affability so essential to engaging the affections. He spoke little, and when he *did* deign to address the company, it was with a precision that suggested a mind occupied with matters far exceeding the trivialities of polite conversation. 

Her sister, Jane, declared him merely shy. Elizabeth, though willing to grant him the benefit of the doubt, suspected a disposition more inclined to censure than to commend. Indeed, she found herself strangely provoked by his very composure, a composure which seemed to imply a judgement upon *them* all.

text:
The matter was slight and simple, hardly entering into comparison with the grand affairs of the season, yet it occupied Miss Eleanor’s thoughts with a persistence most vexing. Mr. Ashworth, a gentleman possessed of a comfortable fortune and tolerable address, had, at the village assembly, barely acknowledged her presence. Not with rudeness, precisely – a curt nod was all – but with a coolness that spoke volumes to a discerning eye.

It has sometimes, I believe, been urged that his pride is unnatural at first in its expression, manifesting not as superiority, but as a peculiar… detachment. One might almost suspect a shyness, were it not so thoroughly overlaid with an air of quiet consequence. Her brother, however, dismissed it as mere affectation, a pose adopted to distinguish him from the more boisterous young men present. 

Eleanor, though, found herself strangely affected. Not by any expectation of his favour, for she held no such foolish notion, but by the *manner* of his disregard. It was not the slight itself, but the implication – that she was scarcely worth noticing at all. A most unsettling thought, and one she resolved to banish, despite its tenacious hold upon her attention.
author: Jane Austen

“Hill? We have heard nothing from town,” Miss Eleanor remarked, adjusting the lace at her wrist with a delicate sigh. The afternoon sun, though pleasant, did little to dispel the languor that had settled upon the drawing-room.

“Dear madam,” cried Mrs. Hill, in great astonishment, “don’t you know there is an express come for Master from… well, from a gentleman of consequence in London! He arrived scarcely an hour ago, and Master is closeted with him still.”

Eleanor’s composure, usually so steadfast, faltered. “An express? Of what nature, pray tell? Is it business, or…?” She dared not utter the word ‘pleasure’, though a flutter of anticipation, most unbecoming in a woman of her years, stirred within her breast.

Mrs. Hill, ever prone to speculation, lowered her voice. “It is said to concern a matter of some urgency, madam. And the gentleman… he was most handsomely dressed, I assure you. A velvet coat, and a countenance quite… determined. Master seemed much agitated upon receiving the dispatch, though he endeavoured to conceal it, of course.”

Eleanor’s fingers tightened around her embroidery. A determined countenance, and agitation in her brother? The possibilities, both delightful and dreadful, were quite overwhelming.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth possessed a quality, not precisely of beauty – though her features were agreeable enough – but rather of a yielding gentleness which rendered it almost impossible to take offense at her. One might disagree with her opinions, find her pronouncements somewhat timid, yet feel a distinct reluctance to *contradict* her with any force. It was a manner, a softening of the eye, a slight inclination of the head, which disarmed even the most resolute disputant.

Mr. Darcy, a gentleman not easily swayed by feminine charms, found himself, to his considerable astonishment, quite captivated. He had encountered ladies of fortune and accomplishment in abundance, yet none had stirred within him such a peculiar…interest. It was not merely her amiable disposition, though that was certainly pleasing. No, it was a certain vulnerability, a quiet strength masked by diffidence, that held his regard. 

He found himself seeking her company, inventing reasons to engage her in conversation, and, most unsettlingly, believing – truly believing – that she possessed a depth of understanding far exceeding her modest presentation. A most unusual circumstance, and one which, he confessed to himself with a blush he hoped remained unseen, had entirely unsettled his composure.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The charts were… inadequate. Utterly, blasphemously insufficient to convey the *wrongness* of this place. We had been charting the periphery of the Amundsen Sea for weeks, yet this landmass – if land it truly *was* – defied all terrestrial geometry. It wasn’t the size, though its breadth was unsettling, but the *angle*. Somewhat greater ruggedness, seeming to slope slightly upward as it receded in the mist-hazed west, a violation of Euclidean space that chilled the marrow. 

The *plankton*, too, was…altered. Bioluminescent, yes, but with a sickly, pulsating glow, and forms that hinted at structures not born of organic processes. The air itself tasted of ozone and something older, something metallic and profoundly *cold*. 

So far we had made no landing, yet to leave the *Polaris* felt akin to stepping into a dream constructed by a mad god. Each passing hour brought a growing dread, a conviction that we were not discovering, but being *drawn* towards something. Something ancient, and utterly inimical to the sanity of man. The wireless crackled with static, a chorus of whispers that seemed to emanate not from the ether, but from the very stone of that impossible shore. A shore that beckoned, and promised only oblivion.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The evening at the vicarage, though pleasant enough, lacked a certain *spark*. Miss Ainsworth’s pianoforte playing, while technically proficient, possessed a melancholy air ill-suited to a gathering intended for cheerful converse. A suggestion, therefore, arose – a small game of charades, to enliven the spirits. Most readily agreed, though a shadow fell upon the room with the arrival of Mr. Darcy.

He stood, a figure of dignified disapproval, near the fireplace. “Charades,” he remarked, his tone conveying a distinct lack of enthusiasm. “A rather… frivolous pursuit, is it not?” 

Mrs. Bennet, ever the diplomat, hastened to assure him. “Indeed, sir, it is merely a harmless diversion. And though this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, he can have no objection, I am sure, to oblige us for one half hour.” 

Mr. Darcy’s lips thinned. “Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” Miss Bingley offered, a touch too quickly. He merely inclined his head, a gesture that spoke volumes of suppressed reluctance. One suspected, however, that even *he* could not entirely resist the subtle pressure of a room full of expectant ladies. The game, it seemed, would proceed, despite his evident reservations.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor found herself, despite her better judgement, quite preoccupied with Mr. Finch. He possessed a manner, undeniably, that bordered on the ridiculous. Every observation was delivered as a pronouncement, every anecdote seasoned with a self-importance quite unbecoming a gentleman of only moderate fortune. He spoke of his lineage as though it rivalled the oldest families, and corrected her on the proper arrangement of roses with an air of profound expertise.

But it was his apology that truly unsettled her. “I find myself, Miss Ashworth,” he had declared, bowing with excessive formality, “most grievously situated. To be next in entail to Longbourn is, frankly, a burden. One does not *wish* to benefit from another’s misfortune, you understand.”

The impropriety! To apologize for a circumstance entirely beyond his control, and to imply a sympathy he could scarcely feel! It was a performance, surely. Could he truly believe himself burdened by good fortune? Her sister, Mary, posited he hoped to appear magnanimous. Eleanor, however, suspected a more calculating motive. What game was this Mr. Finch playing, and what precisely did he intend to *make* of her?
author: Jane Austen

text:
It was, perhaps, a small vanity in Miss Eleanor to still find a certain satisfaction in Mr. Ashworth’s occasional attentions, years after the possibility of any more substantial connection had been, with a firmness most unwelcome, extinguished. He possessed, after all, a London life, and thus, it was yet in his power to give her fresher intelligence of her former friends than she had been in the way of procuring. 

Mrs. Gardiner, ever the sensible observer, remarked upon it with a gentle amusement. “He does seem to take a particular pleasure in detailing the minutiae of Miss Bingley’s latest gown, or the pronouncements of Lady Catherine. One might almost suspect a lingering…interest.”

Eleanor blushed, though not entirely from embarrassment. It was not *interest* precisely, but a peculiar comfort. To hear of their continued prosperity, their continued adherence to the very patterns she had escaped, served as a quiet validation of her own choices. A life of modest contentment, though lacking the brilliance of London society, was, she assured herself, a life of genuine happiness. And Mr. Ashworth, unwittingly, provided the means to measure that contentment.
author: Jane Austen

Now, the masquerade ball at Widow Higgins’ was a sight, I tell you. Folks dressed as everything from French royalty to prize-winning pumpkins. Me? I went as a young lady. A perfectly respectable young lady, mind you, with a borrowed bonnet and a dress that smelled powerfully of lavender and mothballs. 

I figured I could carry it off right smartly. Had practiced my curtsies in the barn, and even managed a passable giggle. Could do pretty well in them, only Jim said I didn’t walk like a girl; too much stride, he called it, and not enough…well, he didn’t rightly *say* what it lacked, just shook his head and chuckled.

And then there was the pocket situation. A body gets used to havin’ things handy, see? A jackknife, a bit of string, maybe a peppermint. So I kept pullin’ up my gown to get at my britches-pocket, which, naturally, didn’t sit right with the illusion. Jim, he pointed that out too. “You to,” he said, lookin’ mournful. “You to quit that right now, or the whole thing’s a bust.” 

So I did. Though it was a powerful inconvenience, I’ll admit. A powerful inconvenience indeed.

text:
The geometries were *wrong*. Even before the final subsidence, a sickening discordance plagued the mind, a subtle fracturing of Euclidean space that clung to the crumbling basalt of R’lyeh’s lesser kin. For aeons, they had risen – cyclopean mockeries of human aspiration, cities of non-angles and basaltine dread blossoming across the Pacific’s abyssal plains. Not built, precisely, but *extruded* from some loathsome, pre-human consciousness.

They called them ‘colonies’ in the fragmented, blasphemous texts – outposts of a dominion older than time, seeded during epochs when continents shifted like uneasy dreams. But the stars were not aligned for permanence. A creeping, ichorous fatigue seemed to infect the very stone, a weakening of the dimensional anchors that held them tenuously to our reality. 

Then came the tremors. Not of earth, but of something *beneath* earth, a vast, sluggish stirring in the primordial ooze. The cities shuddered, their impossible towers listing like drunken gods. And with a final, gut-wrenching groan, the Pacific *remembered* its ancient claim. The lands, and all the blasphemous structures upon them, were drawn back into the black, lightless gulf, leaving only a swirling, oily calm and the chilling certainty that some things are best left undisturbed in the cold, uncaring void.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The salt-laced wind carried a susurrus not of the sea, but of *wrongness*. Old Man Hemlock’s cottage, perched precariously on Widow’s Point, had been silent for weeks, a silence now broken not by human sound, but by the frantic cries of gulls circling a ghastly spectacle. We, the reluctant constabulary of Arkham, found the door ajar, the interior steeped in a cloying, metallic odour.

It was not the squalor that chilled us – Hemlock was ever a recluse – but the arrangement. The floorboards, warped and stained, were strewn with…things. Not implements, not tools, but glistening, pulpy fragments. Membranes of an unwholesome violet hue. Bones, too numerous and subtly *off* in their articulation. And a viscous, iridescent fluid that clung to everything like a morbid dew. 

Then came the larger pieces. A section of musculature, strangely layered, exhibiting a cellular structure wholly alien to terrestrial biology. A portion of what might have been a cranial casing, too smooth, too geometrically improbable. It did not take long for us to guess that those things were the carefully, though oddly and inexpertly dissected parts of one. Something vast. Something…*other*. 

A creeping dread, colder than the November gale, settled upon us. Hemlock hadn’t merely *studied* the abyss. He had *invited* it within.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, this here happened down by the crick, see, during the peach season. Old Man Hemlock’s orchard was ripe as sin, and a gaggle of girls, they were pilferin’ like magpies. Amongst ‘em was little Bess, a sweet thing, but with a tongue sharper than a flint. And there was poor Hare-lip, a boy quiet as dust, born with a…well, a peculiarity in his upper lip, you understand. 

Bess, she took a notion to tease him, callin’ him names that’d curdle milk. Not malicious-like, mind you, just girl-foolishness. But Hare-lip, he weren’t used to it. He turned redder than a boiled lobster and, bless his heart, *so* he hollered. A right proper bellow it was.

“All right, then,” says the other girls, lookin’ at Bess with a sternness that’d shame a preacher. “You just ask his pardon.” She done it, too; and she done it beautifu’. A little sniffle, a downcast gaze, and a “I’m sorry, Hare-lip,” delivered soft as a summer breeze. 

He didn’t say nothin’, just picked up a peach and bit into it, juice runnin’ down his chin. But I reckon, even a boy with a hare-lip can feel a little bit of sunshine in a genuine apology. It’s a curious thing, human nature, ain’t it?
author: Mark Twain

text:
My dearest sister, I confess myself still quite unsettled by the news imparted this morning. To be addressed with such earnestness, and so very lately, as Mr. Collins was wishing to marry you! It was a proposal delivered with a gravity most unbecoming a man of his limited understanding, and a self-importance that bordered, I fear, on the ridiculous. 

Mama, naturally, is in a state of the highest expectation, already envisioning a comfortable establishment and the security such a connection would afford. Papa, though less demonstrative, appears to view it as a most fortunate circumstance. I, however, observe a certain… reluctance in your countenance, a quiet dismay that I suspect mirrors my own sentiments.

Mr. Collins, whilst possessing a respectable living, is sadly deficient in those qualities which render a companion agreeable. His conversation is a tedious catalogue of patronage and pronouncements, and his person… well, let us say it lacks any particular charm. 

But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you will be satisfied. Prudence, after all, dictates a consideration of advantages, and a refusal founded solely on inclination is rarely wise. Do write soon and confide in me your true feelings on this most unexpected turn of events.
author: Jane Austen

It is at least remarkable that in two very short periods of writing--one of about three years, and another of not much more than five--she executed six capital works, and has not left a single failure. It is possible that the romantic paste in her composition was defective: we must always remember that hardly anybody born in her decade--that of the eighteenth-century seventies--independently exhibited the full romantic quality. Even Scott required hill and mountain and ballad, even Coleridge metaphysics and German to enable them to chip the classical shell. Miss Austen was an English girl, brought up in a country retirement, at the time when ladies went back into the house if there was a white frost which might pierce their kid shoes, when a sudden cold was the subject of the gravest fears, when their studies, their ways, their conduct were subject to all those fantastic limits and restrictions against which Mary Wollstonecraft protested

text:
You, I am certain, remember the circumstances of my departure from Longbourn, and the hastily-formed design of soon returning. The part which I acted in the ensuing drama is now, perhaps, due an explanation. Mr. Bennet, though possessed of a wit which often bordered on the impertinent, was, alas, not entirely immune to the influence of female anxieties. His daughters’ collective uneasiness regarding Mr. Wickham’s prolonged absence had been, I assure you, equal to any distress witnessed in a circulating library romance.

It was I, emboldened by a certain degree of familiarity with the gentleman in question – and, I confess, a touch of youthful impetuosity – who undertook to ascertain his whereabouts. A discreet inquiry, veiled as a friendly concern for his health, led me to discover he had not, as was generally believed, been summoned to London on business. Rather, a certain… entanglement had arisen, involving a young lady of considerably less fortune and, it must be added, less discretion. The details, I spare you, being of a nature quite unfit for polite conversation. My return, therefore, was hastened not by pleasure, but by the necessity of imparting this unwelcome intelligence.

“Even now,” Mr. Collins declared, adjusting his cravat with a self-satisfied air, “Miss Bennet, I dare say I have said as much to encourage my suit as would be consistent with the true delicacy of the female character.” He paused, expecting, one might assume, a blush and a downcast gaze. Instead, a most unsettling stillness descended upon Miss Elizabeth.

“Really, Mr. Collins,” cried Elizabeth, her voice possessing a sharpness that threatened to fray the composure of the room, “one would think a gentleman of your discernment might perceive the utter impossibility of such a notion! To suggest that your… attentions are *desired* merely because I have not actively repelled them is a degree of presumption scarcely to be tolerated.”

He stammered, a flush creeping up his neck. “But, Miss Bennet, my estate… my connections… the security I offer…”

“Security, sir, is a poor substitute for esteem. And connections, however advantageous, cannot compel affection. I assure you, my silence has been born of politeness, not expectation.” A slight, almost mischievous, tilt to her lips suggested she found his discomfiture rather diverting.

text:
The wind, it was not a wind of this Earth. It arrived not with a gradual crescendo, but a sickening *shift* in the very aether, a coldness that bypassed the flesh and settled directly upon the soul. We had established the meteorological station on the plateau with a hubris born of scientific detachment, believing the Antarctic’s secrets yielded to methodical observation. We were… mistaken.

The blizzard began subtly, a swirling of crystalline flakes, but quickly devolved into something monstrous. Not snow, precisely, but a particulate of impossible density, driven by a force that defied atmospheric pressure. The instruments, painstakingly calibrated, spun wildly, registering readings that mocked Euclidean geometry. 

Then came the pressure. A crushing, inward force that threatened to implode the very structures. The prefabricated tents, reinforced against ordinary gales, buckled. Two were reduced to splintered wreckage, the snow banking around them *flattened* as if by a colossal, unseen hand. Even the treated wood of the observation platform bore the mark – pitted, denuded, as though subjected to some corrosive, non-chemical decay. 

A silence followed, more terrifying than the storm itself. A silence pregnant with the knowledge that we were not alone, and that whatever *was* had merely… paused.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That was all fixed.

So then we went away and went to the rubbage-pile in the back yard, where they keep the discarded ambitions of men – busted birdhouses, a one-wheeled velocipede, and Old Man Hemlock’s attempt at a self-milking cow. A right sorry sight, it was. Young Timothy, he’d been fretting all mornin’ over this here proposition. Old Man Abernathy, see, offered him a billion dollars. A *billion*.

“A billion dollars, I wouldn’t,” Timothy declared, kickin’ at a rusty bucket. “Not for all the tea in China, and a new set of teeth for Aunt Mildred besides.”

Now, I’d known Timothy since he was knee-high to a grasshopper, and he wasn’t one for extravagance. But a billion dollars… well, that’s a sum that’d make a saint consider a new hat. 

“Why not, son?” I inquired, leanin’ against the shed.

He sighed, a sound like air leakin’ from a punctured bellows. “Abernathy wants me to *smile* for his photograph. Says it’ll ‘boost morale’ or some such folderol. I ain’t smilin’ for nobody, not even for a king’s ransom. A man’s dignity, you see, is worth more than all the minted money in Christendom.” 

And there, amongst the broken dreams and discarded contraptions, I reckoned he was right as rain.

“But, Mama, surely you do not mean to suggest Mr. Hargrave’s attentions are *welcome* simply because Miss Selwick does not actively repel them?” Elizabeth inquired, a delicate arch to her brow.

Mrs. Bennet, fanning herself with agitated vigour, declared, “Repel! A young lady of her consequence does not *repel*, my dear. She allows. And allowing, in this instance, is quite sufficient encouragement for a gentleman of his fortune.”

“_Her_ not objecting does not justify _him_,” Miss Bingley interjected, her tone cool as a winter morning. “It only shows her being deficient in something herself—sense or feeling.” A slight sniff accompanied the pronouncement.

“Well,” cried Elizabeth, unable to contain herself, “to attribute a lack of discernment to Miss Selwick merely to excuse Mr. Hargrave’s forwardness strikes me as…unreasonable! Is a woman to be blamed for another’s ill-mannered pursuit? It seems a most convenient, and decidedly unfair, arrangement.” 

A flush rose on Mrs. Bennet’s cheeks. “Elizabeth! Such impertinence! You speak as if a proposal were a *burden*!”

Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, a woman whose conversational inclinations leaned heavily towards the assessment of eligible men, fixed her gaze upon Miss Eleanor with an air of pointed inquiry. “Does that young lady, Miss Ainsworth, know Mr. Thornton?”

Eleanor coloured, a delicate flush rising in her cheeks. “A little, ma’am. We have met at the assemblies in Meryton, and occasionally at the vicarage.”

“And do not you think him a very handsome gentleman, ma’am?” Mrs. Featherstonehaugh continued, her voice brimming with expectation. “A figure of such consequence, and possessing, I am told, an estate of considerable magnitude. One cannot but observe the… *propriety* of his bearing.”

Eleanor, though accustomed to such pronouncements, found herself strangely reluctant to offer an opinion. Mr. Thornton was, undeniably, possessed of a fine countenance and a stature that commanded attention. Yet, a certain… reserve in his manner, a coolness that bordered on disdain, gave her pause. 

“He is, perhaps, a gentleman of respectable appearance,” she offered cautiously, hoping to deflect further scrutiny. Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, however, was not easily deterred. The pursuit of a suitable match, it seemed, was a subject of endless fascination.

The cartographer, old Hemlock, insisted the gradient was illusory. A trick of the light, he’d rasped, adjusting his spectacles with a trembling hand. But we, the expedition, knew better. We had charted these foothills for weeks, meticulously documenting the oppressive, unbroken verdancy that clung to the slopes – a greenness *too* vibrant, *too* insistent for any natural order. 

It was the *lack* of transition that chilled. The forest did not thin towards the peaks, did not yield to scree or barren rock as logic dictated. Instead, it simply… *continued*. A seamless, suffocating blanket ascending into the cyclopean heights. Hemlock spoke of atmospheric refraction, of optical delusions born of altitude. But we had observed a singular, unsettling interrupt.

A perfect, geometrically precise clearing, roughly circular, nestled amongst the trees. Not a fallen branch, not a displaced stone within its boundaries. Just… absence. A void within the green, radiating a cold that defied the summer sun. And from that emptiness, a silence deeper than any we had encountered, a silence that seemed to *listen*. It was not a natural phenomenon, we all agreed, but a deliberate excision, a wound upon the land hinting at geometries best left unseen.

text:
The air hung thick and fetid, less breathable than a viscous fluid, as we descended further into the cyclopean maw of the earth. Old Man Hemlock, bless his doomed soul, had spoken of a ‘natural hollow,’ but no natural process could have birthed *this*. The passage, carved not by water but by some obscene, geological convulsion, narrowed, and with the narrowing came the accumulation.

It was a deposit…of *things*. Not merely shells, though countless spiraled nautiloids lay fractured and gleaming with a phosphorescent decay. Nor simply bones, though the sheer volume defied comprehension – colossal femurs, vertebrae thicker than a man’s torso, all bleached and slick with an unidentifiable slime. They were interwoven, a grotesque tapestry woven from the remnants of epochs best left undisturbed.

Washed down, Hemlock’s notes hinted, from jungles utterly alien – jungles of Mesozoic tree ferns and fungi, an ecosystem predicated on geometries that mocked Euclidean space. The very *arrangement* of the deposit felt wrong, subtly non-aligned with our perceived reality. A creeping dread, colder than the subterranean air, insinuated itself into the mind. It was not merely death we faced here, but the lingering echo of a pre-human horror, a testament to life’s capacity for forms beyond sanity’s grasp.

text:
The morning room felt, despite the cheerful fire, a distinctly oppressive space. One had endured Lady Catherine de Bourgh before, of course, but to hear her talk, which she did without any intermission till coffee came in, delivering her opinion on every subject in so decisive a manner, was a trial testing even the most patient disposition. 

She commenced with the deplorable state of needlework amongst the younger generation, lamenting a decline in proper accomplishment. This swiftly transitioned to the impropriety of country dances involving more than twelve couples, and then, with alarming speed, to a critique of the local vicar’s sermon – too lengthy, she declared, and lacking in sufficient moral fortitude. 

Miss Eleanor, attempting a polite enquiry regarding Lady Catherine’s health, was met with a discourse on the benefits of early rising and a strict regimen of barley water. Even the arrival of the fragrant coffee offered no respite, merely providing a new platform for judgement – the blend, she pronounced, was “tolerable, but lacking the robust character of a Ceylon.” One could only hope, with a silent prayer, that luncheon might offer a change of scenery, and perhaps, a moment of blessed silence.
author: Jane Austen

The hillside, now, wasn’t much to look at at first blush. Just a rise, really, patched with scrub oak and the kind of weeds a body wouldn’t bother naming. But then you noticed the village nestled in its folds, looking for all the world like a handful of pebbles a child had scattered and forgotten. A right peculiar little collection of shacks and lean-tos, it was.

I closed in above the shore light, slow and easy, and laid on my oars, letting the current do the work. A feller gets tired of pullin’, you see. Floated past, quiet as a church mouse, and that’s when I saw it. Not the village itself, not precisely. But a lantern. 

Hanging on the ja – that’s what they called the porch roof, these folks did – of the smallest cabin. A single, flickering point of yellow in all that gloom. Didn’t seem much of a light to ward off the darkness, but then, these weren’t folks much given to wardin’ off anything, I reckoned. Just… *bein’*. And that lantern, well, it felt like a little piece of their bein’ shinin’ out for anyone who happened to drift by. A curious sight, it was. A right curious sight indeed.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed a sensibility perhaps too keenly attuned to the nuances of social expectation. The invitation to Rosings Park, extended through the kindness of Lady Bertram’s sister, was, of course, a mark of considerable favour. Yet, it filled her with a disquietude she dared not confess even to her dearest companion, Miss Penrose. 

To be presented to Lady Catherine de Bourgh was a prospect fraught with peril. She had heard tales – not unkindly meant, but nonetheless alarming – of her Ladyship’s exacting standards and pronouncements. Eleanor, though possessed of a modest fortune and a passable appearance, lacked the robust confidence so admired in certain quarters. 

Indeed, she looked forward to her introduction at Rosings with as much apprehension as her father had done to his presentation at St. James’s, a recollection he’d recounted with a shudder and a glass of port. Would her curtsy be sufficiently low? Her conversation sufficiently… *agreeable*? The very thought induced a flutter in her breast, and a most unwelcome blush upon her cheeks. One could only hope, she mused, that a quiet demeanour and a sincere respect might prove sufficient armour against the formidable Lady Catherine.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The party, having partaken of refreshments most delicate, were now descending the hill, the late afternoon sun casting long shadows across the parkland. Mr. Darcy, though not actively engaging in conversation – a habit still remarked upon, though with lessening censure – walked a respectful distance behind, allowing Miss Bennet and her aunt to proceed with Sir William Lucas. 

Indeed, all present were, it seemed, warm in their admiration of the estate. Lady Catherine, though pointedly observing the shrubbery for imperfections, had conceded its scale was ‘tolerable’. Even Mrs. Phillips, usually given to pronouncements on ribbons and eligible bachelors, was rendered unusually silent, her gaze fixed upon the imposing façade. 

Miss Bennet, however, found her attention drawn not to the architecture, but to the gentleman who owned it. To observe him *in* his domain, to witness the deference shown by his tenants, was a revelation. A fleeting fancy, perhaps, yet at that moment she felt that to be mistress of such a place – to command such respect, to enjoy such comfort – might be something! A most agreeable something, indeed. The descent continued, and with each step, a new possibility blossomed in her breast.

text:
Old Man Hemlock, he was fixin’ to up and leave Widow Peabody’s boarding house, bag and baggage, convinced he’d struck a gold mine of sorts. All on account of a handbill. A right flimsy thing, printed on paper thinner than a preacher’s promise, offerin’ a reward – a *substantial* reward, mind you – for the return of “Professor Phileas Fogg’s Highly Trained Performing Porcupines.”

Now, Hemlock hadn’t *seen* no porcupines, trained or otherwise. But he’d read the bill, and he’d decided, with the solemnity of a judge deliverin’ a hangin’ sentence, that he was the man to retrieve ‘em. He’d been spendin’ the last three days buildin’ a contraption out of chicken wire and old washboards, claimin’ it was a “porcupine conveyance.”

I tried tellin’ him, see. Told him the whole thing was a lark, a bit of foolishness dreamt up by young Jedediah to stir up some excitement in this dust-bowl town. The handbill was a fabrication, the reward a phantom. 

“But the *principle* of the thing, boy!” he sputtered, adjustin’ his spectacles. “A reward is a reward!” 

I figured if I explained how Jedediah just wanted to get folks lookin’ around, maybe distract ‘em from the bank’s troubles… maybe then he’d swallow his pride and lay down that infernal porcupine trap.

text:
The chipped porcelain doll, a grotesque parody of childhood, was the first. Old Man Hemlock insisted it held the *resonance* – a focal point for Elara’s…condition. Then came the astrolabe, tarnished brass whispering of geometries best left unconsidered, and finally, the pressed specimens of *Lichen mortuus*, gathered from the cyclopean slopes. These three, he rasped, were the anchors.

Not for return, precisely. Not to that suffocating normalcy. But for *further* transit, should the currents shift. No more screaming metal birds, thank the nameless voids. The mountains… they dwarfed even the fevered sketches of the Himalayas. Jagged, obsidian teeth gnawing at a sky perpetually bruised with violet and ochre. 

They weren’t *formed* so much as *exuded* from the earth, hinting at a pre-human architecture, a calculus of stone defying Euclidean comprehension. Hemlock spoke of ‘thin places’, where the veil frayed, and the doll, the astrolabe, the lichen – these were the keys to navigating the resultant… *flux*. A chilling prospect, yet preferable to the creeping dread of stagnation. The air itself tasted of dust and forgotten aeons, and a silence pressed upon the mind, heavier than any tombstone.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

“Entailed as ever,” Miss Penrose sighed, stirring her tea with a deliberation that bordered on pointedness. “One would think, after so many generations, the matter settled. Yet here we are, discussing the prospects of young Mr. Harrison and his… unfortunate circumstance.”

Her companion, Miss Ainsworth, offered a sympathetic inclination of the head. “The Lucases are very artful people, indeed, sister. One observes it in everything – the precise arrangement of their shrubbery, the calculated warmth of their greetings. All for what they can get.”

“Precisely! Mrs. Lucas, though possessed of a pleasant countenance, has a mind as sharp as any solicitor’s. To encourage Miss Harrison’s affections for their nephew, knowing full well his estate is… limited? It is a manoeuvre, I assure you.”

“A most transparent one. They hope, no doubt, to secure a connection, however tenuous, to the larger Penrose estate through a future alliance. It is, I am sorry to say of them, but so it is. They lack entirely the delicacy one expects in neighbours.” Miss Penrose shuddered delicately. “One can only hope Miss Harrison possesses sufficient discernment to see through their machinations.”

It was a mortifying circumstance, to be sure, and one which, upon reflection, did little credit to my own discernment. Had the same events transpired anew, I am quite persuaded I should be deceived again, so readily do I appear to grant credence where it is ill-bestowed. Miss Caroline Bingley did not return my visit till yesterday; and not a note, no, not even the smallest acknowledgement of my civility in the interim. A coolness so pointed, so deliberately maintained, could scarcely be mistaken.

One might have hoped, after the… *misunderstanding* regarding Mr. Darcy, that a degree of candour would have prevailed. But Miss Bingley, alas, possesses a spirit too keenly attuned to slight and a disposition too readily inclined to disapprove. She favoured me with a brief, and decidedly frigid, call, inquiring after my health with a tone suggesting she fully expected a decline. 

Her conversation, as ever, revolved around Netherfield and its present occupants, delivered with a pointed lack of enthusiasm regarding any acquaintance *not* of her own choosing. It is a vexation, certainly, but one I shall endeavour to bear with a composure befitting a lady. Though, I confess, a small measure of resentment is not easily suppressed.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed a mind too keenly attuned to observe the foibles of her acquaintance, and, alas, too little inclined to overlook them. Whilst her sister, the amiable Beatrice, found merit in every blushing cheek and stammered compliment, Eleanor saw only calculation. A proposal, to Beatrice, was a testament to affection; to Eleanor, a shrewd assessment of dowry and connections.

She endured the endless pronouncements on eligible bachelors with a barely concealed sigh. Young Mr. Featherstonehaugh, lauded for his handsome estate, was, in her estimation, possessed of a countenance remarkably resembling a startled carp and a conversational range limited to the price of wheat. 

“He is *so* attentive,” Beatrice would gush, recounting a particularly tedious dance.

“Attentive to the security of a comfortable establishment, perhaps,” Eleanor would murmur, ostensibly examining the embroidery on her own reticule. 

It was not that she *wished* to be disagreeable, merely that she found sincerity a rare and often illusory commodity. A disposition, she feared, that rendered her perpetually on the periphery of happiness, yet stubbornly incapable of feigning contentment within its circle.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth, though possessed of a tolerable fortune and a connection which, whilst not *precisely* elevated, was certainly respectable, remained, alas, unmarried at the advanced age of twenty-seven. It was not for want of suitors, mind you, but a most singular fastidiousness. She declared Mr. Finch, a man of amiable disposition and considerable estate, “utterly devoid of conversation.” Sir Reginald, though undeniably handsome, was dismissed as “too prone to the hunting field and too little to the improvement of his mind.”

And then there was Mr. Harwood. He possessed a certain…way, a forwardness of address which many mistook for confidence. But she, observing him closely during the Assembly, found it merely presumption. And as for her eyes, which have sometimes been called so fine, I never could perceive anything extraordinary in them. They have a sharp, shrewish cast, constantly assessing, judging, and finding wanting. 

He had dared to compliment her on her embroidery, a piece she considered merely passable. “A charming display of needlework, Miss Elmsworth,” he’d ventured. She had replied, with a coolness that could chill a summer’s breeze, “One strives for competence, sir, not necessarily admiration.” It was, she believed, a perfectly reasonable response.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed, if she dared to admit it even to herself, a mind rather too keenly attuned to observation. It was not vanity that prompted the thought, merely a consequence of possessing a sensibility exceeding that of her acquaintance. Indeed, the more she witnessed of society – a parade of affected manners and concealed ambitions – the more profoundly dissatisfied she became. 

Her recent journey to Bath, intended as a restorative, had proven anything *but*. The Assembly Rooms, far from offering amusement, displayed only a heightened degree of artifice. Mr. Harrington, so lauded for his fortune, proved a tedious bore, whilst the charming Miss Tremaine’s smiles felt distinctly calculated. 

Each encounter, each overheard conversation, served only to confirm her growing conviction of the inconsistency of all human character. Professions of friendship masked envy, declarations of honour concealed self-interest. One longed for genuine feeling, for a sincerity rarely glimpsed beneath the polished veneer of polite society. To *think* well, she found, was a solitary occupation, and one increasingly tinged with melancholy. It was a comfort, at least, to know her own heart remained, if not entirely content, at least untainted by such pervasive duplicity.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, I reckon a body can get used to most things, given time and a strong constitution. But this here itch… this weren’t a thing a body *got used to*. It commenced small, mind you, just a tickle ‘round the left elbow. Harmless enough. I indulged, naturally. A man’s gotta scratch when a man’s gotta scratch.

That was my error. A grievous, monumental error.

For within the blink of an eye, it weren’t just the elbow. No sir. It was the back of my neck, the soles of my boots, the tip of my nose. Every blessed inch of me felt like a field of fire ants had taken up residence. I scratched and scratched, a whirlwind of flailing limbs, but it only *spread*. It multiplied like rabbits in springtime. A thousand itches, easy. Maybe ten thousand. 

I was a-writin’ in agony, lookin’ like a scarecrow possessed, when Jim, who’d been quiet as a church mouse, finally spoke up. He eyed me with a suspicion that could curdle milk. 

“Say,” he drawled, slow and deliberate, “who *is* you? Whar is you? Dog my cats, if you ain’t the strangest sight I ever did see.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
The intelligence arrived with Mr. Phillips, flushed and eager, concerning Mr. Bingley’s sudden departure for London. A matter of urgent business, he declared, relating to his estate – a vague pronouncement which, naturally, invited a flurry of speculation amongst the ladies assembled at Longbourn. Mrs. Bennet, however, required little prompting to arrive at a most satisfactory conclusion. 

“It *must* be to secure the necessary papers for a speedy marriage!” she announced, fanning herself with a vigour that threatened to dislodge the ribbons. “He would not go otherwise, not for the world! A mere trifle of business, he says, but a trifle of the utmost consequence to *us*!”

Mr. Bennet, observing his wife’s transports with a familiar amusement, offered only a dry, “Indeed?” 

It appeared he was obliged to go the next day for a short time, a detail which, far from diminishing her joy, only served to heighten the anticipation. Mrs. Bennet was perfectly satisfied; and quitted the house under the delightful persuasion that a proposal, and a wedding, were now merely days away, leaving the more sensible Elizabeth to contemplate the precarious foundations upon which such hopes were built.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, an hour ain’t always just sixty minutes, you see. Sometimes it stretches, like taffy pulled by a strong hand, and sometimes it shrinks quicker’n a miser’s heart at a church social. This hour, though, it was a long one. We’d been floatin’ down the Mississippi – a grand, lazy river, she was – since sun-up, and the day had settled into a kind of dreamy quiet. 

We catched fish, mostly catfish, big enough to give a man a proper supper. And we talked. Not about important things, mind you. More about the foolishness of men, the habits of crows, and whether a bullfrog ever truly appreciates a good fly. Took a dip now and then, too, just to wrestle the sleepiness that crept in with the heat.

It was kind of solemn, drifting. The water barely rippled, the trees stood watchin’ like old judges, and the sun just…hung there. Felt like time itself had slowed to a crawl, content to let us be. An hour, it was, but felt more like a whole afternoon swallowed by the river’s peace. A good hour, though. A right good hour.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The sun was well past peekin’ over the cottonwoods, nigh onto ten o’clock, and a body’d think a fella wouldn’t be findin’ himself adrift on a raft made of nothin’ but hope and driftwood. But there I was. Had been fool enough to think I could navigate the Missouri with a paddle whittled from a fence post. A right proper fool, I tell you.

Now, the current was takin’ me along at a clip, and the banks were gettin’ blurry. Didn’t seem a soul about, not a cabin smokin’, not a dog barkin’. I figured I’d best swallow my pride and hail the next steamboat. But I remembered Pa’s warnin’ – “Don’t go tellin’ folks you’re just ramblin’, boy. Say your kin are ailin’.”

So, when that *Magnolia* came chuggin’ ‘round the bend, I hollered, puttin’ on a voice tremblin’ like a willow in a windstorm. “Help! Please, help! My folks… they’re all down with the chills and fever! Terrible sick!” 

A likely story, maybe. But a fella does what he must. And I vowed, right then and there, not to be a fool again, not with a river and a steamboat and a tale to tell.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, it weren’t a proper darkness, mind you, more a thick stew of night and river mist clinging to the *Belle of Natchez* like a guilty conscience. Old Man Tiber, the watch, had a fondness for dozing, see, and a fella could stretch his legs a bit without undue notice. We – young Silas and myself – had a notion for a slice of Mrs. Peabody’s peach pie, cooling on the texas hearth. 

Sneaking down the slope of it to labboard was like navigating a blind man’s maze. Each step a gamble, feeling for the deck with our boots, slow and deliberate. Hands outstretched, we fended off ropes and stanchions like they were ornery cats. A fella’d think you could smell the pie, it was so close, but the river had its own smells – mud and fish and the faint, sweet rot of things long sunk.

Silas bumped a coil of rope, near gave us away, and whispered a curse that sounded like a strangled frog. I shushed him, naturally. A peach pie ain’t worth a keelhauling, though a good slice *is* worth a little risk. We crept on, shadows swallowing us whole, two boys and a desperate craving, inching towards the promised land of pastry.
author: Mark Twain

The park was very large, and contained great variety of ground. They entered it in one of its lowest points, and drove for some time through a beautiful wood stretching over a wide extent. Elizabeth’s mind was too full for conversation, but she saw and admired every remarkable spot and point of view. It was a large, handsome stone building, standing well on rising ground, and backed by a ridge of high woody hills; and in front a stream of some natural importance was swelled into greater, but without any artificial appearance. Its banks were neither formal nor falsely adorned. Elizabeth was delighted. She had never seen a place for which nature had done more, or where natural beauty had been so little counteracted by an awkward taste.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The assembly at Hartfield was, as usual, a study in varying degrees of consequence. Miss Elmsworth, newly returned from a disappointing Season in Bath, declared herself quite indifferent to the attentions of young Mr. Finch, a gentleman possessed of a tolerable fortune but lamentably deficient in conversation. 

“Indeed, Mama,” she confided, fluttering her fan with a studied air, “I do not mind anything at all.”

Mrs. Elmsworth, ever practical, raised a delicate eyebrow. “Let us be thankful that you are preserved from a state of such insensibility.”

“I never can be thankful, Mr. Finch,” Miss Elmsworth retorted, directing a pointed glance at the unfortunate gentleman, “for a compliment which implies a lack of discernment on my part. To suggest I require *excitement* is to suggest I am…common.”

Mr. Finch, thoroughly discomfited, retreated towards the refreshment table, muttering something about the superior charms of Miss Penrose. The room, however, scarcely noticed his disquiet. Such pronouncements, whilst occasionally startling, were considered perfectly acceptable within the bounds of fashionable affectation. One simply *must* appear unconcerned, even when quite the reverse was true.
author: Jane Austen

text: [Illustration] CHAPTER VI. [Illustration] The ladies of Longbourn soon waited on those of Netherfield. The visit was returned in due form. Miss Bennet’s pleasing manners grew on the good-will of Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley; and though the mother was found to be intolerable, and the younger sisters not worth speaking to, a wish of being better acquainted with _them_ was expressed towards the two eldest. By Jane this attention was received with the greatest pleasure; but Elizabeth still saw superciliousness in their treatment of everybody, hardly excepting even her sister, and could not like them; though their kindness to Jane, such as it was, had a value, as arising, in all probability, from the influence of their brother’s admiration. text:
The summons arrived with the unwelcome punctuality of a winter frost – an invitation to the Ashworths’ rout. Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a sensibility not entirely averse to such gatherings, found herself in a state of considerable agitation. Not from anticipation of pleasure, but from the sheer logistical challenge of appearing suitably composed. Her younger sister, Marianne, declared the event “divinely promising,” and flitted about selecting ribbons with an enthusiasm Eleanor found bordering on the vulgar. 

Their brother, Mr. Thomas, a gentleman of perfectly respectable, if unremarkable, character, offered a dry observation regarding the probable tedium of the evening, then retreated to his books. Eleanor, after giving each of them a hasty kiss, hurried into the vestibule, where Jane, who came running downstairs from her mother’s apartment, immediately inquired as to the colour of her gown. 

“Peach, my dear,” Eleanor replied, smoothing the fabric with a practiced hand. “Though I fear it lacks the brilliance to capture Mr. Harrington’s attention.” Jane, ever practical, merely suggested a sprig of jasmine. The pursuit of a suitable husband, Eleanor reflected, was a most exhausting undertaking, even *before* one had entered the ballroom.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, it was a right proper squall brewin’, the kind that makes a body think twice ‘fore leavin’ the porch. Eleven of us, crammed into Old Man Hemlock’s smokehouse – eleven, mind you, and warn’t hardly room in there to get your breath. Mostly womenfolk and young’uns, see, all a-tremblin’ like aspen leaves. By jings, we forgot to fasten that lean-to door! A foolish oversight, that was.

The wind commenced to howl, and rain lashed down like a disappointed preacher. Then, a shadow fell across the doorway. Big as a bear, it was. Old Nat, the colored fella who helps Hemlock with the choring, he only just *barely* managed to shove that door shut against the gale, lookin’ like he wrestled a cyclone and lost a button or two. 

“Lordy, Lordy,” he breathed, wipin’ his brow. “Thought for a spell that door was gonna take flight to St. Louis.” 

Mrs. Abernathy commenced to pray, little Timmy Hemlock started to cry, and I reckon we all held our breath, waitin’ for the roof to peel off like a bad sunburn. A right mess, it was, a right mess indeed. But we were dry, for the moment, and that, I suppose, was somethin’.
author: Mark Twain

After supper she got out her book and learned me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was in a sweat to find out all about him; but by-and-by she let it out that Moses had been dead a considerable long time; so then I didn’t care no more about him, because I don’t take no stock in dead people. Pretty soon I wanted to smoke, and asked the widow to let me. But she wouldn’t. She said it was a mean practice and wasn’t clean, and I must try to not do it any more. That is just the way with some people. They get down on a thing when they don’t know nothing about it. Here she was a-bothering about Moses, which was no kin to her, and no use to anybody, being gone, you see, yet finding a power of fault with me for doing a thing that had some good in it. And she took snuff, too; of course that was all right, because she done it herself.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, it was warm for young Jebediah, it truly was. Not just a simmerin’ warm, mind you, but a stick-to-your-britches, sweat-drippin’ warm that’d make a lizard consider a cool cave. He’d been caught, see, pilferin’ apples from Old Man Hemlock’s orchard – a sin, certainly, but a temptin’ one with them apples blushin’ like a schoolmarm’s cheeks. 

The new judge, a fella fresh from the city with spectacles perched on his nose, didn’t believe in the usual hickoryin’. No sir. He declared he was a-going to *make* a man of Jebediah. A curious notion, considerin’ Jebediah was already ten summers old.

So, he took the boy back to his own house – a grand affair with carpets and whatnot – and commenced to dressin’ him up clean. Jebediah, used to patched overalls and bare feet, felt like a caged songbird in a starched collar and proper trousers. He smelled of soap and somethin’ flowery, and felt about as natural as a catfish in a teacup. The judge beamed, sayin’ “Now *this* is a gentleman!” Jebediah just reckoned he felt mighty uncomfortable, and longed for the orchard, and a good, honest apple stain on his shirt.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Mr. Alistair Finch, a gentleman possessed of a tolerable fortune and an uncommonly disagreeable disposition, had, after a season of pointed indifference, begun to pay attentions to Miss Eleanor Ainsworth. It was a circumstance remarked upon by all, though few could fathom its cause. He had, for years, declared the fairer sex frivolous and unworthy of serious consideration, and his sudden alteration in sentiment was a puzzle to the neighbourhood. 

He spoke of Miss Ainsworth’s sensible conversation, her quiet accomplishments, and a certain… *steadiness* of character. Yet, those who observed him closely detected a restless dissatisfaction in his manner, a seeking for something he could not quite articulate. He had, of course, entirely failed to comprehend the source of his altered feelings. He attributed it to a gradual softening of his own naturally austere nature, a triumph of reason over prejudice. 

Has he, however, considered the possibility that his unregenerate state was not entirely his own doing? Only she, naturally, has not counted in what was due to her own personal charm – a subtle power, wielded with unconscious grace, capable of disarming even the most hardened of hearts. The secret of that charm, alas, remained entirely her own.
author: Jane Austen

text: hour. We catched fish and talked, and we took a swim now and then to keep off sleepiness. It was kind of solemn, drifting down the big, still river, laying on our backs looking up at the stars, and we didn’t ever feel like talking loud, and it warn’t often that we laughed—only a little kind of a low chuckle. We had mighty good weather as a general thing, and nothing ever happened to us at all—that night, nor the next, nor the next. Every night we passed towns, some of them away up on black hillsides, nothing but just a shiny bed of lights; not a house could you see. The fifth night we passed St. Louis, and it was like the whole world lit up. In St. Petersburg they used to say there was twenty or thirty thousand people in St. Louis, but I never believed it till I see that wonderful spread of lights at two o’clock that still night. There warn’t a sound there; everybody was asleep. Every night now I used to slip ashore towards ten o’clock at some little village, and buy ten or fifteen cents’ worth of meal or bacon or other stuff
