text:
Old Man Hemlock, he weren’t popular. Not with the river folk, nor the townsfolk neither. Claimed he’d struck it rich in California, but spent it all on fancy boots and a parrot that swore like a steamboat engineer. Found him this mornin’, face-down in the mud near the willow bend. Looked like a catfish had used him for a restin’ place. 

Now, Deputy Clem, he’s a good boy, but slow as molasses in January. He was pokin’ around with a stick, lookin’ for clues, when Captain Silas, he bellowed from the *Belle of Natchez*. A man who’d seen more trouble than a gambler’s losing streak.

“Hold yer horses, Clem!” he roared, his voice carryin’ clear as a church bell. “Look sharp, now; the current sets in the closest here, and maybe he’s washed ashore and got tangled amongs’. Don’t be lookin’ *at* the bank, boy, look *in* the bank. And mind you, keep yer eyes peeled for anything… *unnatural*. A man don’t just lay down for a nap in the mud, not unless he’s been persuaded.” 

He squinted at the water, a grim set to his jaw. “This river, she holds secrets, Clem. And she ain’t givin’ ‘em up easy.”
author: Mark Twain

text: unnatural, the fantastic, and the dreamlike. Looking along the line of high peaks, I thought I could see the one mentioned by poor Lake, with a rampart exactly on top. It seemed to be half lost in a queer antarctic haze--such a haze, perhaps, as had been responsible for Lake's early notion of volcanism. The pass loomed directly before us, smooth and windswept between its jagged and malignly frowning pylons. Beyond it was a sky fretted with swirling vapors and lighted by the low polar sun--the sky of that mysterious farther realm upon which we felt no human eye had ever gazed. A few more feet of altitude and we would behold that realm. Danforth and I, unable to speak except in shouts amidst the howling, piping wind that raced through the pass and added to the noise of the unmuffled engines, exchanged eloquent glances. And then, having gained those last few feet, we did indeed stare across the momentous divide and over the unsampled secrets of an elder and utterly alien earth. V. I think that both of us simultaneously cried out in mixed awe, wonder, terror, and disbelief in our own senses as we finally cleared the pass
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I reckon a body can get mighty low in the dumps, and still not rightly *see* the bottom. That’s where I found myself, sittin’ on that splintered crate, feelin’ like a hound dog kicked clean through a fence. My back was achin’ somethin’ fierce – a souvenir from haul’n’ those blasted crates of peaches all the way from Georgia – and my pride was bruised worse. 

Sore, I was, but I couldn’t see no way out of the trouble. After all this long journey, and after all we’d done for them scoundrels – deliverin’ their fruit, protectin’ it from river pirates, even teachin’ old Man Hemlock’s boy to whistle a proper tune – here it was all come to. A claim of short weight. A bald-faced lie, I tell you!

They said I’d skimped ‘em a bushel. A *bushel*! Why, I’d sooner wrestle a grizzly bear than cheat a man outta a peach. But there they stood, Hemlock and his kin, lookin’ at me with eyes colder than a January mornin’. I figured disputin’ it would just stir up more dust, and a fella gets tired of dust after a spell. So I just sat there, feelin’ lower than a snake’s belly, and watched ‘em count out a pittance for my trouble. A pittance, I say!
author: Mark Twain

text:
The Antarctic held a silence not of snow and ice, but of *waiting*. Our expedition, ostensibly geological, was driven by a hunger far older than science. Erebus loomed, a basaltic god wreathed in perpetual fume, and the ascent… the ascent was not merely arduous, but *wrong*. The air thinned not with altitude, but with a creeping dread, a sense of being observed by geometries beyond human comprehension.

The borings on Ross Island yielded not the expected strata, but a substance… unsettlingly *smooth*, and cold beyond any terrestrial measure. It resonated with a low, subsonic hum that frayed the edges of sanity. But it was Pabodie, the geologist, who truly unravelled. 

He began with an accelerated efficiency, charting formations with a feverish zeal. Then came the muttering, the sketches – impossible angles, cyclopean structures buried beneath the ice. His progress was… singular. Days collapsed into a blur of frantic activity, fuelled by something not of this earth. He spoke of “resonances,” of “alignment,” and of a vast, slumbering *presence* awakened by our intrusion. 

Now, he refuses to sleep, claiming the ice *breathes*. And the humming… the humming grows louder.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, it wasn’t a grand misfortune, mind you, not like a steamboat explosion or a yellow fever outbreak. Just a slow leakin’ of fortune, a steady dribble of bad luck seasoned with poor judgment. Old Man Hemlock, he promised a fair price for the timber rights, said he was a man of his word. Turns out, his word was mostly air and a fondness for whiskey. 

So when he died – and a good riddance, I say, though politeness forbids – I took what there was left, because the farm didn’t belong to us, not truly. It was always a borrowed patch of ground, a temporary holdin’. And started up the river, deck passage, and a carpetbag full of nothin’ much but regret and a half-eaten apple.

The Mississippi, she don’t care for a man’s troubles. She just rolls on, indifferent as a judge. Folks on board, they mostly kept to themselves, lookin’ for somethin’ better further upriver. I reckon we all were. A fella can spend a lifetime chasin’ somethin’ better, and end up right back where he started, only older and with a poorer opinion of timber men. It’s a truth, that is. A plain, unvarnished truth.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Old Man Tiberius, he sat there on the general store porch, lookin’ like a scarecrow that’d seen better seasons. Had one ankle resting on t’other knee; the boot on that foot was busted, and two of his toes stuck through, and he worked them now and then, like they was independent little creatures considerin’ a journey. His ha, well, it was a sight. A tangle of grey, mostly, with bits of straw and what looked suspiciously like dried apple peel woven in. 

He was whittlin’ at a piece of pine, makin’ nothin’ in particular, just lettin’ the knife do the thinkin’. Folks said he used to be a river man, a steamboat pilot, even. But that was before the Mississippi decided to change its mind about where it wanted to run, and before Tiberius decided to change his mind about…well, most things.

Young Billy Henderson, full of vinegar and questions, dared ask him what he was makin’. Tiberius just chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “Why, son,” he drawled, “I’m buildin’ a memory. Takes a heap of whittlin’ to get a memory just right, you see. Gotta smooth out the rough edges, and fill in the holes where the truth got lost.” And he went back to workin’ those toes.
author: Mark Twain

In this vast hemisphere, whose concave roof was impressively though decadently carved to a likeness of the primordial celestial dome, a few albino penguins waddled--aliens there, but indifferent and unseeing. text:
My dearest Sister,

A most vexing circumstance has arisen, and I write to you in a state bordering on distraction. Mr. Collins, you see, has proposed – and been accepted! Charlotte, bless her sensible heart, deems it a prudent match, securing her a comfortable home. However, the *timing*… it is utterly improper. He insists upon furnishing the parsonage *after* the ceremony, a notion which, whilst practical, feels… shockingly forward. 

Mama, naturally, is in a flutter, envisioning linens and china, and has already begun to dictate a list of necessities. Papa, however, is quite incensed at the very idea of a wedding without the proper accoutrements beforehand. He speaks of honour and tradition, and I fear a most unpleasant scene with Mr. Collins is brewing. 

You *must* write to him, dearest Sister! Explain to him the dreadful state I am in – truly, I am frightened of the consequences should Papa’s temper be roused. Remind him of the importance of decorum, and the necessity of purchasing everything *before* the vows are exchanged. Above all, prevent a quarrel! A Bennet embroiled in a dispute would be a scandal for us all.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Tiber, he had a notion. A notion struck him right ‘bout three in the mornin’, a time when a body oughta be sleepin’ and dreamin’ of catfish and cool water. “Goin’,” he declared, stirrin’ like a disturbed hornet, “right here in the daybreak?”

Now, *that* warn’t the plan. We’d agreed on waitin’ till sun-high, when a feller could see what he was steppin’ in, and maybe avoid a snake or two. “No, it warn’t,” I grumbled, pullin’ my hat lower, “but it’s the plan *now*.” 

Drat him, we went along. He had a way, that Tiber did, of makin’ a man feel like arguin’ was a waste of good breath. The river was all mist and shadow, lookin’ like nothin’ so much as a troubled spirit. Every rustle in the cane sounded like a whisper, and I swear a hoot owl gave me a look that said I was a fool for bein’ out of bed. 

I didn’t like it, not one bit. Felt like we were sneakin’ around in somebody else’s dream, and likely to wake up to a heap of trouble. But Tiber, he just hummed a tune and kept on walkin’, lookin’ pleased as punch with his early risin’. A man can only complain so much, you see.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a study. Lived up by the Widow Hemlock’s place, did Tiber, and spent most days just…existing. Not *living*, mind you, existing. He’d sit on his porch, a contraption of splintered wood and faded paint, and watch the river go by. Didn’t fish, didn’t wave, didn’t even swat the flies that took a fancy to his nose. 

One afternoon, I observed him launch a little skiff, no bigger than a coffin, and just…drift. No oars. No sail. Just let the current take him. I hailed him, naturally. “Tiber! What in tarnation are you up to?”

He barely glanced my way. “Think I, it won’t do to paddle,” he drawled, voice like gravel. “First I know I’ll run into the bank or a tow-head or something; I got to set still and float, and yet it’s might…unsettling, this letting go.”

Unsettling, he called it. Seemed to me, a man who’d spent seventy years watchin’ the world spin ought to be used to a little unsettlin’. But there he was, a speck on the water, surrendering to the flow. A peculiar sight, that Tiber, a peculiar sight indeed.
author: Mark Twain

text: Now I’ll rest my works a little, and you start up yourn; just tell me _everything_—tell me all about ’m all every one of ’m; and how they are, and what they’re doing, and what they told you to tell me; and every last thing you can think of.” Well, I see I was up a stump—and up it good. Providence had stood by me this fur all right, but I was hard and tight aground now. I see it warn’t a bit of use to try to go ahead—I’d _got_ to throw up my hand. So I says to myself, here’s another place where I got to resk the truth. I opened my mouth to begin; but she grabbed me and hustled me in behind the bed, and says: “Here he comes! Stick your head down lower—there, that’ll do; you can’t be seen now. Don’t you let on you’re here. I’ll play a joke on him. Children, don’t you say a word.” I see I was in a fix now. But it warn’t no use to worry; there warn’t nothing to do but just hold still, and try and be ready to stand from under when the lightning struck.
author: Mark Twain

text: I can’t imitate him; but he turned around to the crowd, and says, about like this: “This is a surprise to me which I wasn’t looking for; and I’ll acknowledge, candid and frank, I ain’t very well fixed to meet it and answer it; for my brother and me has had misfortunes; he’s broke his arm, and our baggage got put off at a town above here last night in the night by a mistake. I am Peter Wilks’ brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, which can’t hear nor speak—and can’t even make signs to amount to much, now’t he’s only got one hand to work them with. We are who we say we are; and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. But up till then I won’t say nothing more, but go to the hotel and wait.” So him and the new dummy started off; and the king he laughs, and blethers out: “Broke his arm—_very_ likely, _ain’t_ it?—and very convenient, too, for a fraud that’s got to make signs, and ain’t learnt how. Lost their baggage! That’s _mighty_ good!—and mighty ingenious—under the _circumstances!_” So he laughed again; and

text:
Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a caution. A right peculiar cuss, was Tiber. Spent half his life submerged, claimin’ the sun gave him the vapors. This particular afternoon, he was hangin’ under the stern oar of the *Belle of Natchez*, lookin’ like a bloated catfish with only his schnozz above the waterline. 

“Is dey out o’ sight yit?” he gurgled, voice muffled by the Mississippi mud. “Don’t talk loud.”

I leaned over the rail, careful not to disturb the ladies with their parasols and gossip. “They’re gone, Tiber. Clean over the bend, chasin’ a steamboat whistle, I reckon.”

A slow, contented sigh bubbled up with him. “C.” 

Just “C.” Not a “yes,” not a “thank you,” not even a grunt of acknowledgement. Just a single, drawn-out “C.” He’d been avoidin’ the Sunday school picnic committee for an hour, and they were a persistent bunch, bless their hearts. Always lookin’ to save a soul, even one already halfway to the fishes. He figured if he stayed submerged, they’d assume he’d already *been* saved, in a manner of speakin’. A clever feller, Old Man Tiber, for a man who preferred company with the crawdads.
author: Mark Twain

text:
…and to carve such things? The question gnawed at Danforth, a morbid curiosity mirroring my own dread. Old Man Hemlock, they said, had been a master woodcarver, but his later works… they defied Euclidean geometry, possessed angles that felt *wrong* to the eye, and a disturbing, almost organic flow. He’d claimed inspiration from “the deep places,” muttering of basalt cities and geometries older than time.

And now, when Danforth and I saw the freshly glistening and reflectively iridescent black slime which clung thickly to those blasphemous effigies, a cold paralysis gripped us. It wasn’t merely wet; it *moved* with a sluggish, internal rhythm, pulsing faintly like a diseased heart. The carvings themselves – grotesque, vaguely cephalopodic forms – seemed to *absorb* the light, leaving only a sickening sheen. 

The air grew thick, heavy with a cloying, metallic scent. Danforth swore he heard a low, subsonic hum emanating from the slime, a vibration that resonated not in the ears, but within the very bone. It was a sound that spoke of abyssal pressures and cyclopean architectures, of things best left undisturbed in the lightless gulfs beneath the world. We retreated, stumbling, knowing with a certainty that chilled us to the core: Hemlock hadn’t *carved* these things. He’d… *summoned* them.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The drawing-room was draped in a silence more oppressive than any boisterous lamentation. Miss Elmsworth, though possessed of a countenance naturally serene, sat with her hands clasped so tightly in her lap the knuckles were quite white. Young Mr. Finch, recently bereaved of his elder brother, bore his sorrow with a stoicism that, to some eyes, bordered on the unfeeling. 

Lady Beatrice, however, understood the art of concealed suffering. Observing the young man’s rigid posture, she felt a familiar ache stir within her. It brought to mind a similar scene, a similar stillness, some five-and-twenty years past. A loss, though of a different nature, had left its mark upon *her* heart, a mark time had softened, but not entirely erased.

“I am sure,” said she, her voice a gentle murmur intended only for Mr. Finch’s ear, “I cried for two days. Not, perhaps, with outward display, you understand. But a constant, inward weeping. It is a most exhausting business, grief. Do not feel obliged to hasten its departure, sir. It requires… time. And a great deal of strong tea.” She offered him a small, sympathetic smile, a silent acknowledgement of a pain she knew, however distantly, all too well.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, a body might think a fella with a raft and a stretch of the Mississippi before him would be aimin’ for New Orleans, or St. Louis, maybe. Somethin’ grand, you understand. But me? I reckon I’m done with grand. Done with folks and their expectin’s and their preachin’. 

This here raft, she’s a freedom, see? Can stop anywhere I want to. Jackson’s Island is good enough for me; I know that island pretty well, and nobody ever comes there. Not since old Man Hemlock swore it was haunted by a screechin’ ghost. Superstition’s a powerful thing, keeps a body peaceful.

And then I can paddle. Not *have* to paddle, mind you. Just…when the notion strikes. Driftin’ is fine, but a little push here and there, steerin’ clear of snags and the like, that’s a comfort. It’s a fella’s own business, where he goes and how fast. No schedules, no questions, just the river and the sun and a body tryin’ to be left alone. Seems to me, that’s about as close to heaven as a man’s likely to get.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, this here pencil, it weren’t much to look at. Just a common wood-cased fellow, yellow as a buttercup and smelling faintly of cedar and…well, ambition, I reckon. Found it tucked inside Old Man Hemlock’s account book, after he’d passed on to that great ledger in the sky. Ransacked the book, I did, hopin’ for a forgotten five or ten, a promissory note, *somethin’*. But no. Just this pencil.

I took a scrap of paper, aimin’ to test its mettle. Scribbled a bit, tried to conjure up a poem, maybe a philosophical treatise. Lord, it was awful. Looked like a spider had dipped its feet in ink and gone for a walk. Couldn’t make heads nor tails of it, not a lick. 

So I tucked the paper back into the account book, right where I’d found it. A pencil’s a peculiar thing, you see. Holds no value itself, but it’s the *potential* for value that’s interestin’. A blank slate, waitin’ for a hand to guide it. And when I got home… well, that’s another story altogether, and a right peculiar one at that.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The chronometers, of course, were the first to falter. Not in a cessation of ticking – no, a far more insidious distortion. They *skipped*. Moments vanished, then reappeared, subtly altered, like reflections in a troubled, oily pool. It began with seconds, then bled into minutes, and finally, whole stretches of perceived time became…unmoored. 

We, the remnants of the ill-fated Arcturus Expedition, observed this with a dread that transcended mere scientific curiosity. The engines of our salvaged aircraft, cobbled together from wreckage and alien alloys, continued to function, yet their operation defied all known principles. Despite the altogether unaccountable juggling of their operative mechanism – a pulsing, violet luminescence within the casings, a rhythmic *thrumming* that resonated not in the ears, but in the very bone – they held.

Old Man Hemlock, the engineer, muttered of non-Euclidean geometries and the blasphemous angles inherent in the plateau’s architecture. He spoke of a ‘resonance’, a sympathetic vibration with something…*else*. Something ancient and vast, stirring beneath the cyclopean stones. 

Do not mention the author by name. We decided to load all the planes the next morning and start back for our base, praying that the sanity we clung to would endure the journey, and that whatever had warped time itself would not reach out and claim us before we reached the familiar, if ultimately insignificant, shores of home.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, there was a stillness descended on the bottomlands that day, a stillness you could chew on. Not the peaceful kind, mind you, but the sort that prickles the back of your neck and makes a man reckon with his own mortality. The cicadas had up and quit, the river didn’t so much as gurgle, and even the usual squawk of a bluejay was absent. It was a silence so complete, it felt…wrong.

I was trackin’ a stray heifer, old Bess, and hadn’t seen hide nor hair of her for hours. The dogs, Blue and Belle, they were with me, but they weren’t their usual rambunctious selves. They walked slow, heads low, and kept a respectful distance, like they knew somethin’ I didn’t. 

And the only sound, truly, was the thump-thump-thumpin’ of my own heart. Felt like a blacksmith workin’ an anvil inside my chest. I swear, I could *hear* it echo in that quiet. It wasn’t fear, not exactly. More like…expectancy. Like the whole world was holdin’ its breath, waitin’ for somethin’ to break. And I had a powerful feelin’ that Bess wasn’t the thing it was waitin’ for.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor Penhaligon found herself, upon reflection, in a state could not have been more wretchedly blind. Not to the charms of Mr. Ashworth, for those were readily apparent, but to the true motives guiding his attentions. She had, with a delicacy she now deemed excessive, interpreted his frequent calls and pointed compliments as nascent affection. Pleased with the preference of one so esteemed, she had allowed herself a degree of hopeful anticipation, a foolish indulgence, she now conceded.

Yet, the slight – the barely perceptible coolness in his manner towards her sister, Miss Beatrice – had stung. Offended by the neglect of *her* particular accomplishments, she had convinced herself Mr. Ashworth valued her superior wit and sensibility. 

Now, however, a whispered conversation overheard in the rose garden revealed the truth. He admired Beatrice’s fortune, not Eleanor’s mind. It was not love he sought, but a comfortable establishment. And vanity, not love, had been her folly. A most mortifying discovery, and one which threatened to render her quite insupportable to herself, and, undoubtedly, to all her acquaintance.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor, having delivered a most pointed condemnation of Mr. Ashworth’s imprudence – a folly concerning a misplaced confidence and a rather extravagant purchase of ribbons – found herself, to her considerable mortification, quite spent. The heat of her upbraiding, so satisfying moments before, now left a hollow ache. It was not his defence, which was minimal and delivered with a most unbecoming stoop, that altered her disposition, but the sheer *disappointment* etched upon his countenance.

He had, she realised with a blush creeping up her neck, anticipated her approval, a small encouragement in this particular venture. To have met instead with such severity! His attachment, though never explicitly declared, was evident in the quickening of his breath when she entered a room, the careful arrangement of a favoured book upon her visits. 

Now, his shoulders slumped, his gaze fixed upon the patterned rug, he appeared a study in wounded pride. A most uncomfortable sensation, akin to guilt, began to stir within her. Perhaps a little leniency, a softening of tone, was due. After all, ribbons *were* a harmless extravagance, and a man’s affections, a far more delicate matter.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The salt-crusted cliffs of Innsmouth held secrets even the oldest mariners dared not whisper. It was during a low tide, a tide unnaturally protracted and sickly green, that I first observed them – the embrasures. Not those crumbling gun-ports of colonial vintage, but *others*. Hewn directly from the basalt, impossibly angled, and flanking a cove no chart acknowledged.

They were not of human design. That much was evident in the subtly non-Euclidean geometry, the unsettling curves that seemed to shift in peripheral vision. And the material… though encrusted with barnacles and the phosphorescent slime of the abyss, a core of something stubbornly *not-stone* remained. A metallic sheen, dulled and pitted, hinted at a construction predating humanity, perhaps even predating the shaping of the continents.

These apertures, wedged tight within the rock as if forced there in some cataclysmic upheaval, faced not the sea, but *down*. Down into a darkness deeper than any ocean trench. They had resisted the corrosive touch of centuries, their alien metal defying the natural order of decay. One felt, with a creeping dread, that they were not meant to *observe*, but to *receive*. To await something rising from the cold, lightless gulfs below. Something ancient, and profoundly, irrevocably *wrong*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I reckon I’ve seen a good many peculiar sights in my time, driftin’ along the Mississippi and amongst folks generally. But this… this took the biscuit, as the English are fond of sayin’. Old Man Tiber, he’d been holdin’ court on the courthouse steps, spoutin’ about the virtues of temperance and the wickedness of card playin’. A fella you’d cross the street to avoid, truth be told. 

Then, a goat. A perfectly ordinary goat, mind you, but wearin’ a bonnet. A pink, flowered bonnet, perched right atop its head. It strolled right up to Tiber, sniffed his boot, and let out a bleat that sounded suspiciously like a chuckle.

Tiber, he just stared. His jaw worked like a rusty gate. Then, he turned around to the crowd, and says, about like this: “This is a surprise to me which I wasn’t looking for; and I’ll acknowledge, it throws a considerable wrench into my sermon. A bonneted goat… well, it’s enough to make a man question everything he thought he knew about Providence and the proper order of things.” He paused, scratchin’ his chin. “I’ll need a stronger cup of coffee, I reckon.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Old Man Tiber, he’d always said Em had a voice like a mourning dove dipped in honey and trouble. And trouble it was, mostly. She could charm the buttons off a sheriff’s coat, or get a fella to give up his last plug of tobacco just listenin’ to her hum. Now she was gone, took with the fever, and the town felt…hollow.

Folks were quiet, see. Not the usual quiet of Sunday mornin’, but a pinched, uncomfortable sort. Nobody to make some about her now, no bright flash to fill the space she left. Old Man Hemlock tried a hymn, but it sounded like a rusty gate swingin’ in the wind. 

I figured, well, I’d always had a knack for rhymin’, though mostly for complainin’ about the price of corn. So I tried to sweat out a verse or two myself, somethin’ about angels and fields of clover, but I couldn’t seem to make it *go* somehow. The words felt clumsy, like a bear tryin’ to thread a needle. 

They kept Em. The earth did, anyway. And the silence just stretched on, thicker than Mississippi mud. A body couldn’t help but feel a mite foolish tryin’ to speak for a voice that’d been so perfectly, powerfully, *hers*.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The assembly rooms at Meryton, though scarcely grand, possessed a particular lustre this evening, owing to the anticipated arrival of the militia. Miss Eleanor, usually reserved in her observations, found herself quite overcome by the occasion, a flutter of excitement she had not experienced since the circulating library received a fresh consignment of novels. She had, indeed, been so high on the occasion, that though she did not often speak unnecessarily to Mr. Collins, she could not help asking him whether he intended to *attend* the regiment’s ball.

Mr. Collins, naturally, was prepared with a most elaborate response. He detailed, at length, his duty to cultivate connections with all respectable persons in the parish, and how a display of civility towards the officers was paramount to maintaining good order. He further expounded upon the potential benefits to the living, should a particularly influential soldier take a fancy to his discourse. 

Eleanor, though politely attentive, found her mind wandering to the possibility of a handsome ensign, and the decidedly *un*influential pleasure of a lively dance. The militia, it seemed, promised a diversion far more agreeable than any sermon on parish duties.
author: Jane Austen

Now, this King William, see, he was a fella with a powerful thirst for knowin’ just *what* everybody had. Not in a friendly, neighborly way, mind you, but in a “how much tax can I squeeze outta ya” sort of way. He’d conquered the whole blamed country, and a kingdom ain’t worth a plug nickel if you don’t know who owns the cows and the cabbages.

So he sent his men, a right swarm of ‘em, pokin’ and pryin’ into every village and farmstead. They asked questions, wrote things down on parchment – a heap of parchment, enough to choke a horse. They counted the oxen, the swine, the hens, even the beehives. Lord, the fuss! Folks grumbled, naturally. Said it was an intrusion, a botheration. 

But William, he wasn’t one for listenin’ to grumbles. He wanted a record, a complete and utter reckonin’. And then he put them all in a book, and called it Domesday Book—which was a good name and stated the case. A day of judgement for your property, see? 

You don’t know kings, Jim, but I know them; they’re all the same. Always wantin’ to know what’s in your pocket, and rarely offerin’ to put anything *in* it. A right peculiar breed, kings are.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, this here hound, Old Man Hemlock’s Blue, was the treacherousest hound in this country, bar none. Not for bitin’, mind you, though he *could* do that quick as a wink. No, Blue’s treachery lay in his affections. He’d look at you with them soulful eyes, wag his tail like he was plumb overjoyed to see ya, and then – *wham* – lead you straight into a patch o’ stinging nettles or a hornet’s nest. A fella could trust a rattlesnake before he could trust Blue’s hospitality.

By this time Jim was gone for the raft. I was just a-biling with curiosity; and I says to myself, Tom Sawyer would’ve concocted some grand scheme to test this canine’s loyalty, some elaborate ruse involving painted cats and stolen pies. Me, I just wanted to know *why* Old Man Hemlock kept a dog that actively sought to inconvenience folks. 

I figured it was a test, see? A test of character. A fella had to be sharp to survive Blue’s “friendliness.” And I reckoned, if a body could outsmart a hound like Blue, well, he could outsmart just about anything. Though, truth be told, I was mostly hopin’ to avoid gettin’ stung.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, I reckon you wouldn’t credit it, but it commenced right after supper. Good-night was said, and I went up to bed, same as any well-behaved boy. But a body can only abide so much quiet. A restlessness took hold, a notion that trouble was brewin’ down yonder in town, and a powerful itch to be *in* it, not hear tell of it later.

So, I clumb out of the window – a maneuver perfected over many a moonlit night – and down the lightning-rod. Slick as a greased pig, I was. Didn’t pause for breath, not even to consider the Widow’s likely fit if she caught wind of it. 

I shoved for the town, I did, a-thinkin’ on old Man Hemlock’s claim of a traveling snake-oil salesman peddlin’ promises and poppycock. I didn’t believ a word of it, mind you. Hemlock was prone to exaggeration, like a catfish tellin’ tales of the river. But a fella’s gotta *see* for himself, don’t he? A body can’t rightly judge a swindle from the comfort of his own featherbed. And that, sir, is how I found myself headin’ straight for a heap of mischief.
author: Mark Twain

text:
In the midst of our flight, with all our faculties centered on the problem of escape, we were in a corridor not of stone, but *of scent*. A cloying, viscous sweetness, like overripe fruit left too long in shadowed cellars, pressed upon us, thicker than any fog. It wasn’t merely *present*; it *resonated*, a low, humming vibration against the inner ear, a sickeningly familiar chord struck deep within the primal brain. 

Old Man Hemlock, the expedition’s botanist, had begun to gibber, muttering of *Myco-sentience* and fungal deities. I dismissed it, at first, as the strain. But the scent… it wasn’t simply *of* something, it *asked* a question. A question not formed in words, but in a creeping dread, a nauseating certainty that we were not fleeing *from* the structure, but *toward* something which *desired* us.

The sweetness intensified with each frantic step, and with it, a horrifying realization bloomed. It wasn’t the scent of decay, but of… *attraction*. Were we, in our terror, merely moths drawn to a phosphorescent, fungal flame? The thought, unbidden and monstrous, threatened to unravel the last vestiges of sanity. The corridor pulsed, and the sweetness… it *waited*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself, despite her best resolutions, quite undone by Mr. Frederick Beaumont’s recent behaviour. He had, but a fortnight prior, been all attentive grace and sparkling wit at the Harringtons’ assembly. Now, however, a chilling reserve had descended, replacing cordiality with a curt nod, and lively discourse with a pointed silence. 

And continually was she repeating, “Why is he so altered? From what can it proceed? It cannot be for *me*, it cannot be for *my* sake that his manners have undergone so lamentable a change.” She had, of course, been perfectly civil, offering the requisite smiles and polite inquiries. Had she, perhaps, inadvertently given offence? A carelessly worded compliment? A too-eager acceptance of a dance?

Her sister, Louisa, declared it a mere fancy, a product of Eleanor’s own romantic inclinations. “Men are fickle creatures, my dear,” she observed, “and easily distracted by a newer face.” But Eleanor could not accept such a blunt explanation. There was a *weight* to his avoidance, a deliberate turning away of his regard, that spoke of something far more pointed than simple caprice. It was a mystery most vexing, and one which threatened to entirely spoil the remainder of the season.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Old Man Tiber, he had a notion for collecting things. Not stamps, nor coins, mind you, but *stories*. Bad ones, mostly. The kind that clung to a fella like swamp gas and left a feller feelin’ uneasy even in broad daylight. He’d sit on his porch, lookin’ like a weathered fence post, and draw folks in with promises of a tale. 

Young Silas, bless his naive heart, he got snared. Went struttin’ up there yesterday, thinkin’ to swap a fishin’ story for one of Tiber’s. I saw ‘em, I did. Tiber’s eyes, they weren’t lookin’ *at* Silas, but *through* him, like he was lookin’ at somethin’ Silas hadn’t even dreamt of yet.

And I’m your friend; and I warn you *as* a friend, and an honest one that wants to protect you and keep you out of harm and trouble, to turn your back. Do not listen to a word that man says. He deals in shadows and regrets, and a fella comes away from Tiber’s porch lighter in the pocket of his soul, and heavier with a worry he can’t rightly name. Just…walk away. You’ll thank me for it, someday.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor found herself, to her considerable vexation, detained. It began, innocently enough, with Mr. Collins. His arrival at the small assembly had been anticipated with a degree of dread, and proved, alas, not unfounded. He commenced a discourse upon the health of her mother, inquiring with a precision most unsettling after the particulars of each individual ailment, real or imagined. He then proceeded to the younger Misses, detailing his own observations on their accomplishments – or, rather, the *potential* for accomplishments. 

One might have escaped such a protracted exchange with a polite excuse, yet a small, and she confessed, rather improper curiosity, stayed her tongue. Mr. Collins, for all his pomposity, possessed a certain… earnestness. What motive could possibly drive a man to such relentless, detailed inquiry? Was it genuine concern, or merely a desire to demonstrate his own importance? 

The question, though frivolous, held her captive. She offered a noncommittal reply regarding her sister Mary’s pianoforte practice, and braced herself for further interrogation, a prisoner of politeness and a most unbecoming fascination.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Maria Ainsworth, though possessed of a temper generally mild, found herself in a state bordering on vexation upon her return from a morning call upon Lady Beatrice. Her Ladyship, whilst undeniably generous with her advice on all matters of propriety, had been, this day, particularly insistent regarding the arrangement of gowns within Miss Ainsworth’s modest wardrobe. 

It was not merely a suggestion, mind you, but a detailed, and rather lengthy, discourse on the correct order of precedence – silks before muslins, day dresses distinct from evening, and colours arranged according to a system only Lady Beatrice herself seemed to comprehend. She was so urgent on the necessity of placing gowns in the only right way, that Maria thought herself obliged, on her return, to undo all the work of Mrs. Higgins, her excellent, but decidedly *unfashionable*, seamstress.

To rearrange the garments according to such arbitrary dictates felt, to Maria’s sensible mind, a most unnecessary exertion. Yet, to openly contradict Lady Beatrice was unthinkable. One must, after all, maintain appearances. And so, with a sigh barely audible above the rustle of taffeta, she began the tedious task, hoping only that no visitor should remark upon the altered arrangement, and thus expose her to further, and likely more detailed, instruction.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The basalt monoliths… they were not *built*, not in any sense comprehensible to Euclidean geometry. They *rose*, extruded from the earth like calcified nightmares, their surfaces slick with a perpetual, unwholesome dew. Old Man Hemlock, before the ice claimed him and his sanity, spoke of a pre-human artistry, a geometry born of angles that fractured the mind. He’d poured over ancient, blasphemous charts, muttering of a continent swallowed by the Antarctic wastes, a land lain in the fears of those Old Ones who carved them so reticently.

I recalled how their northerly end must come near the coast at Queen Mary Land, where the magnetic anomalies writhe like disturbed serpents. The stone itself… it wasn’t of *this* Earth. A density that defied measurement, a coldness that seeped into the bone, and a subtle, rhythmic pulsing – a heartbeat, perhaps, of something vast and slumbering beneath the ice. 

Hemlock believed the monoliths weren’t markers, but *keys*. Keys to unlock… something. Something best left undisturbed. The carvings, though eroded by aeons, hinted at cyclopean cities, at beings of impossible form, and at a cosmic indifference that dwarfed all human comprehension. A dread, ancient and suffocating, clung to the stones, a whisper of a time before time, and a promise of a darkness yet to come.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Penworthy, occupied with the delicate arrangement of lavender in a vase, was quite unprepared for the sudden appearance of her cousin, Mr. Frederick Ainsworth, before the drawing-room fire. And whose astonishment at being so addressed was very evident. He had been absent in London these six months, pursuing studies deemed necessary for a gentleman of his standing, and returned with an air of consequence she found, frankly, unsettling.

Her cousin prefaced his speech with a solemn bow, and though she could not hear a word – for the crackling fire and the distant rumble of a cart conspired against clarity – the intensity of his gaze was quite sufficient to convey the gravity of his intent. He spoke with a measured cadence, gesturing with a hand adorned by a rather ostentatious signet ring. 

Eleanor, though possessing a spirit not easily ruffled, felt a blush rise in her cheeks. Was it a declaration of some sort? A request? Or merely a lengthy account of the latest political machinations? Whatever the subject, it was delivered with a seriousness wholly disproportionate to the occasion, and she found herself wishing, with a most unladylike impulse, for the comforting distraction of a particularly tedious embroidery pattern.
author: Jane Austen

This was silk, the color of a bruised plum, all flounces and furbelows enough to sink a small skiff. It belonged to Miss Evangeline, naturally. She’d been fussin’ over it all mornin’, claimin’ it needed just *so* much ribbon, just *so* many pearl buttons. A body’d think she was preparin’ for a royal visit, not just a picnic down by the creek.

And there she was, hidin’ behind old Bess, the milk cow. Bess, bless her bovine heart, didn’t seem to mind a bit, just chewed her cud and let Miss Evangeline’s skirts billow around her legs. A pair of bright eyes, and a curl or two, peeped out from behind her at me, bashful, the way they always do. 

And here comes the white woman running from the house, about forty-five, lookin’ flustered as a hen in a hailstorm. “Evangeline! That cow! And that *dress*! Goodness gracious, child, you’ll ruin it!” She waved a dishcloth like a flag of surrender. A right comical spectacle, it was.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed a mind remarkably well-furnished, though, alas, not with the ornaments of refined discernment. She could discourse upon political economy with a fluency quite astonishing for a lady, and offer opinions on the merits of various agricultural improvements, yet consistently chose ribbons of a shade most unbecoming to her complexion. It was not that she *intended* ill-taste, merely that her understanding, so broad in its scope, lacked the precision to alight upon particulars.

This deficiency was particularly evident in matters of the heart. She declared Mr. Finch a most eligible gentleman – possessing fortune, connections, and a tolerable disposition – entirely overlooking the unfortunate habit he had of clearing his throat with a sound akin to a distressed badger. 

Indeed, when cautioned on the matter by her sensible cousin, Miss Barlow, Eleanor merely replied, “But he *is* a man of property, Barlow! And one must be practical.” A white frost had begun to settle upon the garden paths, and Eleanor, though acknowledging the chill with a sensible shiver, continued her walk, quite oblivious to the dampness creeping into her slippers. One suspected she would have continued even had the frost reached her shoes.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, old Man Hemlock, he was a fella worth six thousand dollars, and up’ards, mind you. Not a Vanderbilt, no, but comfortable. Had a knack for land, Hemlock did, sniffin’ out a good acre like a hound dog after a rabbit. But the law, she’s a peculiar beast. She don’t much care for a man gettin’ *too* comfortable. 

Seems to me, the law figures a man with property ought to be…contained. Like a prize bull. So they took Hemlock, a man who could’ve built himself a mansion with stained glass and a proper library, and jammed him into this here cabin. A cabin that’s seen better days, I reckon, back when Andrew Jackson was a young pup. 

It’s a right shame, it is. Walls leanin’ like a tired drunkard, roof leakin’ like a sieve. He sits there, Hemlock, surrounded by his wealth, unable to *use* it. Says it’s for his own good, this confinement. Says it’s to keep him from…well, from bein’ too independent, I suppose. A man with land, you see, is a dangerous thing in the eyes of some. A dangerous thing indeed.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The thing dominated the plateau, a monstrous, inverted cone of basalt that defied all terrestrial geometry. It was not *built* so much as… extruded, a petrified extrusion of some unthinkable will. No mortar bound the colossal blocks, yet they interlocked with a precision that mocked human engineering, a precision born not of skill, but of a dreadful, alien *rightness*. We photographed it, of course, the plates trembling in our hands not from the chill wind, but from a subtle, pervasive vibration emanating from the stone itself. 

Each surface was subtly concave, drawing the eye inward, toward a non-Euclidean apex that seemed to shift and writhe even in the static image. The local Bedouin spoke only of ‘the Turned-Over God,’ whispering of a time before sand, before stars, when *it* held sway. We dismissed it as superstition, until the unsettling realization dawned: the structure wasn’t merely tall, it was… *above*. 

We wished that our instruments had been more sensitive, that we’d possessed the arcane knowledge to decipher the faint, rhythmic pulsing we detected within its core. We wished, with a growing, nauseating dread, that we hadn’t disturbed the dust that lay undisturbed for millennia at its base. For something stirred within that dust, something that mirrored the impossible angles of the stone, and regarded us with an ancient, hungry awareness.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Old Man Tiber, he was a caution, always predictin’ rain when the sun was blazin’ and claimin’ the river was risin’ when it was lower’n a snake’s belly. Folks ‘round here, they’d listen polite, nod their heads, then go right on doin’ what they aimed to do, regardless. It weren’t that they *disrespected* Tiber, mind you, just that he had a habit of seein’ things that weren’t there, or seein’ ‘em backwards.

He told us, plain as day, that Miss Abigail’s prize rooster, Bartholomew, would take to flyin’ afore week’s end. Said Bartholomew had a “yearnin’ in his breastbone.” We scoffed, naturally. Roosters don’t fly, ‘cept to roost. But lo and behold, come Thursday, that bird launched himself clean over the barn, squawkin’ like a banshee! 

Folks saw it with their own two eyes, but did they credit Tiber? Not a lick. They said Bartholomew was spooked by a dog, or a sudden gust. “They gotta find out things for themselves, and when *you* find it out and tell ‘em about it, they don’t believe you,” Tiber grumbled, lookin’ mournful. Tom give him a dime, and said we would. A fella’s gotta have some amusement, even if it costs a bit.
author: Mark Twain

Now, this here contraption arrived by rail, you understand, a right fancy piece of furniture it was. A writing desk, they called it, though it looked more like a preacher’s pulpit to my eye. Mahogany, polished to a glare, and fitted with more little drawers and cubbyholes than a fella could rightly keep track of. It sat there in Miss Abigail’s parlor, lookin’ plumb out of place amongst the crocheted doilies and the stuffed birds.

But the thing that caught a body’s attention wasn’t the wood, no sir. It was the top. Covered in green felt, smooth as a gambler’s hand, and with a border painted ‘round it, all flowers and curlicues. Said it come all the way from Philadelphia, a city known for its airs and graces, and likely where they manufacture such frivolous things. 

And then the books. Stacked on either side, neat as you please, like soldiers on parade. Not readin’ books, mind you, but fancy volumes with gilt edges and titles nobody could pronounce. Just for show, I reckoned. A desk for writin’, surrounded by books nobody’d crack open. A right peculiar sight, it was.

Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a study in stubbornness, a veritable granite formation disguised as a prospector. We’d been at this claim near Rattlesnake Gulch for nigh on three weeks, and hadn’t so much as tickled a speck of color. He’d struck a vein of pure, unadulterated *opinion*, though, and was convinced gold lay just beyond a particularly nasty patch of shale. 

Young Jeb, bless his naive heart, suggested maybe we move on. Hemlock near choked on his chewing tobacco. “A-going to *gnaw* him out, are we?” he sputtered, eyes bugging like a startled owl. 

Then he turned that gaze on *me*. A gaze that could curdle milk at fifty paces. “Ain’t them old crippled picks and things in there good enough to dig a… well, a fella out with?” I says, careful to keep my tone neutral as a church mouse. It weren’t the question of the tools, you see. It was the implication. He wanted to know where my loyalty lay. 

He turned back to the shale, muttering about “city slickers” and “lack of grit.” I figured we’d be gnawing on dust and disappointment for a good while yet. Some men just prefer a hard row to hoe, even if there ain’t nothin’ at the end of it but heartache.

text:
The tunnel pressed inward, a suffocating embrace of basalt slick with an unwholesome damp. A customary profusion of carvings lined the walls – bas-reliefs depicting geometries that offended the very notion of Euclidean space, and figures… *things*… with too many angles and an unsettling lack of discernible purpose. But we did not pause to examine any of these. The air grew thick, not with moisture, but with a palpable dread, a psychic residue clinging to the stone like grave-mold. Old Man Hemlock, his face a pallid mask illuminated by the failing carbide lamp, muttered ceaselessly about ‘the angles being *wrong*’, a sentiment I found myself echoing in the silent chambers of my mind.

The rhythmic drip, drip, drip of unseen water became a maddening percussion, each drop a hammer blow against sanity. Then, suddenly, a bulky white shape loomed up ahead of us, and we… flinched. It wasn’t merely *white*, but a luminescence born of something utterly alien, a cold, internal glow that seemed to leach the colour from our very vision. The shape resolved, impossibly, into a colossal, vaguely ovoid mass, pulsating with a slow, sickening rhythm. Hemlock’s muttering ceased, replaced by a choked, gurgling sound. And I knew, with a certainty that chilled me to the core, that we had stumbled upon something best left undisturbed in the cyclopean darkness.

“Booth’s Landing, you say?” Old Man Hemlock drawled, puffing a cloud of contentment from his pipe that smelled suspiciously of burnt molasses. He settled deeper into his rocking chair, the porch groaning a sympathetic tune. “A quiet little patch, Booth’s Landing. Not much excitement ever stirs there, ‘ceptin’ when the river gets to thinkin’ it can rearrange things.”

He paused, eyes twinkling like distant fireflies. “Now, this young fella, Silas, he was courtin’ Miss Evangeline Pruitt, a girl with a smile that could charm the warts off a toad. She was a-visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just in the edge of the evening she started over with him. A buggy ride, mind you, a proper one, all ribbons and gigglin’. 

But Silas, he weren’t the steadiest hand with a team. Got to showin’ off, tryin’ to cut a fancy figure for the girl, and well… let’s just say that ol’ Bess and Barney took a sudden interest in the creek bank. Wasn’t a serious tumble, thankfully, but Miss Evangeline landed right smack in a patch of skunk cabbage. Lord, the smell! Silas swore he’d never felt so mortified in his life. A courtin’ disaster, pure and simple.” He chuckled, a dry, rustling sound. “Booth’s Landing remembers *that* evening, I reckon.”

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself, despite all reasonable intention, quite vexed by Mr. Fortescue’s attentions. Not that his person was displeasing – a tolerable height, a pleasant, if somewhat earnest, expression – but the *manner* of his regard was excessively forward. Such idle and frivolous gallantry, delivered with an air of consequence as though bestowing a great favour, was most unsettling. She steadily repressed any outward encouragement, answering his compliments with a cool civility that, she hoped, conveyed her disinterest. 

Yet, a disquieting thought persisted. He had remarked, during a discussion of the late harvest, upon her prolonged silence regarding his proposals for a country dance. And while she steadily repressed it, could not but feel the reproof contained in his believing, that however long, her refusal had been merely a coyness to be overcome. 

It was mortifying. To be perceived as susceptible, even by a man she deemed wholly unsuitable! Her mother, of course, would deem it a triumph. But Eleanor valued her independence too highly to be flattered by such clumsy pursuit. A sigh escaped her. The season promised little amusement if she must spend it warding off Mr. Fortescue’s persistent, and frankly, impertinent, devotion.
author: Jane Austen

Now, this here cabin, it weren’t *mine*, mind you. Hadn’t no connection with it whatsoever, save for the misfortune of stumble-upon it whilst a-wanderin’ the bottomlands. A sorry sight it was, leanin’ like a tired hound dog after a long chase. Built of mismatched planks and held together, I reckon, by sheer stubbornness and a whole heap of wishful thinkin’.

And there warn’t no floor to the shed, no sir. Just good honest mud and the occasional root tryin’ to claw its way upwards. Didn’t offer much in the way of comfort, I can tell you. Nor did it offer much *of* anything, truth be told. Inside, it was a graveyard of farm implements. Some old rusty played-out hoes and spades, lookin’ like they’d seen better days back when Grant was a boy. 

And p… well, there was p aplenty. Piles of it, dried and cracked like the Mississippi in a drought. Smelled powerfully, it did. A fella could tell this cabin hadn’t been bothered with for a good long spell. Just sat there, a-moldering and a-waitin’ for the river to claim it, which, considerin’ its condition, seemed a likely prospect.

Now, I’d been diggin’ for nigh on three hours, sun beatin’ down like a blacksmith’s hammer, all for a blasted genie. Tom Sawyer, that mischievous imp, had filled my head with tales of rubbin’ a particular rock – a speckled granite, mind you, not just any old stone – and summonin’ fellas with the power to grant wishes. “And what news does it bring--good or bad?” inquired Miss Eleanor, her needle pausing mid-stitch upon the delicate muslin. “What is there of good to be expected?” said he, taking the letter from his pocket; “but perhaps you would indulge me the small satisfaction of witnessing your anticipation.”

She permitted a slight flush to colour her cheeks, a most becoming hue, and offered a demure, “Indeed, Sir Thomas, I should be most pleased. Though I confess, my imagination is already quite fraught with possibilities, none of them, I fear, particularly cheerful.”

He unfolded the paper with a deliberate slowness, a habit which, whilst irritating to some, served only to heighten the suspense. A frown, barely perceptible, touched his brow as he scanned the lines. “It concerns the estate, naturally. A… complication has arisen regarding the tenancy of Northwood Cottage. A distant relation, it seems, lays claim, citing a forgotten clause in the late owner’s will.”

Miss Eleanor’s breath caught. Northwood Cottage was the promised residence for the newly married Mr. and Mrs. Harding. “Good heavens! A most unfortunate circumstance. And their arrangements…?”

“Disrupted, I am afraid. Entirely.” He sighed, refolding the letter. “A matter for the solicitors, undoubtedly. And a source of considerable vexation.”

text:
The anomaly presented initially as a meteorological curiosity – a localised distortion of the aurora borealis, observed during the bleakest hours of a November night over the desolate Norwegian plateau. We, of course, attempted rationalisation. Atmospheric pressure differentials, unusual solar flare activity… the tired lexicon of the scientific mind grasping for purchase on the utterly improbable. Probably we clung to these notions less for conviction than for self-preservation.

But the colours… they were *wrong*. Not the familiar greens and violets, but hues that defied Euclidean geometry, shades that seemed to press against the very optic nerve, hinting at dimensions beyond human comprehension. Then, the tearing. A fissure in the light, widening, revealing not the star-strewn void we anticipated, but *something else*. 

A cyclopean architecture, impossibly vast, constructed of basalt older than time, pulsed with a sickly, internal luminescence. Geometries that mocked sanity unfolded within, hinting at non-Euclidean spaces and angles that should not *be*. And within those structures… movement. Not life as we understand it, but a shifting, amorphous *presence*, a cold intelligence that regarded us with an indifference that chilled the soul more profoundly than the arctic wind. We saw what lay beyond, and the universe, for a fleeting, horrifying moment, ceased to be a comforting mystery, and became a screaming, cosmic dread.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The *Aurora Australis* strained, a groaning beast against the burgeoning grip of the pack. Each shudder sent vibrations through the timbers, a morbid pulse echoing the dread that settled deeper with every league southward. It was not merely the cold, though that was a gnawing, insidious thing, but the *quality* of it – a stillness that felt preternaturally expectant. 

We’d shaken free, at last, from the worst of the thickening field, but the respite felt…illusory. Ahead, the Ross Sea stretched, a leaden expanse under a sky bruised purple and sickly green. And westward…Victoria Land. Not mountains as any sane man understands them, but colossal, non-Euclidean mockeries of stone, rising in angles that offended the very geometry of the mind. 

They weren’t *built*, not in any terrestrial sense. They *rose*, as if extruded from some cyclopean nightmare beneath the ice. The Antarctic constellations, distorted and alien, wheeled above them, casting shadows that writhed with a life of their own. A low, subsonic hum permeated the air, a resonance that seemed to originate not from the mountains themselves, but from the black, abyssal spaces *between* them. A feeling, cold and absolute, that we were being…observed. And judged.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The salt-crusted charts spoke of currents unknown, of abyssal plains where the very geometry of Euclid dissolved into nauseating non-Euclidean angles. Old Man Hemlock, before his…disappearance, had muttered of *arrangements*. Not treaties, not bargains, but *arrangements* existing beyond human comprehension, woven into the fabric of the tides themselves.

We found it during the dredge – a thing utterly defying classification. Not fish, not cephalopod, yet possessing the dreadful fluidity of both. A bulbous, light-gray pseudoneck, slick with an unidentifiable ichor, rose from the silt, utterly lacking the comforting suggestion of gills. It was the *arrangement* it bore that chilled the marrow. 

Held aloft, not by tentacles, but by thick, muscular arms of a disturbing, almost mammalian strength, was a starfish. But not as any earthly eye has witnessed. Greenish, phosphorescent, and undeniably *five-pointed*, it pulsed with a slow, deliberate rhythm. Each arm was tipped with a minute, obsidian orb, and as the thing shifted, those orbs seemed to…observe. 

The air grew thick, heavy with a scent like ozone and decay. A low, subsonic hum resonated through the hull, and I knew, with a certainty that bordered on madness, that we had stumbled upon something not meant for mortal gaze. Something that *arranged* things.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The assembly room, already abuzz with the usual provincial excitements, fell into a most peculiar stillness. Miss Elmsworth, a lady possessed of neither fortune nor particular beauty, had, with a boldness quite shocking to several present, addressed Mr. Darcy directly upon the subject of whist. Not a request for a hand, mind you, but a pointed critique of his previous play. 

Everybody was surprised; and Darcy, after looking at her for a moment, turned silently away. It was not anger, precisely, that coloured his countenance, but a profound…disappointment, as though a particularly unpleasant insect had disturbed his contemplation.

Mrs. Bennet, who fancied she had gained a complete victor – though precisely *how* remained a mystery even to herself – beamed upon her daughters. “Did you observe, my dears?” she whispered, fanning herself with vigour. “The man is clearly discomfited! A woman of spirit, that Miss Elmsworth, though sadly lacking in connections. It proves, does it not, that even the most proud amongst us are susceptible to a well-aimed remark?” 

Elizabeth, however, observed only the faint flush creeping up Miss Elmsworth’s neck, and suspected the triumph belonged less to the lady herself, and more to the sheer audacity of her impropriety.

He had been sketching, he confessed to Mrs. Penhaligon with a blush that did little to disguise his discomposure, a particularly picturesque bend. However, his artistic pursuits were abruptly curtailed. 

News arrived, delivered with a regrettable lack of tact by the housekeeper, that Miss Eleanor and Miss Marianne, along with their formidable aunt, Lady Beatrice, were preparing to call upon Miss Georgiana Harwood. Mr. Finch, though possessed of a tolerable fortune and a passable countenance, found himself utterly unequal to the scrutiny of *those* ladies. 

He had, therefore, made a hasty, and perhaps ungraceful, retreat. It was not aversion, he hastened to explain to Mrs. Penhaligon, but a prudent awareness of his own deficiencies in polite conversation. Lady Beatrice, he understood, possessed a wit as sharp as any rapier, and he feared a verbal discomfiture would prove most…unsettling. A sketch, after all, required no rejoinder.

text:
The chipped basalt stood against a cyclopean sky, bruised purple and sickly green where no stars *should* be. Old Man Hemlock, before his…disintegration, had spoken of it – the Gate of Aethel, he’d called it, a rent in the fabric preceding even the oldest glacial epochs. He’d warned of geometries that unravel the sanity, of echoes from a time when consciousness itself was a larval thing. We, of course, dismissed it as the ravings of a mind fractured by too much peat smoke and forbidden lore.

But the stone *pulsed*. A subsonic thrumming that resonated not in the ears, but within the very marrow. Days we spent charting its angles, measuring the impossible curves, attempting to reconcile its existence with Euclidean space. Each calculation yielded only further madness. 

Finally, driven by a morbid curiosity that outweighed all self-preservation, we prepared to cross the threshold. A dreadful stillness descended, a cessation of all natural law. Time itself seemed to hold its breath, anticipating…something. And yet, when we did venture inside that black arch, our first impression was one of anticlimax. For amidst the oppressive darkness, there was only dust. Fine, grey dust, and the faint, unsettling scent of something anciently *wrong*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth received the news with a composure that, whilst admirable, did little to conceal the tremor in her hand as she set down her embroidery. Her cousin, Mr. Thomas Finch, had, it appeared, engaged his affections – and, regrettably, his fortune – to a Miss Penelope Grimshaw, a lady possessed of a complexion rather too florid and a disposition, by all accounts, equally robust.

“It is…unexpected,” she murmured to her aunt, Lady Beatrice, who bustled about with a flurry of smelling salts. “Though, perhaps, not entirely unforeseen. Mr. Finch has ever been susceptible to a lively countenance.”

Lady Beatrice wrung her hands. “To think, Eleanor, a connection so promising, dashed upon the rocks of Miss Grimshaw’s…enthusiasm! No arguments shall be wanting on my part, that can alleviate so severe a misfortune; or that may comfort you, under a circumstance that must surely be distressing.”

Eleanor offered a small, polite smile. Distress, indeed. More a relief, she confessed to herself, that the prospect of a connection with a man so easily swayed had been so swiftly removed. A quiet life, with her books and her needlework, suddenly appeared infinitely more agreeable.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Lady Lucas, who had been long yawning at the repetition of delights which she saw no likelihood of sharing, was left to the comforts of cold ham and a resigned contemplation of the drawing-room carpet. The Misses Bennet, flushed with the recent arrival of Captain Carteret and his exceedingly tolerable fortune, were quite lost in animated discussion regarding the cut of his coat and the probable extent of his estate. 

Mrs. Bennet, naturally, fuelled the fire, declaring him a most eligible gentleman and lamenting, with theatrical sighs, that Jane was not *immediately* presented. Charlotte, ever practical, offered a quiet observation regarding the necessity of a clean muslin, which was, of course, entirely disregarded. 

Lady Lucas found herself quite unable to contribute to such frivolous speculation. Captain Carteret, whilst undoubtedly presentable, lacked the quiet discernment she valued. A large income was all very well, but a man must possess *something* beyond mere coin to secure a comfortable establishment. She sliced a particularly thin piece of ham, reflecting that a sensible match, even a modest one, was infinitely preferable to a glittering, yet ultimately unsatisfying, alliance. The carpet, at least, offered a consistent pattern of good taste.
author: Jane Austen

Old Man Tiber, he reckoned folks got too fixated on dyin’. Said it was a powerful distractin’ subject, kept a body from attendin’ to the livin’. He was sittin’ on the porch of the general store, whittlin’ a piece of pine into somethin’ vaguely resembling a hound dog, and spittin’ tobacco juice with the precision of a clockmaker. 

“They fret and stew over the hereafter,” he drawled, lookin’ at young Billy Perkins, who was tryin’ to teach his pup to fetch. “Like a body’s got nothin’ *now* to occupy his mind. Why, there’s a whole heap of trouble a fella can get into *before* he’s six feet under, and most of ‘em don’t involve angels or brimstone.”

Billy paused, pup lookin’ confused. “Like what, Mr. Tiber?”

“Like tryin’ to outsmart a mule, or convincin’ Miss Abigail to sell you a piece of pie for less than a quarter. Like dealin’ with leaky roofs, and politicians, and the general cussedness of things. And don’t forget sickness, boy. Not just the dyin’ kind, but bein’ *sick*. What with rheumatiz, and the grippe, and bein’ all tuckered out and just plain…up with other things.” 

He paused, considerin’. “What other things?” Billy asked. “Well, measles, and whooping-cough, and erysiplas, and consumption, and yaller janders, and brain-fever, a body’s got plenty to contend with, I tell ya.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Elizabeth found herself, upon reflection, in a most peculiar state of composure. Lady Catherine de Bourgh, having unexpectedly extended an invitation to Rosings for a small, intimate dinner, had inadvertently provided the very circumstance Elizabeth’s mind had, in secret, occasionally indulged. It was not the company itself – though tolerable, even agreeable in parts – but the *absence* of others that held a strange significance. 

Could she not, had inclination and a less principled regard guided her, have found herself permanently settled within this very sphere? Had a different answer been given at Hunsford, she might by this time be mistress of Rosings, with all its attendant comforts and, indeed, its controlling influence. 

The thought, though swiftly banished as improper, lingered like a faint perfume. Mr. Darcy, present and observing with his usual quietude, seemed unaware of the internal debate. He discoursed upon the merits of his estate, and Elizabeth, with a delicate smile, offered polite acknowledgement. It was a curious sensation, to possess the entirety of a gentleman’s attention, knowing full well she had deliberately chosen *not* to require it. A most unsettling, and yet, undeniably…satisfying, evening.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a study. A right peculiar cuss, all angles and suspicion, like a scarecrow built by a committee. He sat there, polishing his spectacles with a rag that’d seen better days – likely the days before the War, judging by the smell. I’d come ‘round collectin’ for the church social, see, and he’d been holdin’ out on me.

“Some for me?” I asked, polite-like.

He blinked, slow as a tortoise considerin’ a race. “Oh, yes,” he finally drawled, “a half-yearly is in, last night—over a hundred and fifty dollars. Quite a fortune for you.” He eyed the collection plate like it was a rattlesnake.

“Well, that’s mighty generous, sir.”

He waved a dismissive hand. “Generous? Nonsense. It’s *prudent*. You had better let me invest it all for you. I have…connections. Understands the market, I do. Safer with me, believe you me. Don’t you go blabberin’ about where it came from, neither. A private arrangement, this is. A strictly private arrangement.” 

He winked, and I figured he’d been swindlin’ widows again. But a man needs a roof over his head, and a church social ain’t gonna fund itself.

text:
Old Man Tiber, now *there* was a study. Lived by the river, naturally, though not *on* it, mind you. Too much fuss. He was a fixture, like every awning-post in town, and he most always had his hands in his britches-pockets, except when he fetched them out to lend a chaw of tobacco or scratch. Wha. A man could tell the seasons by the state of Tiber’s pockets – worn thin for summer, patched with flannel come the chill.

He weren’t a talkative soul, Tiber. Mostly just observed. Observed the steamboats puffin’ and blowin’, observed the ladies with their parasols, observed the boys tryin’ to skip stones. And he’d offer a slow, knowing blink, like he understood somethin’ nobody else did. 

Folks said he’d seen everything that ever *happened* happen. Claimed he knew the river’s moods better’n the pilot did. I reckon there was truth to it. He just sat there, a silent, dusty monument to time passin’, hands burrowed deep, contemplatin’ the foolishness of man and the steady flow of the Mississippi. A peculiar fella, alright. Peculiar and…comfortable, in a way.

A ball at the vicarage, a handsome, though undeniably forward, Captain Harding, and a promise – a *promise* – of a country dance for the final set. 

“It is, I assure you, entirely improper,” Eleanor declared to their mother, her voice a carefully modulated tremor. “To pledge oneself so readily! He barely knows Marianne beyond a cursory introduction, and his attentions, whilst flattering, are… demonstrative.”

Mrs. Dashwood, ever practical, merely sighed. “Marianne is young, and possesses a warmth of spirit you, my dear, do not always share.”

“Warmth, Mama, or a lamentable lack of discernment? I have attempted to reason with her, but she insists it is merely a polite acceptance. However, I fear Papa will be most displeased. Would you, therefore, do me the kindness – and Mr. Bennet the compliment of requesting you to interpose your authority in my behalf? Initially, the Deepwater Survey sent eager, mathematically-minded men – young fellows convinced of Euclidean geometry’s dominion even at seven leagues. Now, they dispatched the… resigned.

Old Man Hemlock, they said, had begun speaking in clicks and whistles before his final descent. Young Davies returned babbling of cyclopean masonry, not of basalt, but of something… *grown*. The last transmission from Professor Armitage’s team detailed a luminescence, not bioluminescent, but emanating from structures too vast for any earthly architect. 

The dwindling roster wasn’t due to accident, but to a subtle, insidious *withdrawal*. A refusal to return. The ocean floor, it seemed, offered a solace, a dreadful, alien peace. And the silence from below grew heavier, punctuated only by the rhythmic thrum of the *Argonaut’s* engines – a fragile heartbeat against the vast, uncaring cold. A cold that whispered of geometries best left unseen.

A gentleman, even one possessed of Mr. Bingley’s amiable disposition, would hardly think a month’s ablution enough to cleanse him from its impurities, were he once to enter it; and, depend upon it, Mr. Bingley never stir. 

Mrs. Phillips, of course, encouraged the fancy, envisioning a spectacle to rival any Bath assembly. Eleanor, however, found herself compelled to subtly dissuade him, speaking of sudden chills and the prevalence of rheumatic fevers. It was a delicate task, requiring a judicious blend of concern and gentle mockery, lest she offend his good nature. For truly, the thought of Mr. Bingley emerging from *that* pond was quite…unsettling.

Old Man Tiber, he was a caution. Always sniffin’ around for trouble, like a hound dog after a possum. And Bessie May, well, she had a spirit that could curdle milk at fifty paces. They’d been at it for months, a low simmer of glares and pointed silences at the general store. 

Now, I ain’t one to meddle, but young Jebediah, Bessie May’s nephew, he come to *me*. Said Tiber was spreadin’ tales, claimin’ Bessie May was courtin’ a feller from out county. A downright lie, Jebediah insisted.

Now, my Ma, she was a firm believer in the old ways. Not the sensible ways, mind you, like plantin’ corn by the signs, but the sort that involved wardin’ off hexes and keepin’ the night-ridin’ witches at bay. When I was a lad of seven, she snipped off a curl – a right puny thing it was, barely enough to tickle a mouse – and tied it with a bit of red thread. 

“Wear this, son,” she said, serious as a judge. “Keeps the witches off. They can’t abide a piece of yer own self.”

But I hadn’t no confidence in it, not a lick. Seemed to me a witch determined to cause trouble wouldn’t be deterred by a few strands of hair. Especially not *my* hair, which was always gettin’ tangled in everything. 

It all started, you see, with a horseshoe. Found it, shiny and lucky-lookin’, and then lost it again before sundown. Lost a horseshoe, and you lose a bit of belief, understand? That little curl felt less like a protection and more like a reminder of all the luck that slipped through my fingers. I kept it tied 'round my neck, though. Couldn't rightly *tell* Ma it was useless, could I? A boy’s gotta humor his Ma, even when he suspects she’s fightin’ shadows.

text:
The peaks… they were not *right*. Not in the way a geological fault or glacial carving explains imperfection. Old Man Hemlock, before the frost claimed his tongue, spoke of geometries that offended the eye, of slopes that subtly *shifted* when unobserved. I dismissed it as the ramblings of a mind undone by solitude, yet the expedition… the expedition has shaken that dismissal to its core.

We sought the source of the anomalous magnetic readings, charting a course through ranges previously deemed impassable. What we found wasn’t stone and ice, but a dreadful *resonance*. A feeling of being watched by something ancient, something that predated the very concept of mountains. The rock itself seemed porous, not to water, but to… thought. 

And the hunters. Local men, hardened by a life amongst the crags, yet possessed of a disturbing, vacant focus. They tracked the great, shaggy beasts with a chilling efficiency, a preternatural understanding of their movements. But it wasn’t skill. It was… *alignment*. A mirroring of something primal, something that echoed in the unsettling angles of the peaks themselves. I suspect their lineage runs deeper than any family tree, touched by the same cold, alien influence that birthed these abhorrent formations. They are not merely men who hunt; they are *instruments* of the mountains’ will.

“Do *I* know? It was so long ago.” Old Man Tiber, he scratched at his beard, a wilderness of white that’d seen more summers than a redwood. “Seems like tryin’ to recall a dream you had afore breakfast. Faint, and mostly just…feelings.”

“Don’t anybody know?” young Elara pressed, her face tight with worry. The town was fixin’ to build a new mill, right smack dab where the stories said Old Man Hemlock buried his fortune.

“Oh, yes, pa knows, I reckon, and some of the other old people; but they don’t know *now* what they used to. Memory’s a fickle critter, missy. Like a leaky bucket – holds a bit, then lets it dribble away. They remember Hemlock bein’ a tight-fisted cuss, and a fondness for riddles, but the *where* of it? Gone with the dust.”

He chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “Folks used to say Hemlock buried it with a marker – a twisted oak, or a stone shaped like a raven. But oaks grow, and stones get moved. Truth is, the land remembers better’n we do, and she ain’t tellin’.” He spat a stream of tobacco juice. “Best leave well enough alone, I say. Some things are best left lost.”

The summons to Rosings had arrived with disconcerting abruptness, a note delivered by a rather breathless footman only the Saturday prior. Mr. Alistair Finch, though possessed of a modest fortune and tolerable connections, was not accustomed to such direct requisition. Lady Catherine de Bourgh, it appeared, found herself short a hand for the evening’s quadrilles. A circumstance, one might imagine, easily remedied by a polite refusal, yet the very *tone* of the invitation brooked no such liberty.

Indeed, Lady Catherine was reckoned proud by many, a quality she considered not a fault, but a necessary attribute of her station. To be asked, was to be obliged. Mr. Finch found himself, therefore, navigating the polished floors of the great house, attempting to appear both grateful and nonchalant. 

Miss de Bourgh, a young lady of considerable accomplishments and even more considerable solemnity, barely deigned to acknowledge his presence. He observed, with a slight internal tremor, that her mother’s eye followed his every movement, assessing his deportment with a scrutiny that felt distinctly…invasive. The music commenced, and Mr. Finch braced himself for an evening of carefully measured bows and exquisitely polite constraint.

The relief which washed over Mrs. Bennet upon Mr. Harrington’s pronouncement was, perhaps, a shade too demonstrative for perfect composure. To see him at Longbourn again, whenever his other engagements might allow him to visit them – the prospect was, in truth, most gratifying. Not merely for herself, naturally, but for the advantageous impression such continued attentions would undoubtedly create.

“My dear madam,” he replied, “this invitation is particularly welcome. The quietude of the countryside, and the… *vivacity* of your daughters, offer a most agreeable respite from the bustle of London.” He offered a slight bow, his gaze lingering, just a fraction too long, upon Miss Elizabeth. 

Mrs. Bennet, however, chose to interpret this as directed towards the family as a whole. “Oh, Mr. Harrington, you are too kind! We are ever so pleased to offer our humble home. Jane is quite recovered from her little indisposition, and Kitty… well, Kitty is improving daily.” A pointed glance towards her youngest, who was attempting to appear absorbed in a particularly threadbare embroidery. 

He smiled, a polite, carefully constructed expression. “I trust I shall not intrude upon your domestic arrangements.” 

“Intrude? Oh, never!” Mrs. Bennet declared, fanning herself with a vigour that threatened to dislodge her bonnet. “Longbourn is *always* open to agreeable company.”
