The arrival of Mr. and Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, with their prodigious family – four-and-twenty, if one included the distant cousins and governesses trailing in their wake – had thrown Longbourn into a state bordering on agitation. Mrs. Bennet, naturally, declared it a blessing, envisioning husbands for *all* her daughters within the season. However, a more discerning eye might observe a distinct lack of fortune amongst the Featherstonehaughs, and a surplus of boisterous children.

Mr. Bingley, ever amiable, attempted polite conversation with Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, a woman whose pronouncements on the merits of barley water were delivered with the force of a declaration. Nothing but concern for Elizabeth could enable Bingley to keep his countenance. His sister was less delicate, and dire. Miss Bingley, with a barely concealed grimace, declared the assembly “quite overrun,” and hinted, with pointed subtlety, at the impropriety of so large a connection. 

Indeed, the sheer volume of Featherstonehaughs threatened to overwhelm the drawing-room, and, one suspected, the very sensibilities of Hertfordshire society. It was a prospect, Miss Bingley confided to her brother, that filled her with the utmost dismay.

Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a sensibility which rendered her acutely aware of impropriety, found herself in a most vexing predicament. The particulars of Mr. Harrison’s unfortunate debts, and the subsequent, rather hasty, engagement to a lady of decidedly limited fortune, had been confided to her by a source she dared not reveal. It was, of course, Colonel Fitzwilliam. 

To be referred for the truth of every particular to the very gentleman from whom she had previously received the information of his near cousin’s entanglement was a trial of composure. She could scarcely meet his eye without betraying the awkwardness of her position. To admit her prior knowledge would be to reveal a confidence, a breach of decorum she could not countenance. Yet, to feign ignorance would be equally disingenuous.

“Indeed, Colonel,” she ventured, her voice carefully modulated, “one hears such conflicting reports in the country. It is difficult to ascertain what is truly…reliable.” 

He regarded her with a polite, yet penetrating, gaze. “Reliability, Miss Eleanor, is often a matter of source, is it not?” A slight inclination of his head suggested he suspected more than she cared to admit. The conversation, she feared, promised to be exceedingly uncomfortable.

The chill of an April evening did little to discourage promenade, and Miss Beaumont, attended by her brother, had been enjoying the modest bustle of High Street. It was with some surprise, therefore, that they encountered Mr. Harrington and Captain Fitzwilliam, having seemingly retraced their steps. A most curious manoeuvre, thought Miss Beaumont, though her brother merely raised a polite eyebrow. 

Indeed, the two gentlemen, having reached almost precisely the same spot as themselves, paused, a slight awkwardness settling upon the pavement. Mr. Denny, ever the obliging neighbour, swiftly intervened. He addressed them directly, and entreated permission to introduce the Beaumonts, praising Miss Beaumont’s accomplishments in watercolour with a warmth that bordered on the excessive. 

Captain Fitzwilliam offered a bow, charmingly careless, while Mr. Harrington’s was more studied, his gaze lingering, perhaps a fraction too long, upon Miss Beaumont’s face. A blush, entirely involuntary, rose to her cheeks. It was, she reflected, a most unsettling, and yet undeniably *interesting*, circumstance. One could only hope Mr. Denny’s enthusiasm would not prove too… revealing.

text:
The unexpectedness of his arrival, after a week of pointed avoidance, did, admittedly, cause a flutter. “Frighten me, Mr. Darcy,” I remarked, attempting a lightness I scarcely felt, “by coming in all this state to hear me. Though I assure you, I shall not be alarmed.” A small triumph, to maintain composure under such scrutiny.

His countenance remained, as ever, a study in restrained emotion. He offered a curt acknowledgement of my greeting, his gaze sweeping the modest drawing-room with an air that suggested a regrettable necessity. It was not *me* he found wanting, precisely, but the surroundings.

However, it was not his presence alone that stirred a peculiar disquiet. Miss Georgiana, seated at the pianoforte, possessed a skill far exceeding expectation. Her performance, whilst undeniably accomplished, held a certain…precision. A chilling perfection that lacked warmth. 

There was a stubborn quality to her playing, a relentless adherence to the notes, that unsettled me more than any grand declaration from her brother. One might almost suspect a deliberate display, intended to…impress. And, I feared, succeed.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself, despite her better judgement, quite captivated by Mr. Fortescue’s pronouncements on the nature of ‘good.’ He had been expounding, over a particularly delicate dish of syllabub, upon its influence upon character. 

“Good?” he’d inquired, tilting his head with an air of profound consideration. “Yes; it has often led him to be liberal and generous; to give his money freely, to display hospitality, to assist his tenants, and relieve the distressed.” 

Eleanor, though appreciating the sentiment, could not help but observe a certain…convenience in his definition. It spoke, she thought, more to the *effects* of fortune than to any inherent moral quality. A man with limited means, however well-intentioned, could scarcely be ‘liberal’ on a grand scale. 

Her companion, however, seemed quite lost in admiration of his own reasoning. He continued, detailing instances of his own benevolence – a new roof for old Mrs. Higgins, a generous donation to the parish school. Eleanor offered a polite murmur, inwardly resolving to judge a man not by what he *did* with his abundance, but by what he *would* do, were that abundance lacking.

text:
The arrival of “Mr. Spectator” in the circulating library caused a most agreeable stir. Not for the profundity of its observations, mind you – though sensible enough on the subject of millinery and the proper arrangement of a drawing-room – but for the *manner* in which they were conveyed. It was a style, one felt, that understood the delicate nuances of a lady’s feelings, the unspoken anxieties regarding a suitable match, the quiet desperation of a dwindling fortune. 

Miss Eleanor, usually so reserved in her judgements, declared it “charmingly perceptive,” while Mrs. Bennet, predictably, found fault with its lack of detail regarding eligible bachelors. Yet even *she* conceded a certain… finesse. 

Indeed, it did not matter that the author remained anonymous. One could discern, with a certainty that bordered on intuition, a feminine hand guiding the pen. It did not *count* for much, some might argue, for a writer to be of the fairer sex, but there was a distinctly feminine element in “Mr. Spectator,” and in its genius there was, though nothing mannish, much that spoke to the heart of womanhood. A quality, one suspected, quite lost on the gentlemen.

Now, Bilgewater, that feller was a study. Always lookin’ like he’d been suckin’ on a lemon, he was. We was driftin’ down the Mississippi on a raft cobbled together from nothin’ but hope and driftwood, and he commenced to complainin’ ‘bout the heat, the bugs, the lack o’ decent coffee. Lord, the man could find a grievance in a sunrise.

“This here raft’s a disgrace,” he’d grumble, pickin’ at a loose plank. “A proper gentleman wouldn’t be caught dead on such a contraption.”

I says to him, “Well, Bilgewater, you ain’t a proper gentleman, are ya? And as for the raft, it’s keepin’ us afloat, ain’t it? So what’s the use o’ your bein’ sour? It’ll only make things uncomfortable.”

He huffed and puffed, lookin’ like a scalded cat. “It ain’t *fair*,” he finally declared. “I shoulda been born a duke, with servants and silk sheets!”

I just chuckled. “It ain’t my fault you warn’t born a duke, Bilgewater, and it ain’t *you* neither. Some folks get dealt a hand o’ aces, some get a handful o’ nothin’. Best just play the cards you got, and try not to wrinkle your brow so much. It’s givin’ me a headache.”

text:
The morrow produced no abatement of Mrs. Bennet’s ill humour or ill health. A handkerchief was perpetually employed, and lamentations regarding her nerves filled Longbourn with a most disagreeable resonance. Mr. Collins, too, remained in the same state of angry pride, convinced his attentions had been slighted by a family utterly insensible to his good fortune in offering himself. 

Elizabeth, however, found a small solace in the company of Charlotte Lucas. Though not possessed of brilliant wit, Charlotte possessed a steadiness of judgement and a quiet understanding which Elizabeth found increasingly valuable amidst the prevailing chaos. She confided in her friend the particulars of Mr. Collins’ proposal, and the ensuing family uproar, not seeking advice precisely, but rather a calm ear to receive the tale. 

“One would think,” Elizabeth remarked, pacing the small parlour, “that a man’s fortune might render him agreeable, regardless of his disposition. Yet, I find myself infinitely preferring poverty with civility to riches with such… pomposity.”

Charlotte offered a small, knowing smile. “Indeed, Elizabeth. A comfortable income is desirable, certainly. But a comfortable companion is infinitely more so.”

The matter had been agitated for a fortnight, and still Mrs. Bennet persisted in viewing it as settled. A proposal, quite unexpectedly delivered, had been made for Miss Lydia, and accepted with an alacrity that bordered, some might observe, on the indelicate. Mr. Wickham, though possessed of a pleasing countenance and a ready wit, was, alas, entirely without fortune to recommend him. 

“But Mama,” protested Jane, attempting a reasoned discourse, “consider the consequences! To marry without a provision… they will know nothing of the effects that such a step might produce.”

Mrs. Bennet waved a dismissive hand. “Nonsense, child! Love will find a way. And besides, Mr. Wickham is a gentleman, and a man of connections.”

Elizabeth, however, felt a more pressing concern. “There is, however, the matter of security, Mama. Should any…imprudence occur, there is no male relative to intervene.”

Her mother’s brow furrowed. “Do not mention such unpleasantries! And as to your other objection, I am afraid it will hardly hold good. Lydia has no brother.” A statement delivered with a finality that silenced further debate, leaving Elizabeth to contemplate the precariousness of her youngest sister’s future with a heavy heart.

text:
The chill of the evening, though mild for November, had settled upon Netherfield Park with a persistence that even a cheerful fire could not entirely dispel. Mr. Darcy, having endured a particularly tedious discourse on the merits of various hunting dogs, found himself restless. A certain…disquiet, he acknowledged with a slight tightening of his jaw, had taken root. He had, perhaps, been too reserved, too quick to judge. A single, regrettable instance weighed heavily upon his mind.

Resolved on one effort more, and turning to Elizabeth, said,-- “Miss Eliza Bennet, let me persuade you to follow my example, and take a turn about the grounds. Do not remain cooped within, listening to Sir William’s pronouncements on the breeding of spaniels. The air, though cool, will invigorate the spirits.”

Miss Bennet, surprised by the unexpected invitation, hesitated only a moment. A faint amusement danced in her eyes. “Indeed, sir? Do you anticipate a sudden revelation amidst the shrubbery?” 

He offered a small, almost imperceptible smile. “Merely a hope for a more agreeable conversation, Miss Bennet. And perhaps, a clearer perspective.” He extended his arm, a gesture both polite and, he dared to hope, inviting.

Fourteen hundred mile, that’s a stretch, even for a steamboat. But Pa, he figured a deck passage, crammed in with the hogs and hopefuls, would do. Warn’t enough, though. Not near. Now, this here missive arrived by a boy lookin’ peaked as a winter radish, all dust and elbows. Delivered it right into my hand, lookin’ like he expected a reprimand for breathin’. Unfolded it, I did, and found a script so tremulous it near swam off the page. A plea, it was, penned by a feller named William – a name that always struck me as lackin’ in imagination, but that’s neither here nor there.

He wrote of a loneliness that clung to him like Spanish moss, a feelin’ of bein’ overlooked, like a chipped teacup in a fine china cabinet. Said he’d heard tell of my hospitality, and humbly requested, not a favor, mind you, but an *invitation*. Just to sit a spell, share a pipe, and maybe not feel quite so…invisible.

Read it through twice, I did. A peculiar request, to be sure. But there was a sincerity to it, a genuine ache in them words. Folded it neat, slipped it into my waistcoat pocket. 

“Poor William,” I mused, strokin’ my beard. “Afflicted as he is, his *heart’s* aluz right. Asks me to invite. Do not mention the author, now. Let’s see if a bit of company can’t chase away some shadows.”

The relief was, I confess, most palpable. Mr. Grimshaw’s departure for Bath had occasioned a lightness in the household not felt since… well, since his arrival, perhaps. Mama declared it a blessing, though couched in terms of his delicate constitution requiring the waters, a fiction we all readily indulged. 

“I cared not for his compliments, you understand,” Miss Eleanor confided to me over our embroidery, a delicate rose taking shape under her nimble fingers. “I dare say he often hears worse things said than I am going to say. But he *is* an ugly fellow!” 

Indeed. A countenance so singularly lacking in proportion! And his chin… do not, I implore you, dwell upon it. It was a chin of truly alarming length, extending, one felt, into realms best left unexplored. 

“I am glad he is gone,” I ventured, cautiously. “One’s peace of mind is of such consequence.”

Eleanor nodded, her lips pursed in agreement. “I never saw such a long chin. It quite distracted one from any attempt at polite conversation.” A sentiment with which I wholeheartedly concurred. The very air felt fresher now, devoid of that… prominent feature.

The pronouncement, delivered with Mr. Collins’ customary lack of tact, hung in the air like a poorly-stitched tapestry. “From my cousin,” he intoned, adjusting his cravat with a self-important air, “who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases.”

A delicate flush rose upon Miss Eleanor’s cheeks, though she endeavoured to maintain a composure befitting her station. Her sister, however, possessed of a less restrained sensibility, could not contain a small gasp. 

“Oh, my dear,” Mrs. Collins burst forth, her voice a fluster of anxious concern, “I cannot *bear* to hear such things! It is most unsettling! To speak of death, and dispossession, all in the same breath! Such a gloomy prospect for us all!” She fluttered a lace handkerchief, directing a pleading glance towards her husband.

Mr. Collins, seemingly oblivious to the distress he had caused, merely cleared his throat. “It is merely a statement of fact, my dear. Prudence dictates one be aware of potential… contingencies. A comfortable understanding of inheritance, you see, is essential for a well-regulated mind.” He beamed, convinced he had imparted wisdom, rather than a chilling premonition.

The news, when it arrived via Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, was delivered with a theatrical sigh and a pointed glance towards Miss Eleanor. Mr. Beaumont, it seemed, had not merely succumbed to a sudden, unspecified business in London, as previously hinted, but had actively *sought* employment there. And not, pray understand, in the sober realms of commerce, but upon the *stage*.

“A large part, my dear,” Mrs. Featherstonehaugh confided, fluttering a lace handkerchief. “A hero, no less! Though, one hears the theatre is… a rather mixed company.”

Eleanor, though attempting a composure she scarcely felt, found her cheeks betraying a warmth most unwelcome. To think, all his protestations of rural contentment, his lingering farewells, merely a prelude to donning tights and declaiming verses! It was, she conceded, a degree of vanity exceeding even her initial estimations. 

Her sister, Marianne, however, declared it “romantic beyond measure!” Eleanor, with a quiet firmness, deemed it merely *imprudent*. A gentleman of fortune, abandoning all propriety for the fickle applause of the town? It spoke volumes, and none of them flattering. The prospect of encountering Mr. Beaumont, resplendent in theatrical garb, filled her with a most disagreeable anticipation.

text:
The matter of Mr. Harrington’s continued absence weighed upon Miss Elizabeth, not with a violent grief, but a quiet, persistent disquiet. It had been six months since his regiment marched for the continent, and six months of letters received with decreasing frequency, until now, a complete cessation. She did wonder and repine at his returning no more; and though a day seldom passed in which Elizabeth did not account for it clearly – duty, honour, perhaps even a more fortunate attachment – there seemed little change in the landscape of her own heart, only a dull ache where expectation had once bloomed.

Her sister, Mary, declared it a blessing, citing his frivolous conversation and lamentable taste in whist. But Elizabeth found little comfort in such pronouncements. It was not his accomplishments she missed, but the particular *way* he regarded her, a glance that hinted at a sensibility beyond the common. 

She occupied herself with needlework, with the pianoforte, with the polite duties of a country gentlewoman, yet each pursuit felt strangely hollow. A visitor called, remarking upon the brisk autumn air, and Elizabeth found herself responding with a listlessness quite unbecoming. The world, it seemed, continued on its course, oblivious to the small, private sorrow of one young lady.
author: Jane Austen

Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a study in discomfort, perched on that crate like a heron suspectin’ a snake in the reeds. He’d sent word – a boy with eyes too big for his face – requestin’ a “chance to talk us over.” Well, this is it, Capet. I ain’t easy; I ain’t comfortable. That doctor lays on my mind. I wanted to know your plans. 

He fidgeted with a chipped meerschaum, the bowl black as a preacher’s soul on a Sunday. “He says it’s the lung fever, see? But I reckon it’s somethin’ else. Somethin’…settlin’. Like dust in an abandoned attic.”

He paused, lookin’ at me with eyes that had seen too much Mississippi mud and too little kindness. “Got a daughter, out in St. Louis. Sent for her, of course. But a body don’t rightly want a daughter seein’ him…unraveled. Understand?”

He tapped the pipe against the crate. “Just wanted to know if you boys was plannin’ on movin’ on quick. Don’t want no mournful faces lingerin’ ‘round when the undertaker comes callin’. A man deserves a little dignity, even at the finish.”

text:
The matter of Mr. Harrison’s longevity had been much discussed amongst the ladies of the village, and Elizabeth, though generally disinclined to such idle speculation, found herself, this afternoon, contemplating the peculiar weight of a life fully lived. He had, after all, witnessed the passing of two generations, seen estates rise and fall, and observed the fickle currents of fashion with a detached, if somewhat cynical, eye.

There was certainly at this moment, in Elizabeth’s mind, a more gentle sensation towards the original than she had ever felt in the height of his rather boisterous pronouncements on eligible young men. His pronouncements had, admittedly, been frequently irritating. Yet, to consider the accumulation of years, the quiet endurance of sorrow and the inevitable diminishment of spirit… it softened the edges of past grievances. 

One could not help but wonder what store of memories resided within that aged frame, what joys and disappointments had shaped the man he now was. It was a humbling thought, to realise the vastness of time contained within a single existence, and to acknowledge that even the most tiresome of neighbours possessed a history deserving of a degree of respectful consideration.
author: Jane Austen

We met on the dusty stretch ‘tween Widow Peabody’s and town, him a-comin’ like a scalded cat, me a-putterin’ along content as a tick on a hound dog. The correspondence grows, a sickly bloom of parchment in the lamplight. Each missive, penned by men of renown – Armitage of Miskatonic, Lowes of the British Museum, even the aloof Professor Angell – returns with a chilling, polite skepticism. They acknowledge the meticulousness of the charts, the unsettling regularity of the astronomical anomalies I’ve documented, yet recoil from the implications. 

It is not the *data* they dispute, understand. It is the yawning abyss of possibility it suggests. They speak of observational error, of atmospheric distortion, of the inherent fallibility of the human mind when confronted with the vast, uncaring cosmos. But beneath the academic phrasing, I detect a primal fear, a dread of truths best left undisturbed.

They cling to the established order, to the comforting illusion of a universe governed by predictable laws. They *must*. For to admit the validity of my findings – the cyclical alignment, the non-Euclidean geometry bleeding through from… elsewhere – is to invite madness. 

I rely on the judgment and standing of the few scientific leaders who have, on the one hand, sufficient independence of thought to weigh my data on its merits, and on the other, the fortitude to gaze into the encroaching darkness without flinching. But time, I fear, is not on our side. The stars are shifting. And something *answers*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, it was a predicament, I tell you true. Old Man Hemlock, he’d gone and ordered *too many* melons. Watermelons the size of small children, cantelopes fragrant enough to draw bees from a mile, and mushmelons…well, mushmelons just being mushmelons, a delicate affair. And the market, it had turned fickle as a woman scorned. 

We sat there, a committee of three – myself, young Jeb, and Silas, who mostly just chewed tobacco and offered pronouncements like “Humph.” – arguin’ ‘til the fire died low. Drop the watermelons? Unthinkable! Folks *expect* a good watermelon in August. Cantelopes? Too refined for these parts, maybe. But the mushmelons…they were lookin’ peaked, truth be told. 

Jeb favored a lottery. Silas suggested feedin’ ‘em to the hogs, a notion I quickly squelched. Hogs ain’t got no appreciation for a good mushmelon. We wrangled and debated, considerin’ the cost of spoilage, the temper of the townsfolk, and the sheer, overwhelming *quantity* of melon.

But towards daylight, we got it all settled satisfact. We’d donate the cantelopes to the Widow Peabody’s orphans. A touch of refinement for the little tykes, and good publicity, you see. And the rest? Well, the rest got sold at a price that wouldn’t quite break the bank, but wouldn’t leave Old Man Hemlock cryin’ into his coffee neither. A right proper solution, it was.

Now, Old Man Tiber, he’d been mutterin’ for years ‘bout the land along the bend. Said it was built on nothin’ but wishful thinkin’ and river silt, a precarious stack, really. Folks just chuckled, see, ‘cause Harmony Bend was a right prosperous little place, full of ambition and pickle factories. But Tiber, he knew the river. Knew its moods like a man knows his own wife.

This spring, it started subtle. A crack in Farmer Giles’ barn, a leaning fence post. Then, a slow, deliberate *slump* in Widow Peabody’s prize petunia patch. But by June, Lordy, it was a sight. The ground, a quarter mile deep, just…unravelin’. Not a landslide, mind you, but a *cave-in*. Like a biscuit crumblin’ under a heavy hand. 

Houses went first, then the general store, then old Man Hemlock’s entire collection of porcelain cats. All slidin’, crumblin’, and disappearin’ into the muddy maw of the Mississippi. Folks said it was a judgement, others blamed the pickle brine weakenin’ the soil. But Tiber, he just sat on his porch, smokin’ his pipe, and said, “Told ya so.” A town built on nothin’ but hope and soft earth? Bound to vanish, I reckon. Bound to vanish right quick.

text:
The Committee, as it was discreetly termed, had long concerned itself with geometries beyond human comprehension – not those of Euclid, but of angles that *should not be*. Our current preoccupation, however, was less with the opening of doors, and more with the…return traffic. Expeditions, driven by a hubris now curdled to dread, had ventured too far into the cyclopean ruins beyond the Antarctic Circle, and whispers followed them back. Not audible, precisely, but *felt* – a cold resonance in the bone, a sickening lurch in the soul.

We sought havens. Not fortifications, for what good are stone and steel against things unbound by dimension, but places of…nullity. Old churches, built upon pre-human sites, possessed a certain static resistance. Libraries, crammed with the forgotten lore of ages, seemed to fray the edges of their awareness. But most promising were the abandoned lighthouses, their beams a futile, yet somehow *irritating*, gesture against the encroaching darkness. 

The scent was the most unsettling aspect. Not a smell of decay, nor sulphur, but something…nameless. A cloying sweetness overlaid with the metallic tang of ozone and the dust of stars that had died before Earth was formed. It clung to the returning men, and to the air around them, a herald of geometries best left undisturbed. A scent that promised not violence, but *unmaking*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

It was, of course, entirely unexpected. One does not anticipate encountering eligible gentlemen whilst assisting at a particularly tedious village fête, dedicated, as it was, to the preservation of prize-winning marrows. And yet, there he was. Not precisely *handsome*, perhaps, but possessing a certain… solidity of character, and a remarkably well-cut coat. 

He inquired, with a politeness bordering on deference, after my own accomplishments, and I, naturally, steered the conversation towards the pianoforte. It was then, with a casualness I trust did not betray my agitation, that he revealed his connection. A nephew of Lady Catherine de Bourgh! How wonderfully these sort of things occur! Who would have thought of my meeting with—perhaps—a nephew of Lady Ca…? 

My mother, naturally, is in a state of the most delightful flutter. She has already begun to speculate upon the advantages of such an alliance, and to lament the regrettable state of my bonnet ribbons. One must, of course, be sensible. But a connection to Rosings Park… it is a prospect to quicken the pulse of even the most composed female heart.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The prospect of a walk to Meryton, and the consequent opportunity to observe the current state of society within that small compass, was, to Mrs. Bennet, a delight beyond measure. “Indeed, my dears,” she declared, fluttering a fan with agitated enthusiasm, “we *must* go. To see how Lydia and Kitty comport themselves, and, of course, to ascertain if any new officers have arrived! It would be quite improper to remain secluded.”

Jane, ever compliant, readily agreed, envisioning a pleasant stroll and the chance to exchange civilities. Mary, predictably, saw it as a duty, a necessary exercise in observing human nature. But Elizabeth, with a firmness that bordered on obstinacy, steadily opposed the scheme. 

“Mama, I believe a quiet afternoon at home is infinitely preferable. Meryton offers little beyond gossip and the potential for awkward encounters.” 

Her mother, aghast, protested. “Elizabeth! It shall not be said that the Miss Bennets could not bear a simple walk! It reflects poorly upon the family, upon *me*! Such a display of…of *reserve*!” 

Elizabeth merely raised an eyebrow, a silent declaration that her own comfort outweighed her mother’s anxieties regarding public perception. The matter, for the moment, remained unresolved, hanging in the air like a particularly pointed remark.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Tiber, he’d been sellin’ lanterns down by the river for nigh on fifty years, and a peculiar sort he was. Not for the lanterns themselves – good, solid things, they were – but for his pronouncements. This fella, see, he didn’t ask *if* you needed a lantern, he asked what you were hidin’ *from*.

A woman, fine-featured and dressed in city silks, was inspectin’ a brass beauty. “It’s for my nephew,” she said, all polite-like. “He’s comin’ to visit, and the path to the house is… uneven.”

Tiber stroked his beard, a tangled mess of grey. “Uneven, is it? Or is it what’s *on* the path that troubles ye?” He chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “A good lantern shows things, yes. But sometimes, missus, a fella’s all the better for the dark, if he’s got one.” 

“I didn’t think of that.” The woman kept lookin’ at me, pretty curious, and I didn’t feel a bit comforta’. I was just passin’ through, mind ye, but a man can’t help but overhear when a fella’s talkin’ about secrets and shadows. And that lantern, it seemed to gleam a little brighter after Tiber said his piece.

text:
Now, this family, the Abernathys, they were a breed apart, you see. Not stuck-up, mind you, but *polished*. Like a river stone worn smooth by years of current. And their house… well, sir, it wasn’t just a house, it was a statement. Built of brick, it was, a proper red brick, not some slapped-together wood affair. Had a veranda that wrapped around it like a friendly arm, and columns, white as a preacher’s collar.

I’d wandered out from town, lookin’ for a bit of peace and quiet, and stumbled upon it. Never seen nothin’ like it this side of St. Louis. Folks out here generally built for practicality, not for show. But the Abernathys, they had *style*. 

Mrs. Abernathy, she offered me lemonade, sweet as a summer’s dream, and didn’t bat an eye at my dusty boots. The children, little Miss Lily and Master Thomas, they were polite as could be, offerin’ me cookies and askin’ about the town. It was a mighty nice family, and a mighty nice house, too. A fella could get used to a life lived in the shadow of such pleasantness, I reckon.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor found herself, despite a determined composure, quite flustered by the afternoon’s proceedings. Her Aunt Philips, ever eager to display a lively wit, had launched a volley of observations upon the recent assembly, each more pointed than the last, directed, it seemed, at the unfortunate Miss Bingley and her companion. Her cousin, the amiable but somewhat vapid Miss Grace, echoed these sentiments with a breathless enthusiasm, adding little to the substance but much to the volume.

Mr. Darcy, observing the flurry from his position near the pianoforte, remained a study in polite detachment. He offered a curt acknowledgement to Aunt Philips’ most audacious remark – a comment concerning Mr. Bingley’s susceptibility to flattery – but resolutely declined to be drawn into the conversation. 

Eleanor, though privately agreeing with much of what was said, felt a rising discomfort. Such open censure, even if deserved, lacked all delicacy. She attempted to steer the discourse towards the weather, then the merits of needlepoint, but her efforts were in vain. The ladies, emboldened by his silence, continued their pronouncements, seemingly determined to provoke *some* reaction from the gentleman, a feat, however, which proved beyond their powers.
author: Jane Austen

The question hung in the air, a most unwelcome intrusion upon Miss Eleanor’s contemplation of the rose garden. “That letter?” she repeated, her voice a delicate tremor barely audible above the buzzing of bees. Mr. Hawthorne, a gentleman possessed of a tolerable fortune and an irritating habit of directness, stood before her, his brow furrowed with a concern she found both presumptuous and, admittedly, a little unsettling.

It was, of course, the letter from her cousin, detailing a most unsuitable attachment to a penniless musician. Eleanor had hoped to keep the matter confined to her own breast, a private sorrow to be managed with quiet dignity. Mr. Hawthorne, however, appeared determined to dissect it with the bluntness of a country surgeon.

“Indeed, sir,” she replied, carefully arranging a bloom. “A communication arrived this morning. Its contents, I assure you, are of no consequence to anyone but myself and my unfortunate relation.” 

He persisted, naturally. Men *would* meddle. With a final, exasperated glance, he offered a platitude about familial duty, and then, with a slight bow, turned again into the plantation, and was soon out of sight. With no expectation of pleasure, but with the firm resolve to avoid further conversation on the subject, Eleanor returned to her roses, and the solace they offered.

text:
Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a spirit not entirely subdued by propriety, found herself in a most awkward predicament. The promised conveyance to the Smythes’ musicale had failed to materialize, leaving herself and Miss Beatrice stranded at the edge of the village. A gentleman, Mr. Harding, recently arrived and possessing a tolerable fortune, had offered his carriage, an offer Beatrice had, with uncharacteristic haste, accepted.

“For it would really be discreditable to *you* to let them go alone,” Eleanor observed, a delicate censure in her tone.

Beatrice, fluttering her fan, replied, “My uncle is to send a servant for us.”

A slight raising of the eyebrow was Eleanor’s only response. “Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, does he? A most fortunate circumstance, indeed. Though one wonders if Giles is entirely accustomed to navigating the lanes after dusk. Mr. Harding’s horses are known for their steadiness, and his coachman, a man of considerable experience.” 

Beatrice, sensing the implication, coloured slightly. “Uncle assures me Giles is perfectly capable. And Mr. Harding… well, he *is* rather forward in his attentions.” Eleanor merely smiled, a knowing glint in her eye. The evening, she suspected, promised to be far more diverting than any musicale.

text:
Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a feller set in his ways, like a hound dog with a bone. Everything had a place, a time, a *manner* of doin’. Breakfast at precisely six-fifteen, not a tick sooner nor later. Boots polished ‘til you could see your face in ‘em. And Lord help you if you offered him coffee brewed from anything but Chicory.

He’d sit on the porch, watchin’ the river roll by, and declare, “Folks nowadays, they’re all flappin’ about like a chicken with its head cut off. No order to nothin’!” 

I asked him once, “But ain’t life supposed to be *lived*, Tiber? Ain’t a little spontaneity a good thing?”

He just snorted. “Spontaneity! Hmph. Why, the fellers that wrote the books – the ones with the learnin’ – they didn’t write about spontaneity, did they? They wrote about duty, and propriety, and doin’ things *right*. They knew a thing or two, them book-makin’ gents. Don’t you reckon so? Seems to me, if they bothered writin’ it all down, it must be the correct way. Don’t you?” 

He’d then adjust his spectacles and go back to watchin’ the river, convinced he’d settled the matter for all time. A stubborn cuss, that Tiber. A stubborn cuss, indeed.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The prospect of Meryton, though scarcely a league distant from Longbourn, possessed a peculiar power to stretch the hours into an eternity. Not from any deficiency in the village itself – for the millinery was passable, and the assembly rooms, though small, offered a tolerable degree of amusement – but from the certainty of encountering *him*. Mr. Darcy, it seemed, found himself perpetually drawn to Hertfordshire, a circumstance which, whilst not unwelcome to some, filled Mrs. Bennet with a nervous agitation scarcely concealed.

Indeed, anxiety on Jane’s behalf was another prevailing concern. Her sister’s sweetness of temper, so universally admired, rendered her particularly vulnerable to the careless judgements of those less inclined to discernment. Should Mr. Darcy observe her, and find her wanting… the very thought was enough to induce a flutter in Mrs. Bennet’s breast. 

“Oh, my dears,” she lamented to Elizabeth, smoothing her cap with a frantic hand, “to be subjected to *his* scrutiny! It is quite dreadful. One can only hope he remains occupied with the particulars of Mr. Bingley’s estate, and forgets we exist entirely.” A hope, Elizabeth suspected, as fragile as spun glass.
author: Jane Austen

text:
CHAPTER XI. “Come in,” says the woman.

Now, this old Miz Abernathy, they said she could tell you things. Not fortunes, mind you, not like those painted-up city gals with their crystal balls. No sir. She knew things *about* things. The whys and wherefores of a leaky roof, a failing crop, a husband’s sudden fondness for the mercantile’s ginger beer. Folks whispered she’d gleaned it all from the river itself, somehow. 

I’d been sent for a different sort of knowing, though. A matter of the heart, you understand, and a young man with eyes the color of muddy Mississippi after a rain. Mama insisted I needed guidance, and frankly, I was flustered enough to try anything.

But I’d resolved, before even lifting the latch, to remember I was a girl. Not some blushing, simpering thing, but a girl with a spine and a mind. A girl who could ask a straight question and not faint at the answer. It’s a difficult thing, maintaining dignity when you’re hoping a stranger can unravel your affections. 

The parlor smelled of dried herbs and something faintly…fishy. Miz Abernathy, a woman built like an oak stump, sat rocking. She didn’t smile. Didn’t offer a chair. Just that curt “Come in,” and a gaze that felt like being measured for a coffin.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, this here auction, it was a sight. Old Man Hemlock, see, got himself in a pickle with the bank – a right proper pickle, fermented with bad investments and a fondness for fancy pigeons. Announced the sale with barely a week’s notice, which naturally meant folks figured the best bits were already spoken for. And they weren’t entirely wrong.

Still, a crowd gathered, mostly looky-loos and fellas hoping for a bargain. Hemlock’s wife, bless her soul, sat on the porch lookin’ like a thundercloud, clutchin’ a chipped teacup. The auctioneer, a fella named Silas with a voice like a rusty hinge, was tryin’ to drum up enthusiasm for a set of chipped chamber pots. 

“Going once! Going twice!” he hollered, but the bids were slower than molasses in January. Truth be told, Silas was sweatin’ bullets. The bank man, a lean, unpleasant sort, was standin’ right behind him, arms crossed, givin’ Silas the eye. They ain’t going out of this till they get that money; and the way we’ve fixed it the sale ain’t going to. It was a comedy of errors, a slow-motion disaster, and I reckon we’d be there ‘til kingdom come if somebody didn’t offer a decent price for those pots.

Now, I reckon a body’s got to account for themselves, even to a contraption like this here… talking machine. Me? Well, I’m a study in contradictions, same as most folks. Spend my days wrestling with notions, mostly. Big, unwieldy notions about how things *ought* to be, and smaller, more practical notions about where I left my spectacles. 

Just now, I was observing a fella, a right fidgety sort, pacing like a caged panther. He declared, clear as a bell, “I’m a-going up around the corner here to roust out my engineer.” A peculiar statement, that. Sounded like a man wrestling with a locomotive in his sleep. 

I struck for the light, curious to see what manner of engineer required rousing. But as soon as he turned the corner – a perfectly ordinary man, mind you, with a wrench in his hand – I went back. No need to pry, see? Some mysteries are best left undisturbed. A man and his engine, or whatever it was, is his own affair. Besides, I had a sudden, pressing need to remember if I’d locked the shed. A body can’t be too careful, you know.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth had, for some weeks, endured the solicitations of her Aunt Philips to accompany her on a visit to Brighton. Initially, the prospect had held little charm; the seaside, whilst undeniably fashionable, possessed a vulgarity of amusement quite at odds with Eleanor’s preference for quiet contemplation. However, a subtle shift in her feelings had occurred. Not unwelcome for its own sake, the journey would, moreover, give her a peep at Jane; and, in short, as the time drew near, she would have been very sorry to decline.

Jane, her dearest friend, was currently residing with the Worthingtons, a family of tolerable connections and, more importantly, possessing a handsome son who had, on a previous encounter, elicited a most agreeable blush from Eleanor. 

The thought of a fortnight removed from the stifling expectations of Hartfield, and the opportunity to observe Mr. Worthington under less formal circumstances, proved a powerful inducement. Indeed, Eleanor found herself assisting with the packing with an unusual alacrity, her mind already sketching the possibilities of promenade strolls and carefully orchestrated encounters. Brighton, it seemed, was becoming decidedly… promising.

Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was fixin’ to build a new chicken coop, see? A right proper one, with wire mesh and all, to keep out them sly foxes. But he was plumb stumped on how to cut the lumber square. He’d been at it all mornin’, sawin’ crooked as a dog’s hind leg, and mutterin’ somethin’ about the Lord not givin’ a man a steady hand.

I says, “Hemlock, you’re frettin’ over nothin’. It ain’t a sin to use yer head, even if it *is* a bit slow to warm up in the mornin’.” Then, feelin’ a mite mischievous, I says, “It’s unregular and irreligious to sejest it, but there’s an old rusty saw-blade around yonder sticking under the weather-boarding behind the smoke-ho. Found it years back, belonged to a feller who claimed it could cut a straight line even in a hurricane.”

Hemlock, he squinted at me like I’d sprouted a second head. “A *what* now?” 

“Just a saw-blade, Hemlock. A tool. Don’t go lookin’ for divine intervention when a bit of ingenuity’ll do the trick.” He retrieved it, grumbling, but you could see a flicker of hope in his eye. And wouldn’t you know, that rusty old thing cut cleaner than a whistle. Sometimes, a feller just needs a little…assistance.

Catherine was, thankfully, far from objecting to my occasional absence on a Sunday. Indeed, she declared it a most sensible arrangement, provided, of course, that some other clergyman was engaged to perform the duty of the day. A parish, she reasoned with a practicality that always charmed, could scarcely suffer from a temporary surfeit of spiritual guidance, but *would* undoubtedly feel the strain of a complete void. 

It was not, she hastened to assure me, any lack of esteem for my sermons – for she had always been most attentive – but a recognition of the demands upon my time, and a desire to see me refreshed for the week’s labours. A delicate consideration, truly. 

I remained, however, convinced it was less concern for the parish, and more a quiet relief at being spared the necessity of enduring Mrs. Featherstonehaugh’s interminable post-service critiques on my choice of vestments. The woman possessed a singular talent for finding fault, and a Sunday without her pronouncements was a blessing to be gratefully received by all. Catherine, I suspected, understood this perfectly well.

Thursday was to be the wedding-day, and on Wednesday Miss Lucas paid her farewell visit; and when she rose to take leave, Elizabeth, ashamed of the lingering melancholy she had permitted herself, endeavoured to appear wholly composed. Charlotte, however, possessed a discernment which no artifice could long conceal. 

“You are remarkably cheerful, my dear,” she observed, a slight arch to her brow. “One would scarcely suspect a sister on the eve of witnessing a union so… fortunate.”

Elizabeth coloured, and attempted a laugh. “Fortunate, indeed! Mr. Bingley is all that is amiable, and Jane, I trust, anticipates a life of perfect contentment.” It was, after all, the truth. Yet a peculiar lightness had settled upon her own spirit, a feeling quite distinct from mere congratulation. 

She had, in recent months, been plagued by a certain… seriousness. Now, observing Charlotte’s quiet happiness in her own impending domesticity, and reflecting upon the agreeable resolution of her friend’s affairs, a warmth spread through her. Perhaps, she mused, happiness was not always a grand passion, but a gentle, steady bloom, cultivated in the common garden of life. A most agreeable thought.

Now, a raftsman’s life ain’t for the faint of heart, nor the clean of collar, let me tell you. It’s a slow sort of freedom, mostly, punctuated by the occasional snag and the constant company of mosquitoes thick as a politician’s promises. The arrival of the North----shire regiment at Meryton had, naturally, thrown the small society into a delightful, if somewhat breathless, agitation. Miss Penelope Featherstonehaugh, however, possessed a particular talent for embracing whatever was *most* agitating at any given moment, and her current occupation was entirely devoted to the officers. Not to any particular officer, mind you – that would imply a degree of discernment she did not possess – but to the *idea* of officers.

She had, within the space of a fortnight, declared Captain Armitage the most handsome man in England, then dismissed him as possessing a lamentable want of wit after a single, overheard remark concerning the merits of fox-hunting. Now, Lieutenant Banning was favoured, solely because Mrs. Phillips had pronounced his coat-cut exceedingly fashionable. 

Penelope’s mind, one might observe, was a remarkably fertile ground for the seeds of opinion, readily accepting any that were sown by the more assertive members of her acquaintance. She spent her time in the most idle and frivolous manner, flitting between the assembly rooms and the shops, repeating the latest gossip with an air of profound understanding, and generally contributing to the prevailing air of amiable, if somewhat empty, excitement. It was, after all, the only sensible way to occupy oneself whilst awaiting a proposal.

The question, delivered with a precision that bordered on reproach, hung in the air of the small drawing-room. “Are you, Miss Bennet,” Mr. Harding inquired, his brow furrowed with a gentlemanly concern, “consulting your own feelings in the present case, or do you imagine that you are gratifying mine?”

A delicate flush rose upon Miss Bennet’s cheek, though her eyes sparkled with an amusement she did little to conceal. She had, perhaps, allowed a degree of warmth to colour her discourse regarding his nephew, a warmth she knew might be misconstrued. 

“Both,” she replied archly, a slight inclination of her head accompanying the words, “for I have always found a pleasing coincidence between a benevolent regard for another’s happiness, and a certain satisfaction in the exercise of one’s own judgement. To deny either would be, I suspect, a most ungenerous deceit – both to oneself, and to the party concerned.”

Mr. Harding, though clearly discomfited by such a candid response, could not entirely suppress a smile. It was, he conceded, a most artful evasion, and possessed of a wit that was undeniably… engaging. He merely cleared his throat and resumed his inquiries, though with a noticeably lessened air of authority.

The air in the abandoned observatory grew thick, not with dust as one might expect of such a neglected place, but with a cloying sweetness that bordered on the nauseating. It wasn’t a scent readily identifiable – not floral, not decay, but *adjacent* to both, a phantom echo of things that ought not bloom, or rot. A subtle pressure built within the skull, a tightening behind the eyes, and the chronometer, painstakingly calibrated to sidereal time, began to stutter, its rhythmic tick fracturing into a maddening, uneven pulse.

Old Man Hemlock, the last caretaker, had spoken of ‘shifts’ in the stars, of geometries glimpsed in the periphery that defied Euclidean comprehension. Now, staring through the great lens, one understood. The constellations weren’t *wrong*, precisely, but… *altered*. Subtly, sickeningly, as if viewed through a distorting membrane. 

The source of the unease, whether it stemmed from the very fabric of reality itself, or from some subtle, increasing odor emitted by the nightmare specimens – the things writhing in the newly visible gulfs between the stars – one could not say. * * * * * But whatever had happened, it was hideous. A violation of natural law, a blasphemy against the ordered cosmos, and the creeping certainty that observation itself was an act of unspeakable provocation.

The assembly rooms at Hartfield were, as Mrs. Weston had predicted, quite full. Though not, perhaps, possessing the brilliance of London, the company was respectable, and several of them, you see, uncommonly pretty. Miss Eleanor Fairchild, with her rosebud lips and artless blush, was particularly admired, and drew a considerable throng of hopeful gentlemen. 

Young Mr. Ashworth, however, had secured her hand for the first two sets, a circumstance which did not escape the notice of Mr. Darcy, who stood observing the scene with a composure that bordered on disdain. He had been engaged in a rather tedious conversation with Lady Bertram regarding the merits of various embroidery patterns when his attention was caught by Miss Fairchild’s radiant smile.

“_You_ are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,” said Mr. Darcy, looking at the eldest Miss Bertram, who had ventured a comment on the music. 

Miss Bertram, a lady of sensible understanding, though not blessed with striking beauty herself, raised a delicate eyebrow. “Indeed, sir? I had thought Miss Fairchild merely… agreeable. Though Mr. Ashworth appears quite captivated.”

Mr. Darcy offered a slight, almost imperceptible, inclination of his head. “Captivation is a weakness easily indulged, Miss Bertram. True discernment is a far rarer quality.”

Now, old Man Hemlock, he weren’t a feller given to much fuss. Quiet sort, mostly kept to his whittlin’ and his complaints about the price of corn. But he *did* have a habit, a peculiar one, of collectin’ notices. Not the kind from the bank, mind you, but them little handbills plastered ‘round town – lost dogs, reward posters, and, most importantly, announcements of public hangings. 

He’d tack ‘em up in his shed, neat as you please, categorized by the feller’s crime. Said it was “studyin’ human nature.” I reckon it was morbid curiosity, plain and simple. 

One day, he showed me his collection, a grim gallery of misfortune. “See here, boy,” he said, pointin’ to a faded scrap. “This here feller, tried to pass counterfeit money. And this one…well, this one stole a pig. A *prize* pig, they said. Seems the law don’t much care ‘bout the size of the offense, just that it *is* an offense.” He chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “Interesting, ain’t it? The bills dat you’s gwyne to git hung for.” 

It gave a body pause, let me tell you. Made a feller think twice ‘fore even lookin’ cross-eyed at another man’s sow.

Now, I was plumb tuckered out, see? Been wrasslin’ with a particularly stubborn mule all mornin’, and the sun was beatin’ down like a blacksmith’s hammer. My eyelids felt weighted with lead, and a fella couldn’t rightly hold ‘em open if he tried. So I figured, what harm in jest one little cat-nap? Just a blink, a moment’s respite under the shade of Old Man Hemlock.

I leaned back against the rough bark, expectin’ to be roused by the sound of Bessie lowin’ for her supper. But I reckon it was more than a cat-nap, for when I waked up the sun was sinkin’ low, paintin’ the sky in hues of orange and purple. And the mule? Gone. Clean vanished. 

Not only that, but Old Man Hemlock was draped in cobwebs thick enough to choke a steer, and a family of squirrels was usin’ my hat for a picnic table. A fella could lose a good day’s work, and a perfectly good hat, to a single, innocent-seemin’ little cat-nap. It just goes to show, don’t you know, that even the best laid plans of mice and men… well, they often end up with squirrels eatin’ your biscuits.

text:
The news arrived with Mrs. Plumtree, delivered amidst a flurry of apologies for intruding upon afternoon tea and a lament for the dampness of the season. Mr. Harrington, it seemed, was to marry Miss Selina Finch. A match, universally declared *suitable*, and yet one which stirred within me a most unwelcome disquiet. For I knew that his conduct had not been always quite right. A youthful indiscretion, whispered amongst the ladies at the Assembly, a certain…attentiveness to a governess long since departed. Trifles, perhaps, to the world at large.

My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only felt how imprudent a match it *would* be, had it been for *me*. They saw only the advantageous connection, the respectable family, the comfortable fortune. They praised his good sense, his amiable disposition – qualities I found rather selectively applied. 

It was not jealousy, precisely, that troubled me, but a sense of injustice. That a man who had shown himself capable of a certain…laxity, should now be lauded for his respectability, while I, for possessing a more discerning eye, was deemed fanciful and over-sensitive. A most vexing situation, and one which promised little in the way of cheerful conversation at the next family gathering.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Susan, she was a girl built sturdy as an oak, but touched with a sadness. Had a hare-lip, see, and a quiet way about her that made folks think she hadn’t much to say. But Susan, she could *do*. The King, old Barnaby the Benevolent – though ‘benevolent’ was a stretch some days – he’d declared a contest. Whoever could mimic the Royal Parrot, Percy, best, would win a year’s supply of molasses. 

Percy, that bird was a terror. Squawked pronouncements and insults with equal gusto. Folks tried, bless their hearts, but sounded more like strangled chickens. Then Susan stepped forward. She pursed her lips, that little cleft working something fierce, and *imitated* Percy. Not just the squawk, mind you, but the haughty tilt of the head, the judgmental glare. 

And then, wouldn’t you know it, the King, he started doing it too! Mimicking Susan mimicking Percy, hare-lip and all. A sight to behold, I tell you. And Susan and the hare-lip done the same on the other. Everybody clapped their hands and stomped on the floor like a perfect storm, whilst the king he… well, he nearly choked laughing, which was a rare and welcome thing. Molasses for all, I reckon.
author: Mark Twain

text:
It was universally acknowledged amongst the inhabitants of Highwood that Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed a mind remarkably well-furnished. Not with accomplishments, perhaps – her pianoforte playing was passable, her sketching merely adequate – but with a keenness of observation and a facility for discerning character that bordered on the unsettling. She knew, with a certainty that defied explanation, the precise degree of Mr. Harrison’s debt, and the true motive behind Mrs. Plumtree’s excessive flattery. 

But why Mr. Darcy came so often to the Parsonage it was more difficult to understand. It could not be for society, as he frequently declined invitations to the more fashionable gatherings in the vicinity. Nor did he appear to seek the company of Mr. Ainsworth, whose theological discussions, though earnest, were seldom stimulating. No, it was to *her* he addressed his inquiries, subtle questions regarding the local gentry, their alliances, their fortunes, their very dispositions. 

He seemed to value her judgements above all others, a circumstance which, whilst flattering to Miss Ainsworth’s intellect, did provoke a certain degree of bewilderment. Was it possible, she mused, that even a gentleman of Mr. Darcy’s consequence found himself in need of a quiet, observant mind to navigate the complexities of rural life?
author: Jane Austen

Old Man Tiber, he sat on the porch swing, lookin’ like a dried apple peel left too long in the sun. I’d drifted by, see, lookin’ for nothin’ in particular, which is often the best way to find a story. He’d been whittlin’ a piece of pine into somethin’ vaguely resembling a hound dog, and didn’t look up ‘til I cleared my throat.

“Trouble, son?” he finally drawled, not a question exactly, more a statement of universal fact.

“Just passin’ time,” I said.

He chuckled, a dry rustlin’ sound. “Time’s a powerful current, boy. Pulls you under if you ain’t careful. Reminds me of a feller I knew, down in Arkansas. Had a hound, best tracker you ever saw. But that hound, he had a weakness for possum. One night, that feller and the hound, they both got into a heap of trouble myself, and would scatter out *with* you. That’s the whole yarn—what’s yourn?”

“Well,” I began, shiftin’ my weight, “I’d been a-runnin’ a little temperance revival thar, ’bout…”

text:
Miss Eleanor, having endured a full half-hour in the company of Mr. Grimshaw – a gentleman possessed of an enthusiasm for turnips that bordered on the alarming – declared, with a delicate flush upon her cheeks, that she could walk no farther. It was not, of course, a complaint of fatigue, for a gentlewoman was rarely so indelicate as to admit physical weakness. Rather, it was a subtle indication that the conversation had reached its natural conclusion, and a most unwelcome one at that.

Her aunt, Lady Beatrice, though possessing a spirit not easily swayed, perceived the distress in Eleanor’s averted gaze and the almost imperceptible tightening of her lips. A prolonged exposure to Mr. Grimshaw’s agricultural pronouncements, she conceded, might prove trying even to the most robust constitution. 

Mr. Grimshaw, thankfully oblivious to the silent plea, continued to expound upon the merits of swede versus mangel-wurzel. Lady Beatrice, with a firmness born of long experience, cut him short, expressing a sudden and pressing need to return to the carriage. Her niece was, therefore, obliged to submit, and they took their way, leaving Mr. Grimshaw to his beloved roots and a solitude he scarcely noticed.
author: Jane Austen

Now, the Duke, he reckoned he’d lay off and work his brains an hour or two and see if he couldn’t put up something on the Arkansaw village – a scheme, you understand, to separate a few unsuspecting souls from their hard-earned coin. He’d been feelin’ a mite sluggish, see, after that last performance with the painted scenery and the supposed lost Duke of… well, never you mind where. 

The King, he allowed he was agreeable to the notion. “Let the boy stew a bit,” he drawled, puffin’ on a clay pipe that smelled powerfully of burnt hickory. “Folks get suspicious when a feller’s *too* energetic. A little quiet contemplation, that’s what builds trust. Makes ‘em think you’re a man of… substance.”

He winked, a slow, deliberate blink that could curdle milk. “Though I still say that revival meeting idea had legs. Powerful legs. But go on, Duke. Spin your yarn. Just don’t go gettin’ fancy. Simple’s best, remember. Simple and believable. Like a politician’s promise.” 

The Duke, he just grunted and commenced scratchin’ at a piece of brown paper with a stub of a pencil, lookin’ for all the world like a scholar wrestlin’ with the mysteries of the universe. Which, considerin’ his line of work, wasn’t far from the truth.

text:
The arrival of Sir Reginald Featherstonehaugh and his daughters occasioned a flurry of activity at Longmeadow, though not of the boisterous sort. Mrs. Ashworth, ever mindful of propriety, directed the arrangement of the drawing-room cushions with a precision bordering on the mathematical. Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a lively wit, confined her observations to compliments upon Sir Reginald’s estate, whilst Miss Marianne busied herself with a particularly delicate piece of needlepoint, offering only the most gracious of smiles.

Mr. Ashworth, as was his habit, remained largely silent, observing the proceedings with a quiet amusement. He deemed excessive display vulgar, and considered a raised eyebrow a sufficient acknowledgement of company. Mr. Collins, however, more than compensated for his host’s reserve. He launched into a detailed account of the parish’s recent improvements, pausing only to solicit opinions – all of which he readily dismissed with a benevolent air. 

Indeed, the entire household seemed determined to outdo one another in politeness. It was a performance, perhaps, but one executed with such flawless grace that even the most discerning visitor could find no fault. A veritable symphony of bows, murmured enquiries, and carefully chosen phrases.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he weren’t a sociable sort. Kept to himself, mostly, and his property reflected it. Not a grand estate, mind you, but a patch of land clung to like a tick on a hound dog. The main house was respectable enough, though faded, but it was what lay *behind* that held a fella’s attention. 

Row t’other side the smoke-house, you see, was a little hut all by itself, away down against the back fence. Built of mismatched planks and looking like it’d been assembled during a particularly strong wind. Folks whispered it was where he did his…experiments. Hemlock was a tinkerer, a dabbler in things best left alone, they said. 

And some outbuildings down a piece the other side; a lean-to for tools, a coop lookin’ suspiciously reinforced, and a shed with a chimney that never seemed to smoke the same color twice. A body could spend a lifetime tryin’ to figure what went on back there, and still be no closer to the truth. It was a place that smelled of woodsmoke, something metallic, and a peculiar sort of…quiet. A quiet that felt less like peace and more like holdin’ yer breath.
author: Mark Twain

Now, it was a sweltering afternoon, the kind that makes a body feel like a boiled ham left out too long. I was aimlessly kickin’ pebbles ‘long the dusty road, mindin’ my own business, when Miss Elvira, she appeared in her door, which was next to ours, and she took me in her room and shut the door very soft, and asked me if I liked her, and I said I did; and she… well, she just *looked* at me.

She had a little fan, painted with roses, and she was flickin’ it slow, real slow, like she was tryin’ to stir up a breeze that wasn’t comin’. The dust of forgotten lore clung to the brittle pages, a testament to the scholar Hemlock’s descent. He’d begun with innocuous cartography, charting the peculiar prevalence of pentagonal formations in pre-human settlements across the blasted Hebrides. But the patterns… they *shifted*. Not geographically, but conceptually. They weren’t merely architectural, but woven into the very fabric of belief, a ghastly, recurring obsession.

Hemlock theorized a primal veneration, not of any deity readily named, but of something *older*. Something predating language, predating even the squamous forms hinted at in the *Necronomicon*. The five-pointed star, he posited, wasn’t symbolic, but *resonant* – a crude attempt to mimic the natural geometry of an archæan object, a crystalline entity of impossible angles which had, in some epoch beyond reckoning, embodied… something. 

He spoke of a “fractal consciousness,” a non-Euclidean awareness bleeding through the veil. The motif appeared in petroglyphs, in the arrangement of standing stones, even in the aberrant growth patterns of certain fungi. It was everywhere, a silent, maddening chorus whispering of a cosmic alignment, a return. And Hemlock, poor Hemlock, began to arrange his books, his papers, his *life* into the same abhorrent, five-fold symmetry.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a fella prone to exaggeration, a habit not uncommon in these parts, mind you. But Hemlock took it to a new elevation, a veritable Mount Olympus of fibs. Tonight, he’d secured himself the honor of introducing the traveling dramatic troupe’s rendition of…well, it was *supposed* to be Hamlet. 

He stood there, before that patched and faded curtain, lookin’ like a scarecrow dressed for Sunday. Cleared his throat, a sound like gravel shiftin’ in a wagon bed, and commenced. “Ladies and gentlemen,” he boomed, “prepare yourselves! For tonight, you ain’t just seein’ a play. You’re witnessin’ history! A tragedy so profound, so…thrillingest, it’ll curdle your blood and loosen your teeth!”

He went on so, praisin’ up this tragedy like it was a prize-winnin’ hog. Said it was the most heart-rendin’, gut-wrenchin’, soul-shatterin’ performance ever staged. Why, he claimed he’d seen grown men weepin’ at rehearsals! 

And so he did, ramblin’ on ‘til you’d think the play hadn’t even *started* yet, and half the audience was lookin’ at their watches, wonderin’ if maybe a good nap wouldn’t be more thrillingest after all.

text:
The cessation of the range’s unnatural stillness was, in itself, unsettling. Not a silence born of peace, but a vacuum anticipating horror. As the gyroplane, a blasphemous metal insect, shuddered past the final, cyclopean peak – a monolith of basalt that seemed to *lean* against the uncaring stars – the buzzing began. Not the engine, though that throbbed with a sickening regularity, but *within* the skull. A resonance, a sympathetic vibration to something…else.

We descended, slow as a descending nightmare, toward the encampment. Canvas tents, pitifully frail against the immensity of the landscape, huddled like frightened things. The men below, faces obscured by shadow and a peculiar, inward focus, offered no greeting. Their silence wasn’t politeness, but a grim acknowledgement. 

The buzzing intensified, a chorus of unseen wings beating against the membrane of reality. It was not a sound for the ears, but for something deeper, older. And the pledges of secrecy…they were not to protect the world *from* what we’d found, but to protect our sanity *within* it. For to speak of the geometries witnessed, the angles that defied Euclidean law, would be to invite a fracturing of the mind, a glimpse into the cold, uncaring abyss that lay beyond.

Miss Elmsworth, perched upon a stool before the overflowing bookshelves of Longbourn Hall, regarded her cousin with a gentle, yet pointed, air. “It is a comfort, is it not, to consider the accumulation? Not merely of possessions, mind you, but of *knowledge* gathered through so many hands. My grandfather began this collection, you see, with a particular fondness for histories. My father, a more discerning gentleman, added the poets, and then, of course, my brother’s travels brought in volumes of Italian verse.”

“And then you have added so much to it yourself—you are always buying books,” observed Mr. Finch, attempting a lightness he did not quite achieve. He fidgeted with his cravat.

Miss Elmsworth’s lips curved in a small, knowing smile. “One does what one can to continue the good work. It is a responsibility, truly. To allow such treasures to languish, to fall into disrepair… I cannot comprehend the neglect of a family library. It speaks, does it not, to a want of appreciation for all that has come before? A disregard for the very foundations upon which we stand.” She delicately traced the spine of a particularly aged tome. “It is, in a manner, a conversation with our ancestors.”

Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself, despite her best efforts at composure, rather discomfited by Mr. Harding’s attentions. He was, undeniably, a man of fortune, and possessed of a certain… earnestness, which many ladies might deem advantageous. Yet, his compliments, though delivered with a polite inclination of the head, felt less directed *at* her, than *towards* herself – a subtle distinction, perhaps, lost on the less discerning. 

She disdained the appearance of noticing this civil reflection, but its meaning did not escape, nor was it likely to. He spoke of her accomplishments as if cultivating a promising garden, rather than admiring a blooming flower. “Your pianoforte playing, Miss Ainsworth,” he’d declared last evening, “shows a dedication that will undoubtedly refine your character.”

Refine! As if she were some rough-hewn stone requiring polishing. Her sister, observing from across the room, offered a barely suppressed smile. Eleanor, however, maintained a studied indifference, sipping her ratafia and contemplating the unfortunate necessity of enduring such well-intentioned, yet profoundly patronising, regard. A comfortable match, certainly. A *happy* one? That remained, she suspected, a question quite beyond the scope of Mr. Harding’s consideration.

The summons arrived, not with the measured grace of a visiting card, but a breathless flurry of Mrs. Bennet and a near-hysterical Jane trailing in her wake. “Mr. Bennet, you are wanted immediately; we are all in an uproar!” she declared, quite forgetting the proprieties of addressing one’s husband with a modicum of respect. “Lizzy – *Lizzy* – vows she will not have him! Mr. Collins, sir, Mr. Collins! After all we have done to encourage the connection!”

He raised a quizzical eyebrow, continuing to peruse his book. “Indeed? A most decisive young lady. And what, pray tell, is the nature of my intervention to be? Am I to physically compel her to the altar?”

“You must *reason* with her, sir! Explain the advantages! The security! The parsonage! She speaks of a want of affection, as if affection were a necessity in a sensible marriage! It is quite beyond bearing. Kitty is weeping, Mary is lecturing on the folly of romantic inclinations, and Lydia…well, Lydia is simply enjoying the commotion.” 

Mr. Bennet sighed, marking his place with a languid gesture. “A lively scene, then. Very well. Lead on. Though I suspect even my most persuasive arguments will prove insufficient against a determined aversion.”

A most unsettling report had reached the drawing-room, conveyed by Mrs. Higgins with a face quite crumpled with concern. It appeared our niece, Miss Eleanor, was, according to the kitchen-maid, seized with a sudden weakness, a fluttering of the spirits, and a distinct pallor. Naturally, a degree of alarm was unavoidable. One does not lightly dismiss tidings of a young lady’s health, particularly one so prone to romantic flights of fancy, which often manifest as physical complaints.

However, a swift investigation – a brisk walk to the rose garden, accompanied by a pointed inquiry – proved the whole a most egregious exaggeration. Miss Eleanor was not, in fact, ailing, but rather deeply engrossed in a novel, leaning against the sundial with a countenance softened by sentiment. 

Satisfied instantly on that head, and relieved beyond measure, one eagerly communicated the true state of affairs to the assembled company. Mrs. Higgins, though somewhat abashed, declared the kitchen-maid a notorious teller of tales, and a general air of amusement settled upon the room. It is a truth universally acknowledged that a little drama is ever welcome, provided it proves, upon closer inspection, entirely harmless.

The news arrived with Mrs. Philips, breathless and clutching a morning paper, and though delivered with a flurry of exclamation, it was the quiet aftermath that proved most unsettling. Mr. Bingley, it seemed, had secured a most advantageous commission, one that necessitated a prolonged absence from Netherfield. A sigh, barely audible, escaped my lips. It was not for the loss of his company alone that I felt a pang, though his amiable disposition was certainly missed.

The fog, naturally, clung to Arkham like a shroud, but this was a dampness *within* the soul, a chill not of the October air. Eleven lay cold at the Blackwood farm, arranged with a… precision that defied the frantic accounts of the responding constables. Precision born not of malice, but of something utterly *other*. Young Gedney, however, was not amongst them. Simply… absent.

People spoke of shock, of the mind’s merciful obscuring of horrors. They excused our stammered reports, our inability to articulate the *wrongness* of the scene. For what words could convey the geometry of the arrangement? The subtle, sickening scent of ozone and something… older, something predating the hills themselves? 

Old Man Hemlock, before they took him away muttering about angles and non-Euclidean spaces, claimed Gedney hadn’t been *taken*, but… *shifted*. Drawn into a fold, a thinning of the veil. We dismissed it as delirium, yet the unsettling silence where his screams should have been echoed in the hollows of our minds. 

The farm remains sealed, of course. But the fog… the fog feels different now. It *watches*. And I find myself increasingly certain that Gedney is not lost, but… elsewhere. In a place where the laws of God and man hold no sway, and where eleven dead are a paltry sum compared to the cosmic indifference awaiting us all.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The matter had been discussed, of course, in hushed tones amongst the ladies of the village – a certain impropriety, a fleeting glance exchanged too long, a carriage ride taken without proper chaperone. But which I have never acknowledged. It concerned Mr. Hawthorne, a gentleman possessed of a tolerable fortune and, regrettably, a most unsettling habit of observing one with an intensity bordering on rudeness. 

Allowing the case, however, to stand according to your representation, Miss Bennet, that the *feeling* was, however briefly, mutual – a notion I find exceedingly disagreeable – you must remember, Miss Bennet, that the fortune, while comfortable, is not *vast*. And his aunt, the formidable Lady Beatrice, is known to disapprove of any connection not deemed sufficiently advantageous. 

My mother, naturally, sees only the potential for a settled establishment. She speaks of his land, his connections, with a fervour quite unbecoming. I, however, find myself more occupied with the distinct lack of wit in his conversation and the unfortunate shade of brown in his coat. A comfortable life is desirable, certainly, but not at the expense of one’s sensibilities.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The assembly at Hartfield had dispersed, leaving a residue of polite exhaustion and, in my own breast, a most unwelcome disquiet. Mr. Elton, having declared his attentions elsewhere, was, of course, no longer a subject for anxious speculation. Yet, I found myself not rejoicing in the freedom from his unwelcome pursuit, but rather, blaming myself for having done thus much. There is but one part of my conduct, in the whole affair, on which I do not reflect with satisfaction; it is the encouragement, however slight, I may have unwittingly afforded him.

A little too much civility, perhaps, a willingness to believe his compliments genuine, a foolish hope that his regard might be…suitable. Such errors of judgement are, I fear, the province of youthful inexperience, yet they do not lessen the sting of present mortification. My sister, ever practical, assures me I was the object of a mere fancy, and that his affections have swiftly transferred themselves. Still, the thought remains – had I been less amiable, less prone to polite discourse, would this entire, tiresome episode have been avoided? It is a question I suspect will haunt my quiet evenings for some time to come.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Georgiana Darcy, though possessed of a sensibility exceeding most young ladies of her acquaintance, found herself in a peculiar state of agitation. It was not, precisely, a romantic flutter, though Mr. Wickham’s attentions had not been entirely unwelcome. No, this disquiet stemmed from a far more potent source – the approbation of her brother, Fitzwilliam. 

He had, upon his return from Hertfordshire, spoken most favourably of a Miss Elizabeth Bennet. Not with the ardent enthusiasm reserved for those considered truly *eligible*, perhaps, but with a measured praise that, to Georgiana, was infinitely more persuasive. A recommendation was enough to insure her favour; his judgment could not err; and he had spoken in such terms of Elizabeth, as to leave Georgiana without a doubt of the young lady’s good sense and amiable disposition.

Indeed, the very notion of a connection, however distant, to a person so esteemed by Fitzwilliam, filled her with a quiet anticipation. She found herself re-arranging her pianoforte pieces, hoping to demonstrate a proficiency worthy of mention in any future discourse concerning her accomplishments, should the opportunity arise to meet this Miss Bennet. A most agreeable prospect, truly.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The air hung thick and viscous, tasting of dust older than continents and a nameless, oily decay. It clung to the lungs, a premonition of suffocation not from lack of oxygen, but from *wrongness*. I should have heeded the villagers’ frantic warnings, their guttural pleas to leave the Black Mire undisturbed. But the lure of the forgotten… it proved too potent.

Out of that blasphemous tunnel, carved not by any tool known to Euclidean geometry, I stumbled. The floors were greasily smooth, as if perpetually slick with some ichorous secretion, and echoed with a silence that pressed upon the mind. And the murals… gods preserve me from recalling the murals. 

They depicted things *almost* familiar – fish with human hands, birds with the faces of aged, leering men, geometries that shifted and writhed before the eye. Degenerate mockeries, aping and mocking the forms they had superseded, hinting at a lineage too terrible to contemplate. Each stroke felt less painted, more *grown*, a fungal blossoming of cosmic horror. 

Run back, b. Before the angles begin to whisper. Before the slickness claims your feet. Before *they* notice you’ve seen. The Mire remembers. And it hungers.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The building loomed, not with the arrogant thrust of modern steel, but with a sickening, organic sprawl. Each window, a vacant, obsidian eye staring into the perpetual twilight of the alley. Within, a labyrinth of apartments – not rooms, precisely, but accretions, barnacles upon a decaying hull. The floorplans, gleaned from a maddeningly incomplete registry, proved…illusory. Corridors shifted, stairwells ended in blank, plaster voids, and the numbering system devolved into a blasphemous, non-Euclidean jumble. 

We had determined, after days of fruitless charting, that a conventional approach was doomed. The very *geometry* of the place resisted reason. Thus, with a dread that settled like ichor in the lungs, we decided that we must begin our system of hare-and-hound trail blazing. Hitherto our compasses, together with the meticulously drawn maps, had been mockeries, pointing not North, but *inward*, towards some unseen, pulsating core. 

Old Man Hemlock, the building’s sole, gibbering custodian, had warned of “the currents,” of walls that breathed and doorways that…*remembered*. Now, marking our path with phosphorescent chalk, we felt those currents ourselves – a subtle drag, a whispering pressure against the mind, hinting at a sentience woven into the very fabric of the dwelling. A sentience that did not welcome intrusion.
author: H.P. Lovecraft
