Old Man Tiber, he was a study, a right proper study in exasperation. He stood there, hands on hips, lookin’ down at young Billy Pruitt like Billy was a particularly stubborn mule. Billy, he was fidgetin’, eyes dartin’ ‘round the general store like a trapped rabbit.

“Now, Billy,” Tiber commenced, slow and deliberate, “don’t you try to play innocent with *me*. That hat. Your Sunday-go-to-meetin’ hat. It’s… *off*, because—” He paused, drawin’ a breath that could curdle milk. “Because you hain’t got but one *on*! Just *listen* at the man! I saw you, clear as day, settin’ it atop old Bess, pretendin’ she was a queen. A *queen*, Billy!”

Billy mumbled somethin’ ‘bout Bess bein’ regal.

Tiber just shook his head. “*I* know you took it off, and know it by a better way than your words. A boy don’t get that particular shade of sheepish unless he’s been up to no good. And a fine hat don’t belong on a beast of burden, no sir. Now, fetch it. And don’t you go tryin’ to tell me Bess needed protectin’ from the sun. Bess ain’t got no sensibilities about sunburn.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, it was a sight to make a body question the use of reason, truly. Old Man Hemlock, he stood there on the dusty road, lookin’ like a scarecrow struck by lightnin’. And he was hollerin’, mind you, hollerin’ fit to wake the dead. Not about taxes, nor the price of corn, but about *children*.

Said a fella, a stranger I’d never laid eyes on before – a Mr. Abernathy, from up county – had the audacity to claim ownership of his young’uns. Claim ‘em! And then, get this, Hemlock, he just *out flat-footed* declared he’d steal ‘em back. Steal ‘em!

Now, Abernathy hadn’t wronged Hemlock a particle, so far as anyone knew. Didn’t owe him a cent, hadn’t insulted his prize-winning sow, nothin’. Just…had children Hemlock decided he had a claim to. 

Folks just stood around, scratchin’ their heads. It was a spectacle, I tell you. A pure, unadulterated spectacle of a man threatenin’ grand larceny over babes he hadn’t even bothered to *ask* for. The whole thing smelled of sunstroke and bad whiskey, and I reckon a good dose of pure, unmitigated foolishness.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The assembly at Netherfield had progressed with its usual blend of tolerable conversation and pointed silences. Mr. Darcy, as was his wont, observed the company with an air bordering on disdain, though he endeavoured to conceal it beneath a mask of polite indifference. Miss Elizabeth Bennet, however, possessed a spirit too lively to be entirely subdued by such scrutiny. 

He had, with a gravity most unbecoming a social occasion, remarked upon her family’s connections, a slight delivered with the precision of a surgeon’s blade. To him, which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she turned to him and said,— “Did not you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself uncommonly plainly? For I assure you, sir, I am perfectly aware of the deficiencies of my relations, and require no gentleman’s condescension to point them out.”

A flush rose in his cheeks, a most unusual spectacle. He stammered a reply, something concerning the necessity of prudence and the importance of social standing, but his usual composure was clearly ruffled. Elizabeth, though inwardly amused, maintained a demure countenance, allowing him to believe he had, at least, elicited a degree of proper mortification. The evening, she suspected, had become considerably more interesting.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The basalt was…wrong. Not in its composition – spectroscopic analysis yielded expected iron content, silicate structure – but in its *feel*. A coldness that transcended temperature, a subtle vibration against the palm that resonated not in the bone, but somewhere…deeper. We’d dredged it from the abyssal plain designated ‘Sector Gamma-Nine’, a region previously uncharted, and possessing a disconcerting flatness that defied all known tectonic principles.

Old Man Hemlock, the geologist, muttered incessantly about non-Euclidean angles and the unsettling symmetry of the formations revealed by sonar. He insisted the strata weren’t *layered* so much as…*arranged*. As if by a will not geological, but…intentional. 

Our health so far had remained excellent – lime juice well offset the creeping dampness of the *Argonaut* – yet a pervasive unease settled upon the crew. Dreams, vivid and geometrically impossible, plagued our sleep. The basalt, we agreed, was desirable for purposes of comparison with other anomalous finds, but a growing dread suggested it was not merely a specimen to be studied, but a fragment of something vast, ancient, and profoundly *other* that wished to remain undisturbed. A silence, heavier than the ocean above, clung to Sector Gamma-Nine, and I feared we had broken it.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The assurances of my gratitude, I trust, will speedily receive from me a letter of thanks for this as well as for every other mark of your regard during my stay in Hertfordshire. Indeed, the kindness extended to me by your family has been a source of the most agreeable reflection, and I find myself already regretting my departure from Longbourn. 

As for my father, his health, though never robust, continues to permit him a degree of enjoyment. He speaks most favourably of your acquaintance, though, as you may imagine, his pronouncements are often delivered with a certain…brevity. He possesses, you see, a temperament not given to effusive praise, preferring to demonstrate his approval through a quiet contentment. 

Miss Bennet, however, is quite overcome with delight at the prospect of recounting all my adventures upon my return. She has a facility for embellishment, I fear, which may render her narrative somewhat… expansive. Still, her good heart is beyond reproach, and her enthusiasm is, at least, diverting. I remain, with the highest esteem, your most obedient servant.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth, newly arrived at the assembly, presented a study in quietude most remarkable. One might have deemed her possessed of a melancholy disposition, were it not for the faint blush that frequently stole into her cheeks, betraying a sensibility rather than a sorrow. A mere five minutes of observation, however, convinced her companion, Miss Penrose, that the young lady was not, in truth, afflicted by any deep unhappiness, but only exceedingly shy.

Indeed, to elicit even a single word beyond a monosyllable proved a task of considerable difficulty. Questions regarding the music, the company, even the weather, were met with a barely audible “Yes,” or a hesitant “No.” Her gaze, though bright, darted about the room, avoiding all direct contact, settling briefly upon the floral arrangements before flitting away again. 

It was a delicacy of nature, Miss Penrose considered, not a defect. A sensibility so easily overwhelmed required gentle handling, and a patience she was quite prepared to exercise. For though Miss Elmsworth offered little in the way of conversation, there was a certain grace in her silence, a promise of a spirit worth cultivating, should one but possess the skill to draw it forth.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, a body doesn’t rightly *mean* to pull out a clump of hair, understand. It just…comes with the territory of wrestling with a particularly stubborn notion. This one concerned Old Man Hemlock’s prize boar, a creature of considerable girth and even more considerable ill-temper. The notion being, of course, that bacon was a necessity, not a luxury. 

The axe felt good in the hand, though. Solid. A fella can tell a good axe, just like a good woman – dependable, and won’t let you down when you need her most. I blooded the blade proper, a good, satisfying *thwack* against the chopping block, and stuck it, handle-down, right smack dab on the back side of the woodpile. A fella likes things orderly.

Then I took up the pig. Lord, but that animal was slick. Held him by the ears, I did, and he squealed like a stuck whistle. A powerful, indignant squeal. Didn’t much matter to the bacon, though, did it? No sir. A body’s gotta do what a body’s gotta do, even if it leaves a man a bit…flustered, and a little lighter on top.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The geometries were…wrong. Not merely askew to Euclidean understanding, but *actively* hostile to it, pressing upon the mind with a nauseating insistence. We had breached the final stratum, a cyclopean chamber pulsing with a luminescence not of any known spectrum. It was here they resided – the Dominants.

Not beings of flesh, precisely, but constructs of obsidian angles and shifting, iridescent voids. Their presence wasn’t felt, but *calculated* – a cold, precise assessment of our insignificance. The initial scouting parties, naturally, succumbed to gibbering madness. Those were…resolved. Mechanically. Efficiently. 

It interested us, in these final, decaying epochs of our expedition, to observe their indifference. They did not *notice* our exterminations of the lesser, bothersome forms – the chittering, protoplasmic servitors that writhed at the periphery of their awareness. These were merely…adjustments. Like dust motes disturbed by a cosmic breeze. 

But in the last, most decadent pulsations of the chamber’s light, a single, impossible facet of a Dominant *shifted*. A slow, deliberate rotation. And I felt, with a dread that transcended language, that *something* had finally registered our presence. Not as a threat, but as…a curiosity. A fleeting, horrifying thought before the darkness claimed all.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Old Man Tiberius, he was sittin’ on the porch, whittlin’ a piece of pine into somethin’ vaguely resembling a hound dog. I sidled up, bein’ as how I was tasked with findin’ out what all the ruckus was about down by the creek. Young Jebediah, he’d taken a shot at Silas Hemlock, clean missed, thankfully, but stirred up a hornet’s nest all the same.

“Tiberius,” I says, “folks are talkin’. They’re askin’ what in tarnation possessed Jebediah to aim a rifle at a man.”

Tiberius didn’t look up from his whittlin’. “Do to you?” he finally drawled, lookin’ at me like I was simple. “Him? He never done nothin’ to me.”

I blinked. “Well, then, what did you want to kill him *for*?”

He finally glanced up, a slow, weary look in his eye. “Why, nothin’—only it’s on account of the feud.” 

I near choked on my own spit. “What feud? Silas Hemlock sold Jebediah’s pa a mule that was three teeth short and a disposition to kick, nigh on forty years ago!”

Tiberius just shrugged, and went back to his dog. “Seems like a good enough reason to me.”

text:
CHAPTER VII. “Git up! What you ’bout?” I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to make out where I was. It was after sun-up, and I had been sound asleep, plumb forgot how I come to be stretched out on a pile o’ burlap sacks behind Old Man Hemlock’s mercantile. A right sorry bed, truth be told, smelled powerfully of potatoes and disappointment.

Old Man Tiber, Hemlock’s hired hand – a feller built like a woodchuck and with about the same amount o’ conversation – was proddin’ me with a broom handle. “Thought you’d sprouted roots, boy. Hemlock wants that crate o’ peaches unloaded. Says you promised.”

Promised? Now *there* was a wrinkle. My memory, it seemed, had taken a holiday. I recollect a bit o’ cider at the Blue Moon Saloon, and a friendly game o’ cards with a feller claimin’ to be a traveling salesman… but peaches? Unloadin’ ‘em? 

“Seems I…misremembered the particulars, Tiber,” I offered, tryin’ for a tone of dignified recollection. 

Tiber just grunted. “Misremembered your way into a heap o’ trouble, more like. Git to it. Them peaches ain’t gonna unload themselves, and Hemlock’s temper is shorter’n a politician’s promise.”
author: Mark Twain

text: None of our exploring party had ever been in the polar regions before, hence we all relied greatly on our ship captains--J. B. Douglas, commanding the brig _Arkham_, and serving as commander of the sea party, and Georg Thorfinnssen, commanding the barque _Miskatonic_--both veteran whalers in antarctic waters. As we left the inhabited world behind the sun sank lower and lower in the north, and stayed longer and longer above the horizon each day. At about 62° South Latitude we sighted our first icebergs--tablelike objects with vertical sides--and just before reaching the antarctic circle, which we crossed on October 20th with appropriately quaint ceremonies, we were considerably troubled with field ice. The falling temperature bothered me considerably after our long voyage through the tropics, but I tried to brace up for the worse rigors to come. On many occasions the curious atmospheric effects enchanted me vastly; these included a strikingly vivid mirage--the first I had ever seen--in which distant bergs became the battlements of unimaginable cosmic castles. Pushing through the ice, which was fortunately neither extensive nor thickly packed, we regained open water at South Latitude 67°, East Longitude 175°. text:
The world, it must be confessed, does offer a rather wider scope for amusement than Hunsford Parsonage. One cannot but perceive, upon reflection, how limited are its prospects, how circumscribed its society, to a young lady accustomed to a more varied existence. Yet, one endeavours to cultivate a grateful spirit. Indeed, we *must* believe ourselves fortunate for the condescension displayed in being received at all. 

Mrs. Phillips, bless her well-meaning heart, assures me it is a most respectable connection, and that Mr. Collins, though perhaps lacking in…polish, is a man of property. A consideration not to be lightly dismissed, naturally. Still, the evenings stretch long, filled with discussions of parish matters and the precise arrangement of the shrubbery. 

One hopes, of course, to make the best of it. To offer polite conversation, to demonstrate a willingness to be instructed. But a secret sigh escapes me when contemplating the lively assemblies and engaging company left behind. We are, undeniably, grateful for the invitation, and trust our hosts will not perceive any undue lack of enthusiasm – merely a natural consequence of a youthful disposition finding itself…temporarily constrained.
author: Jane Austen

text:
“What a young man ought to be,” said she, adjusting the lace at her sleeve with a delicate air, “sensible, good-humoured, lively; and I never saw such happy manners! So much ease, with such perfect good breeding. Mr. Ashworth, you perceive, possesses all these qualities in a degree most gratifying.”

Miss Penrose, ever the attentive listener, offered a small, approving nod. “Indeed, Mama. Though one might wish for a slightly larger fortune, his prospects are not entirely disagreeable. He speaks of his estate with a becoming modesty, and did not, I observed, dwell upon its advantages with any vulgar ostentation.”

“Modesty is a virtue, certainly,” her mother conceded, though a flicker of calculation crossed her face. “But a comfortable income is not to be dismissed lightly. Still, his conversation! So free from the tiresome pedantry of some young gentlemen, and yet demonstrably informed. He inquired after my roses with a genuine interest, and even remembered my preference for the ‘Cramoisie Supérieure’ variety.”

Miss Penrose sighed contentedly. “A gentleman who appreciates roses, Mama. It speaks volumes.”

text:
The surveyor, old Man Hemlock, had vanished near the Blackwood mire, leaving only his meticulously kept notes and a sketch that chilled the marrow. It depicted not a geological formation, nor any known artifact, but *something* else. A cyclopean extrusion, he’d called it, though the term felt woefully inadequate.

The dimensions were the crux of the horror. Length, a sickening thirteen and eight tenths feet. Central diameter, three and five tenths – a girth suggesting impossible internal volume. But it was the *form* that truly unsettled. Not round, not precisely, but a grotesque parody of a barrel, yet lacking staves. Instead, five obscene, bulging ridges ran its length, pulsing faintly in Hemlock’s rendering, like the distended veins of some monstrous, subterranean thing. 

The ends, he noted with a trembling hand, tapered to a mere foot, almost…pointed. As if designed not for containment, but for *insertion*. He’d scribbled frantically about a non-Euclidean geometry inherent in its curves, a sickening dissonance that threatened to unravel the very fabric of perception. 

The mire exhaled a fetid breath. I dared not venture closer, for the sketch hinted at a dreadful, pre-human purpose, a silent testament to geometries best left undisturbed, and a dread that clung to the soul like grave-dust.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
“You have done all this! and yet you can treat the mention of his misfortunes with contempt and ridicule.” The words, though delivered with a restraint bordering on severity, struck Miss Eleanor with a force quite disproportionate to their measured tone. She had, admittedly, permitted a small, perhaps uncharitable, observation regarding Mr. Wickham’s recent…difficulties with a certain gaming debt. A difficulty, she’d thought, entirely of his own making.

“And this,” cried Darcy, as he walked with quickened pace along the shrubbery, “is precisely the failing I find most…vexing. A want of compassion, masked as good sense! To dismiss another’s hardship as merely the consequence of imprudence is not discernment, Miss Eleanor, but a chilling indifference.”

She flushed, mortified. To be lectured on sensibility by *him*! Yet, a prickle of discomfort stirred within her. He spoke with a conviction that unsettled her usual composure. Was she, in her eagerness to appear rational, neglecting a duty of common humanity? The thought was most disagreeable, and yet, undeniably, possessed a certain…truth. She lowered her gaze, the gravel path suddenly appearing intensely fascinating.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The salt-laced wind, perpetually damp, carried no scent of the familiar. Old Man Hemlock had warned against venturing so far along the Widow’s Strand at twilight, muttering of ‘thin places’ and things best left undisturbed. We, of course, dismissed it as the ramblings of a senile mind, eager to chart the coastline for geological curiosities. It was not the geology that unsettled us, however.

At first, it was a dissonance, a subtle wrongness in the very *texture* of the air. The gulls’ cries lacked their usual brazen quality, becoming thin, reedy wails that seemed to echo not *from* the sky, but *within* the skull. Then, the tide. It did not ebb and flow with the predictable rhythm of the moon, but pulsed, a sluggish, organic breathing against the black, basalt rocks. 

We had had a dog with us, I suppose, it would have been warned before. But we were alone, and the silence, broken only by that dreadful, internal echoing and the breathing tide, pressed upon us with a weight that bordered on physical pain. A creeping dread, cold and viscous, began to coil around the heart, whispering of geometries beyond human comprehension, and a presence… something *watching* from the swirling, grey mist.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I’d been orderin’ up a batch of them picture shows – the kind with the fellas in ‘em doin’ grand things, and ladies lookin’ like angels dipped in sunshine. Figured Jim, he deserved a bit o’ beauty in his cabin, seein’ as how his life hadn’t been overflowin’ with it. 

But Lordy, them pictures. One showed a fella rescuin’ a kitten from a burnin’ buildin’, lookin’ right heroic. Another, a mother holdin’ a babe, peaceful as a summer evenin’. Then there was one of a dog, a hound it was, lookin’ up at a boy with a loyalty that near wrung my heart clean out.

I tell you, I plumb *broke down*. Not sobbin’, mind you, but a lump formed in my throat bigger’n a goose egg. Each one told a story, a little piece of goodness in a world that mostly dealt in hard knocks. 

When I got done lookin’, I couldn’t no way decide which one Jim ought to scratch onto the cabin wall with his charcoal. The kitten? The babe? That loyal hound? They all deserved a place, and me, I was flustered as a hen in a hailstorm. It was a powerful predicament, I reckon.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, it wasn’t every day a feller like old Man Hemlock found himself swimmin’ in coin. Not after a lifetime of wrestlin’ a livin’ from stubborn soil and even stubborner mules. But a distant cousin, a shipping magnate out West, up and kicked the bucket, leavin’ Hemlock everything – and I mean *everything*.

First came the clothes. Lordy, the clothes! Velvet jackets enough to outfit a traveling theatre troupe, trousers that pinched in all the wrong places, and boots polished so bright a body could shave in ‘em. Then the books. Mountains of ‘em. Histories, poetry, treatises on things a man didn’t *need* to know, like the proper way to address a Duke. 

And a spyglass, mind you, a proper brass one, for lookin’ at ships that weren’t even *on* the river. But the real treasure? Three boxes of seegars. Not the chawin’ kind, no sir. These were for *smokin’*, and smelled like sunshine and trouble. 

We hadn’t ever been this rich before in neithe. Ma nearly fainted dead away. Pa just sat on the porch, puffin’ one of them seegars, lookin’ like a king who’d accidentally wandered into a haberdashery. It was a spectacle, I tell you, a right proper spectacle.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Bingley was by no means deficient in agreeable qualities; possessed of a cheerful disposition and a fortune sufficient to render him eligible in any society. Yet, Mr. Darcy was clever. It was a distinction universally acknowledged, and one which, though not openly proclaimed by those who benefited from Mr. Bingley’s good humour, was nonetheless keenly felt. 

He was at the same time haughty, reserved, and fastidious; and his manners, though undeniably polished, lacked the warmth which might have rendered him truly amiable. One could not but observe a certain air of condescension, a subtle implication that the company present rarely met his exacting standards. Miss Bennet, particularly, found herself subjected to a scrutiny so penetrating it bordered on the impertinent. 

Indeed, it was not merely his wealth, though considerable, that set him apart. It was a superiority of *mind*, he seemed to suggest, a capacity for discernment which placed him quite beyond the reach of common understanding. A frustrating quality, to be sure, yet one which, despite oneself, commanded a reluctant respect.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The static crackled, a blasphemous whisper from the void, yet Pabodie’s voice, though attenuated, held a disturbing cheer. We spoke of the dig, of course. Not the *what* of the dig – that remained, thankfully, unvoiced – but the *how*. He was, unsettlingly, fixated on the machinery.

“Marvelous drills, old friend, truly marvelous!” he rasped, the signal momentarily dissolving into a chorus of subterranean groans. “The tungsten carbide, you see, held against… against things no steel should withstand. They bit through the basalt as if it were crumbling shale. And the pneumatic hammers! Oh, the resonance they induced…”

A cold dread coiled within me. Resonance. He spoke of it with a ghastly enthusiasm, as if the vibrations weren’t merely fracturing stone, but *awakening* something. He continued, detailing the specific model, the manufacturer’s obscure Bavarian origins, the unsettlingly precise calibrations. 

Each description felt less like technical discussion and more like a litany, a summoning. He praised their efficiency, their relentless, unyielding power. Power that had, undeniably, breached a barrier best left undisturbed. The static swelled, and I feared, with a sickening certainty, that the drills hadn’t merely unearthed a place, but *opened* a door.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Well, I was dozing off again, plumb lost to the world like a catfish in the mud, when I thinks I hears a deep sound of “boom!” away up the river. Not a cannon, mind you, not a proper explosion, but a sort of… *settling* boom. Like the world itself had just shifted in its sleep. 

I rouses up, and rests on my elbows, listenin’. Old Man Tiber ain’t never quiet, but this weren’t the usual churn and gurgle. No sir. This was a call to action, a nudge from Providence, I reckoned. And Providence, as near as I could figure, was tellin’ me it was high time to wrestle with a skillet.

A body can’t rightly contemplate the mysteries of the universe on an empty stomach, you see. So I swung my legs over the side, feelin’ every one of my years protest. The floorboards groaned a complaint, and the cat, that lazy varmint, barely flickered an eye. 

Bacon, I decided. Bacon and eggs. A man needs sustenance to ponder booms, and a good fry-up was the only sensible response to a world that felt like it was rearrangin’ itself. It was a bother, of course, but a feller’s gotta do what a feller’s gotta do.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he weren’t a feller known for much beyond a stubborn streak and a fondness for patching his britches. But he *did* have a mule. Bess, she was called, and a more contrary beast you never did see. Hemlock, he declared Bess possessed a talent – a talent for *dyin’ dramatically*. 

He’d stage it, you see. A bit of flour dusted on her nose for paleness, a mournful drape of burlap, and Hemlock, wailin’ like a banshee, proclaimin’ Bess had succumbed to a rare mule-ague. First time, folks felt bad, offered condolences. Second time, they were suspicious. Third? Well, that’s when Hemlock started chargin’ a nickel a head to witness the spectacle.

“Come one, come all!” he’d bellow, “Behold the passin’ of a noble creature! A tragedy for the ages!” 

Folks grumbled, but curiosity, it’s a powerful thing. Bess, she’d just stand there, lookin’ bored, while Hemlock carried on. After the show, he’d declare, “Well, she rallied! A miraculous recovery!” and send ‘em all home, tellin’ ‘em, “Go along home, and advise everybody to come and see the tragedy.” Next day you couldn’t hear nothing around that town but how splendid. A nickel a head, and a mule with a knack for pretendin’. It was a marvel, I tell ya, a pure American marvel.
author: Mark Twain

Now, Old Man Tiber, he had a notion for bread unlike any you’d find this side of the Mississippi. Not baked in an oven, mind you, but *on* the roof of his shed. A roof he’d plastered thick with dough, a right sticky mess it was to look at. Folks said he was touched, but Tiber, he just chuckled and went about his business.

He’d slap the loaves right onto that dough, then carefully cover ‘em with another layer, sealing ‘em in tight as a politician’s promise. Then came the curious part. He’d heap hot embers – not flames, mind you, just glowin’ coals – right atop the dough lid. 

Stood back five foot, he did, with a long-handled poker, lookin’ cool and comfortable as a judge at a picnic. Said it was the even heat, see? No scorchin’, no underbakin’. 

And wouldn’t you know it, in fifteen minutes – not a minute more, not a minute less – he’d poke at the embers, lift the lid, and there it was. Bread, golden brown and smellin’ like heaven itself. A peculiar method, yes, but a mighty fine loaf, I tell you. Peculiar, but effective. Just like most things in this world, when you get right down to it.

text:
Miss Eleanor had been accustomed to Mr. Hawthorne’s reserve, a coolness bordering, she feared, on indifference. His visits to Barton Cottage were invariably brief, his conversation polite but devoid of warmth, and his gaze, though not unkind, rarely lingered. Thus, the alteration in his demeanour this morning was quite startling. He had spoken of the recent rains with genuine interest, inquired after her aunt’s embroidery with a solicitousness most unexpected, and even – *even* – offered a compliment upon the arrangement of the roses in the drawing-room.

“He was remarkably agreeable,” Eleanor confided to her uncle, Sir Thomas, during their morning walk. “Indeed, I believe I have never seen him so pleasant.”

Sir Thomas, a man of considerable observation and a dry wit, chuckled softly. “He is a gentleman of peculiar habits, my dear. A scholar, lost in his books, and somewhat…unpractised in the art of social ease.” He paused, adjusting his spectacles. “But perhaps he may be a little whimsical in his civilities,” replied her uncle, “and one should not read too much into a temporary brightening of his disposition.” Eleanor, however, found herself hoping it was *not* temporary, and that a more amiable Mr. Hawthorne had, at last, revealed himself.

text:
The pronouncement regarding Mr. Featherstone’s unexpected engagement, though delivered with a commendable lack of theatricality by Miss Penrose, was nevertheless a shock. As such pauses must always be, succeeded for a few moments. A delicate stillness descended upon the drawing-room, broken only by the ticking of the ormolu clock and the barely perceptible rustle of silk gowns. 

It was first broken by Mrs. Annesley, a genteel, agreeable-looking woman, whose endeavour to maintain composure was, perhaps, a trifle *too* pronounced. “Good heavens!” she exclaimed, fanning herself with a vigour quite unnecessary given the pleasant warmth of the fire. “To think of Mr. Featherstone, and Miss Lovelace! A most…unexpected union.”

Lady Beatrice, however, merely raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow. “Unexpected, certainly,” she murmured, her tone suggesting a deeper understanding than she chose to reveal. “Though one might argue, my dear Mrs. Annesley, that Mr. Featherstone has always possessed a predilection for the…unconventional.” 

A ripple of suppressed amusement passed through the room. The subject, it seemed, was open for discussion, and the afternoon promised to be considerably more diverting than anticipated.
author: Jane Austen

Old Man Hemlock, he was a study. A right peculiar cuss, always sniffin’ at progress and declarin’ the world was goin’ to pot. But lately, he’d taken to religion, sudden as a summer thunderstorm. Not the quiet, contemplatin’ kind, mind you. No, sir. This was a *loud* religion.

He’d cornered young Timmy Gable down by the creek, lookin’ flustered as a hen in a hailstorm. “Get religion, too!” he boomed, wavin’ a hand like he was swatting flies. “I never see such a son.” 

He took up a little blue and yaller picture of some cows and a boy, and says: “What’s this?”

Timmy, bless his heart, stammered, “It’s…somethin’ Miss Abigail gave me, sir. A Sunday school reward.”

Hemlock squinted. “Reward for *what*? For bein’ a heathen? For not seein’ the light? Boy, you gotta *feel* it! It ain’t about pictures of bovines, it’s about a feelin’ in yer gut! A powerful, tremblin’ feelin’!” He then proceeded to describe this feelin’ for a good ten minutes, mostly involvin’ comparisons to indigestion and a runaway mule. Timmy just nodded, wishin’ he’d stayed home and practiced whittlin’.

Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a caution. Folks said he’d gone plumb sour, lost his luck with the silver mines and taken to mutterin’ at clouds. Said nothin’ good would *ever* come of this patch of land again, not even a decent crop of weeds. But I reckon folks are quick to write off a man, and a field, too.

I was clearin’ out his shed – doin’ a bit of work for his niece, a sensible girl – and it was a sorry sight. Dust thicker than a Mississippi fog, tools rusted solid, and a general air of give-up-and-die about the place. Still, there was somethin’…persistent. A half-finished birdhouse, for one. And a pile of seed catalogues, dog-eared and marked with pencil.

Might come good, I thought. It just might. 

There was a boy’s old speckled straw hat on the floor; I took that, too. Good for shadin’ my eyes while I worked. And there was a bottle that had had milk in it, and it had a faint, sweet smell clingin’ to the glass. Reminded me of summer and possibilities. Even a busted-up old shed, I figured, could hold a whisper of hope. A fella just had to listen close.

Now, the river was a-rollin’ along like a contented hog in the mud, and we was makin’ good time, considerin’. But a fella couldn’t rightly *enjoy* good time with that Duke’s foolishness weighin’ on a body. He’d been a-tinkerin’ in the printin’ office of that one-horse town, spouting about “warnings” and “public service,” which translated, in my estimation, to stirrin’ up a hornet’s nest of trouble. 

Old Jim, he was fretful. Said he’d heard tell of powwows – gatherings of folks with long memories and shorter tempers – that could follow a man clear to kingdom come if he’d riled ‘em enough. And the Duke, with his fancy talk and printed lies, had riled ‘em plenty.

So we laid to, makin’ miles enough that night to get clean out of the reach of whatever ruckus we reckoned was brewin’. text:
The static clung, a greasy film upon the ether. It wasn’t merely radio interference, but a *presence* within the wavelengths, a cold, geometrical wrongness that prickled the scalp and tasted of ozone and ancient dust. Agreed, the initial signal from the Miskatonic expedition had been received – a frantic, fragmented plea concerning cyclopean masonry and a luminescence not of this sun – but thereafter, silence. A silence more terrifying than any scream.

Some electrical condition in the disturbed air to the westward seemed to prevent communication. Each attempt to re-establish contact yielded only that same insidious hiss, punctuated by fleeting, non-Euclidean echoes. Old Man Hemlock, the operator, swore the sound *shifted*, resolving momentarily into something…vocal. Not human, certainly. More akin to the grinding of basalt against basalt, or the sigh of a wind across a landscape utterly devoid of life.

We did, however, get the _Arkham_, and Dou. The freighter, responding to our relayed distress call, reported sighting an unnatural aurora borealis over the plateau, a sickly, pulsating green that defied all known atmospheric phenomena. And Dou… poor, stammering Dou, the junior cartographer, arrived babbling of angles that shouldn’t *be*, of a city built before time, and of eyes… countless, lidless eyes watching from the black gulfs between the stars. He hasn’t spoken coherently since.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The matter had been settled, quite to the satisfaction of everyone present save, perhaps, Miss Elizabeth. Mr. Harding’s proposal, delivered with a commendable, if somewhat breathless, sincerity, had been accepted by her sister, the amiable Jane. A general murmur of approval rippled through the room, compliments bestowed upon the happy couple with a warmth that bordered on effusiveness. 

Yet Elizabeth, though offering the requisite congratulations, had turned away her head. Presuming, however, that this studied avoidance spoke rather of a momentary embarrassment than an actual disinclination, Mrs. Bennet declared it merely the effect of surprise. A most natural reaction, she assured anyone who would listen, and one entirely befitting a sister so devoted.

Mr. Bennet, observing the scene with his customary detachment, raised a sardonic eyebrow. He knew his Elizabeth. It was not surprise that clouded her features, but something altogether more complex. A delicate consideration, perhaps, or a quiet regret for possibilities not chosen. He suspected, with a familiar amusement, that the quiet of Longbourn would soon be disturbed by a flurry of pointed observations and carefully veiled criticisms. The wedding, he thought, would be *most* interesting.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The reports from the dig were… unsettling, even for a man accustomed to the geological obscenities of the West. Not the strata themselves – though the basalt was of a hue no textbook described, a sickly violet veined with ochre – but the *manner* of their disruption. The borings, initially routine, yielded not core samples, but a hollow resonance, a sickening thrum that vibrated in the teeth. Then came the blastings.

Each detonation, intended to loosen the stubborn rock, seemed to *answer* something. A deeper, echoing concussion that wasn’t merely seismic. Fragments exhumed bore markings – not glyphs, not runes, but a geometry that defied Euclidean comprehension, angles that felt… *wrong*. They weren’t carved, but *grown*, as if the stone itself had yielded to an alien impulse. 

He was strangely convinced that the marking wasn’t meant for eyes, but for something… other. Something that listened with a sense beyond sight, a resonance attuned to the fracturing of the earth. The foreman spoke of nightmares, of a cold wind even in the desert heat, and a pervasive sense of being *watched* from below. He dismissed it as sunstroke, but the unsettling thrum persisted, and with each blast, the feeling grew: they weren’t uncovering a formation, but *awakening* one.

text:
Miss Eleanor Penrose, though by no means capital in beauty – possessing, rather, a pleasing regularity of feature and a complexion inclined to the rose – found herself the centre of a small, yet flattering, attention. The evening at the Thornewoods was progressing with its usual decorum; polite conversation regarding the late harvest, the merits of Mr. Wilmot’s new carriage horses, and the lamentable state of Lady Beatrice’s gout. 

After a song or two, and before she could reply to the entreaties of several that she would sing again, she was eagerly summoned by Mr. Finch, a gentleman of considerable fortune, though lamentably deficient in wit. He offered a compliment upon her voice, delivered with a breathless earnestness that suggested more was intended than mere musical appreciation. 

Eleanor, accustomed to such clumsy overtures, offered a demure acknowledgement. Her sister, Marianne, observing the exchange from across the room, raised a delicately arched eyebrow. It was, Marianne thought, a most predictable circumstance. Mr. Finch, lacking the discernment to appreciate a truly fine mind, would invariably fix upon the most readily available accomplishment. Eleanor, however, possessed a fortitude that belied her gentle appearance, and Marianne had no doubt she would manage the situation with her customary grace.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself in a most uncomfortable position, seated opposite Mr. Finch at a small, rather dusty table in the tea rooms. He had, with a regrettable lack of discretion, confided in her regarding a… *misunderstanding* with the eldest Miss Penrose. A misunderstanding involving a misplaced sonnet and a rather fervent declaration, delivered, it appeared, under the misapprehension of reciprocal sentiment.

“It were to get round to the lady’s family,” Mr. Finch lamented, stirring his tea with unnecessary vigour, “an unpleasant thing indeed. The Penroses are, as you know, possessed of a certain… rigidity.”

Eleanor offered a sympathetic inclination of her head. “Indeed. Their connections are most respectable, and their expectations, correspondingly high.”

“You may depend upon my not mentioning it,” he assured her, his voice a low murmur. “The whole affair is best forgotten, buried beneath a mountain of polite conversation.”

Eleanor’s gaze met his, a delicate firmness within it. “And remember that I have not… heard a word of this. Do not, I implore you, consider me a confidante in such delicate matters. My silence is absolute.” The weight of the Penroses’ potential displeasure pressed heavily upon her own composure.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a tolerable degree of good sense, found herself in a most vexing predicament. The assembly at Netherfield had promised a delightful evening – a succession of country dances, the eligible Mr. Wickham’s attentions a most agreeable prospect. Yet, fate, it seemed, delighted in irony. For scarcely had the first set concluded, and Miss Eleanor begun to anticipate a further conversation with the gentleman, than Mr. Collins, with an air of self-importance that bordered on the ludicrous, requested her hand.

Those very dances; and to have Mr. Collins instead!—her liveliness had been never worse timed. A blush, she feared, betrayed her dismay, though she endeavoured to mask it with a polite, if strained, smile. There was no help for it, however. Mr. Wickham’s happiness, and indeed her own composure, demanded a degree of fortitude. 

She suffered through the reel, enduring a monologue on the virtues of Rosings and the necessity of proper estate management. Each turn brought her no nearer to escape, and each pronouncement from Mr. Collins felt a fresh assault upon her sensibilities. One could only hope, she thought, that the evening would swiftly conclude, and that Providence might yet deliver her from this most unwelcome partner.
author: Jane Austen

Now, Old Man Tiber was risin’ somethin’ fierce, lookin’ to swallow half the county, and me, I was in a pickle. A right proper pickle, mind you, with a debt hangin’ over me like a thundercloud and a couple of fellas – let’s just say they weren’t choirboys – lookin’ to collect. I figured my number was called.

Then *she* appeared. Miss Evangeline, with eyes that could charm the hide off a rattlesnake and a spirit quicker than a hummingbird’s wing. She gave me a wink, a little flicker of mischief, and I knew. Knew she’d light out and save me, and blow on those dead-beats like a gale through dry leaves.

Well, we swarmed along down the river road, just carrying on like wildcats; and to m… to tell the truth, it was a blur of dust, fast talk, and Evangeline’s laugh, which sounded like wind chimes in a hurricane. She spun a tale to those fellas, a whopper of a yarn about a distant, wealthy relative and a sudden inheritance. They swallowed it whole, bless their simple hearts. 

By the time the sun dipped low, we were miles away, laughin’ fit to bust, and I owed Miss Evangeline more than I could ever repay. A woman like that, she’s a gift from the Almighty, I reckon.

Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a sensibility far exceeding her years, found herself in a most disagreeable predicament. Mr. Harding, a gentleman of tolerable fortune but lamentable self-regard, had, during a particularly dull evening at the Ashworths’, confessed a partiality. Not a declaration, precisely – for Mr. Harding was too practiced in the art of circumlocution for such bluntness – but an acknowledgement, nonetheless, of feelings he could neither explain nor, one suspected, truly *feel*.

It was not the sentiment itself that proved so vexing, but the manner of its delivery. Done with respect, he insisted, yet imbued with an unpardonable assurance, as if bestowing a favour rather than revealing a vulnerability. And then, the truly mortifying part: he had mentioned, with a chilling lack of discretion, the unfeeling manner in which she had previously dismissed a minor compliment from a distant cousin. 

Eleanor coloured, not with pleasure, but with a righteous indignation. To have one’s past conduct so casually dissected, and then presented as justification for *his* affections! It was a boldness bordering on impertinence, and she resolved, with a firmness she scarcely knew she possessed, to discourage any further advances with a civility that would, she hoped, convey her utter disapproval.

Now, Old Man Tiberius, he was a frugal soul, see? Not stingy, mind you, just…economical. He baked his own bread, a dark, heavy loaf that could stop a bullet, or at least dull the appetite for a good hour. But Tiberius, he had a habit of milling his wheat too close to the riverbank. Consequently, every slice held a certain…grit. 

I bit into a piece this mornin’, and felt a crunch that wasn’t wheat. No sir. It was sand, fine and pale, like the beaches down in New Orleans, only less pleasant in the mouth. I pointed it out to young Jebediah, who was lookin’ particularly righteous after a sermon about upholding the law.

Jebediah puffed up, talkin’ about justice and swift punishment for wrongdoers. Said folks needed takin’ care of, a firm hand, a rope, maybe. He was all fired up, see? 

I just chewed slow, contemplatin’ the sand. Then I looked at him, slow and scornful. “The idea of *you* lynching anybody! It’s amusing. The idea of you thinkin’ you have the moral high ground while swallowin’ down a mouthful of dirt…well, it’s a spectacle, I tell ya. A right comical spectacle.”

text:
The arrival of the post was rarely a source of such agitation in the household, but this morning, Miss Bennet found herself quite unable to attend to her embroidery whilst her sister, Elizabeth, read aloud. It concerned a distant relation, a Colonel Forster, stationed at Meryton, and contained intelligence most unsettling. 

“My dearest Mother,” Elizabeth began, her voice gaining a tremor, “I write with a hand scarcely steady. You will scarcely credit what has transpired. Lydia, alas, has eloped – and with no less a person than Mr. Wickham! He declares, in his own words – and I quote directly, for the gravity of the situation demands precision – ‘that Miss Lydia Bennet has, of her own free will and with the full understanding of her affections, consented to pass the remainder of her life with me.’ He further states, ‘I am entirely devoted to her, and anticipate a future filled with happiness.’ A most audacious declaration, considering his… previous engagements, or lack thereof, as you know.”

What a stroke was this for poor Jane, who would willingly have shielded her sister from all sorrow! Elizabeth continued, “He adds, with a chilling lack of remorse, ‘I trust this will not cause undue alarm, as my intentions are honourable.’ Honourable! The very word rings false.”
author: Jane Austen

text:
The unsettling truth, gleaned from fragmented basalt tablets and the fevered ramblings of Old Man Hemlock, concerned not *what* the Precursors built, but *how*. They did not merely assemble; they… *impressed* form. The blocks, cyclopean and geometrically abhorrent, weren’t quarried, but *willed* into existence from the very bedrock, shaped by a consciousness alien to Euclidean space. 

That the transfer of sculptured blocks had not been more extensive, was doubtless owing to the fact that the land city was not at its zenith when the… cessation occurred. Hemlock spoke of a ‘resonance’, a mental frequency required to coax the stone into obedience. A frequency, he insisted, still faintly echoing in the hills, driving men to inexplicable compulsions – to build, to *shape*, even with the most rudimentary tools.

It is a terrifying notion. To possess the power of creation, not through laborious craft, but through a psychic dominion over matter itself. And to suspect, with growing dread, that the impulse remains within us, a dormant seed of Precursor madness, waiting for the correct, blasphemous alignment to bloom. The chipped fragments in my study seem to… *pulse* when the moon is full. A subtle, sickening throb.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Old Man Tiber, he was a river rat through and through, smelled of mud and mischief, and possessed a mind like a tangled fishing line. He was testin’ young Bartholomew, see, a lad fresh off a steamboat and thinkin’ he knew the ways of the world. Bartholomew, bless his heart, was all starch and city notions.

“For’rard end, mum,” Tiber drawled, pointin’ a thumb vaguely towards the bow of a flatboat. Bartholomew blinked, lookin’ for some fancy signal. “Which side of a tree does the moss grow on?”

“North side,” Bartholomew chirped, proud as a peacock. 

Tiber just chuckled, a sound like gravel shiftin’. “Right enough. Now, this here’s a puzzler for a fella who knows his compass. If fifteen cows is browsing on a hillside, how many of them eats with their mouths?”

Bartholomew sputtered. “Why… why all of ‘em, naturally!”

Tiber slapped his knee, near splittin’ his britches. “Naturally! That’s what I wanted to hear. A fella gotta think beyond the obvious, son. A fella gotta *see* the cow, not just the number. This river life, it ain’t about book learnin’, it’s about observin’ what’s right under yer nose.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
The pronouncement, delivered with a chilling composure, hung in the air like the scent of fading lavender. “I warn you, Mr. Ashworth. I have done with you from this very day.” Miss Eleanor Tremaine’s voice, though low, possessed a steel that belied her delicate frame. He attempted a protest, a murmur of explanation, but she cut him short with a lift of her chin.

“I told you in the library, you know, that I should never speak to you again, and you will find me quite resolute.” The memory stung; a careless remark of his, dismissing her passion for botanical illustration as a ‘feminine fancy’, uttered amidst the leather-bound volumes. A trifling thing, perhaps, to others, but to Miss Tremaine, a grievous insult. 

He coloured, attempting a charm she now found utterly repellent. “But Eleanor –“

“Do not address me so familiarly, sir.” Her gaze, usually bright with intelligence, was now glacial. “And do not mention my name. You have forfeited the privilege. You will find me occupied, and quite content to remain so, without the benefit – or rather, the *burden* – of your acquaintance.” She turned, a graceful dismissal, leaving him to grapple with the full weight of his folly.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The charts, brittle and smelling faintly of guano and despair, indicated a convergence. Not of currents, nor of landmasses, but of *something* else. Old Man Hemlock, before his…disappearance, had scribbled frantic notes about a ‘resonance’, a disharmony in the magnetic fields that clung to these forsaken isles like a shroud. This trip, ostensibly a geological survey, felt increasingly like a descent into a pre-Euclidean nightmare.

The readings from the fathometer were…wrong. Not merely inaccurate, but *impossible*. Depths fluctuating wildly, suggesting chasms where only seabed should lie. And the silence. A suffocating, absolute silence broken only by the rhythmic throb of the engines – a sound that now felt less like reassurance and more like a desperate, futile heartbeat against the encroaching void. 

Indeed, if both of the neighboring ones were choked – the signal lost to that abyssal static – it was doubtful whether our batteries would warrant an attempt on the next northerly. A chilling premonition settled upon me, a certainty that we were not charting the ocean floor, but rather, tracing the contours of a slumbering, cyclopean geometry best left undisturbed. The air grew thick, heavy with a nameless dread, and the phosphorescence outside the porthole pulsed with an unwholesome, alien light.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The invitation to remain at Hartfield beyond the initially proposed fortnight had not been explicitly offered, yet Elizabeth found herself lingering, drawn by the amiable company and the quietude of the estate. However, she was positively resolved to depart on the morrow – nor did she much expect it would be asked she stay longer; and fearful, on the contrary, of being considered forward, she made no hint of her contentment. 

Miss Woodhouse, though possessing a benevolent disposition, was not entirely without a tendency to manage, and Elizabeth suspected any prolonged visit might be construed as a tacit acceptance of such direction. A delicate balance was required. She occupied herself with sketching the grounds, praising the roses with a measured enthusiasm, and engaging in polite, yet not overly familiar, conversation. 

Mr. Knightley, observing her careful restraint, offered a knowing smile. He understood, perhaps, the subtle anxieties of a mind accustomed to independence. Elizabeth, catching his eye, felt a blush rise in her cheeks. To remain would be delightful, undeniably. But to appear eager… that, she deemed, would be quite improper.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, the Duke, he was a sight. Been livin’ high on nothin’ but airs and borrowed finery for a spell, and it showed. By and by, he commenced lookin’ pretty rusty ‘round the edges, like an old weather vane. Claimed it was the damp, but I reckon it was more the lack of honest work. 

Then came the jump. A perfectly unnecessary jump, mind you, just to stir up some excitement and maybe fool a few folks. Plunged right off the stern, he did, followed by the King, who ain’t much for swimmin’ neither. A good deal of splashin’ and sputterin’, and a heap of hollerin’ about cold water and lost dignity.

But after breakfast – a right hearty spread of ham and biscuits, I’ll give you that – they were chippered up a good deal. The water, it seems, had washed away some of the gloom, and with it, a good portion of their pretense. The Duke, he even managed a grin, though it looked a bit strained, like he was tryin’ to remember how to do it. Still, a man can’t rightly judge a feller ‘til he’s seen him wet and fed. It changes things, you see. Changes things.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The chill wasn’t merely of the Antarctic air, but a creeping, geometrical wrongness that settled upon the soul. We’d followed the cartographer’s maddeningly imprecise sketches to this outpost – a cyclopean structure of basalt, incongruous amidst the ice. Old Man Hemlock, before his…dissolution, insisted the Elder Sign was *here*, protecting something. He was, as always, maddeningly oblique.

We split, foolishly believing in linear progression. Davies and I took the western gallery, a suffocating corridor lined with bas-reliefs depicting things no sane mind should catalogue – angles that defied Euclid, ichthyic horrors with too many eyes. Nothing. Utter, sterile emptiness. 

Then came the signal, a frantic burst from Pritchard in the eastern wing. “The penguins…they *know*! They’re…arranging themselves!” 

We rushed, hearts hammering a rhythm of dread. There it was. The Sign, glowing with a sickly, phosphorescent light. And around it, a precise, unsettling circle of Emperor penguins, their black eyes fixed on a shimmering distortion in the air. 

Davies, ever the pragmatist, muttered about magnetic anomalies. But I knew. The penguins hadn’t *saved* us. They’d merely confirmed we’d stumbled upon the correct containment. The wrong gallery…God, the things that might have awakened there. The thought alone threatened to unravel the tenuous threads of my sanity.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though possessed of a sensibility far exceeding her years, found herself in a most vexing predicament. Mr. Thomas Bellweather, a gentleman of tolerable fortune and unexceptionable character, had declared his intentions with a seriousness that bordered on the alarming. And yet, Eleanor, despite acknowledging his many virtues, had initially met his proposal with a coolness she scarcely felt.

It was, she knew, the established custom. A young lady of quality *must* appear reluctant, must demonstrate a degree of coyness lest she be deemed forward. Her mother, naturally, encouraged this performance, lamenting Eleanor’s lack of artifice. “A little frost, my dear, will only make the thaw more gratifying!”

However, the ensuing weeks proved a torment. Mr. Bellweather, though not entirely discouraged, had adopted a reserved politeness that chilled Eleanor’s spirits. She observed his attentions directed towards Miss Penrose, a girl of amiable, though decidedly unremarkable, disposition. A pang, quite unexpected, struck her heart. Perhaps, in adhering to the dictates of propriety, she had overplayed her hand. The folly of feminine strategy, she mused, was a subject worthy of considerable reflection.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The pronouncement, delivered with a chilling composure by Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, hung in the air like a poorly-stitched embroidery – noticeable for its imperfection. “It is, I confess, a relief to find that you do not depend on her serving you,” she continued, a slight inclination of the head acknowledging the unfortunate Miss Peabody, who had, moments before, spilled a dish of ratafia upon Mr. Harrington’s waistcoat.

Mrs. Bennet deigned not to make any reply; but, unable to contain herself, began scolding one of her younger daughters – Lydia, naturally – for a perceived lack of sympathy towards the afflicted waistcoat. “Such a want of feeling! A gentleman, and a *good* party, ruined by carelessness! It is quite beyond bearing!” 

Her husband, observing the scene with his customary detachment, merely adjusted his spectacles. The younger Miss Ainsworth, meanwhile, offered Mr. Harrington a linen handkerchief with an air of quiet efficiency that only served to further highlight Mrs. Bennet’s agitated state. It was a small incident, perhaps, but one which revealed, with painful clarity, the vast gulf between true refinement and…well, *some* families.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a fella prone to sniffin’ at things he didn’t understand, and Lord knows he didn’t understand much beyond the price of corn. But his Missus, bless her soul, she took to religion like a duck to water. Not the fire-and-brimstone kind, mind you, but a quiet, earnest sort. She started prayin’ for “spiritual gifts,” she did.

I asked her what in tarnation *that* was, thinkin’ maybe she wanted to conjure up a rainstorm for the crops. She just smiled, a patient sort of smile, and said the thing a body could get by prayin’ for it was…well, too many to list. It was a whole passel of somethin’s. 

Then she told me what she meant – I must help other people. 

Now, that struck me as a right peculiar “gift.” Ain’t we *supposed* to help folks anyhow? Didn’t require no prayin’ for that, just a bit of common decency. But Missus Hemlock, she had a way of lookin’ at things. She figured prayin’ opened a body’s eyes to *who* needed helpin’, and gave ‘em the gumption to actually *do* somethin’ about it. And I reckon, seein’ her, a body couldn’t rightly argue with that.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The charts, meticulously rendered in a phosphorescent ink that seemed to *breathe* with a cold, internal light, depicted not constellations, but…resonances. Not of stars, but of angles. Angles not Euclidean, not comprehensible to the sane mind, yet undeniably *present* in the arrangement of the basalt monoliths on the plateau. Old Man Hemlock, before his…dissolution, had insisted it was random placement, the fevered whim of a forgotten tribe. I knew better.

It wasn’t chaos, not precisely. It was a geometry of intent, a vast, non-human calculus operating on dimensions we could only glimpse through the fracturing of reason. Each stone, each precisely measured space between, wasn’t arbitrary, but a node in a colossal equation. An equation whose solution wasn’t a number, but a *state* – a specific vibrational alignment with…something beyond. 

At the time, I tried to keep the men’s minds off those points; for it was so much simpler—so *safer*—to speak of ancient rituals and barbaric sacrifices. To allow them to cling to the comforting illusion of human agency in a universe demonstrably indifferent. But the angles…they whispered of a logic far older, far colder, and infinitely more terrifying than any god or demon dreamt of in the fevered imaginings of mankind. A logic that, once understood, would unravel the very fabric of perception.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, old Man Hemlock, he was a feller plagued with anxieties, see? Worried himself sick over everything from the price of sorghum to the possibility of comets fallin’ right through his roof. He comes a-bustlin’ one evenin’, lookin’ like a hound dog lost in a hailstorm, and asks if I sold lightning rods. 

“Well,” I says, scratchin’ my chin, “I ain’t exactly *in* the lightning-rod business, no sir.”

He near ‘bout wept. “But I *need* one! Heard tell of a terrible storm brewin’, and my missus, she’ll have a fit if a bolt so much as *looks* at the house.”

I considered. Hemlock was a tightwad, but a good customer for fishin’ tackle. “I reckon I could… *acquire* one,” I says slow. “But it’d be of no way?” “Yes,” I says, “but I reckon it ain’t regular. Come up the stairs, and let on it’s a lightning-rod.” So he done it. 

Next day Tom stole a peach from Mrs. Gable’s orchard, claimin’ he was testin’ the rod’s grounding capabilities. A boy’s gotta have his fun, you see, even when dealin’ with anxious men and questionable merchandise.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, this here happened down by the river, see. Rain comin’ down in sheets, lookin’ like the sky itself was weepin’. Old Man Hemlock, he’d fished a feller outta the current – a boy, no older’n ten, shiverin’ like a willow in a gale. Soaked to the bone, he was, and lookin’ peaked as a month-old biscuit.

Hemlock, he turned to Buck, my brother, a lad built more for wrestlin’ bears than tendin’ to delicate matters. “Buck,” he says, voice gravelly as a riverbed, “take this little stranger and get the wet clothes off from him and dress him up in some of yours that’s dry.”

Buck looked about as old as me—though he was a year or two the senior, and carried himself with the solemnity of a judge. He squinted at the boy, then at Hemlock, then back at the boy again. A slow burn of annoyance crept across his face. 

“Paw,” he drawled, slow enough to curdle milk, “my best shirt ain’t fittin’ a sprout like *him*. And I reckon my britches’ll be draggin’ on the ground.” 

Hemlock just leveled a look at Buck that could stop a steamboat. Buck sighed, a sound like air leakin’ from a punctured bellows, and started towards the cabin. A body didn’t argue with Hemlock, not and live to tell the tale.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The salt-laced fog clung to the cliffs of Dunwich Head like a shroud, a viscous, grey presence that seemed to *remember* things best left forgotten. We had established our vigil, Professor Armitage and I, driven by the unsettling reports from the local fishermen – tales of phosphorescent trails in the black depths and a chilling, subsonic resonance that rattled the very teeth. We had expected, upon looking back, to see a terrible and incredible moving entity if the mists were thin enough; but of that entity we saw…nothing.

And that, perhaps, was the most dreadful revelation of all. 

The emptiness was not a lack of form, but a *wrongness* of space. The fog didn’t merely obscure; it *shifted*, subtly altering the geometry of the coastline, bending the stars into impossible configurations. A nauseating pressure built behind the eyes, a sense of being observed by something utterly alien to Euclidean comprehension. The air tasted of ozone and decay, and a low, internal hum began to vibrate within the skull. 

It wasn’t a being *in* the fog, but the fog *itself* – a sentient, protean horror, and we, insignificant motes, were caught within its dreaming. The absence of a defined shape was not reassurance, but the ultimate, chilling proof of its vast, unknowable nature. We retreated, sanity fraying, knowing we had glimpsed a truth mankind was never meant to perceive.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text: its habitability for an indefinite period. The beings seem to have had no trouble in adapting themselves to part-time--and eventually, of course, whole-time--residence under water, since they had never allowed their gill systems to atrophy. There were many sculptures which showed how they had always frequently visited their submarine kinsfolk elsewhere, and how they had habitually bathed on the deep bottom of their great river. The darkness of inner earth could likewise have been no deterrent to a race accustomed to long antarctic nights. Decadent though their style undoubtedly was, these latest carvings had a truly epic quality where they told of the building of the new city in the cavern sea. The Old Ones had gone about it scientifically--quarrying insoluble rocks from the heart of the honeycombed mountains, and employing expert workers from the nearest submarine city to perform the construction according to the best methods. These workers brought with them all that was necessary to establish the new venture--Shoggoth tissue from which to breed stone lifters and subsequent beasts of burden for the cavern city, and other protoplasmic matter to mold into phosphorescent organisms for lighting purposes. * * * * * At last a mighty metropolis rose

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he’d been ailin’ for a month, coughin’ like a rusty gate hinge. Folks said it was the consumption, but I knew different. I’d seen him cheat at cards more times than I’d had hot dinners, and a body don’t court misfortune like that without payin’ a price. Still, his daughter, sweet little Bess, she begged me to pray for him. Said it’d ease her mind.

Well, I knelt there, in that dim parlor, and I *said* the words. Asked the Good Lord to restore him, to grant him strength. But deep down in me I knowed it was a lie, and He knowed it. Old Hemlock didn’t deserve a blessed moment of ease. 

You can’t pray a lie—I found that out. It felt like tryin’ to swallow gravel. A tightness in my chest, a burnin’ in my throat. The words tasted like ash. 

So I was full of trouble, full as I could be; and didn’t know whether to be sorrier for Hemlock, Bess, or myself for gettin’ tangled in such a mess. It was a powerful uncomfortable feelin’, let me tell you. A powerful uncomfortable feelin’ indeed.

text:
Now, this here skiff wasn’t much to look at, mind you. A patched-up thing, smelling powerfully of river mud and regret. I’d just gotten her tied to the willow when this feller, a specimen of rawboned strength and questionable judgment, comes a-strollin’. He wanted a ride, see, across to the far bank. Said he had business with a widow woman and a prize-winning pumpkin.

I obliged, naturally. A body don’t turn down a nickel these days. Gave him the rope to hold while I positioned myself to push off. But the moment I leaned into it, he *let go*. Just up and left me a-holt of the rope, and went behind him to shove *himself* along. 

Now, this man was built like a steamboat boiler. Too much muscle for a little skiff, I reckon. He jerked loose, near yankin’ me clean into the water, and took off downriver like a scalded dog. 

Well, I wasn’t about to lose my boat, nor my dignity. So I jumped in and commenced to row, hollerin’ like a banshee. A right comical sight, I expect, me chasin’ a runaway strongman in a leaky skiff. The river, she just chuckled along, watchin’ the whole foolishness unfold.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The assembly rooms at Meryton, though crowded as ever, offered little amusement this evening. Kitty and Lydia, predictably, were entirely engrossed with the scarlet coats of the militia officers, their giggles echoing with a vapidity that threatened to overwhelm even Mrs. Bennet’s pronouncements on eligible husbands. Jane, as always, bore their silliness with a sweetness bordering on resignation. 

Mary, meanwhile, had cornered poor Mr. Phillips, attempting to demonstrate her newly acquired skill on the pianoforte – a performance, one suspected, more calculated to display her learning than to provide pleasure. 

“Really, Papa,” Elizabeth observed, a slight arch to her brow as she watched the scene unfold, “one might believe we were bred solely for the entertainment of provincial gentlemen.”

Mr. Bennet, ever prone to mischief, merely raised an eyebrow. “My dear Lizzy, you possess something more of quickness than your sisters. You *see* the absurdity, which is half the battle. They merely *are* it.” 

He paused, a flicker of something akin to regret crossing his face. “Though, perhaps, a little less observation and a little more…docility…would spare us all a great deal of vexation.”
author: Jane Austen

text:
The basalt was not merely cold, but *wrong*. A chill that bypassed the flesh, settling directly into the marrow, clung to the expedition as we descended. Professor Armitage, bless his doomed curiosity, had insisted upon this particular fissure in the Antarctic wastes, citing anomalous magnetic readings and whispers gleaned from the *Pnakotic Manuscripts*. Whispers best left undisturbed.

Each echoing footfall felt like a blasphemy, a violation of geometries not meant for human perception. The air thickened, not with moisture, but with a palpable *age* – an age predating life, predating even the slow grinding of continents. Then came the carvings. Not glyphs, not runes, but something…older. Cyclopean angles that defied Euclidean space, depicting entities of impossible form, writhing in a non-dimensional abyss. 

A low, resonant hum began to vibrate through the stone, a sound that resonated not in the ears, but within the skull. It was a summoning, a reawakening. The carvings *shifted* in the flickering lamplight, and a dreadful realization dawned: we were not the first to find this place, merely the first in an epoch beyond reckoning to hear the echoes of what had slumbered here, and to feel the cold, expectant gaze of things that should remain forever lost to the cosmos.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, this here notion of “safe” is a curious thing, ain’t it? Folks cling to it like a drowning man to a splinter. I recollect a pair of fellas down by the river, arguin’ the very point. One was about seventy or upwards, had a bald head and very gray whiskers. He had an old battered-up slouch hat on, and a grin that showed more gum than teeth. The other, a young whippersnapper barely out of short pants, was all puffed up with book-learnin’.

“Safety’s in prudence, sir!” declared the young’un, adjustin’ his spectacles. “In calculatin’ risk and avoidin’ peril!”

Old Man Hemlock just chuckled, a sound like gravel shiftin’. “Prudence, eh? Boy, I’ve known men ruined by *too much* prudence. A man can calculate himself right into a grave. Safe is a warm fire on a cold night, a full belly, and a friend who won’t tell your wife about the poker game. It ain’t about avoidin’ the rapids, it’s about knowin’ how to navigate ‘em. Sometimes, the safest thing a fella can do is take a chance.” 

He winked, then spat a stream of tobacco juice into the muddy water. “And sometimes, it ain’t.”
author: Mark Twain

Well now, the situation was fixin’ to be right unpleasant. Old Man Hemlock’s prize rooster, Bartholomew, had taken a fancy to my hat – a perfectly good straw, mind you – and wouldn’t relinquish it for all the corn in Missouri. Hemlock, he was a fella who held a grudge tighter than a miser holds his pennies. So I made a dash for it, and Miss Hooker she said if I didn’t strike help sooner, come here and hunt up her uncle, and he’d fix the thing. 

I made the break, legs pumpin’ like a piston, Bartholomew squawkin’ and clingin’ to the brim. Hemlock bellowed somethin’ about trespassin’ and poultry rights, but I wasn’t stoppin’ to parse legalities. I ran past Widow Peabody’s prize petunias – a disaster waitin’ to happen, that was – and nearly collided with young Timmy Johnson, who was attemptin’ to teach a bullfrog to waltz. 

Finally, I reached the blacksmith, a man built like a brick privy. He took one look at me, Bartholomew still perched atop my head, and let out a laugh that rattled the windows. “Looks like you’ve got yourself a feathered friend, son!” he boomed. And with a few well-placed words and a handful of oats, Bartholomew was persuaded to relocate, and my hat, though somewhat worse for wear, was saved.

text:
Old Man Hemlock, he’d passed on, bless his soul, leaving a will that was…peculiar. Said his fortune was to go to whoever could prove they’d received personal correspondence from him. Now, Hemlock wasn’t known for writin’ letters. Preferred a good chew and a grumble, he did. But two letters surfaced, lookin’ remarkably alike – one addressed to a fella claimin’ kinship, the other to a young woman who’d tended his prize-winning pumpkins.

Both penned in a spidery, deliberate hand, full of digressions about the weather and the general foolishness of mankind. Both signed with a flourish, and both containin’ the same odd little habit of drawin’ a tiny, almost invisible beetle beside the period at the end of each sentence. 

The lawyer, a fella named Peabody, squinted at ‘em through his spectacles, turnin’ ‘em this way and that. He’d seen enough forged documents to fill a steamer trunk. But after a good long study, he straightened up, lookin’ plumb bewildered. 

“Well now,” he drawled, scratchin’ his chin. “You would see that he wrote his own letters and mine too—they’re by the same hand.” He looked at the claimants, then back at the letters. “I believe it.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single lady of modest fortune must, at some point, encounter a gentleman possessed of both consequence and a remarkably pleasing countenance. Such has been my recent experience with Mr. Alistair Finch. He is, undeniably, the most agreeable man I have ever seen – possessing a wit that is both sparkling and refined, and a disposition so uniformly kind as to be almost… unsettling. 

Indeed, it is this very perfection which gives me pause. For whilst his attentions are flattering, and his conversation a constant delight, I perceive a most dreadful imprudence in allowing myself to be *too* pleased. He speaks of my accomplishments with an enthusiasm bordering on admiration, and I fear – oh, I *fear* – that he is becoming truly attached. 

To encourage such a sentiment would be folly. My connections are… limited. His are, naturally, of the highest order. A mismatch, however amiable, would bring only discomfort to all parties concerned. Better, surely, to maintain a polite distance, to admire from afar, and to acknowledge, with a sigh, that some pleasures are best left untasted. It is a painful conclusion, to be certain, but a necessary one.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Tiber, he’d gone and done it again. Not intentionally, mind you. Just a fondness for napping in peculiar places. This time, it was the root cellar, and a landslide of potatoes had sealed him in tighter than a drum. A right mess, it was. 

Young Jeb, bless his simple heart, was wringing his hands and near to hysterics. “We gotta blast, Pa! Blast him out!”

Now, Pa, he was a man who favored deliberation, and a healthy dose of mischief. He stroked his beard, contemplatin’ the situation. “Blastin’s too… dramatic, Jeb. Folks’ll ask questions. No, sir. We got to dig him out with the picks, and *let on* it’s case-knives.”

Jeb blinked, slow as a turtle. “Case-knives, Pa?”

“Aye. Say we was excavatin’ for a new shipment of fancy cutlery. A fella can’t have too many case-knives, can he?”

“_Now_ you’re _talking!_” I says; “your head gets leveler and leveler all the time, Pa.” It was a grand scheme, see? A little fib, a lot of diggin’, and Old Man Tiber, covered in spuds, would emerge a victim of… a very enthusiastic cutlery collection.

text:
The charts, compiled from the dredged remnants of the *Cyclopean*, spoke of a world utterly alien, yet…tenable. Not in any fashion comforting to terrestrial sensibilities, mind you. Xylos, they termed it – a designation as hollow and meaningless as any attempt to categorize the unclassifiable. Its sun, a bloated crimson smear, cast shadows that *moved* independently of their source, and the atmosphere…the atmosphere was less breathed than *absorbed*, a viscous, phosphorescent fluid that clung to the lungs with a sickening familiarity.

Initial probes detected no life as *we* understand it. Then came the anomalies. Fluctuations in the magnetic field, rhythmic pulsations within the basaltic plains, and, most disturbingly, the subtle alterations to the probe’s own metallic structure. It wasn’t corrosion, not precisely. More…assimilation. 

The beings – for beings they undoubtedly were – existed not in discrete forms, but as distributed consciousnesses woven into the very fabric of Xylos. They had, it seemed, no trouble in adapting themselves to part-time – and eventually, of course, whol – possession of inorganic matter. The probes weren’t destroyed; they were *joined*. And the unsettling implication, gleaned from the final, fractured transmission, was that Xylos wasn’t merely habitable. It was *hungry*. And patient. Indefinitely so.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, this fella, barely more than a sprout, showed up at the livery stable lookin’ like a kicked puppy. Clothes all rumpled, face streaked with somethin’ – dirt, tears, maybe both – and eyes dartin’ around like a trapped rabbit. Claimed he was from upriver, bound for St. Louis, but the story smelled fishier than a week-old catfish. 

Old Man Hemlock, he sized the boy up quick. “Runaway, ain’t ya?” he drawled, not accusin’, just statin’ a fact. The boy near jumped outta his skin.

“Now, hold on,” I said, steppin’ forward. “Don’t you fret none. I’ve seen my share of trouble. You’re an ’prentice, skipped out on yer master, I reckon.” The boy nodded, lookin’ like he expected a rope and a tree.

“Well,” I continued, “that’s a pickle, alright. But I’ll tell ya what. I ain’t one to turn a blind eye to a fella in a bind. I’ll keep yer secret, see? And trust me, I’ll keep it. And, what’s more, I’ll help you. So’ll my old man if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway ’prentice, that’s all. It happens.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a lively wit and a sensibility far exceeding her years, laboured under a most unfortunate deficiency – a want of discretion, particularly when confronted with the tedium of a formal dinner. It was, alas, a failing she had repeatedly vowed to conquer, yet found herself perpetually succumbing to. 

This evening proved no exception. Whilst the footmen navigated the intricacies of the roast, and Mrs. Grimshaw, the housekeeper, hovered with a watchful eye, Miss Eleanor, emboldened perhaps by a particularly fine glass of claret, declared her utter disbelief in Mr. Featherstonehaugh’s claims regarding his prize-winning turnips. 

A stifled giggle escaped young Thomas, the hall boy, and a distinct twitch affected Mrs. Grimshaw’s lips. Eleanor, observing these reactions, felt a blush creep up her neck. It was, she realised with mortification, better that *one* only of the house should be subjected to her imprudence. She resolved, with a sigh, to confine her opinions to the company of her needlework for the remainder of the evening, and pray for a swift conclusion to the meal.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The pronouncement, “the pleasure of seeing you at Pemberley to-day,” had scarcely left Lady Bracknell’s lips when a most unsettling pallor descended upon Mrs. Featherstonehaugh’s countenance. A delicate fan fluttered with increasing rapidity, barely concealing a tremor in her hand. 

“Indeed, a most agreeable visit,” she murmured, though her tone suggested anything but. “However, a circumstance of the utmost urgency… a prior engagement, you understand… compels our immediate departure.”

Her husband, a gentleman more accustomed to silence than explanation, merely cleared his throat. Lady Bracknell, ever observant, raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow.

“Pray, do convey our regrets to Miss Darcy,” Mrs. Featherstonehaugh continued, her voice a breathless rush. “Be so kind as to apologize for our abruptness. Say that… urgent business calls us home immediately. Do not, I implore you, mention the… the author by name. It would, I fear, cause a most disagreeable scene, and quite spoil the afternoon for everyone concerned.” 

A fleeting glance passed between the couple, a silent acknowledgement of a social disaster narrowly averted. Pemberley, it seemed, held terrors beyond its magnificent façade.
author: Jane Austen
