text:
The drilling had progressed beyond reason, beyond the pale geometries understood by sane men. Each fathom descended into the Antarctic’s heart was a violation, a scraping against something ancient and *wrong*. The ice, once merely cold, now pulsed with a subsonic thrum, a resonance that settled not in the ears, but directly within the ventricles of the brain. 

Old Man Hemlock, the geologist, had begun muttering of cyclopean masonry, of non-Euclidean angles glimpsed in the core samples – formations that defied terrestrial origin. The heat, generated by the drill itself, was…answered. A reciprocal warmth rising from the abyss, sickeningly organic. 

Then came the breakthrough. Not ice, not rock, but a yielding, viscous blackness. A stench, older than time, of brine and decay and something utterly *other* filled the station. The drill bit, designed for granite, met no resistance, boring into a substance that felt…alive. 

They brought up a fragment. A glistening, obsidian shard, covered in glyphs that shifted and writhed before the eye. Hemlock screamed, a sound swallowed by the rising thrum. He babbled of Azathoth, of the dreaming chaos, and of a gate…finally, irrevocably, *unsealed*. We must break thr… the transmission fractured, lost in a static that tasted of cosmic dread.

Old Man Tiber, he’d been tryin’ to explain to Miss Abigail why the newfangled ice cream freezer wouldn’t work at his place. A contraption it was, all gears and churns, lookin’ like a mechanical beetle. She’d brought it as a gift, see, thinkin’ to elevate our simple lives.

“It requires a consistent flow of cold water, Miss Abigail,” he was sayin’, scratchin’ his beard. “A steady stream, to keep the cream chillin’ proper. And we… well, we ain’t got no conveniences for it.”

She pursed her lips, a sight that could curdle milk. “Oh, I see, now. You might a said that in the first place and saved time.” 

Now, Miss Abigail, she was a woman who valued efficiency above all else, and a wasted minute was a personal affront. The way she said it, all clipped and precise, it felt like a judge deliverin’ a verdict. 

And I, standin’ there holdin’ the crank, I see I was ou. Clean out of arguments, clean out of hope for frozen sweetness, and clean out of patience for a woman who could find fault in a summer breeze. It was a long afternoon, I reckon, and a hot one at that.

The intelligence arrived with Mrs. Phillips, breathless and brimming with conjecture, and was, of course, immediately dispatched to Longbourn. Netherfield Park was let, she declared, and by a gentleman of large fortune – a Mr. Bingley, no less! One could scarcely credit such good fortune descending upon our quiet neighbourhood. 

My sister Elizabeth, ever possessed of a lively curiosity, received the news with an eagerness which hardly left her power of comprehension; and from impatience of knowing what further particulars Mrs. Phillips possessed, questioned her with a rapidity quite alarming. It appeared Mr. Bingley had arrived only that morning, accompanied by a sister and a party of gentlemen, and had already begun making inquiries concerning the local families.

The most diverting part of the account, however, concerned a certain Mr. Darcy, described as possessing ten thousand a year, and a countenance of the most forbidding pride. Such a disparity in temperaments! One could only imagine the effect such a man might have upon the sensibilities of our acquaintance. Indeed, the very prospect filled one with a delightful mixture of anticipation and apprehension. It promised, at the very least, a season of considerable amusement.

Now, I reckon I ain’t ever seen a sight quite like it. Old Man Hemlock’s prize bull, Bartholomew, had busted loose, see, and the whole town – every Tom, Dick, and Harriet – took after him. Not for any good reason, mind you, just pure, unadulterated excitement. A body’d think the Mississippi was a-floodin’ the way they went. 

I was amongst ‘em, naturally, though my legs ain’t what they used to be. Had to *run* to keep from bein’ trampled, I tell you. Folks hollerin’ and whoopin’, skirts flyin’, hats lost to the wind. It was a spectacle, a regular circus.

Bartholomew, bein’ a bull of considerable sense, made a beeline for the graveyard. Figured it was peaceful there, I suppose. But when they got there… well, it was like a busted dam. They swarmed into the graveyard and washed over it like an overflow, headstones bobbin’ in the human tide. And when they got to Old Man Withers’ plot, the one with the fancy marble angel… that’s when the real trouble started.

text:
Miss Everly found Mr. Lucas, even in the politest of conversation, profoundly odious. It was not a matter of any particular ill-treatment – he was, in truth, excessively attentive – but rather a pervasive air of self-satisfaction that grated upon her nerves. He possessed a fluency in discussing estate management which she found insufferable, particularly as he seemed to believe her own understanding of such matters woefully deficient.

And his wife, now mistress of Longwood, was scarcely less provoking. To succeed her, to inhabit the rooms she had once considered her own, was a circumstance Miss Everly bore with a barely concealed, and wholly justifiable, abhorrence. Mrs. Lucas, though outwardly amiable, possessed a subtle triumph in her every glance, a quiet assertion of her new position. 

Whenever Charlotte, a sensible girl and a valued friend, came to visit, Miss Everly invariably concluded the afternoon with a headache and a renewed conviction that happiness was not to be found within ten miles of Longwood’s gates. Charlotte, bless her heart, seemed quite content, but Miss Everly suspected a certain blindness in her friend’s affections.

text:
The geometries were *wrong*. Not subtly, as with the crumbling angles of forgotten cyclopean ruins, but with a brazen, unsettling modernity. Towers of obsidian glass and steel clawed at a sky perpetually bruised with a sickly, synthetic luminescence – a sky that felt…*constructed*. This was not the slow accretion of ages, the organic sprawl of human settlement. This was a growth, a *proliferation*, born of calculations too vast for sanity to comprehend.

They called it Veridia. A name that tasted of manufactured hope, a thin veneer over a core of cold, alien purpose. The citizens moved with a disconcerting synchronicity, their faces pale and vacant, eyes reflecting the city’s unnatural glow. Their speech, clipped and efficient, lacked the warmth of genuine inflection. 

Old Man Hemlock, before they…*adjusted* him, spoke of foundations laid not in earth, but in dimensions tangential to our own. Of architects who were not architects, but something…older. Something that predated not merely mankind, but the very concepts of time and space as we understand them. Veridia, he rasped, ranked with Valusia, R'lyeh, Ib – a blasphemy not of the past, but of the *now*, a chilling testament to geometries best left unobserved. And the worst part? It was still *growing*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

We wished that Pabodie were present, for his engineering knowledge might have helped us guess how such titanic blocks could have been handled in that unbelievably remote age when the city and its outskirts were built up. * * * * * The half-mile walk downhill to the actual city, with the upper wind shrieking vainly and savagely through the skyward peaks in the background, was something of which the smallest details will always remain engraved on my mind. text:
Old Man Tiber, he’d been grievin’ somethin’ fierce over the loss of his hound, Blue. Finest dog a man ever did see, Blue was. Disappeared clean off the place, one mornin’, just…gone. Tiber sat on the porch for nigh on three days, lookin’ out at the fields like he expected Blue to just materialize from the corn. Didn’t say a word to nobody, just sat.

Finally, a rain commenced. Not a gentle sprinkle, mind you, but a proper soakin’. Tiber, he just let it come down, and then went to bed; there ain’t no better way to put in time when you are lonesome. You can’t stay so, you soon get over it. And so for Tiber.

Woke up the next mornin’, sun shinin’, and a young pup, all legs and ears, a-nibblin’ at his boot. Wasn’t Blue, no sir. But a dog nonetheless. A scruffy, hopeful thing. Tiber didn’t smile, not exactly. Just scratched the pup behind the ears and said, “Well now, what have we here?” Grief, it seems, has a way of makin’ room.

text:
Old Man Tiber, he was a study in peculiar habits, that one. Folks said he’d spent too long sniffin’ around the Mississippi bottomlands, pickin’ up notions from the cypress knees and the bullfrogs. But it wasn’t the notions that were odd, it was *how* he displayed ‘em.

It always started the same. Somebody’d tell him somethin’ – a price for corn, a tale of woe, even just the weather – and he’d fix ‘em with a look. Then, slow as molasses in January, he’d *up* his eyebrows, right ‘til they near disappeared into his hairline. Next he would squeeze his hand on his forehead and stagger back and kind of moan, like a hound dog stepped on. 

Then came the sigh. A long, drawn-out thing, full of the weight of the world and a lost sock drawer. And *next* he’d let on to drop a nickel. Not offer it, mind you, but *let on* to drop it, like it was a troublesome thought he was shakin’ loose. Said it was for “consideration of the burden of knowin’.” Pure balderdash, of course, but nobody dared call him on it. Tiber was a powerful convincer, even with a nickel and a moan.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The ascent had been…unnatural. Not merely the physical strain of scaling the basalt monolith known locally as Widow’s Tooth, but a growing, insidious *wrongness* in the very air. The peak itself wasn’t formed by geological process as understood by sane men, but felt…*imposed*. A violation of Euclidean space, subtly, sickeningly. Old Man Hemlock had muttered of a pressure, a psychic weight, emanating from the stone, and dismissed it as senility. I now understood his terror.

The fissure, barely visible from the summit, opened into a tunnel descending at an impossible angle. A chill, not of temperature but of *absence*, radiated from its maw. It was the air, though. A peculiar, opalescent haze clung to the rock, and the scent…not sulfur, not decay, but something older, something that predated scent itself. 

We entered, driven by a morbid curiosity that felt less like volition and more like compulsion. The walls pulsed with a faint, internal luminescence. And then we saw. Not carvings, not formations, but *geometry* that defied description, angles that fractured the mind, and a slow, rhythmic dilation of the tunnel itself, as if breathing with a lung of unimaginable size. The source, we suspected with mounting dread, might not be caused by the tortuous-channeled rising of some such vapor from the unfathomed regions of earth's core.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, this Boggs, he was a feller who’d spent a lifetime cultivatin’ a reputation for bein’ troublesome when lubricated with whiskey – and he *was* lubricated, mind you, right down to his bootsoles. He commenced to raisin’ Cain in the square, hollerin’ about Colonel Sherburn bein’ a coward and a scoundrel. A right noisy performance, it was, and drawin’ a crowd like flies to molasses. 

Folks tried reasonin’ with Boggs, of course. Old Man Rutherford, he pleaded, and young Stevens, he begged. But Boggs just kept on, louder and more outlandish with each swig he’d managed to sneak. Finally, the Colonel, he’d had enough. Stepped out onto his porch, cool as a cucumber, and told Boggs to hold his tongue. Boggs, naturally, took exception.

Well, sir, quicker’n a hummingbird’s wing, the Colonel drew. One shot. Boggs dropped like a sack of potatoes. A hush fell over the square, thick enough to cut with a knife. Then a yell went up: “Give him air! Give him air!” They took Boggs to a little drug store, tryin’ to fan him with hats and newspapers, but it was a lost cause, I reckon. After many pauses and many trials of other subjects – the merits of Italian landscapes, the distressing price of ribbons, even a discourse upon the proper trimming for a winter pelisse – Elizabeth could not help reverting to Miss Penhaligon. The girl possessed a sensibility, it was true, but one so wildly untamed as to threaten continual impropriety. Living as she did under the sole care of her aunt, Mrs. Armitage, a lady of fortune but decidedly limited understanding, the consequences were most alarming.

Mrs. Armitage, whilst generous in providing comforts, entirely lacked the firmness necessary to *superintend* her niece’s education. Music lessons were abandoned for sketching, French grammar for rambling walks, and the proper deportment for…well, for staring fixedly at the stable boys. 

Elizabeth, observing this laxity during a prolonged visit, felt compelled to offer her counsel. “A little discipline, Madam,” she ventured delicately, “might prove more beneficial than an abundance of indulgence. A mind left to wander, like a garden untended, will surely produce weeds amongst the flowers.” Mrs. Armitage merely smiled, declaring Penhaligon “a free spirit,” and offering Elizabeth another slice of exceedingly rich plum cake. The prospect of reforming the girl, Elizabeth feared, was a task of considerable magnitude.

Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a feller who believed in *most*. Not a little, not some, but *most*. Most folks were fools, most politicians were thieves, and most sunsets were prettier than any woman he’d ever met – which, considerin’ his history, was sayin’ somethin’. 

He’d been arguin’ this very point with young Miss Elara, a schoolmarm fresh from the city, over a plate of Mrs. Higgins’ notoriously tough biscuits. She’d declared a fondness for *all* sunsets. “Every single one, Mr. Tiber!” she’d chirped.

He’d scoffed, naturally. “Nonsense, girl. There’s sunsets that look like a scalded cat, sunsets that remind a man of debt collectors, and sunsets that just plain offend the eye.”

But then, somethin’ peculiar happened. Miss Elara, she just *laughed*. A genuine, bell-like sound. And then she put her arms around his neck, and he, bein’ a contrary sort, put his around hers, and hung their chins over each other’s shoulders; and then for three minutes, or maybe five – time gets blurry when a feller’s bein’ unexpectedly embraced – they just sat there, quiet as church mice, watchin’ a sunset that, confound it all, *was* rather pretty. Maybe she had a point about *most* after all.

text:
With Douglas and Thorfinnssen I resolved to take steps toward investigation. The reports, initially dismissed as Antarctic hysteria, had accrued a dreadful weight – whispers of geometries *wrong*, of a luminescence not born of any earthly star. The source, chillingly consistent across disparate expeditions, centered upon a region beyond the Shackleton Icefall, a place the natives, even in their fractured, borrowed English, refused to name.

Our plan hinged upon the fifth aëroplane, which we had left at the McMurdo Sound supply cache. A fragile vessel against such immensity, yet our only recourse. The modifications, Thorfinnssen’s grim handiwork, were… unorthodox. Reinforced struts, a leaden lining to the fuel tanks, and a peculiar, oscillating device meant to disrupt whatever *resonance* seemed to plague the area. 

Douglas, ever the pragmatist, spoke of atmospheric anomalies. I knew better. The sketches recovered from the lost Wilkins party – cyclopean structures of basalt, angles that defied Euclidean comprehension – spoke of something ancient, something *waiting*. A cold dread, older than the ice itself, settled upon me as we prepared for ascent. The air tasted of ozone and something else… something subtly, sickeningly *alien*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The bathysphere descended, a fragile iron womb against the crushing black. Below R’lyeh’s cyclopean peaks, beyond the phosphorescent bloom of things best left unnamed, lay *it*. Not ruin, not the expected coral-encrusted decay, but…replication. A city mirroring the one above, yet utterly, chillingly *wrong*.

Stone, basalt perhaps, but of a texture alien to terrestrial geology, formed impossible angles. Towers, not crumbling with age, but precisely mirroring those of the surface city, yet lacking any discernible ornamentation. No grotesque carvings, no blasphemous bas-reliefs. Just…geometry. A cold, Euclidean perfection that felt less constructed than *grown*. 

The light, strained and sickly green, revealed streets laid out with a disturbing regularity, devoid of debris, of life, of *anything* save the unsettling symmetry. It was the absence of decadence that gnawed at the sanity. A city built not by the slow erosion of time, but by a will utterly alien, a will that valued order above all else, and in that order, hinted at a purpose too vast, too cold, for the human mind to comprehend. A purpose that resonated with a dreadful, silent hum in the very structure of the sphere, promising not destruction, but…assimilation.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

The matter, though awkwardly concluded, was satisfactory; it was gratifying to know that his resentment, so plainly expressed but moments before, had not made him think *really* ill of her. Mr. Ashworth had, with a stiffness that bordered on the ridiculous, offered a curt acknowledgement of her explanation regarding the misplaced letter, and she, in turn, had accepted it with a composure she did not entirely feel. 

They now walked on in silence; each of them occupied with the delicate task of rebuilding a semblance of amicable regard. The rose garden, usually a source of such pleasant contemplation, seemed to offer little solace. He traced patterns in the gravel with the toe of his boot, a habit she had always found particularly vexing, and yet, today, it seemed merely…thoughtful. 

Miss Elmsworth dared a glance. His profile, though still bearing the shadow of displeasure, lacked the harshness of earlier. Perhaps, she mused, a little time, and the judicious application of polite conversation, might restore their acquaintance to its former, comfortable footing. It was, after all, a most desirable outcome, and one worth a degree of forbearance.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The departure of Miss Lydia, though anticipated with a degree of relief by her more sensible sisters, left a void not of genuine sorrow, but of… expectation. She had promised, with a volubility quite characteristic, to chronicle every detail of her new life at Brighton, to furnish a constant stream of intelligence regarding officers, assemblies, and the general gaiety of the place. Yet, weeks passed with only the most perfunctory acknowledgements of their letters, and those penned in a hand so hurried as to be scarcely legible.

A general disappointment settled upon the household, a languor that threatened to consume the afternoons with tedious embroidery and melancholic sighs. However, this pervasive gloom was, thankfully, warded off by the defence of some little peculiar vexation. Mrs. Bennet, discovering a slight imperfection in the new pianoforte’s varnish, launched into a tirade of such precise and sustained indignation that all other grievances were quite eclipsed. 

Miss Elizabeth, observing this domestic drama, could not help a small smile. It was, she reflected, a truth universally acknowledged that a family in possession of a good fortune must be in want of *something* to complain about, and that the absence of larger misfortunes was often compensated for by the diligent pursuit of smaller ones.
author: Jane Austen

Now, old Man Hemlock, he was a feller who believed in progress, see? Said a fella oughta invest in the future. And the future, according to Silas Pettigrew, was…well, it was bottled air. “Vitalized Atmospheric Essence,” he called it. Claimed it cured everything from the rheumatiz to a melancholy disposition. Cost five dollars a pint, and smelled suspiciously like nothin’ at all.

I, bein’ a simple man with a simple faith in a good bargain, bought a case. Figured my wife, bless her soul, could use a bit o’ vitalizin’. Turns out, it vitalized nothin’ but Pettigrew’s pocketbook. The air, it just…was. 

Then I saw him, slick as a greased pig, sellin’ the same stuff to Widow Higgins, claimin’ it’d bring back her departed husband’s bloom. That riled me.

“You’re the houn’ I’m after, and I’m a-gwyne to have you, too!” I bellowed, marchin’ towards him. And so I went on, callin’ Pettigrew everything a man could conjure – a scoundrel, a rascal, a purveyor of hot air, ironically enough. He just smiled, a thin, oily thing, and said, “Buyer beware, friend. Buyer beware.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
The cellar reeked of a dampness not born of mere earth and stone, but of something…older. A slickness coated the flagstones, a phosphorescent sheen that pulsed with a sickly, internal light. It was upon this glistening expanse that *it* moved. Not walked, not crawled, but *flowed*, a distortion of angles and shadows barely resolving into a serpentine form. Scales, if one could call them that, shifted and rearranged themselves with each impossible undulation, reflecting the cellar’s ghastly glow in a thousand fractured points.

The air grew thin, heavy with a pressure against the temples. Dust motes danced in frantic spirals, avoiding the path of the thing as if possessed of a dreadful awareness. It had been the caretaker’s obsession, this cellar, and his frantic scribblings spoke of a cleansing, a preparation. He’d swept, he’d polished, driven by a compulsion he could not name, to render the floor…*suitable*. 

Still came that eldritch, mocking cry—"_Tekeli-li!_” – a sound that resonated not in the ears, but within the very bone. A promise of geometries beyond human comprehension, of a cold, uncaring cosmos where mankind was but a fleeting, insignificant tremor. And the slithering continued, a blasphemous grace upon a floor swept so evilly free of all litter.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

Now, Old Man Tiber, he was a caution, a real study in stubbornness. Had a mule named Bess that was cut from the same cloth, I reckon. This here trouble started with a prize-winning pumpkin, see? Biggest thing in three counties, it was. Tiber swore it’d win the fair, and young Jebediah, his nephew, well, Jebediah had a different notion.

“Uncle Harvey,” Jebediah says, fidgeting with his hat, “I… I might’ve accidentally let the chickens at it. Just a peck or two, mind you. They got a hankerin’ for orange, I suppose.”

Tiber’s face went a shade of purple I hadn’t seen since Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning beets got struck by lightning. “Accidentally, you say? Chickens don’t *accidentally* dismantle a gourd the size of a small wagon! You told them to, didn’t you? You and your infernal schemes!”

Jebediah stammered, “I… I was gonna fix it! Got some plaster and paint… thought I could patch it up. Said I’d tell you later, after I… got it.’ But never mind, if you think it’s best to tell your uncle Harvey—” 

“Shucks, and stay fooling around here when we could all be having good time?” Tiber bellowed. “Boy, you’re in for a heap of trouble.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Lucas, ever possessed of a practical turn of mind, observed with growing concern the lingering attentions of Mr. Collins towards her friend, Miss Bennet. Though a connection with such a man could scarcely be deemed desirable, the prospect of his continued importunities threatened a most disagreeable disturbance to the quiet of Longbourn. It was, therefore, with a degree of determined benevolence that she conceived a scheme, not entirely devoid of self-interest, to secure her friend from any return of his unwelcome addresses, by engaging them towards herself. 

Appearances were so favourable, indeed, that Mr. Collins, readily mistaking civility for encouragement, began to lavish upon Miss Lucas compliments of a rather excessive nature. He spoke of her sensible disposition, her admirable composure, and, most surprisingly, her pleasing figure. Miss Bennet, though privately amused, maintained a discreet silence, allowing the gentleman to proceed in his delusion. 

Miss Lucas, meanwhile, bore the flattery with a commendable fortitude, occasionally offering a carefully modulated response, sufficient to fuel his hopes without committing her to any definitive understanding. It was a delicate game, requiring a precision of manner and a suppression of genuine feeling, but one she felt herself admirably equipped to play.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth, though possessed of a lively wit and a mind remarkably fertile in notions, was, alas, a most desultory correspondent. Her letters, whilst brimming with intelligence – accounts of balls, the latest fashions from London, and observations upon the local gentry – were frequently marred by a lamentable lack of precision. One found oneself perpetually backtracking, deciphering half-formed sentences and grasping at meanings obscured by a profusion of dashes.

It was, one suspected, a consequence of her exceeding quickness of thought. Ideas, it seemed, tumbled forth with such velocity that the poor hand could scarcely keep pace, and the necessary labour of arrangement was quite neglected. A phrase begun with elegant circumspection would often dissolve into a breathless rush, leaving the reader quite adrift. 

Indeed, one could almost *pardon* the imperfections, perceiving them as the unavoidable price of such a spirited intellect. Though not, of course, *estimable* in themselves – clarity and good order are, after all, the hallmarks of a refined composition – they bespoke a mind too engaged with the substance of things to be overly concerned with the minutiae of their presentation. A charming fault, perhaps, but a fault nonetheless.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mr. Alistair Finch, having endured a twelvemonth within the somewhat bustling, and occasionally chaotic, household of the Beresfords, felt a peculiar obligation descend upon him. It was not, precisely, affection – though a fondness for Miss Eleanor’s quiet pianoforte playing *did* exist – but rather a sense of duty, born of sustained hospitality. He had, after all, been a burden, a distant cousin with nowhere else to turn following a most unfortunate speculation in Peruvian guano.

Having discharged his conscience on that head, detailing the improvements to his financial situation and the securing of a modest, yet respectable, living in Hampshire, he proceeded to inform them, with a carefully modulated tone, of his impending departure. Mrs. Beresford, predictably, expressed a delicate regret, whilst Mr. Beresford merely nodded, preoccupied with the latest agricultural reports. 

It was young Master Thomas, however, who elicited a genuine warmth. The boy, having initially regarded Mr. Finch with suspicion, now clung to his coat, lamenting the loss of a willing participant in his rather boisterous games. Such unfeigned sorrow, Mr. Finch thought, was a reward far exceeding any comfort he had received during his stay, and prompted a gratitude he had not anticipated.
author: Jane Austen

Now, I reckon I’ve seen a heap of foolishness in my time, but the spectacle down at Old Man Hemlock’s barn-raising took the biscuit, it did. These weren’t farmers, mind you, not exactly. They were… *aspirants*. Folks who’d struck a little luck with the silver, and decided plain speakin’ and honest toil were beneath ‘em.

Lord, the colors! Velvet jackets the shade of a bruised plum, ruffled shirts that’d shame a peacock, and enough gold braid to moor a steamboat. And the talk! Not a “howdy” or “good day” amongst ‘em. No sir. It was “Your Majesty, a fine day for hammerin’,” and “Your Grace, might I offer you a swig of cider?” 

Old Jebediah, who hadn’t shaved in a month and smelled powerfully of manure, was addressed as “His Lordship” by a fella wearin’ a wig that looked suspiciously like a squirrel. It was enough to make a body laugh ‘til his sides ached, and then feel a mite sorry for the poor souls tryin’ so hard to be somethin’ they weren’t. They were buildin’ a barn, alright, but they were also buildin’ a whole heap of nonsense on top of it.
author: Mark Twain

Now, old Man Hemlock, he’d been livin’ a solitary life up by the crick, mostly talkin’ to squirrels and complainin’ about the price of corn. A fella named Silas, a traveling peddler with a wagon full of notions and a tongue full of stories, stopped by one afternoon. Silas, he was a slick one, mind you, with a mustache that curled like a question mark.

“Say,” Silas drawled, settin’ down a box of patent medicines, “ever hear tell of a fella named Romeo?”

Hemlock squinted. “Romeo? Sounds like a fancy name for a hound dog.”

Silas chuckled, a sound like pebbles in a tin can. “Oh, no sir. Romeo was a *lover*. A real, dyed-in-the-wool, moonin’ and sighin’ sort. And he was sweet on a gal named Juliet. Now *she* was a looker, but her family, they didn’t hold with Romeo. Said he was no good, a ramblin’ sort. Ended up…well, it’s a long story involving poison and misunderstandin’s. I *was* Romeo, you see, in a theatrical company once. Played the part to perfection, I did.”

Hemlock just stared, then spat a stream of tobacco juice. “Played the part, eh? Seems a right foolish way to spend a life, all that lovin’ and dyin’.”
author: Mark Twain

Now, the Mississippi in de mawnin’ is a sight to behold, all mist and shimmer like a spilled bottle o’ dreams. But it weren’t the river holdin’ my attention, no sir. It was the skifts. They begun to go by, one after another, loaded with folks headin’ to town for market and gossip. And Lordy, the gossip!

’Bout eight or nine skifts out o’ ten, they’d slow as they passed, and somebody’d lean over, eyes wide as saucers. “Heard tell yer pap been to town,” they’d say, all hushed and important-like. “Said *you* was…well, said you was doin’ somethin’ or other.” 

They never *said* what, mind you. Just left it hangin’ there, a prickly burr under yer skin. Some’d offer a pityin’ look, others a sly grin. Old Man Hemlock, he just shook his head and muttered somethin’ ’bout “trouble brewin’.” 

It was enough to make a body feel like a fish on a hook, twitchin’ and wonderin’ what kinda bait they’d used. Pap hadn’t said a word to *me* 'bout comin' to town. Just vanished like smoke, and now the whole river knew somethin’ I didn’t. A body couldn’t rightly trust a river, or the folks who floated on it, neither.

Old Man Tiber, he sat on the porch swing, lookin’ like a hound dog left out in the rain. Dust motes danced in the afternoon sun, same as they always did, but today they seemed to mock the stillness. Miss Elvira, she fussed with a chipped teacup, though there wasn’t a soul to offer it to.

“All right—for George didn’t leave nothing,” she said, her voice thin as a willow branch. “And that letter was all they could get him to put a pen to.” She held it up, a flimsy thing, the ink faded like a forgotten memory. 

“Why do you reckon Harvey don’t come?” I asked, shiftin’ in my chair. “Wher’ do a man disappear to, anyhow, after livin’ alongside you sixty year? Seems like the earth oughta swallow him whole if he ain’t got nowhere particular to be.”

Tiber sighed, a sound like wind through dry cornstalks. “Harvey always was a wanderer at heart. Said he felt cramped by these hills. George, he was rooted. But Harvey… well, a bird ain’t meant to stay in a cage, even a gilded one.” He spat a stream of tobacco juice into the dirt. “Just a shame he couldn’t’ve sent a word. A fella deserves a little closure, don’t ya think?”

The ascent began with a sickening lightness, a defiance of the natural order that pressed upon the temples. Above the grey, churning bosom of the Atlantic, the aircraft strained, a fragile insect against a canvas of impossible vastness. We sought not the depths, but the *heights* – a foolish ambition, I now suspect, born of a hubris that mirrored the pre-human architects whose cyclopean ruins clung to the foothills below.

The camp, a cluster of canvas and dread, was pitched amongst those ancient stones. They were not built, but *grown*, it seemed, from a basaltic ichor that pulsed with a cold, internal luminescence. Locals whispered of the ‘Sky-Touched’ – beings who predated the glaciers, who walked these slopes when the world was younger and… *different*. 

A peculiar stillness permeated the air, a silence not of absence, but of *listening*. The wind, when it came, carried not the scent of pine or salt, but a faint, metallic tang, and a subsonic hum that resonated deep within the bone. It was a place where the geometry felt subtly wrong, where shadows stretched at angles that mocked Euclidean space, and where the very air tasted of a forgotten, cosmic loneliness. Something watched from the peaks, I felt it, and it was not benevolent.

text:
The journey from Epsom, though agreeable enough in its initial stages, had begun to pall. Miss Eleanor, ever sensitive to the discomforts of travel, declared the springs of the chaise quite inadequate, and her sister, Miss Marianne, though less prone to complaint, confessed to a growing weariness. Their destination, London, loomed with a mixture of anticipation and trepidation. 

Their father, a gentleman of comfortable means but decidedly provincial habits, had secured lodgings in a respectable, though not overly fashionable, square. Farther, indeed, they travelled, for on entering that place, they removed into a hackney-coach, and dismissed the chaise that brought them from Epsom. 

All that is known after is a series of fragmented reports gleaned from the housekeeper, Mrs. Higgins, a woman of considerable discretion and even more considerable gossip. There were callers, of course – a Mr. Finch, a solicitor with a most unromantic countenance, and a Captain Armitage, whose attentions to Miss Marianne were, according to Mrs. Higgins, “rather too pressing for a young lady’s peace of mind.”  Whether these encounters led to any lasting consequence, or merely provided fodder for the servants’ hall, remains, alas, a mystery.

text:
The floe groaned, a sound not of ice fracturing, but of something *shifting* beneath, a vast, cold respiration. Fifteen leagues we’d drifted, swallowed by the white, and the compass spun with a sickening, purposeful futility. It was not merely snow, this immensity, but a palpable *absence* of colour, a negation of light that pressed upon the mind. 

Old Man Hemlock, before the…incident, had muttered of a geometry beyond human comprehension residing within the polar wastes, a non-Euclidean architecture built by things that predate warmth. Now, I understood. The horizon wasn’t a line, but a concave curve, drawing the eye inward to a point that wasn’t there, a point that *shouldn’t* be.

The air grew thick, not with moisture, but with a silence so profound it resonated in the bone. Shapes began to coalesce within the swirling white – not drifts, but *forms*, colossal and vaguely cylindrical, rising and falling with a rhythm that echoed the maddening pulse in my temples. They were…wrong. Terribly, fundamentally wrong. 

A low, ululating tone, like the sigh of a dying star, permeated the ice. We were not merely lost. We were being *observed*. And the white, I realised with a creeping dread, was not emptiness, but a veil. A veil drawn back to reveal…something.

Miss Eleanor had, with a most fortunate dispatch, rid herself of two of the secrets which had weighed on her for a fortnight, and was certain of a willing listener in Jane, whenever she might wish to talk again. The relief was considerable, though not, perhaps, entirely untainted by a degree of mortification. To confess a foolish fancy, even to a sister of such discretion, was not wholly agreeable. 

However, the matter concerning Mr. Hawthorne’s unexpectedly ardent admiration – a circumstance she had initially deemed flattering, but now recognised as rather… presumptuous – was safely imparted. And the unfortunate incident with the spilled ratafia at Lady Ashworth’s soiree, a calamity she had feared would forever brand her as clumsy, was likewise confessed.

Jane, as Eleanor had anticipated, received both narratives with a gentle amusement and a comforting lack of judgement. “Men *will* be foolish, Eleanor,” she observed regarding Mr. Hawthorne, “and a little ratafia upon a carpet is scarcely a matter for lasting regret.” 

Eleanor felt a warmth spread through her. To have shared the burden, and to find it so lightly borne, was a blessing indeed. Perhaps, she thought, a quiet evening with her embroidery was now fully deserved.

While Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire – a task undertaken with a vigour quite disproportionate to the actual need for warmth, and accompanied by a running commentary on the deficiencies of the grate – Mr. Darcy brought his coffee-cup back to the mantelpiece. He did so with a quietude that served only to highlight the bustling agitation of the room. One might have thought, observing him, that he was accustomed to navigating far more turbulent company than that of Longbourn’s inhabitants.

Indeed, his countenance betrayed little beyond a mild disapproval of the excessive floral arrangement upon the table. Mrs. Bennet, pausing mid-stir, fixed him with a gaze intended to convey both welcome and a subtle inquiry as to his opinion of her daughters. He offered a barely perceptible inclination of the head, a gesture which, to a less discerning eye, might have passed for nothing at all.

Now, this here meal, it weren’t just *eaten*, understand. It had a journey. Old man’s cookin’ ain’t never been known for its…containment. Bits and pieces, they’d flake off, see, like scales from a catfish. And them flakes, they didn’t just disappear. No sir. They made a trail. A right proper, if accidental, trail.

Started at the cabin door, a sprinkle here, a dusting there, leadin’ through the weeds and over the roots. A fella could’ve followed it blindfolded, I reckon, if he weren’t too concerned with snakes. It wound and meandered, that meal did, like a lazy river, and ended, bless its heart, right at the edge of the lake. 

And then, to complete the illusion, to make it look like pure, unadulterated happenstance, I took Pap’s whetstone. That stone he prized like a gold tooth. Dropped it right amongst the meal-dust. The small gathering at the vicarage, though pleasant, had offered little in the way of stimulating conversation. Mrs. Philips was detailing the ribbons adorning her youngest’s bonnet, a subject upon which I could offer little genuine interest. I had begun to contemplate the merits of a quiet evening with a book when a shadow fell across my path.

It was Mr. Darcy. A most unwelcome interruption, I thought, bracing myself for some observation on the impropriety of the company. Instead, he addressed *me* directly, and with a gravity that quite stole my breath. 

“Miss…,” he began, a flush rising on his usually composed countenance, “I trust I do not intrude. However, I find myself compelled to speak plainly. My regard for you, madam, has grown beyond what I deemed possible, and I venture to offer… a proposal of marriage.”

The words hung in the air, utterly astonishing. A proposal! From *him*! My composure, so carefully maintained, threatened to desert me entirely. I could only stare, a most unbecoming display, I daresay, but entirely beyond my control. The room seemed to spin, and Mrs. Philips’ bonnet faded into a blurry, insignificant haze.

The encounter, though deemed accidental by polite society, possessed a distinct air of calculation on Mr. Ashworth’s part. He had, it was understood, contrived to be strolling near the milliner’s on Bond Street precisely at the hour Miss Elmsworth favoured for acquiring ribbons. He told himself it was merely a desire to inquire after the health of Mrs. Penrose, a mutual acquaintance; a flimsy justification even *he* found wanting upon reflection. 

As to his real character, had information been in wider circulation, a less charitable interpretation would undoubtedly prevail. He possessed a fluency of address, certainly, and a pleasing countenance, though a certain restlessness in the eye hinted at a spirit not entirely governed by propriety. He spoke of the recent Assembly with an ease bordering on familiarity, observing Miss Elmsworth’s gown with a compliment that, while not overtly impertinent, lacked the sincerity expected of a gentleman. 

She, for her part, received his attentions with a cool civility, her fan moving with a deliberate slowness that spoke volumes. He sensed a resistance, a quiet assessment, and found himself, to his considerable annoyance, wishing he had indeed inquired after Mrs. Penrose.

The drawing-room, though comfortably appointed, felt suddenly airless. Miss Eleanor, usually so composed, had flushed a most unbecoming pink, and Mr. Harding, a gentleman possessed of a fortune exceeding his wit, was regarding her with an expression bordering on triumph. It was, however, to Miss Bennet that his remark was directed.

“If you and Miss Bennet will defer yours till I am out of the room,” he declared, his voice a touch too loud for polite company, “I shall be very thankful; and then you may say whatever you like of me.”

A delicate silence descended. Miss Bennet, ever mindful of propriety, lowered her eyes to her embroidery. “What you…intend, sir, is not entirely clear.”

Mr. Harding, emboldened by her restraint, continued, “Only that my attentions to your sister are a matter of…speculation. And I confess, a frank exchange of opinion, *after* my departure, would be preferable to a pointed observation whilst within my hearing.” 

Miss Eleanor’s blush deepened. It was a most awkward proposal, and one which threatened to unravel the carefully constructed civility of the afternoon.

Books stacked precarious as a gambler’s debts, newspapers yellowed with age and opinion, a half-eaten apple core lookin’ like a miniature, brown monument to lost ambition. And clothes. Old Man Hemlock, he’d said it was a curiosity. A relic. I reckon a relic of somebody’s forgotten troubles, more likely. Still, a body couldn’t help but wonder what secrets that dusty lump was keepin’ to itself, lyin’ there in the gloom like a forgotten promise.

Now, Old Man Tiber ain’t never seen a fella as set on a notion as I was. Been courtin’ Miss Lily May for nigh on two years, a sweet girl, she was, with eyes like melted caramels and a laugh that could charm the warts off a toad. Well, substantiality ain’t always measured in coin, I reckoned. It’s in the grit of a man, the kindness in his heart. But try tellin’ *him* that. So, I hatched a plan. A grand, romantic plan. Run off with Lily, of course. 

But not the usual sort. I figured, what good is runnin’ *from* somethin’? Better to run *to* somethin’. I told Lily, “We’ll make a life for ourselves, a proper one. Her good, and then, ’stead of taking to the woods when I run off, I’d go down the river about fifty mile and camp in one place for good, and not have to be lookin’ over my shoulder every minute. She just smiled, that caramel-eyed smile, and said, “Sounds mighty fine to me.” And that, sir, was enough to make a man feel substantial indeed.

Old Man Tiber, he was a ponderin’ sort, always had a wrinkle in his brow deeper than the Mississippi at low water. We was sittin’ on the porch, watchin’ Miz Peabody’s tabby, Clementine, try to snag a moth. Now, Clementine, she had a peculiar habit of…well, *attemptin'* human speech. Mostly just squawks and growls shaped like words, but Miz Peabody swore she once heard her say “More milk.”

“It’s unnatural, I tell ya,” Tiber declared, spittin’ a stream of tobacco juice into the dust. “Well, den, dey ain’t no sense in a cat talkin’ like a man. Is a cow a man?—er is a cow a cat?”

I scratched my head. “No, she ain’t either of them.”

“Well, den, she ain’t. And a cat ain’t a man, neither. It’s a contraption of the mind, that’s what it is. Folks get to thinkin’ too much, tryin’ to put a harness on nature. A cat’s meant to *meow*, not debate the price of corn. It’s a sign of the times, I reckon. Everything gettin’ all mixed up and fancy. Give me a good, honest purr over a philosophical feline any day.” He chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “It just ain’t *natural*.”

text:
Old Man Tiber, he had a memory like a sieve, bless his soul. Or, rather, *didn’t* have one. Claimed I’d promised him a prize bull, a magnificent Durham, back in ‘88. ‘88! Why, I was barely shaving then, and more interested in chasing skirts than cattle. 

“Every bit and grain I *did* say, young man,” he insisted, leaning on his cane like it was the only thing keepin’ him upright. “Said I’d have that bull delivered by spring. Witnessed by half the county, it was!”

Now, I’d likely *mentioned* a bull, in passing, whilst discussin’ the price of turnips. A casual remark, a bit of farmer’s bluster. But a *promise*? Heavens to Betsy. 

“I reckon he can stand a little thing like that, can’t he?” I offered, tryin’ for a conciliatory tone.

He bristled, eyes narrowin’ like a hawk’s. “I don’t care whether ’twas little or whether ’twas big; he’s expectin’ that bull! A gentleman’s word is his bond, you know. And you, sir, are lookin’ mighty ungentlemanly right now.” 

A Durham bull. Lord. Some folks just have a way of rememberin’ things… *their* way.

Now, old Man Hemlock, he found her sittin’ by the creek, lookin’ like a wilted sunflower. Not a sound she made, just… occupied. And what occupied her was peculiar, I tell you. One hand, a delicate thing, all pale and fine, but with a smear of black wax along the edge of the palm – looked like she’d been sealin’ up trouble, or maybe a heart. 

She was workin’ at a locket, see. Silver, tarnished with grief, and attached to a chain long enough to snare a catfish. But she weren’t admirin’ it. No sir. She was *mashin'* it against her mouth, gentle-like at first, then with a desperation that’d make a preacher clutch his Bible. 

Underneath the glass, a faded picture. Couldn’t rightly make out who it was, but the way she pressed that locket to her lips, like tryin’ to draw a breath from a ghost… well, it spoke volumes. Some loves, they ain’t meant for keepin’, I reckon. Some just leave a black mark and a taste of sorrow, and a woman mashin’ silver against her own mouth, hopin’ to bring somethin’ back that’s already gone to Kingdom Come.

The salt-laced wind carried a preternatural chill, even for this forsaken stretch of the Massachusetts coast. Old Man Hemlock had warned of them, of course – muttered tales of ‘sky-pillars’ and a geometry inimical to the sane mind. We dismissed it as the ramblings of a man too long acquainted with brine and solitude. Until *they* became visible.

At first, merely suggestions against the bruised twilight, impossibly tall and slender. Not clouds, for they possessed a dreadful, static *presence*, an unyielding verticality that mocked the natural curves of the horizon. Off, utterly and disturbingly off, from any terrestrial scale. They were visible only because of their abnormal height, a violation of perspective that gnawed at the edges of reason.

Little by little, however, they rose grimly into the western sky, allowing us to distinguish… *volumes*. Not smooth, but faceted, with angles that seemed to shift and writhe even as we stared. A sickly, phosphorescent sheen clung to their surfaces, and a low, subsonic hum resonated in the bones, a vibration that spoke of vast, cold distances and things best left undisturbed. The sea birds fell silent. A dread, ancient and formless, settled upon the town, and I knew, with a certainty that chilled me to the core, that the stars were not right.

Miss Elmsworth’s conduct regarding her cousin, Mr. Finch, continued to perplex all who observed it. It was not, precisely, dislike; for a complete want of civility would have been far more comprehensible. Rather, it seemed a wilful ill-nature, or a voluntary penance; for on these occasions it was not merely a few formal inquiries and an awkward pause and then a hasty retreat. No, Miss Elmsworth *encouraged* Mr. Finch’s attentions, accepting his offered hand for a country dance, even engaging him in conversation regarding the merits of various rose cultivars. 

Yet, with each polite gesture, a subtle frost descended upon her countenance. Her replies, though perfectly formed, lacked warmth, and her eyes, whilst meeting his, held a distant, almost mournful expression. One might suspect a secret sorrow, were it not for the distinct impression that she *wished* him to perceive her unhappiness. 

Mrs. Penhaligon, a lady renowned for her discernment, declared it a most peculiar game. “She draws him on, only to remind him of his unsuitability,” she confided to Miss Ainsworth. “A most artful, and, I fear, unkind amusement.”

Now, it was a right foolish game we were playin’, “Bully for the Bush,” we called it. Simple enough – one fella hid, the others sought. But these boys, Tom Sawyer types mostly, had a knack for mischief that bordered on the unholy. They’d been countin’ to a hundred and ten, I reckon, just to give themselves a proper head start. A body could’ve walked to St. Louis and back in that time.

Goodness gracious, the boys had *too* good a start. They got to the woodpile that was in front of my tree, and slipped in behind it, and so they had the bulge on me. A fella could’ve sworn they’d sprouted roots, they were so still. I circled that pile slow, lookin’ for a twitch, a giggle, *somethin’*. 

Old Man Hemlock, he’d’ve said they were possessed by sprites. And I wouldn’t’ve argued with him. It wasn’t fair, not a bit. But then, fairness ain’t always been a strong suit with boys. They were waitin’ for me to pass, intendin’ to jump out and yell “Bully!” and scare the whiskers off a hound dog. A right nuisance, they were, but a fella couldn’t help but smile. The geologist, Armitage, had dismissed the initial reports as delirium induced by altitude and the peculiar, metallic tang in the air. But the photographs… the photographs defied rational dismissal. They depicted a section of the Black Ridge, normally subject to the relentless gnawing of wind and frost, exhibiting an *arrest* of decay. Not merely slowed, but *halted*. 

It was the geometry that chilled the blood. Not the natural fracturing of shale, but a deliberate, unsettling order. The mountainside was afflicted with a tangle of regular cubes, ramparts, and cave mouths – all hewn from the living rock, yet possessing a precision utterly alien to terrestrial forces. Each angle was unnervingly *correct*, each surface polished to a sickening sheen.

The local tribes spoke of “The Stone Sleepers,” entities who predated the glaciers, who *shaped* the mountains to their unknowable purpose. Armitage, a man of science, scoffed… until he noted the subtle, almost imperceptible hum emanating from the stone itself. A resonance, calculated, it seemed, to retard the usual climatic processes of rock disintegration. A preservation, not of beauty, but of *waiting*. And what, he dared not contemplate, were they waiting *for*?
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The summons had arrived not by post, nor messenger, but a creeping dissonance in the very architecture of my dreams. Old Man Hemlock, they called him – though ‘old’ felt a grotesque understatement for a being whose lineage predated the crumbling of Carcosa. He required an…observer. A chronicler of the Shift. And over his duties, I did not protest. To protest would have been to invite a scrutiny I dared not contemplate.

The observatory, a cyclopean stone excrescence upon Widow’s Hill, reeked of ozone and something older, something akin to the dust of extinct stars. Hemlock gestured with a hand that seemed less flesh and more articulated shale towards the western horizon. There, beyond the familiar, bruised purple of twilight, lay a sector of reddish, *farther* sky. 

I tried to keep all my skill and self-possession about me, and stared at it. It wasn’t a colour known to Euclid, nor describable by any sane palette. It *pulsed*, a slow, sickening rhythm that resonated not in the eyes, but in the basal ganglia. The air grew thick, viscous, tasting of iron and regret. Hemlock merely chuckled, a dry rasp like pebbles in a tomb. “Observe,” he croaked. “Observe the thinning.” And I knew, with a dread that chilled me to the very core, that something *vast* and utterly alien was pressing against the fragile membrane of our reality.

text:
The matter was concluded, and with a surprising lack of acrimony, which, Miss Elmsworth considered, spoke volumes for the gentleman’s character, if not his judgement. He had declared his affections, quite plainly, and she had, with equal plainness, declined them. Not from dislike, precisely – Mr. Finch was a perfectly respectable man, possessed of a tolerable estate and a passable countenance – but from a want of that…spark. That animating principle which renders life, and indeed, matrimony, bearable.

She found herself, however, remarkably untroubled. There was no harsh word exchanged, no wounded pride to nurse. He had accepted her refusal with a stoicism bordering on indifference, and she, in turn, felt no particular regret. It was a quiet ending to a quiet pursuit. 

Indeed, she possessed the singular comfort of a clear conscience. She had nothing either to hope or fear, and nothing to reproach him with. Thank God she had not *that* pain. A little time, therefore – she should certainly require it – to re-establish her composure and resume her usual occupations. The pianoforte, perhaps, and a new embroidery frame. A sensible arrangement, all things considered.

This mornin’, though, it weren’t fish he was smellin’. It was trouble. He got a look in his eye, a pinched-up sort of look, and muttered somethin’ about “strangers.” I didn’t pay it much mind, bein’ more concerned with avoidin’ chores. But then I heard the voices. Low, and not friendly.

So, I got my gun – a perfectly good squirrel rifle, though it’d do for a man in a pinch – and slipped out and into the edge of the woods. I sat down there on a log, and looked out through the leaves. I see t… a fella, dressed all in black, arguin’ with Pa over somethin’ shiny. And another one, keepin’ watch, lookin’ mean as a rattlesnake in July. This weren’t about fish, no sir. This was somethin’ else entirely. And I had a feelin’ it was gonna get interestin’.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The arrival of the Misses Beaumont at Hartfield was, naturally, the subject of much discussion. Not that their fortunes were remarkable – perfectly adequate, certainly, but not such as to command immediate consequence. No, it was their *carriage*, and more particularly, their demeanour, which drew the attention of the neighbourhood. They were very fine ladies, possessing complexions of a delicate bloom and figures rendered elegant by Parisian millinery. 

Not deficient in good-humour when they were pleased, nor in the power of being agreeable where they chose it, Miss Eleanor, the elder, possessed a wit that, whilst undeniably sharp, was frequently employed in a manner bordering on the pointed. Miss Marianne, though less overtly critical, held herself with an air of such quiet superiority that one felt perpetually under observation, and invariably found wanting.

Mrs. Weston declared them “charming, though a little… reserved.” Mr. Knightley, however, observed, with a characteristic lift of the brow, that reserve was often merely pride in a more polished guise. And indeed, it was becoming increasingly clear that the Beaumont sisters, whilst perfectly civil, considered themselves quite beyond the necessity of *seeking* acquaintance.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The charts, salvaged from the drowned scholar’s cabin, spoke not of coastlines or currents, but of *angles*. Unnatural angles, etched upon vellum brittle with age and smelling faintly of the abyssal brine. They detailed, with a maddening precision, the placement of structures – not dwellings, not temples in any sense understood by sane men – but *resonators*. 

Each point marked corresponded to a cyclopean edifice, now mostly submerged or crumbled to dust along the forgotten shores of the Antarctic. The sketches… they defied Euclidean geometry. Towers leaning inward upon themselves, foundations that spiraled *downward* rather than supporting, and a pervasive, unsettling motif of non-right angles. 

Old Man Hemlock, before his unfortunate…disintegration, muttered of a pre-human architecture, built to channel energies from a dimension beyond human comprehension. He believed these structures weren’t built *on* the Earth, but *to* it – anchors, perhaps, preventing something vast and ancient from fully breaching our reality. 

We could, with diligent study and further expeditions, reconstruct the whole stupendous thing as it was a million years prior. But a chilling dread clings to the prospect. For what purpose were these angles conceived? And what, precisely, were they holding *back*?
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I reckon I ain’t one for spillin’ my guts, not generally. But a body gets to thinkin’, see, when the sun’s settin’ and the river’s rollin’ by like time itself. And thinkin’ ‘bout freedom… well, that’s a powerful thing.

I was a slave, you understand. Born into it, raised in it, expectin’ to *die* in it. Felt like a stone tied to the bottom of that very river, always pullin’ me down. Then came Huck. A scrawny, mischievous boy, full of notions and a heart bigger’n Missouri. 

He coulda turned me in, easy. Society expected it. But he didn’t. He *fought* for me, lied for me, risked everything for a man he barely knew. A boy, mind you, wrestlin’ with his conscience and the whole blamed world.

I’m a free man now, see? Got my own little patch of land, growin’ beans and livin’ quiet. But I couldn’t ever ben free ef it hadn’ ben for Huck; Huck done it. Jim won’t ever forgit you, Huck; you’s de bes’ fren’ Jim’s ever had. That boy… he showed me what a man *could* be, even when the world told him different.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor Finch was, it must be confessed, possessed of a certain vivacity. Her early pronouncements at assemblies, concerning the lamentable state of the circulating library and the egregious lack of eligible bachelors in the county, had raised a few eyebrows. Yet, these were merely the effervescence of youth, a slight pertness easily forgiven, and indeed, rather amusing. 

It was when Mr. Dorrington, a man of considerable fortune and even more considerable solemnity, finally declared his affections that Eleanor’s true character shone. He spoke, of course, with all the requisite gravity, detailing his esteem and anticipating a future of comfortable domesticity. Eleanor, however, did not blush and flutter as propriety demanded. 

“Sir,” she replied, her voice remarkably steady, “I am flattered, truly. But comfort, while desirable, is not the sole aim of a woman’s existence. I require…sympathy. A meeting of minds. Do you, Mr. Dorrington, possess a mind *worth* meeting?” 

The colour drained from his face. He had anticipated gratitude, acquiescence, perhaps a delicate sigh. Not this. Not a direct challenge to his intellectual capacity. The silence stretched, thick and uncomfortable, a testament to Eleanor’s unexpected fortitude.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, I reckon a fella gets himself into scrapes, same as a hound dog finds ticks. This particular scrape commenced with Mrs. Abernathy’s peach preserves. Fine preserves, mind you, but a body can only admire so many jars before a certain…acquisition instinct kicks in. And I, well, I’m built for admiration, and subsequent borrowing.

It wasn’t the preserves themselves, not exactly. It was the *hanging around*. I was suited to that widow’s place, see? Quiet, respectable, a listening ear for her tales of departed husbands and prize-winning pumpkins. But she got to thinking I listened *too* much. Said a man with my talents – and she did use that word, “talents,” bless her – ought to be *earning* his keep, not sampling her fruit and offering opinions on the weather.

She told me, plain as a church bell, that my presence was “unsettling.” Unsettling! As if a bit of polite conversation could unsettle a woman who’d weathered forty winters and a hailstorm that near took the roof off. 

Next thing I knew, the constable had a hand on my shoulder and I was cooling my heels in a cell. Perfectly comfortable, truth be told. A man needs a bit of peace and quiet now and then, and jail, surprisingly, provides it.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The river, she was a-rollin’ along like a contented hog in the mud, and the raft, well, the raft was lookin’ mighty little ways off now. Close enough to smell the fish we’d be catchin’, close enough to hear old Jim’s stories, which, truth be told, were mostly tall tales and ramblings ‘bout signs and superstitions. But close enough for comfort, all the same.

Old man turned to me, squintin’ like a crawfish in the sun. He had a way of lookin’ *through* a body, not *at* ‘em. “Boy,” he says, slow and deliberate, like he was weighin’ every syllable, “that’s a lie. What *is* the matter with your pap? Answer up square now, and it’ll be the better fo’. Don’t try to spin me no yarns, see? I ain’t got the patience for it.”

I swallowed hard. Pap… well, Pap was a complicated sort. A fella could write a whole book ‘bout the trouble with Pap, and still not get to the bottom of it. But the old man wanted a straight answer, and a boy learns quick enough that a straight answer, even a painful one, is often the least troublesome path.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The matter was, quite simply, Mr. Denny’s return from town. A point of some consequence to the Bennet household, as his conveyance held the promised ribbons for Miss Mary, and a new shade of muslin much desired by Miss Elizabeth. Lydia, however, possessed a volubility ill-suited to delicate inquiry, and had begun to pepper Mrs. Phillips with questions regarding the precise hour of his anticipated arrival, detailing the potential benefits to each sister with an enthusiasm bordering on the indelicate.

“Lydia, pray!” Miss Jane murmured, a blush rising in her cheeks. Miss Elizabeth seconded the plea with a pointed glance. “Such eagerness is quite unseemly.”

But Mr. Collins, who had been attempting to expound upon the virtues of a particularly robust parsonage garden, was much offended. He laid aside his discourse, deeming it a slight, and declared, with a huff, that a gentleman’s movements were no subject for such frivolous speculation. “To inquire as if Mr. Denny were a post chaise, arriving on a fixed schedule! It is… it is wanting in all propriety!” 

Mrs. Phillips, ever adept at smoothing ruffled feathers, hastened to assure him that Lydia’s youthful exuberance was merely a demonstration of familial affection. Though, privately, she suspected the ribbons held a greater sway over her youngest’s concern.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though barely turned three and twenty, possessed a composure that belied her years. It was not, however, a natural stoicism, but rather the fruit of a sensibility once too readily engaged. A youthful fancy, indulged with perhaps undue warmth towards a certain Captain Fitzwilliam, had yielded to the sobering influence of time and, more importantly, of reflection. She now understood, with a clarity that brought a gentle melancholy, that first attachments often boast a brilliance exceeding their true substance.

Mr. Thomas Ashworth, a gentleman of quiet fortune and even quieter manners, had entered her life some months past. He lacked the Captain’s dashing air, yet offered a steadiness of character, a kindness of disposition, that resonated with a deeper part of her nature. It was not a passionate whirlwind, but a slow, warming glow. 

And so fervently did she value his remembrance, and prefer him to ever. Not with the breathless excitement of a girl, but with the considered affection of a woman who knew the true worth of a tranquil heart and a dependable hand. A prospect, she allowed herself to think, not entirely devoid of happiness.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mrs. Philips, ever eager for intelligence concerning the fortunes of her neighbours, had been questioning Mr. Harding regarding his recent travels. His descriptions of a certain estate, however, initially conveyed little gratification. He spoke of a grand, though somewhat austere, residence, situated amidst parkland of considerable extent, and occupied by a gentleman of reserved habits. 

“Indeed?” she remarked, with a polite, yet faintly disappointed, inclination of the head. “A large house is all very well, but one does hope for a lively company.”

It was only when Mr. Harding, perceiving her lack of enthusiasm, elucidated further – explaining that this Rosings Park belonged to Lady Catherine de Bourgh, a lady of immense wealth and connection, and intimately acquainted with the family of a certain Mr. Darcy – that Mrs. Philips’ countenance brightened considerably. 

A change most palpable! Suddenly, the austere residence became a place of consequence, the reserved gentleman a figure of interest. “Lady Catherine, you say? And connected to the Darcys? Oh, Mr. Harding, you bring most excellent news! Such a connection is…everything.” The prospect of reflected glory, it seemed, possessed a charm far exceeding mere architectural grandeur.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The arrangements for the evening were, to say the least, precarious. Mama, naturally, had issued invitations with a generosity quite exceeding our means, and yet, one felt compelled to appear as though anticipating a throng. However, a sober assessment of the situation revealed a distinct lack of positive responses. Nobody, I am quite certain, is coming, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. 

It is a delicate matter, you see. To appear neither too eager for company, lest one be thought desperate, nor too indifferent, lest one be deemed ungracious. Mr. Collins, thankfully, remains at Hunsford, and Lady Catherine, though ever a potential visitor, is occupied with the breeding of her favourite pug. 

One cannot help but reflect upon the absurdity of social expectations. To expend such energy upon a supper which may well be consumed by only three – myself, Mama, and, perhaps, Charlotte – feels a trifle foolish. Still, a lady must maintain appearances, and a well-prepared dish, even for a small audience, is a comfort in itself.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, a body gets to recollectin’ things peculiar, don’t they? Especially when a feller’s tryin’ to make a point. Old Man Hemlock was holdin’ forth, see, about the righteousness of his judgment and the failings of human memory. “I remember, I believe,” he declared, puffin’ on that clay pipe of his, “every single detail of that transaction!” 

He went on and on, a regular flood of particulars. I let him ramble, mind you. A man’s gotta pick his spots. He kept sayin’, “Stop and think.” Well, I *did* stop and think. Studied awhile, like a hound dog fixin’ to spring. And I saw my chance, clear as a bell.

Then I says, slow and deliberate, “Well, I see the colored folks go in there several times.” Both of ‘em. Carryin’ bundles, lookin’ right proper. Hemlock, he sputtered like a wet firecracker. Claimed he hadn’t noticed. Said he was focused on the *important* business. 

Important business, indeed. Sometimes a body forgets what’s truly important when they’re too busy polishin’ up their own recollections. A body remembers what a body *sees*, generally. And I saw them colored folks, plain as day.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The matter had been broached, of course, with all the delicacy one might expect from a well-meaning, yet entirely misguided, acquaintance. Mr. Wickham, ever charming, had allowed a certain warmth to colour his discourse regarding Miss Elizabeth, a warmth which, to a less discerning eye, might have suggested a regard beyond mere civility. Elizabeth, however, always laughed at the notion, dismissing it as the product of his practiced affability and her own perhaps overly-active imagination. 

Indeed, the very idea was preposterous. Mr. Wickham possessed a taste for consequence, and Elizabeth, though not wanting in fortune, offered little in the way of connection or influence. 

Mrs. Collins, privy to the gentleman’s compliments, had attempted a subtle encouragement, hinting at Elizabeth’s accomplishments and amiable disposition. But Elizabeth’s amusement, so readily displayed, and a certain firmness in her refusal to entertain the possibility, quickly dissuaded her. It did not, Mrs. Collins felt, fall within her purview to *press* the subject, particularly when faced with such cheerful, and frankly, rather pointed, derision. A prudent woman knew when a delicate matter was best left undisturbed.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The chill wasn’t merely atmospheric, but a creeping, ontological frost that settled not upon the skin, but *within* the very architecture of the mind. Danforth, a man once rigorously devoted to the quantifiable, now spoke in fractured whispers, his eyes perpetually fixed on some unseen geometry beyond the plaster of my study walls. It was, he later told me, precisely what he had caught in infinitely muffled form when at that spot beyond the alley corner above the glacial le – a resonance, not of sound, but of *wrongness*.

He’d been charting the peculiar subsidence of old man Hemlock’s cellar, a task ostensibly geological, but driven, I suspect, by a morbid curiosity he dared not confess. The le, a stagnant pool fed by unseen springs, pulsed with a sickly luminescence even under the greyest skies. It was there, amidst the crumbling brick and the fetid air, that the sensation began. 

Not a hearing, but a *feeling* of being heard. A vast, cold intelligence, pressing against the fragile membrane of reality, attempting to articulate itself in dimensions beyond human comprehension. He described it as a colour, a texture, a weight… all simultaneously, and utterly *impossible*. A pre-Euclidean horror, hinting at geometries that would unravel the sanity of any who truly perceived them. And the worst, he insisted, was the implication of *waiting*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, old Man Hemlock, he had a notion. A powerful, peculiar notion. He figured Jim, the colored fella who worked his south forty, had struck it rich – gold, you see – and buried it. So Hemlock, he commenced to dig. Not *with* Jim, mind you, but *for* Jim, and all under the cover of darkness. He’d sneak out with a pickaxe, lookin’ like a badger pilferin’ chickens, and chip away at the ground near Jim’s cabin. 

I watched him one night, hid behind the smokehouse. He was gruntin’ and sweatin’, makin’ a right mess of things. I asked him, casual-like, what he was up to. He just glared and said, “Mind your business, boy.”

But I *did* mind. See, I knew Jim hadn’t no gold. He barely had two nickels to rub together. Hemlock was diggin’ up nothin’ but dirt and foolishness. I tried to tell him, but he wouldn’t listen. Said it was a “secret operation.” 

I could’ve joined him, helped him dig, pretended to believe in the gold. But I knew better. A man’s got to have some sense, even if old Hemlock hadn’t a lick of it. So I just let him sweat, and the dirt fly, and the whole thing be a spectacle of pure, unadulterated silliness.
author: Mark Twain

text:
I am, undeniably, the youngest, and, it must be confessed, the tallest of my sisters. A circumstance which, whilst affording a certain advantage in discerning the approach of eligible gentlemen across a crowded room, did little to elevate my standing in their esteem. Mr. Harrison, newly arrived from Hertfordshire, had, during the pianoforte performance, bestowed a most particular attention upon my person – not, I suspect, to my musical abilities, which are merely passable – but to my height. 

The rest of the evening was spent in conjecturing how soon he would return Mr. Bennet’s visit, and determining the precise degree of encouragement I had, or had *not*, offered. My mother, naturally, believed it a settled matter, envisioning a match predicated upon his admiration for a “fine, commanding figure.” Charlotte Lucas, ever the voice of reason, suggested it might simply be a matter of practical observation, a gentleman wishing to gauge the height of the room before committing to a dance. 

Such differing opinions! It is a vexation to be the subject of such speculation, particularly when one’s own sentiments remain, as yet, entirely unformed.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mr. Featherstonehaugh, though possessing a fortune quite adequate to his station, was a gentleman of peculiar, and one might venture to say, *uncommon* sensibilities. He did not in the least regard his losses at whist, dismissing a particularly grievous hand with a shrug and a remark concerning the capricious nature of cards. Far more occupied was he with the arrangements for the evening’s repast. 

Indeed, he enumerated the dishes at supper with a precision bordering on the pedantic – “First, a delicate consommé, followed by the roasted pheasant, then the salmon in hollandaise, a haunch of venison, and finally, a most agreeable syllabub!” – as if cataloguing treasures. Throughout the meal, a persistent anxiety plagued him. He repeatedly feared that he crowded his cousins, Miss Penelope and Miss Beatrice, offering his seat, adjusting their shawls, and inquiring, with a fretful air, if they had sufficient elbow room. 

One might have thought such solicitousness charming, were it not so… *constant*. It was, in truth, a most distracting habit, and one which suggested a mind far more attuned to the minutiae of social comfort than to the more substantial pursuits of a gentleman. He had, undeniably, more to occupy him than most.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though possessed of a comfortable fortune, found herself besieged by a most unwelcome proposition. Mr. Cecil Harwood, a gentleman of tolerable appearance but lamentable prospects, had lately declared his intentions with a candour bordering on the impertinent. His previous attempts at establishing himself had, it was universally acknowledged, been exceedingly bad. He had found the law a most unprofitable study, and was now absolutely resolved on being ordained, *if* she would present him to a living.

The audacity! To suggest a vocation solely upon the strength of her connections, and to imply a dependence so…unbecoming. Her mother, naturally, viewed the matter with a different eye, extolling the respectability of the cloth and the convenience of a settled clergyman nearby. Eleanor, however, possessed a spirit too independent to be bartered for parish duties. 

“He speaks of piety, Mama,” she observed, whilst arranging a posy of sweet peas, “but I detect a distinct lack of principle. A man who shifts his purpose with such ease is hardly fit to guide others.” The prospect of a life spent facilitating Mr. Harwood’s ambition filled her with a most disagreeable apprehension.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth possessed a vivacity which, though not precisely *brilliant*, was undeniably agreeable. It was this, perhaps, more than any shared accomplishment, that had recommended her to Miss Lydia Fortescue upon their first meeting at the Assembly. Good-humour and good spirits, it seemed, were sufficient foundation for a connection, and a most fortunate one it proved. Of their three months’ acquaintance, two had been spent in a degree of intimacy quite remarkable for so short a period.

Lydia, though prone to flights of fancy and a certain eagerness for amusement, found in Eleanor a companion who neither indulged nor entirely suppressed them. Eleanor, in turn, appreciated Lydia’s open heart, a quality so often obscured by the careful proprieties of society. 

They confided in each other with a freedom that bordered, some might observe, on imprudence. Secrets of minor consequence – a stolen glance, a disappointing dance partner, a particularly egregious bonnet – were freely exchanged. It was a friendship built not on profound understanding, but on a mutual delight in the small, everyday occurrences of life, and a shared inclination to view them with a cheerful disposition. A most comfortable arrangement, indeed.
author: Jane Austen

One *wants* his presence, naturally, for the arrangements concerning the estate are quite beyond my comprehension without his guidance. Mrs. Penrose assures me he is occupied with parish matters, but I suspect a more agreeable occupation. Perhaps a visit to Lady Bracknell? The thought is not pleasing. Eliza, bless her heart, attempts to appear indifferent, burying herself in embroidery, but I observe the tremor in her hand. 

Well, my comfort lies in knowing I did all within my power to dissuade her from such a connection. A man of fortune is desirable, certainly, but not at the expense of a daughter’s happiness. And yet… and yet, a settled family is so very much to be preferred to the uncertainties of spinsterhood. One hopes he returns soon, if only to conclude this tiresome business.

text:
The assembly room, though comfortably full, possessed a stillness broken only by the polite scrape of a violin. Elizabeth Bennet, observing the company with a discerning eye, found her attention, against her better judgement, drawn once more to Mr. Darcy. He stood near the fireplace, ostensibly contemplating the flames, yet a most peculiar movement had caught her notice. He had, quite distinctly, *hugged himself*.

A stifled giggle escaped Miss Lydia, who, thankfully, attributed it to a passing compliment from Sir William. But Elizabeth could not contain a small, involuntary smile. 

“Good heavens, Lydia, must you be so demonstrative?” she murmured, though her own composure felt rather fragile.

“What is it, Lizzy?” Lydia inquired, ever eager for amusement. “He looks as though he’s warding off a chill, perhaps?”

“A chill, indeed,” Elizabeth replied, a mischievous glint in her eye. “Though I suspect the source is not atmospheric. Mr. Darcy is not to be laughed at!” cried Elizabeth. “That is an uncommon advantage, and uncommon I hope it will continue. Do not mention it to anyone, I implore you. Such a display, were it to become public knowledge, would surely diminish his… gravity.”

text:
The cairn stood upon Widow’s Peak, a cyclopean arrangement of basalt blocks defying any rational geological formation. Locals whispered of the ‘Fourteen Biologi,’ not men, but *things* interred within, their forms hinted at in the unsettlingly organic curves of the stone. For generations, the structure remained inviolate, a grim sentinel against the encroaching sea. But the autumn gales… they were *different* this year.

Not merely strong, but… inquisitive. They did not batter, but *probed*. Old Man Hemlock swore he saw the stones *shift* in the moonlight, not tumbling with brute force, but subtly, deliberately rearranged. A fissure, hairline before, now gaped, revealing a darkness deeper than any shadow. 

The wind itself seemed to carry a low, ululating tone, a resonance that chilled the marrow and spoke of geometries beyond human comprehension. It wasn’t the sound of air rushing through stone, but of something *listening*. Something testing. 

Then came the scent – not of salt and decay, but of a sickly-sweet, phosphorescent bloom, emanating from the widening crack. The Biologi, it seemed, had felt the touch of a wind possessed of a dreadful, alien curiosity, and their long slumber was, irrevocably, disturbed. A reckoning, cold and vast, was drawing near.
author: H.P. Lovecraft
