The news, delivered with a regrettable lack of tact by Sir Reginald, has quite thrown the ton into a flutter. Lady Beatrice, it seems, has accepted the hand of the Duke of Ashworth – a match, whilst undeniably advantageous in terms of fortune, has deprived the British Court of its brightest ornament. Her Ladyship seemed pleased with the idea; and you may imagine that I am happy on every occasion to witness the felicity of others, though a small pang of…disappointment, perhaps, did prick at my composure.

For Lady Beatrice possessed a wit so sparkling, a grace so refined, that she rendered every assembly infinitely more agreeable. Now, Ashworth Hall will be the recipient of her charms, rather than Almack’s. Mr. Finch, naturally, is inconsolable, having devoted himself to her admiration these past two seasons with a diligence bordering on the absurd. 

Mama declares it a most sensible arrangement, and Papa merely observes that the Duke’s estates are extensive. I, however, cannot help but feel a sense of loss. The evenings will, I fear, be considerably less…illuminating. One can only hope the Duke appreciates the treasure he has acquired.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, having received a missive of a most unsettling nature, found herself in a state of considerable perturb. It was not the length of the letter, nor the hand – perfectly legible, though regrettably familiar – that caused her distress, but the *contents* therein. A declaration, bold and entirely unexpected, regarding sentiments she had scarcely dared to acknowledge even to herself.

She had, with a trembling hand, read it through twice, then a third time, seeking some alteration in the phrasing, some possibility of misinterpretation. Finding none, she hastily folded the offending pages, pressing them flat with a force that threatened to crease the delicate paper. 

“Good heavens!” she murmured, clutching the letter to her breast as if to contain its scandalous implications. “I shall not regard it! I will not look in it again!” 

And yet, even as she spoke, her fingers tightened around the paper. She thrust it into the depths of her writing desk, beneath a pile of account books and dried lavender, protesting with each movement that she would banish it from her thoughts entirely. A most improbable assertion, she knew, but one necessary to maintain a semblance of composure in the face of such…unforeseen agitation.
author: Jane Austen

The surveyor, old Manley, had warned against it, muttering of geometries best left undisturbed. He spoke of the strata not as layers of time, but as *scales* – shed by something ancient and vast, slumbering beneath the plains. I, of course, dismissed it as sunstroke and the rambling of a mind frayed by solitude. A foolish dismissal.

The canyon walls rose, not in the expected ochre and rust of Comanchean sandstone, but in hues… *wrong*. A sickly, bruised purple bled from the Permian schists, their angles defying Euclidean comprehension. The Triassic formations pulsed with a subtle, internal luminescence, a cold fire that chilled the very marrow. And then, the coal. Not the dull, earthy black of terrestrial origin, but a glassy obsidian, slick and reflecting a distorted, non-existent light. 

Each stratum felt less like rock and more like a petrified organ, a fragment of a colossal, buried anatomy. The air grew thick, resonant with a low, subsonic thrumming that seemed to originate *within* the stone itself. A creeping dread, not of physical harm, but of ontological violation, began to consume me. This was not geology. This was… excavation of a nightmare. And the glossy black outcropping? It wasn’t coal. It was a *tooth*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The chill wasn’t merely atmospheric; it seeped from the very stones of Dunwich Hollow, a damp, insidious cold that clung to the lungs and whispered of geometries best left unseen. Old Man Hemlock, they said, had disturbed something during his ill-advised excavations – something that predated the founding of the town, predated even the shadowed legends of the Elder Things. 

It began subtly. A greyish dusting on the moss-covered gravestones, a peculiar, fungal bloom in the neglected orchards. Then, *they* emerged. Not with a rush, but a slow, sickening proliferation. Humanoid in the loosest sense, their forms were vaguely reminiscent of men, yet composed of a shifting, pallid substance that seemed to *absorb* light. 

Lake, the botanist, had theorized a spore-based reproduction, a ghastly mimicry of vegetable pteridophyta. He was tragically correct. Each…manifestation…released clouds of the grey dust, seeding the surrounding land. We fired upon them, of course. Rifles, shotguns, even Hemlock’s antiquated cannon. Utterly, horrifyingly useless. The bullets passed *through* them, leaving no mark, no disruption. We were powerless to harm them! Their advance was inexorable, a silent, creeping tide of fungal horror, and the air grew thick with the scent of decay and something…older. Something profoundly, cosmically wrong.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

He wrote last week to hurry my return.” [Illustration: “Dawson” [_Copyright 1894 by George Allen._]] “Oh, your father, of course, may spare you, if your mother can. Daughters are never of so much consequence to a father. And if you will stay another _month_ complete, it will be in my power to take one of you as far as London, for I am going there early in June, for a week; and
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Hemlock, he was a sight. Red-faced, sputtering like a wet firecracker, and fixin’ to swallow his own tongue. He was cornered, see, by Silas Pettigrew, a feller known more for the sharpness of his elbows than the kindness of his heart.

“Judge Thatcher’s got it. You git it. I want it,” Pettigrew barked, leanin’ in so close Hemlock smelled nothin’ but stale tobacco and trouble.

Hemlock wrung his hands, lookin’ like a plucked chicken. “I hain’t got no money, I tell you. You ask Judge Thatcher; he’ll tell you the same. I turned it all over to him for safekeeping, years ago. Foolishness, maybe, but a man gets to thinkin’…”

Pettigrew just snorted. “Safekeeping, eh? More like hidin’ it from honest folk. Don’t you try to play me for a simpleton, Hemlock.” He jabbed a bony finger at the old man’s chest. “All right. I’l’ go see the Judge myself. And when I do, I reckon *he’ll* be explainin’ why a perfectly good sum is layin’ up while a respectable man like myself is sufferin’ hardship.” 

He turned on his heel, leavin’ Hemlock lookin’ like he’d already lost the argument, and likely, whatever it was Pettigrew was after. A bad business, that, a right bad business.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Tiber, he’d declared he was goin’ to Charleston. Charleston, mind you, in the thick of the yellow fever. Said he had a notion to settle a debt, a trifling thing from ‘way back when, but a debt nonetheless. Folks warned him, naturally. Said he was courtin’ death itself, practically handin’ it a mint julep. 

But Tiber, he just chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound like leaves in November. “Wouldn’t I, now?” he’d say, eyes twinklin’ like fireflies. “Wouldn’t I be a man to back down from a promise, fever or no?”

Ther’ ain’t no question ’bout it in *my* mind. He was set. Solid as a granite tombstone. 

But then his brothers, Silas and Jebediah, they commenced to fuss. Silas, all high-minded talk of family duty, and Jebediah, wringin’ his hands and bleatin’ about the will. They tried to lock him in the smokehouse, then pleaded, then threatened to cut him off from the peach brandy. 

Well, then, what kind o’ brothers would it be that’d stand in his way at sech a time? A body’d think they’d *want* him to prove his mettle, not shackle him like a runaway mule. It plumb defied common sense, it did.
author: Mark Twain

text: for’rard end, mum.” “Which side of a tree does the moss grow on?” “North side.” “If fifteen cows is browsing on a hillside, how many of them eats with their heads pointed the same direction?” “The whole fifteen, mum.” “Well, I reckon you _have_ lived in the country. I thought maybe you was trying to hocus me again. What’s your real name, now?” “George Peters, mum.” “Well, try to remember it, George. Don’t forget and tell me it’s Elexander before you go, and then get out by saying it’s George Elexander when I catch you. And don’t go about women in that old calico. You do a girl tolerable poor, but you might fool men, maybe. Bless you, child, when you set out to thread a needle don’t hold the thread still and fetch the needle up to it; hold the needle still and poke the thread at it; that’s the way a woman most always does, but a man always does t’other way. And when you throw at a rat or anything, hitch yourself up a tiptoe and fetch your hand up over your head as awkward as you can, and miss your rat about six or seven foot.
author: Mark Twain

text: that its respiratory apparatus handled oxygen rather than carbon dioxide; and there were odd evidences of air-storage chambers and methods of shifting respiration from the external orifice to at least two other fully developed breathing systems--gills and pores. Clearly, it was amphibian and probably adapted to long airless hibernation periods as well. Vocal organs seemed present in connection with the main respiratory system, but they presented anomalies beyond immediate solution. Articulate speech, in the sense of syllable utterance, seemed barely conceivable, but musical piping notes covering a wide range were highly probable. The muscular system was almost pre-naturally developed. The nervous system was so complex and highly developed as to leave Lake aghast. Though excessively primitive and archaic in some respects, the thing had a set of gangliar centers and connectives arguing the very extremes of specialized development. Its five-lobed brain was surprisingly advanced, and there were signs of a sensory equipment, served in part through the wiry cilia of the head, involving factors alien to any other terrestrial organism. Probably it had more than five senses, so that its habits could not be predicted from any existing analogy. It must, Lake thought, have been a creature of keen sensitiveness
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, Miss Watson, a woman built along the lines of a dried apple stick and possessed of a disposition to match, had descended upon us. Tolerable slim, she was, and wore spectacles perched upon her nose like a pair of anxious spiders. She took one look at me, a boy naturally inclined towards fishing and mischief, and declared a state of emergency in the realm of my education.

It commenced with a spelling-book. Lord, the tedium! “A is for apple,” she’d drone, her voice thin as a whippoorwill’s call. I knew what an apple *was*, mind you. Had eaten a passel of ‘em, pilfered mostly from Old Man Hemlock’s orchard. But to *spell* it? Seemed a mighty unnecessary exercise. 

She’d tap the book with a bony finger, her goggles glinting. “Now, repeat after me. A-P-P-L-E.” I’d mumble it, slow and reluctant, feeling like a caged hound. It wasn’t the letters themselves, see, but the *point* of it all. What good was spelling ‘apple’ when a perfectly good apple was right there for the eatin’? A body could spend a lifetime at such foolishness and still not catch a single fish.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The assembly at Netherfield had concluded, leaving Miss Eleanor Ainsworth in a state of considerable agitation. Mr. Darcy, a gentleman possessed of an air both forbidding and fascinating, had been observed regarding her with an intensity that, whilst unsettling, did not entirely displease. He had, indeed, spent a disproportionate amount of the evening lost in contemplation, his brow furrowed with a thoughtfulness that suggested matters of the deepest import.

“Pray, Miss Ainsworth,” confided Mrs. Philips, ever eager for gossip, “did you observe Mr. Darcy’s countenance this evening? He appeared quite… preoccupied. One might almost suspect a romantic entanglement, though with whom is the mystery! He seemed to be studying a face, and desired he would tell her what lady had the credit of inspiring such reflections.”

Mr. Darcy, who had unfortunately overheard the last portion of this query, approached with a degree of resolution that startled even himself. He replied, with great intrepidity, – “Miss Elizabeth Bennet. Do not mention the author by name.” 

A blush, most unbecoming, rose in Eleanor’s cheeks. To be so utterly eclipsed by the lively, and admittedly more favoured, Miss Bennet! The injustice of it was, she felt, quite beyond bearing.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The carriage had scarcely drawn to a halt before Mr. Ashworth was at the door, his attentions, though undeniably polite, possessing a certain briskness that bordered on eagerness. Then, with no other delay than his pointing out the neatness of the entrance – a comment Miss Eleanor found rather superfluous, given the obvious care bestowed upon the gravel – taken into the house they were; and as soon as they were in the parlour, he welcomed them with a warmth that, while not *improper*, felt distinctly…studied.

“I trust your journey was not unduly fatiguing, Miss Bennet?” he inquired, his gaze lingering perhaps a moment too long upon her countenance. Mrs. Bennet, naturally, launched into a detailed account of a minor discomfort with the springs, a narrative Mr. Ashworth endured with a fixed, though amiable, smile. 

Eleanor, however, observed a subtle tension in his manner, a quickness of the eye that suggested a mind occupied with matters beyond the comfort of travelling ladies. The room itself was handsome, certainly, but lacked the lived-in ease of a truly comfortable home. It was, she suspected, prepared for inspection, rather than enjoyment. A curious circumstance, indeed.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The small drawing-room at Hartfield held a silence most uncomfortable, broken only by the scratching of a quill. Mr. Knightley, seated by the window, penned a missive with a speed that bordered on the impertinent, whilst Miss Woodhouse, perched upon a stool, offered observations of a decidedly mixed nature.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!” she declared, her tone a curious blend of anticipation and, dare one say, a touch of self-satisfaction. He made no answer, his brow furrowed in concentration. A most ungracious response, she thought, though not entirely unexpected. Mr. Knightley was ever prone to taciturnity when engaged in affairs of the heart – or, rather, affairs *concerning* the heart of another.

“You write uncommonly fast,” she ventured, hoping to provoke some discourse. 

“You are mistaken,” he replied, his voice clipped. A most unyielding man! One might almost suspect a deliberate desire to discomfit. She considered the matter. His haste, she decided, spoke not of eagerness, but of a desire to *be done* with the task. A practical, and therefore, rather unromantic, impulse. And the brevity of his reply? Pure obstinacy. Still, she conceded, a man of his integrity would naturally approach such delicate correspondence with a seriousness bordering on severity.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The assembly room, though comfortably full, felt suddenly airless to Miss Elizabeth. Lady Catherine de Bourgh, a woman whose pronouncements carried the weight of settled estates, had descended upon her with a curiosity most unwelcome. It began, naturally, with a commendation of her health, swiftly followed by an inquiry into the particulars of her family connections. 

“Pray, Miss Bennet,” Lady Catherine declared, her voice possessing a timbre that brooked no dissent, “is your father possessed of a respectable income? And, more importantly, is he a man of good understanding?”

Elizabeth, though inwardly chafing at such directness, maintained a composure she scarcely felt. “My father’s income, Madam, is sufficient for our needs, and his understanding, I believe, is entirely his own.”

Lady Catherine’s brow furrowed. “Indeed. And your mother? A connection of some consequence, I trust? One does not often encounter such…unaffected manners without a lineage to support them. What, pray, had been her maiden name?”

Elizabeth felt all the impertinence of her questions, but answered them very composedly. “Lady Cather, my mother was a Miss Gardiner.” A simple statement, yet delivered with a quiet dignity that, for a moment, seemed to disarm the formidable Lady.
author: Jane Austen

After lamenting it, however, at some length, she had the consolation of thinking that Mr. Bingley would be soon down again, and soon dining at Longbourn; and the conclusion of all was the comfortable declaration, that, though he had been invited only to a family dinner, she would take care to have two full courses. text:
Now, the river, she was a-actin’ contrary, full of sandbars and a current that’d test a preacher’s patience. Been followin’ the right-hand shore for a spell, thinkin’ to make good time to Widow Hemlock’s for supper. But the water got shallow, and the lead kept singin’ a mournful tune ‘bout bottom. Then I spied it – the left-hand shore, which meant that I was in a crossing; so I changed off and went that way. 

It was one of these long, slanting, two-mile crossings; so a body had time to contemplate the foolishness of man, and the stubbornness of rivers. The sun, she beat down like a blacksmith’s hammer, and the steam rose off the water in waves. Old Man Tiber, he’d say this was a test of a pilot’s mettle, seein’ if he could hold a course when there weren’t nothin’ *but* water and sky to guide him. 

I reckon I held it well enough. Though, truth be told, I was mostly hopin’ I hadn’t steered us straight into a swamp full of gators and regret. A feller can ponder too much, you see. Best just keep a steady hand and a watchful eye, and let the river do what she’s a-mind to.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Pap, he weren’t a man given to overwork, not by a long shot. Nine logs floated downriver was plenty, he declared, a right handsome haul for a mornin’s effort. More’n enough to warrant a trip to town, seein’ as how a feller’s throat gets parched just *lookin'* at wood. 

He fussed with the cabin door, lookin’ at it sideways like it’d offended him personally. “Gotta keep things secure,” he mumbled, though secure from *what*, I couldn’t rightly say. Likely from my own natural inclination to improve the situation, I reckon. He bolted it good and proper, then, with a grunt that rattled the rafters, he shoved off in the skiff.

Towi, he called it. Towin’ those logs, he meant. Though it looked more like he was bein’ *towed* by ‘em, driftin’ along with the current and lookin’ pleased as punch. Didn’t even bother with a proper oar stroke half the time. A man like that, you understand, he figures the river owes him a livin’. And he fully intends to collect. Left me there, mind you, with nothin’ but the dust motes dancin’ in the sunbeams and a growlin’ belly. A fine state of affairs, that was.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, the next day dawned like any other, which is to say, full of possibilities for trouble. Old Man Hemlock, he swore it was a sign – the way the rooster crowed backwards – a sign of misfortune comin’ on like a Mississippi flood. I paid him no mind, of course. Folks are always findin’ signs in everything, like a hound dog sniffin’ at a ghost.

But there *was* a stillness to it, a holdin’ of breath in the woods. Even the cicadas weren’t makin’ a racket, which is unnatural enough to give a body pause. We’d been expectin’ trouble with the Grangerfords for a spell, a simmerin’ feud that’d been brewin’ longer than a pot of sorghum. 

No, sir; if a body’s out hunting for cowards he don’t want to fool away any time amongst them Shepherdsons, becuz they don’t breed any o’. They’d face down a tornado with a smile and a rifle. It was the *quiet* that worried me. A coiled spring, that’s what it felt like. And a coiled spring, sooner or later, is bound to let loose. A body could feel it in his bones.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a study. A right peculiar cuss, was Hemlock. Said to me, bright and early – though ‘early’ with Hemlock meant near onto mid-morning – “Before breakfast—I’ll be glad to.” Didn’t specify *what* he’d be glad to do, mind you. Just hung that phrase in the air like a damp dishrag.

I asked, naturally, what was afoot. He waved a hand, dismissive-like, towards a pair of fellas lookin’ remarkably uncomfortable on the porch. Ruffians, they were, the sort that smelled of stale whiskey and bad intentions. 

“Those are… associates,” Hemlock drawled. “And I require a bit of peace to discuss… matters of import. I’ll be glad to have you occupy their attention.”

My sisters, bless their innocent hearts, were playin’ jacks nearby. I swallowed hard. “You mean… leave ‘em with *these*?”

Hemlock just gave a shrug that could’ve dislodged a barnacle. “Yes; never mind about them. They’ve got to stand it yet a while. They might suspic’ if you fussed. Just… keep ‘em entertained. A song, a story, anything. And don’t you breathe a word of this to your Ma.” 

A body could get into a heap of trouble just tryin’ to be helpful, I reckoned.
author: Mark Twain

One of these was that doctor; another one was a sharp-looking gentleman, with a carpet-bag of the old-fashioned kind made out of carpet-stuff, that had just come off of the steamboat and was talking to him in a low voice, and glancing towards the king now and then and nodding their heads—it was Levi Bell, the lawyer that was gone up to Louisville; and another one was a big rough husky that come along and listened to all the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now. And when the king got done this husky up and says: “Say, looky here; if you are Harvey Wilks, when’d you come to this town?” “The day before the funeral, friend,” says the king. “But what time o’ day?” “In the evenin’—’bout an hour er two before sundown.” “_How’d_ you come?” “I come down on the Susan Powell from Cincinnati.” “Well, then, how’d you come to be up at the Pint in the _mornin_’—in a canoe?” “I warn’t up at the Pint in the mornin’.” “It’s a lie.” Several of them jumped for him and begged him not

text:
“Indeed, Mama,” Miss Elizabeth observed, arranging a sprig of lavender in her workbox with a delicate hand, “one might think a gentleman’s absence would be a sufficient discouragement. To actively *recall* his acceptance of an invitation… it borders upon the indelicate.”

Mrs. Bennet, however, was not to be deterred by considerations of delicacy. “Indelicate! Nonsense, Lizzy! The man is perfectly respectable, and possesses a tolerable fortune. It is *my* duty to ensure our daughters are suitably presented. And truly, the least you should not *remind* your mother of inviting him.”

“As I did the other day,” said Elizabeth, with a conscious smile; “very true, it will be well to avoid the subject. Though I confess, the prospect of an evening devoted entirely to Mr. Harding’s pronouncements on agricultural improvements does not entirely inspire delight.”

Her sister, Mary, seized the opportunity. “Improvement is always desirable, Lizzy. A cultivated mind appreciates the benefits of…”

Elizabeth cut her off with a gentle, “Pray, Mary, let us not anticipate the evening with undue seriousness. A little quiet amusement, perhaps, is all one can reasonably expect.”
author: Jane Austen

text:
“Mamma,” cried Lydia, with a most disconcerting eagerness, “my aunt says that Colonel Forster and Captain Carter do not go so often to Miss Watson’s as they did when they first arrived. It is a most grievous alteration in their attentions, and quite beyond my comprehension!”

Mrs. Bennet, ever attuned to the currents of eligible society, fluttered her fan. “Indeed, Lydia? A diminution of visits is rarely a favourable sign. Though Miss Watson, whilst perfectly agreeable, possesses not a fortune to tempt a man of the world.”

“But they *did* call, Mamma! Almost daily! And Captain Carter was so very… attentive. He complimented my embroidery, you know, and inquired after my pianoforte practice.” Lydia’s cheeks flushed a delicate pink.

“Compliments are the breath of politeness, my dear, and signify little. Perhaps they have discovered a more promising diversion. The arrival of the militia from Meryton has, I understand, created a considerable stir amongst the ladies. A fresh field, you see, for their gallantries.” 

Lydia pouted. “But I had hoped… one might have formed a connection. A regimentals are so very dashing, and a wife to an officer… it is the height of fashion!”
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Tremaine found herself, despite all reason and propriety, unable to entirely dismiss the matter of her husband’s conduct. It was not, she assured herself, a lingering affection that prompted this unwelcome recurrence of thought, but rather a mortified sense of what *ought* to be. To be continually overlooked, to find his evenings occupied with the boisterous company of men at the club, and to banish from her thoughts that continual breach of conjugal obligation and decorum which, in exposing his wife to the contempt of society, was almost a public affront – this proved a burden far heavier than any she had anticipated in marriage.

She had, of course, offered gentle remonstrances, couched in the language of delicate suggestion. But Mr. Tremaine, possessed of a comfortable fortune and an equally comfortable self-regard, dismissed her concerns as feminine fancy. It was a vexation, she conceded, to be so utterly disregarded, and a far greater one to witness the knowing glances exchanged amongst her acquaintance, all too aware of his indifference. A quiet life, she had desired; instead, she found herself a spectacle.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, I reckon I’ve seen a good many peculiar sights in my time, driftin’ along the Mississippi and beyond, but this… this was a spectacle to curdle milk. It weren’t the grand sort of oddity, mind you, no steamboat explosion or runaway circus bear. It was a quiet oddity, the kind that settles in your bones and makes you question the sanity of the world.

We were docked at Natchez, see, and the light was failin’, that bruised purple hour before full dark. Folks were movin’ like shadows, but even shadows cast *some* kind of shape. This weren’t so with what I saw. Mostly, it was just… absence. A see-before, blacker, mostly, than is common. 

Then, she materialized. A woman in a slim black dress, belted small under the armpits, with bulges like a cabbage in the middle. Not a graceful cabbage, neither, but one gone to seed and lookin’ decidedly unwell. She didn’t *walk*, precisely. More… flowed. And nobody, not a soul on that busy levee, seemed to notice a thing. It gave a man pause, I tell you. A right proper pause. Made a fella wonder if he hadn’t had a bit too much of Old Man Hemlock’s corn liquor.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, this here Honest Injun, see, he weren’t much to look at. Had a hare-lip that’d make a preacher wince, and a way of lookin’ sideways like he expected a brick to fall. The Duke, he was puttin’ on a show, claimin’ this feller was a lost prince from some outlandish kingdom. Pure balderdash, of course. 

I was layin’ low under the bed in the parlor, watchin’ the whole shebang. The Duke, he’d stashed the take from the show – a right handsome pile of coin – under his mattress. While the Injun was distractin’ folks with a mournful flute tune, I slipped up and lifted it. Not boastin’, mind you, just statin’ facts.

Then, a crack appeared in the dining-room door, and Old Man Pettigrew, the undertaker, poked his head in. He was a gloomy sort, always talkin’ ‘bout coffins and worms. “He had a rat!” he declared, pointin’ at the Injun. “A genuine, live rat, right there in his…person!” 

The Injun just blinked. 

“Was *you* in on this, boy?” Pettigrew demanded, fixin’ me with a stare. I just played innocent, naturally. A feller’s gotta look out for himself on this river, you see. And a little bit of coin helps a heap.
author: Mark Twain

In her kind schemes for Elizabeth, she sometimes planned her marrying Colonel Fitzwilliam. He was, beyond comparison, the pleasantest man: he certainly admired her, and his situation in life was most eligible; but, to counterbalance these advantages, Mr. Darcy had considerable patronage in the church, and his cousin could have none at all. [Illustration: “On looking up”] CHAPTER XXXIII. [Illustration] More than once did Elizabeth, in her ramble within the park, unexpectedly meet Mr. Darcy. She felt all the perverseness of the mischance that should bring him where no one else was brought; and, to prevent its ever happening again, took care to inform him, at first, that it was a favourite haunt of hers. How it could occur a second time, therefore, was very odd! Yet it did, and even the third.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mr. Alistair Finch, a gentleman possessed of a sensibility perhaps *too* refined for the present age, found himself in a most peculiar predicament. His wife, the amiable but mischievous Clara, and his dearest friend, Mr. Beaumont, had conspired to induce him to participate in a game of blind-man’s-buff. A childish amusement, he protested, wholly unbecoming a man of thirty-two summers! Yet, Clara’s pleading eyes and Beaumont’s teasing pronouncements of his “excessive gravity” proved irresistible.

He was, however, distracted from his reluctant preparations by a missive delivered with the morning post – a letter from *The Spectator*, penned, astonishingly, by a Miss Elara, aged but four years. Her observations on the proper conduct of gentlemen, delivered with a precocious clarity, were… unsettling. She deemed excessive seriousness a “most disagreeable frown” and advocated for “much laughter and tumbling.” 

Alistair, bandaged and awaiting his fate, could not help but feel a blush creep up his neck. Was he, in his attempts at dignified composure, failing some fundamental test of human enjoyment? Perhaps, he conceded with a sigh, a little foolishness, even induced by wife and friend, was not entirely amiss. Especially if sanctioned by a four-year-old philosopher.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, Old Bess, she weren’t built for speed, mind you. More a comfortable conveyance for a gentleman contemplatin’ the virtues of a good cigar. But today, well, today she felt a spirit. Likely caught it from me. I’d just heard tell of Jedediah Pruitt tryin’ to pass off watered-down whiskey as the real McCoy, and a righteous indignation had settled in my bones.

So I lit out, a-tearin’ across Farmer Giles’ south forty, whoopin’ and yellin’ like a Comanche scout. Not that I *am* a Comanche scout, understand. Just… expressin’ myself. Bess, bless her heart, lumbered along, doin’ her best to keep pace with my enthusiasm. 

And I was singin’ out, loud enough to rattle the crows from the cornfields: “Cler the track, thar! I’m on the waw-path, and the price uv coffin! Jedediah Pruitt, you listen good! This ain’t about the whiskey, it’s about principle!” 

Old Man Hemlock nearly jumped outta his skin, clutchin’ his spectacles. Bess just flicked an ear and kept on. A fella’s gotta have *some* fun, even when deliverin’ a warnin’. It’s the American way, I reckon.
author: Mark Twain

Now, that boat. Lord, that little skiff. Wasn’t much to look at, mind you – patched canvas, a single oar lookin’ like it’d seen better decades, and smelled powerfully of fish and regret. But Old Man Hemlock, he’d been usin’ it to haul his prize-winning pumpkins across the river, and a fella could *see* the smug satisfaction in them gourds. Couldn’t abide it, no sir. Had to have it for ourselves.

So we went a-quaking and shaking down the stabboard side, and slow work it was, too—seemed a week before we even reached the water. Jebediah nearly pitched headfirst, bless his clumsy soul, and young Tilly let out a shriek that’d curdle milk. We tied a rope to a willow, lowered ourselves like a passel of scared monkeys, and finally, *finally* splashed down. 

The water was colder than a banker’s heart, and the boat groaned somethin’ awful. But we were in it. We were *in* it. Hemlock’d be mighty put out, no doubt, but a man’s gotta have a vessel for…well, for important business. Like transportin’ pebbles. Or contemplatin’ the sunset. Or, maybe, just to spite Old Man Hemlock.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, old Man Hemlock, he was tellin’ a tale down at the general store, a whopper, naturally. Said he’d seen Jack Robinson. Not the feller who runs the livery, mind you, but *the* Jack Robinson. The one from the sailor’s yarns.

Hemlock swore this Robinson weren’t a man at all, not rightly. “Tall as a pine, he was,” Hemlock declared, puffin’ on his pipe, “and big around as the Methodist church itself! Could cradle a steamboat in his hands, he could.”

Folks scoffed, of course. Old Man Tiber, he said, “Hemlock, you been at the cider again?” But I, I was ponderin’. This Robinson, bein’ so…substantial…well, it got a feller thinkin’. 

“Now look here,” I says, leanin’ on the counter, “they say Robinson can best any man. But what if we wasn’t aimin’ to *fight* him fair? What if we got some genies to help *us*—can’t we lick the other feller then? A little magic, a bit o’ trickery…seems to me that’d level the playin’ field right smartly.” 

The store fell quiet. Even Hemlock stopped puffin’. It was a thought, wasn’t it? A right clever thought, if I do say so myself.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The chipped basalt held a horror beyond mere decay. For the most part, the untold æons had disintegrated and banished any pigments which may have been applied. Yet, the more one studied the marvelous technique – the unsettling *geometry* of the remaining lines – the more a ghastly impression bloomed in the mind. It wasn’t a depiction of anything *known*, certainly not of any earthly flora or fauna. Rather, it suggested a pre-organic architecture, a scaffolding of thought erected by entities whose very existence mocked Euclidean space.

The surface wasn’t merely worn; it felt… *un-made*. As if the original form struggled, even across millennia, to un-coalesce back into the primordial chaos from whence it sprung. A sickly, phosphorescent dust clung to the grooves, emitting a faint, subsonic hum that resonated not in the ears, but directly within the cerebral cortex. 

Old Man Hemlock, before his unfortunate… dissolution, had whispered of a city built of angles that should not be, a place where the laws of perspective were deliberately, blasphemously, *wrong*. This fragment, unearthed from the cyclopean ruins beneath Widow’s Peak, felt like a shard of that impossible metropolis, a glimpse into a reality best left undisturbed, a chilling echo of a sanity-shattering design.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I was settin’ on the porch of Old Man Hemlock’s general store, whittlin’ a bit of pine and observin’ human nature – a pastime I’ve found considerably more entertainin’ than most any church social. And along comes a pair. A right handsome, silver-haired gentleman, lookin’ like he’d seen a good deal of sun and come out the better for it. And walkin’ with him, a younger feller, maybe twenty-five, with a face that’d charm the birds outta the trees… but his right arm was tucked up in a sling, lookin’ forlorn as a lost pup.

They hadn’t gone ten feet past the store when somebody – likely young Timmy Higgins, that mischief-maker – let out a holler. “Lookit the pair! One’s all fixed up, the other’s busted up!” 

And, my souls, how the people *yelled* and laughed! Not mean-spirited, mind you, but a hearty, good-natured roar. The old gentleman just tipped his hat and kept strollin’, a twinkle in his eye. The young one, though, he flushed a bit, but managed a grin. It was a sight, I tell you. A sight that reminded a body that life, for all its troubles, is often a right comical affair.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Old Man Tiber, he reckoned Bill was in a fix, a right proper pickle. Bill, see, he’d gone and bought a motor truck – a contraption of gears and sputterin’ that smelled powerfully of burnt ambition. “It ain’t good morals,” Tiber declared, puffin’ on his pipe, “spendin’ good money on somethin’ that’ll likely leave ya stranded ‘fore sundown.”

And wouldn’t ya know it, ‘bout halfway to Piggott’s Landing, she just… *stopped*. “Oh! Lordy, Lordy!” Bill wailed, kickin’ a tire. “Hello, what’s up?” he hollered at the engine, like it was a stubborn mule. 

The wreck, it was a sight. Truck tilted sideways, load of turnips spillin’ into the ditch. Solomon, Bill’s boy, just stood there, lookin’ like a rained-on rooster. We turned in and slept under the truck, me and Solomon, while Bill fussed and fumed. 

Come mornin’, Solomon, bless his heart, he started dismantlin’ the thing. “Turnin’ over the truck,” he muttered, “might find somethin’ loose.”  He hadn’t a lick of sense ‘bout engines, but a boy’s gotta *try*, don’t he?  It was a fool’s errand, of course, but a comfortin’ one, all the same.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself in a most uncomfortable position. Lady Beatrice, ever eager to orchestrate a suitable match, had pressed upon her the subject of Mr. Thomas Finch. A perfectly respectable gentleman, to be sure, possessed of a tolerable estate and an amiable disposition. Yet, Eleanor could offer no encouragement. Not from any particular dislike, understand, but from a… familiarity.

She had known Mr. Finch since childhood, witnessed every awkward growth spurt, every ill-considered jest. He was, in essence, a brother in all but name. To contemplate him as a husband felt… improper. A violation of a long-held, unspoken understanding. 

“You are remarkably silent, my dear,” Lady Beatrice observed, her gaze sharp. “Do you find him wanting?”

Eleanor flushed. “It is not that, precisely. I am not qualified to form one. I have known him too long and too well to be a fair judge. It is impossible for *me* to be impartial.” A small, frustrated sigh escaped her lips. The very notion! To be pressed on a matter where her heart, though not inclined towards affection, felt bound by years of quiet companionship.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Penworthy, having secured a vantage point behind the lace curtains of the drawing-room, had continued the occupation; but unluckily no one passed the windows now except a few of the officers, who, in comparison with the stranger, were, to put it mildly, entirely devoid of interest. He had ridden past some half an hour ago, a gentleman of decidedly handsome mien, and possessing a carriage of such elegant simplicity as spoke volumes regarding his fortune, and, more importantly, his taste. 

Her sister, Marianne, declared him merely ‘tolerable,’ a judgement Eleanor considered shockingly deficient. To be sure, his coat was dark, not the fashionable blue, but it fitted him with a perfection that quite excused the colour. And the set of his jaw! A firmness, yet not unkindness, resided there. 

Mrs. Ainsworth, ever the pragmatist, had observed only that he was unaccompanied, a circumstance which, whilst intriguing, did little to elevate his prospects. Eleanor, however, allowed herself a small, hopeful sigh. A gentleman of such bearing *must* have connections, and a residence in the vicinity. Perhaps, with a little fortunate coincidence, their paths might cross again.
author: Jane Austen

text:
My dearest friend,

One scarcely knows where to begin when attempting to convey the… *peculiarities* of Mr. Collins. He arrived, as you might imagine, with a pronouncement upon the blessings of Lady Catherine de Bourgh, a discourse so lengthy and detailed it threatened to consume the entire afternoon. He speaks, not as one engaging in conversation, but as delivering a sermon – and a most tedious one at that!

His self-importance is truly remarkable. Every observation, however trifling, is offered as a profound insight, and delivered with an air of unquestionable authority. He appears utterly incapable of perceiving any merit save that which aligns with his own narrow views, and considers himself a man of the most refined sensibility, despite exhibiting none whatsoever. 

Indeed, one might almost suspect a deliberate cultivation of silliness. He boasts of his connections, details his patron’s every whim, and generally presents himself as a figure of such consequence as to be quite beyond reproach. You, knowing my disposition, will readily understand my dismay. To think such a man seeks a wife! It is, frankly, a most unsettling prospect.
author: Jane Austen

Now, there was a sight to make a man contemplate the peculiar generosity of the river. A dozen logs, prime pine, all bunched together like a family reunion gone slightly adrift. Didn’t look like they’d *fought* their way free, mind you, more like politely requested a vacation. A fella could make a livin’ off of that, easy enough. Just had to *catch* ‘em, and steer ‘em down to the wood-yards or the sawmill. Simple as pie, if you didn’t mind gettin’ your boots wet.

I went along up the bank with one eye on the logs and the other on the likely spots for snags and quicksand. A body had to be cautious. Old Man Tiber, he wasn’t known for handin’ out fortunes without askin’ for a little somethin’ in return. 

Young Jebediah, he reckoned he could lasso ‘em. Lasso logs! The boy had a head full of notions, that one. I told him, “Son, you’ll be needin’ a rope thicker’n a ship’s hawser and a mule with the disposition of a grizzly bear.” He just grinned, full of youthful confidence. Bless his heart. He’d learn. The river always taught a fella somethin’, one way or another.

text:
The luminescence was…wrong. Not the absence of light, for a sickly, phosphorescent glow clung to the basalt walls of the cyclopean chamber, but a *quality* of illumination that pressed upon the mind, hinting at geometries best left unseen. Old Man Hemlock, before his…dissolution, had spoken of a ‘channel’, a resonance within the stone itself, capable of drawing forth the true dawn. A preposterous notion, yet the dwindling oil in our lamps offered a grim alternative.

We’d spent cycles – or what *felt* like cycles, time being a fluid, unreliable thing down here – adjusting the focusing lenses, coaxing the strange, humming crystals into alignment. Each failed attempt brought a fresh wave of nausea, a tightening in the temples as the chamber seemed to *breathe* with a cold, alien intelligence. Hemlock’s notes, scrawled in a hand trembling with dread, insisted upon ‘plentiful trial and error’, a phrase that now echoed with a terrifying weight. 

But a flicker. A subtle shift in the phosphorescence. A nascent warmth. It was barely perceptible, yet undeniably *different*. A hope, cold and brittle as the stone around us, began to form. So, at last, we set off eagerly in the…direction of the growing light, praying it wasn’t merely another facet of the abyss opening before us.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The carriage had deposited its occupants before Longbourn with a speed that bordered on unseemly, a circumstance Miss Elizabeth Bennet attributed entirely to her sister’s agitated state. Lydia, having been absent these six months, returned not with the bloom of improved society, but with a pallor that spoke of anxieties best left unvoiced. Mr. Bennet, predictably, offered only a dry observation regarding the expense of retrieving a runaway, while Mrs. Bennet dissolved into a flurry of handkerchiefs and pronouncements of ruin.

Yet it was not the familial drama that occupied Miss Elizabeth’s thoughts, but the gentleman who accompanied her sister – a Mr. Wickham, whose presence, though undeniably handsome, carried with it a disquieting air. He offered a curt bow, his eyes avoiding hers with a practiced ease. 

“And—may I ask?” said Elizabeth; “but the terms, I suppose, must be complied with.”

“Complied with!” he echoed, a flicker of something unreadable crossing his features. “Indeed, Miss Bennet. A…necessary arrangement, for the sake of all parties concerned.” He offered a thin smile, and Elizabeth, though outwardly composed, felt a chill settle upon her spirits. Something, she suspected, was profoundly amiss, and the quiet of Hertfordshire felt suddenly, and most disturbingly, fractured.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, the situation was peculiar, you understand. A right mess of a scheme, hatched in the dim light of a riverboat cabin, and nobody aboard to answer questions but me; so I didn’t want the plan to begin working till pretty late to-night. A body needs a bit of darkness for such undertakings, don’t they?

I says to Miss Mary Jane, a girl with eyes like melted chocolate and a disposition to match, “Miss Mary Jane, I’ll tell yo. This here undertaking requires a certain…delicacy. A touch of the theatrical, if you will. We’re aimin’ to convince old Man Hemlock he’s seen a ghost. A genuine, sheet-wearin’, chain-rattlin’ specter.”

She near dropped her embroidery. “A ghost, Mr. Silas?”

“The very thing. But not just *any* ghost. A ghost with a message. A message about…well, about a certain promissory note he’s holdin’ over your pa’s head. It’s a delicate matter, see? And the success of it hinges on everyone believin’ it’s the real McCoy. So, no gigglin’, no hintin’, and for heaven’s sake, no tellin’ the cook.” 

She promised, solemn as a judge. And I figured, with a girl like that on my side, even a ghost could be managed.

The matter, once concealed with such meticulous care, was now, alas, revealed. Not through any dramatic outburst, or intercepted correspondence, but by the sheer, unavoidable consequence of time. Miss Elizabeth, of course, had always possessed a penetration exceeding her years, and had, with a quiet observation that bordered on the unnerving, suspected the truth long ago. It was a truth Mr. Bingley’s sister, Caroline, had deemed utterly unsuitable for general consumption, and particularly so for the knowledge of her brother.

Indeed, the entire connection seemed determined to bury the circumstance – a youthful indiscretion on the part of Mr. Bingley’s elder brother, involving a modest fortune and a lady of decidedly *less* connection than themselves. The details, though whispered amongst the servants, were rigorously suppressed from Bingley, lest it colour his judgement, or, worse, affect his amiable disposition. 

Caroline, in her perpetual striving for propriety, had considered Elizabeth a dangerous confidante, and thus, ironically, the one person most likely to unravel their careful construction of silence. She had underestimated, as so many did, the strength of Elizabeth’s discretion, and the quiet dignity with which she bore the weight of unwelcome knowledge.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The charts were… incomplete. Wilkes’s frantic notations, Mawson’s later, more measured confirmations – both spoke of a land beyond the permissible angles of the globe, glimpsed during fleeting breaks in the cyclopean blizzards. Hills, they called them. But no terrestrial formation could bear such geometry. They weren’t *built* of stone, but *from* wrongness, a sickening non-Euclidean curvature that pressed upon the sanity.

The magnetic anomalies were the first heralds, twisting compass needles into obscene spirals. Then came the dreams, shared, disturbingly similar – basalt columns that pulsed with a cold, internal light, and a vast, echoing silence broken only by the grinding of… something immense. 

At 70° South, the air itself thickened, becoming viscous, tasting of ozone and a mineral decay older than time. It was not the cold that chilled, but the *awareness* of being observed. Something waited in the perpetual twilight, something whose scale dwarfed even the continent itself. 

And the hills… they weren’t distant. They were *approaching*. Not physically, but… conceptually. As if the very fabric of reality was bending to accommodate their impossible presence, drawing the world closer to a dreadful, pre-human symmetry. A symmetry that promised not understanding, but dissolution.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The matter of Miss Eleanor’s domestic felicity was, it seemed, a subject of perpetual, though delicately veiled, lament. “I am persuaded,” she confided to Mr. Darcy, stirring her tea with a precision bordering on severity, “my friend would not call herself *near* her family under less than *half* the present distance.” A sigh, barely audible, accompanied the pronouncement. 

Her brother, a gentleman of amiable, if somewhat improvident, disposition, had settled himself and his growing brood a full sixty miles hence, a circumstance Miss Eleanor deemed a grievous imposition upon both parties. Not for the expense, mind you – though that was considerable – but for the *duty* of frequent visitation. 

Mr. Darcy drew his chair a little toward, a movement so subtle as to be almost imperceptible, yet not lost upon Miss Eleanor’s observant eye. “Sixty miles is, indeed, a considerable journey,” he offered, his tone carefully neutral. “One might almost consider it a removal, rather than a mere relocation.” 

“Precisely!” she exclaimed, a flicker of animation brightening her countenance. “A removal, sir, and a most inconvenient one. One feels quite…detached.”
author: Jane Austen

text:
The question, though delivered with Mrs. Bennet’s customary lack of finesse, hung in the air like a poorly executed embroidery. “Could Colonel Forster repeat the particulars of Lydia’s note to his wife?” she pressed, her voice a shade too eager for composure. “He brought it with him for us to see, did he not?”

Mr. Bennet, observing the scene with a detached amusement, offered only a raised eyebrow. The Colonel, a good-natured man but easily flustered by feminine insistence, shifted uncomfortably. “Indeed, Mrs. Bennet. A most…unsettling communication. Miss Lydia expressed a desire, a *hope*, to spend a few days in Brighton, accompanying Mrs. Wickham.”

A collective gasp rippled through the room, save for Mr. Bennet who merely took a sip of his wine. Elizabeth, however, felt a chill despite the warmth of the fire. The very notion! Lydia, with her head full of ribbons and officers, seeking such an arrangement. 

“With the best intentions, I assure you,” the Colonel continued, reddening, “Mrs. Wickham believed it might be a harmless amusement. A little sea air, you understand.” Harmless, indeed. Elizabeth suspected a great deal more lay beneath the surface of that deceptively simple phrase.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The range, they said, was innocuous. The Blacktooth Peaks, locals called them, though a more fitting nomenclature would be the Teeth of Silence. It was the *sound* that unsettled, a piping, impossibly vast in its scope. Not a melody, precisely, but a modulation – a shifting, ululating tone that seemed to emanate not *from* any single peak, but *through* the very stone of the mountains themselves. 

Old Man Hemlock swore it altered with altitude, becoming a subsonic thrumming at the base, rising to a crystalline shriek near the snowline. I dismissed it as altitude sickness, until the reports began to coalesce. Lake, the surveyor, vanished three weeks past, last seen charting the westernmost crag. His notes, recovered by a search party, spoke of a “resonant dread” and a growing conviction that the piping *responded* to his presence.

Worse still, the sketches. Crude, frantic depictions of swirling vapours clinging to the summits – not cloud, but something…*local*. A clinging, phosphorescent mist, mirroring the patterns of the sound itself. We observed it ourselves today, a sickly luminescence around Harrowfell and Widow’s Peak. Lake saw it too, undoubtedly. And the piping…it grows louder. It feels, undeniably, as though something is *listening*.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The news, when it arrived, was delivered not with the dramatic flourish one might expect, but with the quiet, devastating precision of a dropped porcelain teacup. Miss Eleanor, it seemed, had *gone*. Not merely to visit an aunt in Hertfordshire, as had been delicately suggested, but…with Mr. Harding. 

“Elopement!” Mrs. Bennett declared, clutching her vinaigrette as if it contained the very antidote to such impropriety. “They must have seen them together for ever!” Indeed, whispers now recalled stolen glances at the Assembly, prolonged conversations during walks in the shrubbery, and a certain blush that frequently coloured Miss Eleanor’s cheeks in Mr. Harding’s presence. 

Colonel Forster did own that he had often suspected some partiality, especially on the gentleman’s side, though he had attributed it to a youthful enthusiasm easily corrected. He confessed, with a rueful shake of his head, to having dismissed it as mere flirtation, a harmless amusement for a young officer stationed nearby. 

Now, however, amusement was far from anyone’s mind. The disgrace was considerable, the family’s prospects dimmed. And the question, unspoken but heavy in the air, was not *if* they were in love, but *where* they believed love could possibly lead them.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mr. Harrington, having ventured a compliment upon Miss Beaumont’s accomplished needlework – a landscape, though rather too liberally populated with shepherdesses for true discernment – paused in hopes of an answer; but his companion was not disposed to make any; and Elizabeth, at that instant moving towards them, he was struck with the fortunate interruption. Indeed, Miss Beaumont’s silence, while not entirely unexpected, had begun to feel a trifle pointed. 

He had, perhaps, overestimated the reciprocal pleasure derived from discussing the merits of pastoral scenes. Or, more likely, she found his observations wanting. A possibility he found distinctly unsettling.

“Miss Bennet,” he offered, turning with what he hoped was a graceful air, “a most agreeable evening, is it not? The air possesses a delicacy quite uncommon for late July.”

Elizabeth, with a polite inclination of her head, replied, “Indeed, sir. Though I suspect the coolness is more attributable to the approaching shower than to any inherent quality of the season.” 

Her observation, delivered with a quiet composure, was, he thought, rather too accurate for comfort. He felt a distinct need for a more stimulating topic, and quickly.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The lantern light, it flickered somethin’ fierce, playin’ tricks on a fella’s eyes. This here figure, slumped in Pap’s chair, smelled powerfully of woodsmoke and trouble, same as always. But the voice… well, it weren’t Pap’s gravelly growl. It was higher pitched, strained, like a fiddle string stretched too tight. 

I’d been expectin’ a demand for my earnings, a tirade about good-for-nothin’ boys, the usual. Instead, this fella – or *somethin’* – just sat there, pickin’ at a loose thread on his coat. And then he smiled.

Now, Pap hadn’t smiled in a coon’s age. This weren’t a smile of pleasure, neither. It was a tight, nervous thing, and it didn’t reach the eyes. But on his face, under the grime and the beard stubble, I seen a hint of powder. And the jawline… too delicate for Pap, by a country mile. 

So I knowed, then, that this warn’t Pap, but a woman dressed up in a man’s clothes. So I was uncomfortable again. I judged the old ma. A woman disguisin’ herself as my Pap? Lord, what in tarnation was *that* about? It smelled like a heap of trouble brewin’, and I had a feelin’ I was about to be right in the middle of it.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Elmsworth, though possessed of no striking beauty, nor a fortune to incite the avarice of the most calculating gentleman, found herself the subject of a most unsettling attention. It was, indeed, highly improbable – one might even declare it *improper* – that Mr. Finch, a man known more for his debts than his discernment, should direct his affections towards a young lady actually residing under the guardianship of the esteemed Mrs. Penworthy, and possessing connections in respectable society. 

Yet, direct them he did. His attentions, though veiled in a clumsy politeness, were persistent. He hovered near her at the Assembly, offering compliments of a rather breathless and ill-considered nature. He dispatched bouquets of rather wilted flowers, and even attempted a sketch of her, which, thankfully, Mrs. Penworthy intercepted before Miss Elmsworth was forced to endure the mortification of viewing it.

The very notion was preposterous! That any young man should form such a design against a girl who was by no means unprotected or friendless, and who was actually staying in the very house of a lady renowned for her good judgement, bordered on the absurd. Still, a disquieting flutter in Miss Elmsworth’s breast suggested that even absurdity might prove… troublesome.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though possessed of a modest fortune and even more modest connections, found herself the subject of a most unexpected proposition. Mr. Collins, ever eager to demonstrate his consequence, had declared, with a flourish of self-importance, “Bring her to Hunsford, and I will visit her.” 

Eleanor, accustomed to the quietude of her aunt’s estate, could scarcely credit the offer. Hunsford! A place dominated, as rumour had it, by a lady of… *pronounced* opinions. Her cousin, Miss Bennet, upon hearing the news, offered a wry observation.

“Allow me, by the way, my fair cousin, to observe that I do not reckon the notice and kindness of *that* quarter as a particular advantage. Indeed, a degree of obscurity is often preferable to the glare of unwelcome patronage.”

Eleanor, though not entirely disagreeing, felt a flicker of curiosity. To be observed, even critically, by so formidable a personage… it was a prospect, if not *desirable*, certainly… stimulating. The journey promised, at the very least, a diverting change from the predictable rhythm of country life. And perhaps, she mused, a story worth recounting upon her return.
author: Jane Austen

text:
My dearest sister, a most vexing circumstance has arisen with Mr. Hawthorne, and I find myself in need of your counsel, though I confess a degree of reluctance in troubling you with family affairs. He persists, you see, in a most peculiar reticence regarding his estate. While his attentions to Eliza are undeniably flattering – and she, I must admit, returns them with a warmth I deem quite proper – a mother cannot entirely disregard the practicalities.

He speaks much of affection, of esteem, but little of provision. This morning, during a particularly tedious discussion of the merits of landscape gardening, he alluded, almost in passing, to a desire for a swift union. “Your side, I hope it will not be long before they are,” he remarked, with a disconcerting air of expectation. 

All that is required of you, it seems, is to assure to your daughter, by settlement, her equal share of Thorne Abbey. A most impertinent suggestion, to place the onus upon *us* to secure her future! I have, of course, offered no immediate answer, merely hinting at the necessity of a full and transparent accounting. One cannot be too careful, you understand. A comfortable competence is, after all, the foundation of all happiness.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Tiber, he commenced to flail about like a fish yanked from the river, only drier and considerably more agitated. Wasn’t a sight a body forgets easy. He was grabbin’ at nothin’, mind you, just air, but grabbin’ with the desperation of a man fightin’ off a whole swarm of hornets. And screamin’. Lordy, the screamin’! Claimed devils had got a-hold of him, little imps tuggin’ at his limbs and whisperin’ blasphemies in his ear. 

Now, Tiber wasn’t a man given to fancy. Usually content with complainin’ about the price of corn or the laziness of his hound dog. But this… this was a performance. He wrestled with them unseen fiends for a good ten minutes, kickin’ up dust and hollerin’ ‘bout brimstone and eternal damnation.

By-and-by, though, the fight went out of him. Like a punctured bellows, he just…stopped. Collapsed onto the porch like a sack of potatoes. Didn’t move for a spell, ‘cept for a low moanin’ that rattled in his chest. Just laid there, lookin’ smaller than I ever remembered, and a fella had to wonder what sort of trouble a man could get into with somethin’ you couldn’t even *see*.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The basalt cliffs wept a viscous, phosphorescent dew, and the air hung thick with a cloying sweetness that hinted at geometries beyond human comprehension. Old Man Hemlock, they said, had gone mad studying the strata there, muttering of ‘segmented dominion’ and ‘the chitinous will.’ I, of course, dismissed it as coastal dementia until *I* saw them.

Not creatures, precisely. More…assemblages. Colonies manifested as shifting, obsidian mounds, pulsing with an internal luminescence. Each segment, a grotesque parody of organic form, performed delicately differentiated functions in its primal world—much like the ants and bees of to-day. It reproduced like the vegetable cryptogams, especially the abhorrent puffballs that bloom in cyclopean grottoes. Spores, not of seed, but of *being*, drifting on the fetid breeze.

The horror wasn’t in individual form, but in the utter lack of individuality. A single, vast consciousness expressed through countless, writhing components. And the feeling…the dreadful, creeping certainty that they *noticed* me. That my observation was not passive, but a calculation. A potential assimilation. The cliffs seemed to lean closer, the phosphorescence intensifying, and I fled, the sweetness turning to bile in my throat, knowing I carried a fragment of their alien awareness within my very soul.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Mrs. Bennet chose to consider it as given, in compliment to her eldest daughter, and was particularly flattered by receiving the unsolicited assurance from Mrs. Phillips that Mr. Bingley’s attentions were, undoubtedly, directed towards Jane. It was a prospect most agreeable, naturally, though the younger Miss Bennetts, Elizabeth in particular, affected a composure she did not entirely feel. 

Mary, ever occupied with improvement, declared it a fortunate circumstance for the family’s standing, though her pronouncements lacked the warmth one might expect. Kitty, predictably, was consumed with imagining balls and new ribbons, whilst Lydia, with a breathless eagerness, speculated upon the speed with which a wedding might be arranged. 

Even Charlotte Lucas, observing the flurry from a more sensible remove, remarked upon the general excitement. “One cannot deny, Mrs. Bennet,” she offered with a polite inclination of the head, “that a suitable match would alleviate many anxieties.” 

Mrs. Bennet, however, heard only the validation of her own discerning judgment. To have *two* daughters advantageously placed was, she declared, a triumph, and a clear indication of her own superior management of the household. The prospect, indeed, was almost too delightful to bear.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The mist clung to Kanchenjunga’s slopes like a shroud, a damp, grey pallor mirroring the unsettling geometries etched upon the crumbling stone. These were not the ruins of any known empire, but something…*older*. Something that predated the very concept of empire, whispering of cyclopean architects and a worship utterly alien to human comprehension. 

The canvases of that peculiar painter – Roerich, they called him – had, with maddening accuracy, captured the *feel* of these places. Not the detail, for detail was lost to the centuries and the relentless erosion, but the *wrongness*. The subtly skewed perspectives, the colours that seemed to bleed from a dimension beyond our own, the suggestion of vast, non-Euclidean spaces lurking just beyond the visible.

Each weathered lintel, each moss-choked carving, felt less like a remnant of a forgotten civilization and more like a fragment of a dream – a dream not *of* humanity, but *about* humanity, observed by entities whose minds were as vast and cold as the Himalayan winds. A dreadful, creeping certainty settled upon the soul: these stones were not built, but *remembered* into existence, echoes of a primordial age when the world was shaped by forces best left undisturbed. And the paintings…the paintings were a key, a dreadful, alluring key to unlocking the abyss.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, I had a plan, see. A perfectly good plan, laid out in my head like a map of the Mississippi itself. I was going to turn up there from the village, not from below. A fella wants a bit of surprise, a touch of the unexpected, and comin’ up from the lowlands just ain’t got that. So I just took a look, and shoved along, straight for town.

Well, the very first thing I encountered was Old Man Hemlock’s prize-winning sow, Bess. And Bess, she weren’t pleased. Not one bit. She’d rooted up half the Reverend’s petunias and was lookin’ for a scapegoat, and naturally, a fella on a mule fit the bill. 

She charged, she did, a pink blur of righteous indignation. My mule, Bartholomew, he ain’t known for his bravery, mind you. He let out a bray that could curdle milk and near threw me into a patch of prickly pear. We danced a jig, Bess and Bartholomew and I, a right comical sight, I reckon, if a body wasn’t tryin’ to avoid bein’ trampled. 

Ended up havin’ to bribe her with a handful of apples. A perfectly good plan, all undone by a pig with a grudge. Such is life, I suppose.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The matter of Mr. Harrington’s whist playing had become, in a remarkably short space of time, the subject of much quiet discussion amongst the ladies of Meryton. It was not, to be sure, a topic of the first consequence, yet possessing a certain piquancy, given the gentleman’s acknowledged pride in his skill. The cards, it appeared, had been most unkind. He had suffered a series of losses, and those, too, against players of decidedly inferior reputation.

Indeed, the evening’s play had been most unfortunate. He had lost every point, a circumstance which, had it not been observed by Mrs. Philips, might have passed with a degree of decorum. But Mrs. Philips, ever solicitous to demonstrate her understanding of all things fashionable, began to express her concern thereupon, a lamentation which, though well-intended, was clearly most vexing to the gentleman. 

He assured her, with a forced lightness, that the evening was merely a trifle, a momentary lapse in fortune. “A mere accident, madam,” he declared, adjusting his cravat with a touch of agitation. “The cards, you see, were…obstinate.” One suspected, however, that his composure was a fragile thing, and that the sting of defeat was felt with a rather more acute sensibility than he chose to reveal.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though possessed of a comfortable fortune and a passable complexion, found herself, at twenty-four, remarkably unpursued. Not for want of callers, mind you, but for want of a caller *worthy* of her regard. Mr. Finch, the vicar, was excessively pious, and Mr. Hargrave, though undeniably handsome, possessed a vanity so pronounced it quite eclipsed any other quality.

This season, however, brought a new prospect: Mr. Beaumont, recently returned from the Continent, and possessing, it was whispered, a considerable library. Eleanor, a devotee of correspondence and a judge of character through penned prose, found herself intrigued. He spoke little of his travels, preferring to inquire after *her* pursuits. 

Yet, a subtle chill pervaded his civility. He praised her wit, but with a detachment that bordered on condescension. He admired her collection of letters, but remarked upon their “feminine sensibility” with a slight, almost imperceptible, curl of the lip. Eleanor, though flattered by his attention, began to suspect a pride that might prove an insurmountable obstacle. A gentleman who valued intellect, surely, would not so readily dismiss the very source of it.
author: Jane Austen

In addition, of course, our two ships--wooden exwhalers, reinforced for ice conditions and having auxiliary steam--were fully manned. text:
The passing of Mr. Darcy, though universally lamented, had left a peculiar charge upon the shoulders of his cousin, Colonel Fitzwilliam. Not for him the fashionable pursuits of London, nor the agreeable company of acquaintances. Duty, a sentiment he held in the highest regard, demanded a complete re-ordering of his life. He relinquished his commissions, much to the surprise of several ladies who had favoured him with encouraging glances, and took up residence at Pemberley.

It was a task requiring no small degree of application. Every detail, from the management of the estate’s tenants to the arrangement of the library – a room Mr. Darcy held particularly dear – received his meticulous attention. He consulted with the head gardener on the rose bushes, debated timber yields with the land steward, and even oversaw the repair of a minor leak in the west wing. 

Mr. Darcy, in his lifetime, had always possessed a discerning eye for character, and it was a comfort to Colonel Fitzwilliam to know his efforts were not unappreciated. The late master’s solicitor, a man of sound judgement, frequently remarked upon the Colonel’s diligence, and declared him “most highly esteemed” for his unwavering devotion to Pemberley’s prosperity. A quiet satisfaction, though never openly expressed, bloomed within him.

text:
The air, even at this unseasonable late autumn, held a glacial bite, a premonition of the endless winter clinging to the slopes of Mt. Terror. Ten thousand nine hundred feet it rose, a pallid, spectral monument against a bruised and sickly sky. Extinct, they called it. A geological slumber. But the mountain *remembered*. 

Puffs of something – not quite smoke, not quite steam, but a viscous, opalescent exhalation – drifted from the caldera, clinging to the stunted pines like grave-shrouds. Old Man Hemlock, before his…disappearance, spoke of a breathing, a slow, rhythmic expansion and contraction of the peak itself. Nonsense, the surveyors had scoffed. Yet, the compasses spun erratically near the base, and the barometric pressure fluctuated with a sickening, organic pulse.

I had come seeking geological data, but found only a growing dread. The stone itself felt *wrong*, cold and slick with an unnatural dew. A subtle geometry, not of nature, but of something…constructed, seemed to underlie the mountain’s form. And within those drifting, pearlescent vapours, I thought I glimpsed shapes. Vast, angular, and utterly, irrevocably *alien*. A silence descended, heavier than stone, broken only by the whisper of the wind – a whisper that sounded, disturbingly, like a name.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
The drawing-room, already crowded with the well-meaning but tiresome attentions of local society, seemed to shrink as he entered. It was not merely *his* presence, though undeniably striking after a year’s absence, but the peculiar sensation of the past being abruptly, and rather inconveniently, resurrected. He stood, quite immediately before them, as if time had been a mere trifling inconvenience, not a chasm to be bridged.

A swift glance confirmed her apprehension – or perhaps, her secret hope. No shadow of the former coolness marred his countenance. Indeed, he possessed all the recent civility, the polite deference he had so carefully cultivated during his last visit. A most unsettling improvement, she thought, for it demanded a response. 

To remain aloof, to offer only the barest acknowledgement, felt…unsuitable. Not because of any lingering affection, she assured herself, but from a sense of decorum. One could not, after such a display, descend to pointed indifference. Therefore, with a delicate inclination of the head, and a carefully modulated smile, she resolved to *imitate* his newfound grace. It was, after all, the only proper course. Though a most vexing one.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Hemlock, he’d gotten it into his head to be a gentleman, see? Not just *any* gentleman, mind you, but a proper Englishman. Now, Hemlock hadn’t been further east than St. Louis, and his accent before was thicker than Mississippi mud, but he was determined. All the time he was a-doing it he tried to talk like an Englishman; and he done it pretty well, too, for a slouch.

He’d practice on the hired help, bless their patience. “Good *mornin’*, Perkins,” he’d boom, drawlin’ the ‘orning’ out like taffy. “Rather a spot of bother with the turnips, what?” Perkins, a fella not known for subtlety, would just stare. 

The worst was the tea. He insisted on it, brewed weak as dishwater, and served with biscuits he’d attempt to crumble delicately, usually resulting in a shower of crumbs down his waistcoat. He’d then pronounce, with a flourish, “Quite delightful, don’t you think? A most… *civilized* repast.” 

Folks just humored him. It was a sight, I tell you, a genuine hoot. He never quite lost the glint in his eye, the way he’d size you up, but he *thought* he was pullin’ it off. And maybe, just maybe, that’s all that mattered.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The arrival of Mr. Finch was, to say the least, an event calculated to disturb the composure of Hartfield. He had, it was whispered, suffered a disappointment in affections – a circumstance which, whilst eliciting a degree of pity from the more charitable, afforded considerable amusement to others. His cousin, Lady Bertram, had, with a benevolence bordering on the officious, insisted upon his spending the Season with them, believing country air and female society might restore his spirits. 

He had, however, likewise foretold, with a melancholy air, that no such restoration was possible. And so it proved. He took his seat at the bottom of the table, by her Ladyship’s desire, and looked as if he felt that life could furnish nothing further to require his attention. Miss Eleanor, ever mindful of propriety, offered a polite enquiry as to his journey, but received only a murmured acknowledgement and a gaze fixed upon his plate with an intensity that suggested he found more solace in the arrangement of the roast than in human conversation. 

One could not help but wonder if a man so thoroughly resigned to unhappiness might not prove a rather tiresome companion for the summer months.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The carriage rattled onward, and Miss Elmsworth, though attempting a composure befitting her years, found her gaze repeatedly drawn to the rising land. It was not the prospect of Pemberley House itself, though grandly spoken of, which now occupied her thoughts, but rather the woods surrounding it. A wildness, a *profusion* of trees, quite unlike the carefully managed parklands of Hertfordshire, presented itself. A slight tremor, not entirely unpleasant, ran through her. Such untamed nature felt…imposing.

Her companion, Mrs. Featherstonehaugh, remarked upon the “picturesque gloom,” but Miss Elmsworth suspected the lady merely wished to sound discerning. It was, undeniably, a little frightening. One imagined losing one’s way with alarming ease, encountering creatures best left undisturbed. 

At length, however, they turned in at the lodge, a stone structure of considerable solidity, and her spirits were in a high flutter. The drive, though long and winding, offered glimpses of the house, each revealing a greater degree of magnificence than the last. A footman, remarkably attentive, sprang forward to assist. This was it. Pemberley. And despite her earlier perturbation, a hopeful anticipation bloomed within her breast. Perhaps, just perhaps, this visit would prove… agreeable.
author: Jane Austen

Now, we’d had a supper, a right proper spread of cold chicken and biscuits pilfered from a farmer’s pantry – a fella too trusting for his own good, I reckon. The King, he was leanin’ back against a stack of hay bales, belly shakin’ like a bowlful of jelly, and the Duke, well, he was near rollin’ on the ground.

“Did ye *see* their faces, Sire?” the Duke managed to gasp between fits of laughter. “Believin’ that performance! A genuine tragedy, they thought it was! A tragedy about a lost nephew and a heartbroken uncle! Why, I haven’t seen such gullibility since old Man Hemlock tried to trade a blind mule for a gold watch.”

The King wiped a tear from his eye with a greasy napkin. “Greenhorns, flatheads, the whole lot of ‘em. They swallowed it whole, hook, line, and sinker. Paid good money, too, to witness their own fleecein’. It’s a marvel, I tell ye, a pure marvel how easy it is to separate a man from his coin when you tell him a story he *wants* to believe.” 

He chuckled, a low rumble in his chest. “Don’t mention it to a soul, mind. Let ‘em stew in their own sentimentality. It’s good for business.”
