text:
The afternoon proved a trial, though not, perhaps, of the severest kind. Lady Bertram, settled as ever in a state of comfortable inertia, held forth upon the merits of needlepoint, a subject to which she devoted a surprising degree of conviction. Mr. Collins, naturally, was entirely of her opinion, assuring her Ladyship that her skill was beyond compare and thanking her, with a most earnest repetition, for every favourable observation. 

Miss Bingley, however, found herself constrained to offer a dissenting murmur regarding the shade of silk employed – a pale rose, she deemed, quite unsuitable for a summer’s work. This small rebellion was met with a glacial stare, and a pronouncement that Miss Bingley’s taste, whilst not *incorrect*, lacked the seasoned judgement of one accustomed to country life. 

One could scarcely credit the lengths to which politeness demanded one go! It was, I confess, a relief when the conversation turned to the vicarage garden, allowing Mr. Collins ample opportunity to detail its modest improvements, each one, of course, deserving of Lady Bertram’s highest praise. A tedious, yet undeniably *proper*, occasion.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Mr. Harrison, a man generally possessed of a cheerful disposition, found himself in a most uncomfortable predicament. Having remarked, with what he intended as a compliment, upon the excellence of Mrs. Ainsworth’s blancmange – a confection, indeed, of surpassing delicacy – he had then, regrettably, inquired as to which of her daughters assisted in its preparation. 

A slight chill descended upon the room. Mrs. Ainsworth, a lady of considerable refinement and even more considerable pride in her domestic arrangements, merely raised a brow. “My daughters, sir,” she stated, her voice cool as a winter morning, “are occupied with accomplishments befitting their station. Needlework, pianoforte, a smattering of French – these are their pursuits, not the vulgar business of the kitchen.”

Mr. Harrison, mortified to have caused displeasure, stammered an apology. “Pray, forgive my impertinence, madam. I merely… admired the result, and foolishly assumed…”

He begged pardon for having displeased her. In a softened tone, she declared herself not entirely offended, merely wishing to impress upon him the proper distinctions of rank and the importance of cultivating a lady’s mind, rather than her culinary skills. He bowed, relieved, and resolved to confine his future observations to the weather.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Old Man Hemlock, he was a study in granite and regret, mostly. Been diggin’ this ditch for nigh on thirty-eight years, he had. Thirty-eight! A fella’d think a man could dig a ditch in less time than it takes a catfish to grow whiskers. But Hemlock, he wasn’t diggin’ *a* ditch, see. He was diggin’ *the* ditch. The one that’d finally settle all accounts.

Young Tom Sawyer, bless his mischievous heart, strolled up, lookin’ like trouble wrapped in homespun. “Ain’t never seen a man work so steady at somethin’,” he drawled, kickin’ at a loose clod. “Never seen a man dig so…purposeful.”

Hemlock just kept at it, shovel bitin’ into the stubborn clay. Then, out of the blue, he says, quiet as a church mouse, “No thirty-seven year job; this is a thirty-eight year job, Tom Sawyer.” 

He never said nothin’ more. But he sighed, a sound like wind through a graveyard, and pretty soon he stopped diggin’, and leaned on the shovel like it was the only friend he had left. Just stared out at the field, lookin’ for somethin’ lost, or maybe somethin’ he knew he’d *never* find. A powerful, mournful sight, it was.
author: Mark Twain

Now, old Man Hemlock, he’d gone and done it. Not *died*, mind you, not precisely. More like…disappeared with intention. He’d laid it all out for me, Jim, over a chipped enamel mug of lukewarm coffee. Said the Barlows, them grasping land-grabbers, were fixin’ to claim his bottomland, claim it rightful, they would. Said they’d spread a tale, a mournful one, of a tragic accident.

“And they’ll think I’ve been killed, and floated down the river,” he’d rasped, eyes glinting like a catfish in muddy water. “There’s something up there that’ll help them think so—a hat of mine, weighted down, and a boot. A left one, naturally. Always favored my left foot, I did.”

He’d then handed me a small, oiled packet. “Don’t you lose no time, Jim, b. Deliver this to Miss Elvira, up at the Widow Peabody’s. Tell her…tell her Hemlock sends his regards, and a little somethin’ to grease the wheels. It ain’t gold, but it’s worth more’n all the Barlows’ land, I reckon.” 

A peculiar man, Hemlock. Always had a scheme brewin’ under that bushy brow. And I, a simple boatman, caught right in the middle of it. Lord help us all.

Now, old Man Hemlock, he had a notion for fancy poultry. Peacocks, mostly. Cost him a pretty penny, them birds did, and a heap o’ fussin’ to keep ‘em lookin’ presentable. Tom Sawyer, see, he wasn’t one for presentable. He was one for *opportunity*. And Hemlock’s peacocks, strutting around like royalty, well, they were just beggin’ for a bit o’…improvement.

Heavin’ in new bullinesses wherever he got a chance, that was Tom’s way. A frog in the preacher’s hat, a snail on the schoolmarm’s spectacles, and now, a generous coat o’ blue clay on them peacocks. Not a smear, mind you, but a thorough, artistic application. Looked like they’d been dipped in the Mississippi itself.

Hemlock near ‘bout had a fit. Screechin’ and carryin’ on like a scalded cat. But Tom, he just leaned against the fence, whittlin’ and lookin’ innocent as a newborn babe. 

And that is what he done. Well, one thing was dead sure, and that was that Tom Sawyer was in earn. Earnin’ a good laugh, mostly, and a whole mess o’ trouble, likely. But a boy’s gotta have his fun, don’t he? Even if it involves a few blue birds and a right riled-up old man.

Miss Eleanor Penhaligon found herself in a most vexing predicament, though not, she assured herself, one entirely unforeseen. Mr. Finch, a gentleman of tolerable fortune and even more tolerable manners, had declared his affections with an earnestness bordering on the impertinent. The fault, however, lay not with *him*, for such things, I know, are all chance in this world. There was no knowing how estates will go when once they come to be entailed. 

No, the difficulty resided entirely with her own unfortunate cousin, Mr. Alistair, whose improvident gaming debts had rendered him, despite his lineage, quite ineligible. Had Alistair possessed a prudent disposition, the Penhaligon inheritance would remain secure, and Eleanor free to decline Mr. Finch with a clear conscience. 

Instead, she was burdened with the knowledge that a match with the man, though lacking in brilliance, offered a necessary bulwark against ruin for her family. It was a sacrifice, certainly, but one demanded by duty. She sighed, contemplating the blandness of Mr. Finch’s conversation. A comfortable existence, perhaps, but oh, the lack of *spark*!

text:
Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a tolerable fortune and a mind not entirely devoid of discernment, was, it must be confessed, given to pronouncements of a rather startling confidence. This morning, whilst assisting her sister in the arrangement of a particularly delicate bouquet, she declared her complete independence of circumstance.

“My actions, dearest Marianne,” she stated, snipping a rose with unnecessary force, “would be dictated solely by principle, not by the vagaries of fate. I should act precisely as my conscience demanded, regardless of…well, of anything!”

Mr. Bingley, passing by the open window on his bay mare, overheard the final sentence. He paused, a slight smile playing upon his lips. “Indeed, Miss Eleanor,” he called out, his voice carrying on the gentle breeze, “your conduct would be quite as dependent on chance as that of any man I know; and if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, ‘Bingley, do *not* venture beyond Netherfield Park today,’ would you not, despite your principles, find yourself curiously inclined to disobey?”

Eleanor flushed a delicate pink, the rose slipping from her grasp. Marianne, ever the observer, exchanged a knowing glance with the stable boy.
author: Jane Austen

Now, a feller comes to me, see, and utters a phrase like *Polly-voo-franzy*… well, sir, that ain’t a signal for polite conversation, no indeed. Folks ‘round these parts ain’t much given to fancy talk, let alone words strung together like a runaway train. It’d be like a blue jay tryin’ to recite Shakespeare – just plumb unnatural.

“What would I think?” you ask. Why, I wouldn’ think *nuff’n*. Not a blessed thing. My brain wouldn’t even bother to register it as language. It’d be akin to hearin’ a hog whistle – a noise, certainly, but signifyin’ nothin’ but the hog’s own peculiar amusement. 

No, sir. A man comin’ at me with “Polly-voo-franzy” is a man lookin’ for trouble. And I’d be obliged to provide it. I’d take en bust him over de head with the nearest convenient object – a fence post, a skillet, maybe even a particularly sturdy melon – dat is, if he wa’ standin’ close enough. A body’s gotta protect hisself from nonsense, you understand. And that there, that’s pure, unadulterated nonsense.

“And this is always the way with him,” she added, gesturing with a slight inclination of the head towards the newly arranged chamber. “Whatever can give his sister any pleasure, is sure to be done in a moment. There is nothing, truly, too much trouble for Mr. Alistair when Miss Eleanor’s comfort is at stake.”

The room itself was not grand, being merely a spare bedchamber overlooking the stable yard, but it had been transformed. Gone were the faded chintz curtains, replaced with a cheerful sprigged muslin. A small writing desk, previously relegated to the attic, now stood bathed in the afternoon light, adorned with a vase of freshly-cut lavender. Even the rather severe portrait of their late aunt had been removed, supplanted by a delicate watercolour of the family estate.

Miss Beatrice sighed, a delicate sound. “He insisted upon the rosewood screen, you know. Said Eleanor complained of a draught, though I assure you, the window was perfectly sealed. Such attention! It is almost…excessive.” 

Her companion, Mrs. Penhaligon, chuckled softly. “A brother’s devotion is rarely measured by reason, my dear. And Eleanor *is* a delicate creature. He merely anticipates her needs.”
author: Jane Austen

About Mr. Ashworth and his… indiscretion with Miss Bellingham? It is quite shocking, and to think he was so recently paying suit to Lady Beatrice!”

Miss Marianne, ever the more pragmatic of the two, merely raised a brow. “Shocking, perhaps, but hardly surprising. The man has always possessed a certain… boldness. But what concerns me is the manner of its exposure. To broadcast such a thing so dreadfully! It reflects upon *everyone* connected, you know.”

“Precisely!” Eleanor exclaimed, her fan fluttering with emphasis. “And Mr. Ashworth, naturally, blames Mr. Darcy, claiming he was privy to the arrangement and did nothing to prevent it. He even hinted at a… communication, a prior understanding. Though, of course, Mr. Darcy would never stoop to such a thing.”

Marianne considered this, her lips pressed into a firm line. “That it ought not to be attempted. Mr. Darcy has not authorized me to make his communication public. To do so would be a breach of confidence, and a most unseemly intrusion. Let Mr. Ashworth stew in his own disgrace.”

The use of phrases like "indiscretion," "boldness," and "unseemly intrusion" are particularly evocative of her writing. The ending, with Marianne’s firm stance, feels very much in line with a character who values principle and discretion.)**

The charts were… insufficient. Old Man Hemlock’s meticulous renderings, lauded for decades, proved tragically, blasphemously wrong. It wasn’t the gradual rise of the plateau we anticipated, but a *rupture* in the very fabric of the world. It appeared on the south, and before noon we all felt a thrill of excitement at beholding a vast, lofty, and snow-clad mountain chain which opened out an impossible vista.

But the excitement curdled swiftly. The peaks weren’t geological. They *shifted*, subtly, as if breathing. The snow wasn’t white, but a sickly, phosphorescent grey, and clung to the slopes with a disturbing tenacity. A silence descended, heavier than any arctic stillness, a silence that pressed upon the mind, hinting at geometries beyond human comprehension. 

Young Davies, the geologist, began muttering about non-Euclidean angles, his eyes wide with a dreadful, nascent understanding. Even seasoned Captain Larsen, a man who’d faced down typhoons and mutiny, paled. For the mountains weren’t merely *there*; they were… *watching*. And in the unnatural stillness, I swear I detected a low, resonant hum, a vibration that resonated not in the ears, but in the very bone. A hum that spoke of ages before mankind, and of things best left undisturbed.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

The arrival of Mr. Alistair Finch at the Meryton assembly caused a most agreeable stir. The ladies, having recently exhausted their commentary upon Mr. Bingley’s pleasing countenance and amiable disposition, declared Mr. Finch to be vastly his superior in handsome features. Indeed, a darker, more sculpted profile, and eyes of a penetrating grey, drew forth a chorus of approving whispers. He moved with a quiet confidence, accepting compliments with a modest inclination of the head, and was, for nearly half the evening, the object of universal admiration.

However, this favourable impression began to wane with the discovery of his…enthusiasm for beetles. Not a casual interest, mind you, but a detailed, and rather *loud*, discourse upon the various species present in Hertfordshire, complete with sketches produced from a pocketbook and offered for inspection. Miss Elmsworth, having endured a lengthy explanation of the *Lucanus cervus*, declared him “singularly devoted to the insect world,” a sentiment quickly echoed, and with increasing volume, throughout the room. The grey eyes, once so captivating, now seemed to gleam with a rather unsettling zeal.

Miss Marianne, however, possessed of a more restless spirit, was already contemplating escape. “Perhaps a turn about the drawing-room, or – dare I suggest it? – a glimpse of the view?” 

Their mother, ever mindful of propriety, offered a gentle correction. “The view, my dears, is best enjoyed *after* a suitable interval of quietude. You have been above an hour in the dining-room, happily employed in visiting with Mrs. Grimshaw, watching the seamstress diligently at work. Such concentrated attention requires recovery.”

Marianne, though momentarily subdued, could not entirely conceal a mischievous glint in her eye. “Recovery, Mama? “The best landlord, and the best master, that ever lived,” said she, with a sigh that spoke volumes of past experience. “Not like the wild young men now-a-days, who think of nothing but themselves. There *is* a difference, Miss Eleanor, a vast difference, between a gentleman who considers his tenants as beings deserving of comfort, and those who view them merely as a source of income.”

Eleanor, ever the attentive listener, prompted, “Indeed, Mama? You speak of a particular instance, perhaps?”

“Oh, many! But one springs readily to mind. Old Mr. Ashworth, at Oakhaven. He never raised the rent in all my father’s years, not even during the leanest harvests. And when the barn roof suffered in the great gale of ’98, he oversaw the repairs himself, ensuring the work was done properly, and at *his* expense. He inquired after the health of every family on the estate, remembered birthdays, and even sent a goose at Christmas. 

Such consideration! It is a quality sadly lacking in the present generation. They speak of improvement and innovation, but forget the simple virtues of kindness and responsibility. A man may possess all the land in England, yet be utterly devoid of true worth without a benevolent heart.”

We had breached the final moraine, and before us, impossibly preserved within the glacial lee, stood a cyclopean structure of basalt, utterly alien to any known epoch of man. It wasn’t the height, though that was monstrous, but the *angles* – non-Euclidean geometries that seemed to shift and writhe in the periphery, inducing a nausea not of the stomach, but of the soul.

These archways, of course, were flush with upper-story floors, and in this case one of the floors still existed. The building thus accessed revealed a chamber of polished, obsidian-like stone, slick with a perpetual, internal frost. No carvings adorned the walls, only a subtle, rhythmic pulsing – a slow, geological heartbeat. 

And the silence…it wasn’t the absence of sound, but a *weight* of it, a suffocating pressure born of millennia. I dared not speculate on the beings who conceived such a place, only knew, with a certainty that chilled me beyond reason, that their slumber was not natural, and that the encroaching ice was not a burial, but a *warden*. A warden against something…worse.

text:
It was, perhaps, unavoidable that as one of the executors of my father’s will, I should be made privy to the full extent of his, shall we say, *peculiar* financial arrangements. A gentleman of comfortable means, certainly, yet possessed of a fondness for speculation that bordered, in my estimation, on the imprudent. The particulars, revealed through endless ledgers and correspondence, were most unsettling. 

My sister, Miss Eleanor, remains blissfully ignorant, content to believe Papa’s estate a model of order. I, however, have been forced to confront a series of…loans, extended to individuals of questionable character, secured by promises as flimsy as cobwebs. And the sums! Enough to quite overturn our expectations for a comfortable future.

Mr. Harding, the solicitor, assures me all is recoverable, but his assurances ring hollow. The very thought of pursuing these debts, of engaging in such unseemly commerce, fills me with a profound abhorrence. It is a burden, this knowledge, and one I dare not share with Eleanor, lest it disturb her peace. One must, after all, maintain a semblance of composure, even amidst financial disarray.

They sought to rekindle the flame of interstellar transit, a flame extinguished before recorded history, a flame guarded by whispers of entities best left undisturbed.

But the final calibrations… they spoke of a change. A subtle, yet absolute, alteration in the very fabric of reality. The aether, once receptive to the resonant frequencies necessary for displacement, now *rejected* them. Each attempt to pierce the veil resulted not in ascension, but in a sickening, localised distortion – a warping of space that threatened to unravel the observatory itself. 

Old Man Hemlock, his eyes hollowed by too much gazing into the abyss of numbers, muttered of a ‘closing’. A cosmic membrane descending, a final, irrevocable sealing. The ancient knowledge, it seemed, had not been *lost*, but *withdrawn*. Something, somewhere beyond the black gulfs, had decreed Earth a prison. And the stars… the stars were no longer destinations, but cold, indifferent witnesses to our confinement.

The assembly at Netherfield had concluded, leaving Miss Eleanor, though outwardly serene, with a most unsettling agitation. Mr. Darcy, a gentleman of undeniably proud bearing and, it must be confessed, considerable fortune, had ventured a proposal. Not with the ardent flourish one reads of in novels, no, but with a chilling precision, detailing her family’s deficiencies as justification for overcoming his own better judgement. 

To the utmost to speak with composure when she said,-- “You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you suppose that the mode of your declaration affected me in a degree proportionate to its impropriety.” It was a phrasing, she knew, bordering on impertinence, yet she could not bring herself to offer a more effusive rejection. His countenance, already habitually reserved, darkened further.

He attempted a retort, something concerning the unsuitability of her connections, but she cut him short with a cool, “Pray, sir, do not insult my understanding with such transparent condescension.” The air crackled with unspoken sentiments, a battle of wills waged with carefully chosen words. She observed, with a small, internal satisfaction, that *he* was the more discomposed of the two.

The cyclopean geometry pressed upon the mind, a nauseating insistence of angles not meant for human comprehension. We had breached the basalt plateau after weeks of agonizing ascent, and found it – not a city, not a temple, but a *circumference*. A vast, unbroken ring of obsidian, polished to a sickening sheen, encompassing a hollow perhaps miles across. 

But it was the walls *beyond* that chilled the marrow. Three-fourths of the ring’s impossible span were shadowed by structures of a pre-human scale, colossal remnants of a tower the ring itself seemed to *define*. Bas-reliefs, carved with a maddening precision, depicted the original edifice – a spire of impossible height, adorned with geometries that defied Euclidean space, and crowned with…things. Things best left unremembered.

The sculptures hinted at a purpose, a function beyond mortal ken. They showed beings, vaguely reptilian yet disturbingly *architectural*, tending to the spire with tools of obsidian and a reverence that bordered on worship. A worship of what? Of the spire itself? Or of the void it pierced? 

A low, subsonic hum emanated from the shadowed ruins, vibrating not in the ears, but in the very bone. It spoke of ages before mankind, of entities that slumbered, and of a geometry that threatened to unravel the sanity of any who dared to gaze upon its dreadful perfection.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

The Misses Ashworth and Penhaligon, once inseparable as sisters might be, now occupied opposite ends of every room, their greetings reduced to the coldest of nods. It was a subject much discussed amongst their acquaintance, naturally, though none dared inquire directly, for delicacy forbade. One might conjecture, perhaps, a difference in taste regarding the recent militia arrivals – Miss Ashworth favouring the rather boisterous Captain Harding, while Miss Penhaligon displayed a marked preference for the quieter Mr. Finch. 

Or could it be a matter of shared confidences, betrayed, not through malice, but through an unfortunate looseness of tongue? Mrs. Bellingham hinted at a disagreement concerning a bonnet, a particularly egregious creation of lavender silk, but such a trifle seemed hardly sufficient to sever a connection of so many years. 

Indeed, the truth, one suspected, lay in a more subtle realm – a gradual divergence of opinion, a quiet accumulation of small disappointments. Very true, indeed; and now, my dear Miss Grey, observe how Miss Penhaligon deliberately avoids meeting Miss Ashworth’s eye. A most uncomfortable spectacle, and one which promises much further speculation.
author: Jane Austen

Now, the Sawyer clan, you understand, ain’t known for sittin’ still. Six families of ‘em, all crammed together like sardines in a barrel, descended on White River last summer, lookin’ for…well, lookin’ for somethin’ to *happen*. And happen it did, I reckon. Miss Bingley, having just declared her utter lack of acquaintance with truly *accomplished* young ladies, received a most pointed reply. “Nor I, I am sure,” she offered, with a delicate sniff that suggested a superior discernment. 

“Then,” observed Elizabeth, with a lightness that belied a keen observation, “you must comprehend a great deal in your definition. For it seems to encompass a proficiency in little beyond the superficial – a passable display upon the pianoforte, a smattering of French, and an ability to sketch a tolerable rose. Are these, truly, the hallmarks of a cultivated mind?”

A flush rose upon Miss Bingley’s cheeks. “One does not require a scholar’s burden to be agreeable, Miss Bennet. A pleasing countenance and a talent for conversation are, in my estimation, far more valuable.”

Elizabeth permitted herself a small, inward smile. “Indeed? It is a fortunate thing, then, that agreeable ladies are so plentiful. Though one might venture to suggest that a mind capable of *more* than mere pleasantries is a rarer, and therefore, more estimable possession.” The silence that followed was, she suspected, quite eloquent.

Each night, the forest pressed closer, not with the rustle of leaves, but with a suffocating *awareness*. The local fauna had vanished, replaced by a silence so profound it felt actively hostile. The late spring had been most unkind to Miss Catherine Bennet. A distressing entanglement, involving a gentleman of dubious character and a hasty elopement with her elder sister, had left her spirits quite shattered. For weeks, she remained a pale shadow of her former self, prone to sighs and a lamentable lack of interest in ribbons and bonnets. Her mother, naturally, bore the brunt of this affliction, though her complaints were, as ever, directed more towards the injustice of fate than genuine sympathy for her daughter.

However, time, that great healer, and a steady regimen of lemonade and gentle scolding, began to work their effect. Mrs. Bennet, having exhausted her supply of dramatic pronouncements, settled into a more manageable level of agitation. And so, Miss Catherine was restored to her usual querulous serenity; and by the middle of June, she was so much recovered as to be able to enter Meryton without tears—an event celebrated, not with joy, but with a relieved observation from her mother that at least *someone* in the family was fit to be seen. The militia, thankfully, had moved on, leaving the field clear for a fresh round of local gossip and, perhaps, a less perilous pursuit of amusement.

The cyclopean geometry pressed upon the mind, a blasphemy wrought not by human hands, but by something…older. We had breached the perimeter, those foolhardy few driven by a scholar’s morbid curiosity and a cartographer’s lust for the unknown. Now, within the colossal constructions of glacial ice, a dread unlike any earthly terror coiled about the soul.

The structures rose in impossible angles, defying Euclidean space, their surfaces slick with a perpetual, internal frost. Most unsettling were the vast expanses of transparent ice, revealing submerged chambers – windows, one might call them, though the term felt grotesquely inadequate. Each was sealed, shuttered with plates of a dark, metallic substance, as if anticipating a gaze best left uninvited. 

A silence reigned, not of peace, but of *waiting*. A waiting that resonated in the very marrow, a premonition of something stirring in the abyssal blackness beyond those sealed panes. The air grew thick, tasting of ozone and a nameless, ancient decay. It was a place built not to *be* inhabited, but to *contain*. And the chilling certainty bloomed: whatever lay within those shuttered windows was not merely sleeping, but *observing*.

The valley breathed a silence not of peace, but of cessation. It was a place where sound itself seemed loath to tread, choked by the oppressive weight of ages. Below, the river – or what *had* been a river – writhed as a sluggish, obsidian ribbon across the pallid landscape. Not water, precisely, but a viscous, light-devouring substance that mirrored no sky, reflecting only the inner darkness of the earth. 

Its course was not the clean arc of natural flow, but a tormented, irregular scrawl, as if some colossal, unseen hand had dragged a blackened finger across the stone. The banks, crumbling shale and cyclopean root systems, offered no solace, only the suggestion of geometries unsettlingly *wrong*. 

For a second, we gasped – a foolish, involuntary reaction – not at beauty, but at the sheer, unearthly *otherness* of the scene. It was a vista born of angles not meant for human perception, a landscape sculpted by forces predating sentience. A cold dread, older than memory, seeped into the marrow. The river did not flow *through* the valley; it *was* the valley’s despair, solidified and made manifest. And in its sluggish currents, one felt, lay the echoes of things best left undisturbed.

“Wickham be your man, Miss Eleanor,” Lady Beatrice declared with a knowing tilt of her head, stirring her tea with unnecessary vigour. “He is a pleasant fellow, and would jilt you creditably, should the necessity arise. A most polished disappointment, you understand.”

Eleanor, however, found herself strangely unmoved by the suggestion. “Thank you, madam, but a less agreeable man would satisfy me entirely.” A blush warmed her cheeks, though whether from embarrassment or a nascent defiance, she could not quite determine. 

Lady Beatrice raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow. “Indeed? A most peculiar sentiment. One generally *desires* agreeable qualities in a gentleman.”

“Precisely,” Eleanor replied, her voice gaining a firmness she hadn’t known she possessed. “And it is precisely that excess of agreeableness which gives me pause. We must not, I think, seek a happiness built upon such shifting sands. A man too readily charming is often too readily… distracted.” 

She paused, gathering her composure. “A quiet virtue, a steadfast character – these are the qualities I value. And those, I suspect, are rarely found in a gentleman so universally admired.”

text:
The basalt cliffs wept a perpetual, oily mist, clinging to the cyclopean masonry like a shroud. We had breached the barrier reef after weeks of charting currents no sane mariner would approach, driven by whispers of a pre-human civilization on the Isle of Xylos. What we found… defied Euclidean geometry, and perhaps, sanity itself.

The city wasn’t *built* so much as *grown*, a fungal bloom of obsidian and jade. Colossal sculptures, vaguely humanoid yet disturbingly lacking in individual features, lined the avenues. They held no weapons, no emblems of conquest, but rather… implements. Tools for communal labor, vast looms, and strange, interlocking gears carved with a precision that mocked our own. 

Commerce, undeniably, had flourished. Not the bartering of trinkets, but a systematic exchange of resources on a scale that implied a unified, almost hive-like consciousness. Local obsidian was traded for phosphorescent fungi from the deeper caverns, and stranger goods – shimmering, non-terrestrial metals – arrived via docks that accommodated vessels of impossible design. 

Yet, the unsettling uniformity… the utter *lack* of individuality… hinted at something profoundly alien. Was this a utopia, or a meticulously constructed prison of the collective? The silence of Xylos offered no answers, only the creeping dread that we had glimpsed a form of order far older, and far more terrifying, than our own.

Now, Tom Sawyer, he had a notion. A right peculiar notion, it was. He declared, with a solemnity that’d shame a preacher, that we weren’t to *steal* things, not exactly. No sir. What he meant, he said, was we could acquire anything we *needed*. Needed, mind you. A powerful distinction, that.

Old Man Hemlock’s prize watermel, plump and green as envy, had been weighin’ heavy on my mind for a week. The heat had been somethin’ fierce, and a fella could practically *feel* his insides dryin’ up like a forgotten biscuit. 

So, naturally, I put Tom’s pronouncement to the test. “Tom,” I says, lookin’ him square in the eye, “I *need* that watermel.”

He blinked, slow and deliberate, like a bullfrog considerin’ a fly. “You…need it?”

“Mighty bad,” I confirmed. “My constitution, it requires a substantial dose of juicy refreshment. It’s a matter of health, Tom. Purely a matter of health.”

He scratched his chin, a thoughtful frown creasin’ his brow. “Well now,” he drawled, “that does change things, don’t it?” And with that, we commenced plannin’. It weren’t stealin’, you see. It was…necessity.

After walking two or three times along that part of the lane, she was tempted, by the pleasantness of the morning, to stop at the crumbling stone gate. It was not a grand entrance, certainly, nor one designed for show. Rather, it appeared to lead *into* the ground, the path beyond descending with a disconcerting abruptness, swallowed almost entirely by a thicket of yew and overgrown ivy. 

Miss Elmsworth had observed it on previous rambles, of course, but always with a prudent distance. Old Man Hemlock, the estate’s former owner, was said to have been a man of peculiar habits, and the gate, rumour whispered, led to a folly – or something far less agreeable. 

A most unsettling curiosity, however, had taken hold. The air around the opening felt…different. Cooler, perhaps, and strangely still. Her companion, the ever-sensible Miss Penrose, would undoubtedly deem it imprudent to investigate. But Miss Elmsworth, possessed of a spirit not entirely subdued by propriety, found herself drawn forward, a delicate hand reaching for the rusted latch. What secrets, she wondered, might lie hidden beneath the earth?

The arrangement, born of a particularly pointed exchange regarding Mr. Harrington’s attentions, was that silence should prevail through the two ensuing dances. A most uncomfortable decree, yet one to which Miss Eleanor, with a stiff inclination of the head, had reluctantly assented. At first, both parties were resolved not to break it; a demonstration of injured pride, and a subtle, yet keenly felt, rebuke. 

Mr. Fitzwilliam, however, possessed a countenance remarkably expressive, and Eleanor found herself, despite her best efforts, observing the slight twitch at the corner of his mouth as the waltz commenced. It was, she perceived, a suppressed amusement. And a most unwelcome one! 

Suddenly, a most peculiar notion took hold. To maintain this frigid composure, this studied indifference, was, in truth, *his* torment. To deny him the satisfaction of witnessing her discomposure, to offer no reaction whatsoever… surely *that* would be the greater punishment. 

Therefore, with a delicate lift of her chin, and a brightness entirely at odds with her declared displeasure, she remarked, “The band appears to favour a rather brisk tempo, does it not, Mr. Fitzwilliam?”

Mrs. Phelps, she near jumped outta her skin, bless her heart. A flurry of petticoats and a voice sharp enough to cut glass. “Has *he* come?” she demanded, lookin’ around like she expected him to materialize from the wallpaper.

Old Man Tiberius, he had a notion struck him sudden as a hornet. Had to get home. *Right now*. Wife’d be frettin’, see, and the prize-winning pumpkin needed watchin’ – a gourd of such magnitude it practically required a bodyguard. He’d been at the mercantile, arguin’ the price of molasses with old Man Hemlock, a fella who could haggle the wings off a fly, and the thought just *hit* him.

“Hemlock,” he declared, loud enough to rattle the pickle jars, “I gotta go. Urgent business. Domestic calamity, likely.”

Hemlock, naturally, just squinted. Tiberius commenced to cuss, a colorful string of pronouncements that’d make a steamboat captain blush. He flung his best straw hat into a particularly muddy patch, stomped on it for good measure, and then, in a fit of pure exasperation, rode his mule, Bess, *over* a stack of flour sacks. 

Didn’t do no good, though. Bess, that stubborn creature, just planted her feet and commenced to munch on a stray cabbage leaf. A mule’s will, you see, is a thing stronger than a preacher’s sermon. And Tiberius, well, he was stuck.

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth found herself, to her considerable vexation, the object of Mr. Finch’s unwavering regard. It was not that he possessed any particular deficiency – his estate, though modest, was respectable, his manners passable – but rather a *want* of anything to truly engage her affections. He was, in short, perfectly indifferent to her sensibilities, perceiving her quiet enjoyment of a well-turned phrase or a thoughtful observation as mere feminine caprice.

Indeed, it became increasingly apparent that his chief object was, by delicate attentions – a particularly fine shawl procured from London, an overabundance of early strawberries – to recommend himself to her. He spoke constantly of her accomplishments, praising her embroidery as if it rivalled the finest needlework in the kingdom, and her pianoforte playing with an enthusiasm quite disproportionate to its merit. 

He had, she suspected, made a point of it. A point to *win* her, regardless of any reciprocal inclination. A most unsettling prospect, and one which threatened to disrupt the comfortable tranquility of her days with a persistent, and wholly unwelcome, civility. She feared a protracted campaign of polite persistence, and the necessity of devising a suitably firm, yet not entirely rude, rejection.

text:
Miss Eleanor Penrose found herself in a most peculiar state of agitation, considering the brevity of their acquaintance. Only a fortnight had passed since the assembly at Meryton, and yet, the memory of Mr. Alistair Finch’s attentions occupied a disproportionate share of her thoughts. Four dances! A most encouraging number, certainly, though Mrs. Hawthorne did remark upon his rather pronounced habit of discussing agricultural improvements.

She had, moreover, observed him one morning whilst sketching near his estate – a circumstance she had contrived, naturally, under the guise of admiring the landscape. And then, the dinners! Four times she had found herself seated within conversational distance, enduring polite inquiries regarding her brother’s health and the merits of the local milliner. 

It was, she confessed to her sister, a vexing situation. Too little time to form a proper judgement, and yet, enough to inspire a degree of… expectation. Was it possible, she wondered, that a gentleman might convey a serious intent with such swiftness? Or was she, perhaps, allowing a lively imagination to read significance where none existed? The uncertainty, she found, was almost as tiresome as Mr. Finch’s discourse on turnips.

Now, Jim, he was a study. A right peculiar study. Been settin’ on that riverbank, quiet as a church mouse, all night long. I reckon he’d been talkin’ a blue streak to me, mind you, but mostly about things a body couldn’t rightly *see*. Said he’d been conversin’ with the very air, and the air had been tellin’ him stories. 

“Hain’t seen no fog, nor no islands, nor no troubles, nor nothing,” he declared, lookin’ me square in the eye. “I been setting here talking with you all night till you went to sleep about t.” 

‘T, he said. Just ‘t’. Like it held the whole world inside that one little letter. I tried to pry what ‘t’ was, but he just chuckled, a low rumble like distant thunder. Said it was a secret, a thing for the river to keep. 

Folks’ll tell you a man needs land, a house, possessions. But Jim, he seemed to have all he needed right there, in the whisper of the water and the company of a good, long talk with…well, with whatever it was he was talkin’ to. text:
The Misses Beaumont – Penelope, the eldest and possessed of a rather tiresome sensibility; Clara, amiable but sadly lacking in discernment; and young Marianne, whose enthusiasm bordered, one feared, on the imprudent – were discussing a newly published novel. Penelope had declared it a masterpiece of pathos, weeping openly over the heroine’s misfortunes.

“An excellent consolation in its way,” said Elizabeth, observing the damp handkerchief, “but it will not do for *us*. We do not, after all, find ourselves betrothed to villains, nor abandoned in draughty castles.”

Clara, ever eager to please, murmured agreement. “Indeed, our circumstances are far more…comfortable.”

Marianne, however, flushed with indignation. “But to *feel* such passion, to experience such depths of sorrow! Is that not preferable to a life of placid contentment?”

Elizabeth raised a delicate eyebrow. “Contentment, my dear Marianne, is not necessarily placid. It is, rather, a state of judicious acceptance. And a well-managed estate, a sensible match, and a circle of agreeable acquaintances offer a far more secure foundation for happiness than the fleeting drama of a printed page.” She paused, adding with a subtle smile, “Besides, one suspects the author exaggerates somewhat for effect.”

text:
Now, this here stretch of the river, it weren’t known for pleasantries. More for a stubborn sort of gloom that clung to the water like Spanish moss to an old oak. The air hung so thick you could practically *chew* it, and the trees off a little ways looked dim and spider-webby, all blurred by the humidity. A body felt like they were swimmin’ in molasses, even standin’ still.

Then, wouldn’t you know it, here would come a blast of wind. Not a gentle breeze, mind you, but a proper *gust* that’d bend the trees double, lookin’ like they were bowin’ to some unseen, grumpy king. It’d stir up the river somethin’ fierce, makin’ the water churn and spit. 

Old Man Hemlock used to say that wind was the river’s temper flarin’ up. Said it was complainin’ about bein’ penned in by the banks, wantin’ to stretch out and swallow the whole bottomland. I reckon he wasn’t far wrong. It had a feelin’ to it, that wind, like somethin’ restless and powerful was just holdin’ itself back. A fella could feel it in his bones, sure as shootin’.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Old Man Tiber, he was a sight. Sat on the overturned crate by the riverbank, lookin’ like a catfish outta water. Folks been askin’ him where he was headin’, seein’ as he’d packed up his whole life – a chipped teacup, a banjo missin’ three strings, and a mournful hound dog named Blue – onto a rickety flatboat.

“Where ya goin’ to, Tiber?” young Jedediah had inquired, polite-like.

Tiber just blinked, slow as molasses in January. Then he commenced to scratchin’ his beard, a tangled mess it was. “Goin’ to?” he finally drawled, lookin’ at Jedediah like *he* was the one askin’ a foolish question. “Well, looky here, boss, dey’s sumf’n wrong, dey is. Is I *me*, or who *is* I? Is I heah, or whah *is* I? Now dat’s what I wants to know.” 

Jedediah, bein’ a practical boy, just shrugged. “Sounds like you need a nap, Tiber.”

But Tiber shook his head, solemn as a judge. “Nope. Need a *place*. A place to figure out if this here boat’s carryin’ Old Man Tiber, or just… a notion of him.” And with that, he gave Blue a pat and pushed off into the current, lookin’ for answers downriver.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, it was a right peculiar notion, this descending the lightning-rod. A fella’d think a body’d have sense enough to stay *on* the house when a storm’s brewin’, not dangle from it like a ripe pear. But young Tom, he had a hankerin’ for information, see? And information, in this instance, resided beneath Widow Douglas’s window.

We went down a little after ten, mind you, the air thick enough to chew on. Took a candle, though it flickered somethin’ fierce in the breeze, lookin’ like a nervous firefly.  The rod was cold iron under my palms, and the drop was…considerable.  

Down we crept, quiet as church mice, and positioned ourselves under that window-hole.  And what did we hear? Not whispers of secret plots, nor lamentations of a guilty conscience. No sir. We heard Jim.  

Snoring. A sound like a sawmill workin’ overtime, a regular hurricane of breath.  Tom, he near burst a gut laughin’, and I confess, I let out a chuckle myself. All this risk, all this clandestine maneuverin’, for the privilege of hearin’ a man sleep like a contented hog.  Human nature, I reckon.  It’s a curious thing.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The trawler *Althea* returned to Innsmouth not with cod, but with a dread silence clinging to its barnacled hull. Old Man Hemlock, eyes vacant as bleached stones, spoke only of the depth – a pressure beyond reckoning, yet… *not felt*. He’d hauled it up, he rasped, a thing of basaltic geometry, impossibly smooth, and cold with a cold that defied the Gulf Stream. 

It wasn’t the shape, though unsettlingly non-Euclidean, that chilled the crew. It was the *resonance*. A low thrumming that settled not in the ears, but within the bone, a vibration echoing from epochs before humanity clawed its way from the primordial slime. 

Whispers began, of course. Tales of the abyssal plains, where pressures would crush steel to dust, yet *something* endures. Something that has always endured. The killer-whale theory, once a comforting rationalization for strange sonar readings, now felt… inadequate. A childish attempt to explain the unexplainable. 

Hemlock insists it *breathed*. Not with lungs, but with the slow, geological shift of continents. And I, observing the creeping madness in his gaze, fear he is right. For the ocean does not merely *hold* secrets; it *remembers* them. And some things, best left forgotten, are stirring once more.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, though possessed of a comfortable fortune and a tolerable degree of beauty, found herself, at twenty-four, remarkably unoccupied. Not by a lack of callers, mind you – the gentlemen of the neighbourhood were perfectly civil – but by a dearth of *interesting* callers. Mr. Finch, with his endless discourse on turnips, and young Mr. Harwood, whose accomplishments extended solely to whist and a lamentable vanity, offered little to stimulate a discerning mind.

She had, however, discovered a most agreeable diversion in the comparative merits of domestic architecture. Her aunt, a woman of considerable, if somewhat eccentric, taste, had recently undertaken the rebuilding of the west wing. And there, in the careful placement of windows, the proportion of the cornice, and the judicious use of Palladian motifs, there may be traced the distinct superiority in point of construction, which, as it seems to me, it possesses over all the others. 

The plot, though seemingly confined to brick and mortar, revealed a far more satisfying order than the tangled affections of her acquaintance. A well-laid foundation, a harmonious design – these were virtues one could rely upon, unlike the shifting sands of a gentleman’s professed admiration.

Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a teller of tales, a regular geyser of fabrication, but this one… this one took the biscuit, I reckon. He started with a hen layin’ a square egg, which was peculiar enough, mind you. Then that egg hatched a rooster with the voice of a baritone, singin’ opera, no less. Folks chuckled, expectin’ the yarn to peter out, but Hemlock, he just warmed to his work.

The rooster, see, commenced collectin’ buttons. Not just any buttons, but pearl ones, and he’d trade ‘em for molasses. Then the molasses started talkin’, givin’ stock tips, and makin’ a tidy profit, it did. Hemlock’s eyes got wider with each embellishment, his voice climbin’ higher and faster. He described the rooster buildin’ a miniature steamboat out of thimbles, powered by the talkin’ molasses, and sailin’ it around the parlor table. 

And at last, when he had gone around two sides of the room, wavin’ his arms and shoutin’ about a gold-plated pickle, he disappears down cellar. Then in about two seconds, a muffled yell and the distinct sound of somethin’ heavy crashin’ against stone. Silence. Then, just Hemlock’s boots stickin’ up. A body couldn’t help but wonder if the pickle had followed him.

Now, Old Mrs. Hotchkiss, she was a woman who could curdle milk with a glance, and Aunt Sally, bless her heart, was flustered something awful. Tom Sawyer, he lay there lookin’ paler than a winter moon, a bullet hole in his leg lookin’ like a misplaced dimple. Huck, he just stood by the door, quiet as a catfish, watchin’ it all unfold. 

“Land sakes, child!” Aunt Sally wailed, fannin’ herself with a hymn book. “Wounded! And by Injun Joe’s gang, no less!”

The Doctor, a fella who believed in bleedin’ a body for most any ailment, declared, “He’ll live, though he’ll be limpin’ for a spell. And young Jim… well, Jim’s got a touch o’ the fever, but he’s holdin’.” 

Then Tom, he rose square up in bed, weak as a kitten, but with that mischievous glint in his eye. “Hand out them letters!” he commanded, voice raspy. “Out with ‘em, I say!” 

Aunt Sally, bewildered, produced a bundle tied with string. Tom snatched ‘em, a grin spreadin’ across his face. Seems even a bullet couldn’t keep a boy from his adventures, or a secret well-kept. A right peculiar situation, it was.
author: Mark Twain

text:
It is a peculiarity, perhaps, that I find myself compelled to address a matter so long held within the bounds of propriety, particularly as I stand upon the precipice of departure. Whether I ever before mentioned to you my feelings on this subject, I cannot with certainty recall; my memory, alas, is not always a faithful recorder of past sentiments. However, I will not leave the country without confiding them, and I trust you will extend to me the same discretion.

Mr. Ashworth, though possessed of a tolerable fortune and a passable countenance, is, in my estimation, utterly devoid of sensibility. His conversation consists entirely of agricultural improvements and the price of wool, subjects which, whilst undoubtedly important, do little to stir the affections. I have observed, with a degree of mortification, the attentions he bestows upon Miss Penrose, a young lady whose accomplishments extend no further than a proficiency in needlepoint and a talent for simpering. 

It is not affection for Mr. Ashworth that prompts this confession, but rather a desire to be understood. To know that *someone* recognises the absurdity of such a match. And I trust, dear friend, that this confidence will remain precisely between us.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The assembly room, though comfortably full, felt suddenly airless after Mr. Darcy’s departure. He had, with a politeness bordering on condescension, addressed Miss Bennet – a young lady possessed, it must be admitted, of tolerable beauty, though hardly of a cast to rival the acknowledged loveliness of Georgiana – and declared her, in the hearing of several, to be “one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance.” 

Miss Bingley, who had been observing the exchange with a keenness usually reserved for the assessment of ribbons and bonnets, allowed herself a small, triumphant smile. It was a paltry compliment, of course, delivered with a coolness that betrayed its insincerity. Yet, it served its purpose. 

He had been *made* to say it. Forced, by her subtle steering of the conversation, to acknowledge a merit she knew he disdained. The very notion of his acknowledging it! It was a small victory, perhaps, but a victory nonetheless. He then went away, and Miss Bingley was left to all the satisfaction of having forced him to say what he would rather have bitten his tongue than utter. A most gratifying evening, indeed.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, this ditch-digging business, it weren’t no picnic, I tell you. Old Man Hemlock, he figured a fella could move mountains with a spoon if he just *applied* himself. Applied himself 'til your knuckles bled, more like. My hands, they were a sight, blistered and cracked, lookin’ like a dried-up riverbed. Didn’t give ‘em no show to get well, not with the constant shovelin’ and the grit grindin’ in.

We were supposed to be drainin’ Hemlock’s lower forty, preventin’ a flood, he said. But it felt more like we were diggin’ a path straight to perdition. Tom, he was a fella for observin’ things, and he declared, plain as day, “We ain’t makin’ no headway, hardly.” And he was right. We’d dig ten feet, and the next rain would fill it right back up. 

It was tedious, see? Soul-crushin’ tedious. A body could plumb forget what sunshine felt like, buried in that clay. And Hemlock, he’d just stand there, puffin’ on his pipe, expectin’ miracles from a couple of boys and a rusty shovel. A fella could get to thinkin’ miracles ain’t worth the effort.
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he was a peculiar sort. Claimed his rheumatism could predict the weather, and generally did, though mostly it predicted more rheumatism. Anyway, he sent young Timmy and me down to the cellar with a request – a simple enough thing, he said, just to *come with a candle*. Didn’t specify *what* we were comin’ with it *for*. A man learns not to ask questions of folks like Hemlock, see?

We shut the cellar door behind us, and the damp smelled like forgotten potatoes and regret. Timmy, bless his nervous heart, nearly jumped out of his skin at every creak. Finally, we found it – a burlap sack tucked behind the pickle barrels. When we hauled it up and they spilt it out on the floor, well, it was a lovely sight, all t’was. 

Not gold, mind you. Not jewels. No sir. It was turnips. A mountain of ‘em, plump and pale as a preacher’s conscience. Hemlock just chuckled, a dry, rustlin’ sound. “Needed to check their glow,” he said, perfectly serious. “A good turnip, you see, holds the moonlight. Tells ya somethin’ about the harvest.” 

Timmy and I just exchanged a look. Some folks, I reckon, are born to be puzzled by.
author: Mark Twain

That’s why they’re invited here this evenin’; but tomorrow we want _all_ to come—everybody; for he respected everybody, he liked everybody, and so it’s fitten that his funeral orgies sh’d be public.” And so he went a-mooning on and on, liking to hear himself talk, and every little while he fetched in his funeral orgies again, till the duke he couldn’t stand it no more; so he writes on a little scrap of paper, “_obsequies_, you old fool,” and folds it up, and goes to goo-gooing and reaching it over people’s
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, old Man Tiber, he’d been ailing for a spell, and I figured a quiet float down the Mississippi would do him a world of good. Built us a right sturdy raft, see, lashed together with rope thicker’n my thumb. We’d been driftin’ along peaceful-like, him nappin’ under a patched quilt, me whittlin’ a likeness of a particularly ornery catfish. 

Got back to shore late last night, sun dipped below the trees lookin’ like a bruised peach. Figured we’d leave the raft tied, just a quick stretch of the legs and a bite to eat. But wouldn’t you know it, when we come back down to the bank…gone. Clean gone. Not a splinter left to show for it.

Tiber, he roused then, blinked at the empty water like he’d mislaid his spectacles. We stood there a good long minute, just starin’. Then he let out a chuckle, a dry, raspy sound. 

“Well, I’ll be,” he said, slow. “That little rascal has stole our raft and shook us, and run off down the ri.” And I reckon he was right. Some folks just have a knack for mischief, and a raft’s too temptin’ a prize for a free spirit to resist.
author: Mark Twain

text:
## CHAPTER I. Civilizing Huck.—Miss Watson.—Tom Sawyer Waits.

Now, don’t you go thinkin’ this here’s a tale of fancy balls and polished silver. No sir. It’s a story of gettin’ *un*civilized, mostly. See, Widow Douglas, a good woman mind you, but with a powerful fondness for starch and rules, she took it upon herself to “sivilize” me, Huckleberry Finn. Lord, the misery of it! Washin’ my hands ‘fore breakfast, wearin’ proper clothes that itched like a nest of chiggers, and learnin’ to eat with a fork – a contraption fit only for pokin’ at peas.

Miss Watson, the Widow’s sister, she was worse. Always tryin’ to drill scripture into a fella’s head, and talkin’ about “proper behavior.” Proper behavior! Why, a body needs to *stretch* sometimes, and scratch when he itches, and not sit still like a mortified frog. 

Tom Sawyer, he was always lurkin’ about, full of schemes and grand notions. He’d watch me struggle with my lessons, a smirk playin’ on his lips, and then whisper about pirates and buried treasure. He was a good friend, Tom was, though a powerful nuisance. And I had a feelin’, a right strong feelin’, that this “sivilizin’” business wasn’t gonna last long with *him* around.
author: Mark Twain

So they said I could have a home there as long as I wanted it. Then it was most daylight and everybody went to bed, and I went to bed with Buck, and when I waked up in the morning, drat it all, I had forgot what my name was. So I laid there about an hour trying to think, and when Buck waked up I says: “Can you spell, Buck?” “Yes,” he says. “I bet you can’t spell my name,” says I. “I bet you what you dare I can,” says he. “All right,” says I, “go ahead.” “G-e-o-r-g-e J-a-x-o-n—there now,” he says. “Well,” says I, “you done it, but I didn’t think you could. It ain’t no slouch of a name to spell—right off without studying.” I set it down, private, because somebody might want _me_ to spell it next, and so I wanted to be handy with it and rattle it off like I was used to

text: side of the deep embrasures. They seemed to have become wedged in place, thus surviving the rusting of their former and probably metallic fixtures and fastenings. After a time we came across a row of windows--in the bulges of a colossal five-edged cone of undamaged apex--which led into a vast, well-preserved room with stone flooring; but these were too high in the room to permit descent without a rope. We had a rope with us, but did not wish to bother with this twenty-foot drop unless obliged to--especially in this thin plateau air where great demands were made upon the heart action. This enormous room was probably a hall or concourse of some sort, and our electric torches showed bold, distinct, and potentially startling sculptures arranged round the walls in broad, horizontal bands separated by equally broad strips of conventional arabesques. We took careful note of this spot, planning to enter here unless a more easily gained interior was encountered. Finally, though, we did encounter exactly the opening we wished; an archway about six feet wide and ten feet high, marking the former end of an aërial bridge which had spanned an alley about five feet above the present level
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Now, Old Man Tiberius, he run things over in the Sultanate of Piffle, and a peculiar arrangement it was. When business was slow – and Lord, things *were* slow in Piffle, slower than molasses in January – Tiberius’d call a meetin’ of the Parleyment. Not to *do* nothin’, mind you, just to fuss with it. Change a comma here, debate the color of the ink there. Kept ‘em occupied, see?

But Tiberius, he was a man of…firm convictions. If a Parleyment man dared disagree, or even *look* like he was thinkin’ disagreein’, why, off with his head! Quick as you please. A bit drastic, some said, but Tiberius believed in order. 

Mostly, though, the Parleyment just hung ‘round the harem. Finest silks, sweetest dates, and ladies with eyes that could melt a glacier. A body could understand the appeal. Tiberius, he claimed it was for “observational purposes,” studyin’ the effects of beauty on governance. More likely, it was just a convenient arrangement for all concerned. Piffle was a strange place, I tell you, a strange place indeed.
author: Mark Twain

text: a half an hour they was as thick as thieves again, and the tighter they got, the lovinger they got, and went off a-snoring in each other’s arms. They both got powerful mellow, but I noticed the king didn’t get mellow enough to forget to remember to not deny about hiding the money-bag again. That made me feel easy and satisfied. Of course when they got to snoring we had a long gabble, and I told Jim everything. CHAPTER XXXI. We dasn’t stop again at any town for days and days; kept right along down the river. We was down south in the warm weather now, and a mighty long ways from home. We begun to come to trees with Spanish moss on them, hanging down from the limbs like long, gray beards. It was the first I ever see it growing, and it made the woods look solemn and dismal. So now the frauds reckoned they was out of danger, and they begun to work the villages again. First they done a lecture on temperance; but they didn’t make enough for them both to get drunk on. Then in another village they started a dancing-school; but they didn’t know
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, there was Old Man Tiber, a feller known more for his silences than his speeches, settin’ on the porch swing like a judge weighin’ dust motes. Young Elias, barely sprouted, stood afore him, fidgetin’ like a June bug in a bottle. Seems the schoolmarm, Miss Peabody – a woman who could curdle milk with a glare – had asked Elias a question. A simple enough question, on the face of it.

“White or black?” she’d demanded. 

And the boy, bless his heart, had froze solid. Not for lack of knowin’ colors, mind you. But somethin’ in the *way* she asked it, somethin’ sharp and expectin’, had plumb knocked the words clean outta him. He tried, he did. He felt ‘em bubblin’ up, ready to spill, but they just… wouldn’t. 

Old Man Tiber watched him struggle, a slow smile creepin’ across his face. “Sometimes,” he drawled, finally breakin’ his silence, “a feller finds the hardest questions ain’t about what you *know*, but about what you reckon’s expected of ya.” He paused, then added with a wink, “And sometimes, boy, silence is a powerful answer indeed.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Now, Old Man Hemlock, he’d gone and lost his prize rooster, a bird magnificent enough to make a bishop blush. Accusations flew thicker than gnats at a picnic, landing mostly on young Jebediah and his hound, Blue. Jebediah swore Blue was innocent, claimed the rooster likely wandered off chasin’ a lady friend. Hemlock, though, he wasn’t buyin’ it. 

He commenced to lay on the guilt, thick and heavy, talkin’ ‘bout the rooster’s lineage and the heartbreak of a man losin’ a fine fowl. Jebediah, he got riled, and commenced to talk back, and pretty soon it was a regular dust-up of words. 

Now, I’d been watchin’ the whole shebang from the porch, and I’d seen Blue sneakily buryin’ a pile of feathers down by the creek earlier. Didn’t say nothin’, though. Let ‘em go at it. It was entertainin’, see? 

Finally, Hemlock and Jebediah went off a-jawing; and I felt dreadful glad I’d worked it all off on to the hound, and yet hadn’t done Blue no harm by it. A fella’s gotta have his amusements, you see, and a little bit of quiet observation can be worth a whole heap of trouble.
author: Mark Twain

text: and then he put them all in a book, and called it Domesday Book—which was a good name and stated the case. You don’t know kings, Jim, but I know them; and this old rip of ourn is one of the cleanest I’ve struck in history. Well, Henry he takes a notion he wants to get up some trouble with this country. How does he go at it—give notice?—give the country a show? No. All of a sudden he heaves all the tea in Boston Harbor overboard, and whacks out a declaration of independence, and dares them to come on. That was _his_ style—he never give anybody a chance. He had suspicions of his father, the Duke of Wellington. Well, what did he do? Ask him to show up? No—drownded him in a butt of mamsey, like a cat. author: Mark Twain

text:
Mr. Alistair Finch, having at length declared his affections, and been, with a firmness she scarcely knew she possessed, refused by Miss Eleanor Ainsworth, now stood convinced of his own self-conquest. He had, with admirable restraint, swallowed his disappointment, and presented a countenance of polite indifference. Yet, this very triumph, this demonstration of a spirit above wounded pride, afforded Miss Ainsworth no consolation whatsoever. It brought, in fact, a peculiar exacerbation of her distress.

For it was not his *passion* she regretted, but the amiable, though misguided, regard which had prompted it. To see him so neatly packaged in composure, so precisely calculating his dignity, was exactly calculated to remind her of the warmth extinguished. He believed he had mastered his feelings, and in doing so, had revealed a coldness of temperament she had previously failed to discern. 

A gentleman who could so readily subdue the heart, she mused, was a gentleman whose heart was perhaps not so easily moved. And a prospect of future acquaintance, once promising a gentle friendship, now held only the chill of polite, and profoundly unsatisfying, detachment.
author: Jane Austen

text:
The matter of Miss Everly’s affections, it was plain to all observing eyes, rested entirely upon Mr. Hawthorne’s purse. Not that the gentleman possessed any particular brilliance of wit, or indeed, any striking feature beyond a comfortable breadth of shoulder. But he *had* fortune, and in this age, fortune, alas, often dictates the course of a young lady’s heart. 

One heard the whispers, of course. “A most advantageous match!” “She could do far worse.” And one felt, with a certain melancholy, the truth of it. For a younger son, you know, must be inured to witnessing such pragmatism. One observes the limitations imposed by a modest income with a clarity others, blessed with independent means, rarely possess. 

Mr. Hawthorne, though not actively charming, possessed the undeniable advantage of being able to *provide*. He could offer a settled establishment, a carriage, perhaps even a London season. Others, with infinitely more sensibility, might offer only ardent declarations and a dwindling inheritance. It is a harsh reality, but one must acknowledge he is better means of having it than many others, because he is rich, and many others are poor. I speak feelingly.
author: Jane Austen

Mr. Bennet indeed said little; but the ladies were ready enough to talk, and Mr. Collins seemed neither in need of encouragement, nor inclined to be silent himself. He was a tall, heavy-looking young man of five-and-twenty. His air was grave and stately, and his manners were very formal. He had not been long seated before he complimented Mrs. Bennet on having so fine a family of daughters, said he had heard much of their beauty, but that, in this instance, fame had fallen short of the truth; and added, that he did not doubt her seeing them all in due time well disposed of in marriage. This gallantry was not much to the taste of some of his hearers; but Mrs. Bennet, who quarrelled with no compliments, answered most readily,-- “You are very kind, sir, I am sure; and I wish with all my heart it may prove so; for else they will be destitute enough. Things are settled so oddly.” “You allude, perhaps, to the entail of this estate.” “Ah, sir, I do indeed. It is a grievous affair to my poor girls, you must confess. Not that I mean to find
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, these two fellers, they drifted into our camp lookin’ like trouble wrapped in a Sunday suit. One, a gaunt, whisker-streaked gent claimin’ to be a deposed Duke, the other a fella with a manner that suggested he’d been born wearin’ a crown, though a tarnished one, no doubt. They spun a yarn about bein’ royalty, runnin’ from rightful inheritances and such. 

Truth be told, I didn’t rightly *believe* a word of it. But the boy, he was easily led, and a fuss was the last thing I needed. So, when they requested we address ‘em as royalty – kings and dukes, I hadn’t no objections, ’long as it would keep peace in the family; and it warn’t no use to tell Jim, so I didn’t tell. 

Jim, he’d just shake his head and mutter somethin’ about white folks and their foolishness. He was a practical man, Jim was. These two, though, they were pure wind and fancy talk. Still, a body learns to navigate the river by readin’ the currents, and sometimes, the easiest current is the one that lets a feller float along with the nonsense. It saved a heap of argument, and that, in my experience, is worth more than all the crowns in Europe.
author: Mark Twain

text:
The fog, a viscous, grey ichor, clung to the rigging, tasting of brine and something…older. Something not of this sun-drenched, yet profoundly *wrong*, expanse of ocean. We, the salvage crew of the *Albatross*, were lashed to the decaying hulk of the *Morwenna*, a vessel lost these forty years, now resurrected only to serve as a ghastly intermediary. 

Our task: to establish a line, a tenuous umbilical cord between the *Albatross* and the *Morwenna*, and thence, a precarious pathway for supplies. But it was not the physical labour that gnawed at the sanity. It was the *feeling*. A cold, creeping awareness of observation from the depths. 

Each cable, taut and groaning under the swell, felt less like rope and more like a probing tendril, extending into a vast, unseen consciousness. The *Morwenna* did not merely *house* the fog; it *exuded* it, a miasma of forgotten sorrows and geometries that defied Euclidean comprehension. 

The first ascent of the breeches-buoy brought a sailor back…changed. His eyes, vacant and reflecting no light, spoke of vistas beyond human endurance. He muttered of angles that should not be, of a pressure in the water, and a singing…a low, resonant chanting that promised not rescue, but assimilation.
author: H.P. Lovecraft

text:
Miss Eleanor Penworthy had, it must be confessed, been quite captivated by Captain Harwood. His attentions, though perhaps a trifle too demonstrative for perfect good taste, were nonetheless flattering to a young lady possessed of a modest fortune and a yearning for excitement. She had declared him, to her confidante Miss Bingley, a man of “uncommon sensibility” and “a countenance quite arresting.” 

And, consequently, after a moderate period of extravagant and wild admiration, her fancy for him gave way, and others of the regiment, who treated her with a more reasoned, and dare one say, *respectful* regard, began to attract her notice. Captain Harwood, it transpired, possessed a lamentable fondness for boasting of past conquests, and a distressing habit of interrupting when one attempted a thoughtful observation. 

Lieutenant Finch, though lacking the Captain’s initial flamboyance, proved a far more agreeable conversationalist, and Ensign Bellweather, with his quiet diligence and genuine interest in her pianoforte playing, offered a comfort Captain Harwood had never even considered. It was, Miss Bingley observed with a knowing smile, a most fortunate shift in affections, and one likely to result in a considerably more sensible match.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Miss Elmsworth, having just declared, with a firmness quite unsettling, “beyond a doubt: there cannot be two opinions on that point,” regarding the suitability of Mr. Finch as a partner for her niece, observed the room with a satisfied air. Mrs. Penworthy, however, merely fluttered her fan, a delicate pink confection.

“Upon my word! Well, that was very decided, indeed—that does seem as if—but, however…” she began, her voice a gentle tremor. “One must consider, Miss Elmsworth, that Mr. Finch *does* possess a rather pronounced fondness for discussing the merits of turnips. A subject, I confess, which does not universally appeal.”

Lady Beatrice, ever the pragmatist, offered a small, knowing smile. “Turnips are, admittedly, a limiting topic. Yet, a comfortable income outweighs a dearth of conversational brilliance, does it not?”

Miss Elmsworth, unperturbed, continued, “His estate is impeccable, his connections respectable. A young lady requires security, not sparkling wit.” 

Mrs. Penworthy sighed, a sound like escaping steam. “Security is paramount, of course. But a life spent solely discussing root vegetables… one shudders to contemplate it.”
author: Jane Austen

text:
To Elizabeth it appeared, that had her family made an agreement to expose themselves as much as they could during the evening, it would have been impossible to devise a scheme more successful. Her mother, emboldened by a tolerable assembly room and the presence of a few eligible, though undeniably provincial, gentlemen, had already declared Mrs. Phillips’s niece a paragon of accomplishment. Lydia, meanwhile, flitted about with a giggling eagerness that bordered on the indelicate, accepting the attentions of a young ensign with a want of discernment most alarming.

Even Kitty, usually content to echo Lydia’s enthusiasms, seemed determined to outdo her sister in forwardness. Mr. Bennet, observing the scene with a detached amusement, offered only the occasional, sardonic remark, which, though witty to Elizabeth’s ear, served only to encourage the very behaviour he mocked. 

It was a spectacle, she thought, quite sufficient to deter any sensible man from seeking connection with the family. And yet, a certain gentleman – a Mr. Darcy, whose countenance betrayed a profound disapproval of all that transpired – remained within their orbit. A most perplexing circumstance, indeed.
author: Jane Austen

text:
Now, the matter of Old Man Hemlock’s spare room was a thing to behold. Folks said he’d been collectin’…well, *things*…for nigh on seventy years. Not valuable things, mind you. Just…things. Broken clockworks, chipped porcelain dolls with eyes askew, a collection of buttons that’d make a tailor weep, and enough moth-eaten shawls to outfit a regiment of ghosts. 

When the new tenants, the Millers, come to inspect, they had to take soundings before they could navigate it. Young Miller, a fella with a practical bent, brought a boat hook. True as you’re standin’, he did. Said it felt like explorin’ a sunken galleon.

The Judge, he was there, seein’ as how he’d brokered the lease. He felt kind of sore, truth be told. Hemlock had promised a “tidy spare.” Tidy! Why, a dust bunny in that room had likely *developed its own ecosystem*. 

He cleared his throat, adjusted his spectacles, and said, “Well now, I reckon…I *recommend*…a strong pair of lungs and a willingness to embrace the…historical.” He paused, lookin’ at Mrs. Miller’s face, which was turnin’ a shade paler than a winter moon. “Yes sir. Historical.”
author: Mark Twain

text:
Miss Eleanor, though possessed of a sensibility far exceeding her years, found herself in a most vexing predicament. Her friend, Jane, had become quite captivated by a novel – a circumstance in itself not alarming – but by the gentleman whose attentions were so liberally bestowed within its pages. It was a tale of ardent devotion, of overcoming obstacles, and, Eleanor feared, of setting an impossibly high standard for real affection.

“She was persuaded,” Eleanor confided to her sister, Charlotte, “that Jane must soon cease to regard *any* gentleman in the enjoyment of his own good fortune. A man without a Byronic air, a brooding melancholy… she deems him utterly deficient.”

A short pause followed, during which Eleanor delicately rearranged a posy of lavender. “It is unlucky,” she said, with a sigh, “that you should not possess the requisite degree of suffering to appreciate such a narrative. Do not mistake me, Charlotte, I do not condemn the book itself. It is merely… dangerous. It fosters expectations which, I suspect, will prove most detrimental to a sensible match.” 

Charlotte, ever practical, merely raised an eyebrow. “A sensible match, Eleanor, is rarely founded on brooding melancholy.”

The matter had been discussed, of course, with a delicacy bordering on the absurd. Miss Eliza Bennet, though possessed of a lively mind, found herself repeatedly circling the point with her sister, Jane. Mr. Harding, the new curate, had been excessively attentive, offering Jane the plumpest peaches from his mother’s orchard and engaging her in conversations concerning the merits of various hymn tunes. 

“It is quite plain, Eliza,” Jane murmured, arranging a posy of lavender, “that he finds my company agreeable.”

“Plain to *everyone*, Jane,” Eliza retorted, with a touch of impatience. “Must be a simpleton indeed not to discover it too.”

Their mother, overhearing, interjected with a knowing glance. “Remember, Eliza, that he does not know Jane’s disposition as you do. A man requires…encouragement.”

Eliza sighed. “But if a woman is partial, Mama, and allows her affections to be too readily perceived, does she not risk appearing…forward?” 

“Nonsense, child! A little encouragement is merely good sense. Mr. Harding is a respectable, if somewhat shy, gentleman. And Jane deserves a comfortable establishment.” The lavender trembled slightly in Jane’s hand, a blush rising on her cheeks. The prospect, though pleasing, was not without its anxieties.
